George S. Green, P. G. M.
LOUISIAN.A.

BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LoDGE:

As we grow older, time seems to go more swiftly, and the past
twelve months have gone so rapidly that I can hardly realize that
a year has passed since we were assembled here as Masons and
members of the Grand Lodge.
No doubt some who were here last year have since passed away;
others are perhaps unable to attend by reason of illness, and of the
older members who are with us again we can observe in a few the
changes wrought by time, and see that their step is a little less
steady, and th.at they are not quite so vigorous as they were one
year ago. The great majority of those present are, as a matter of
course, new men, and it is their first appearance as members of
the Grand Lodge. It is a pleasure to see so many old familiar faces,
and also to greet those who are with us for the first time.
To me the recollections of our Annual Communications are of
the most pleasant nature, and the friendships formed here. will be
dearly treasured by me all through life. Coming, as we do, from
every portion of this g.reat State, belonging to this noble Fraternity,
and bound together by . the most ·sacred ties, we do not meet . as
strangers, but as ·brothers, and as lmch I extend to you all a Fra·
ternal greeting and cordial welcome, and I hope tl~at this meeting
wlll be so pleasant and profitable to each of you that it may !Ong
dwell in your memory.

· Samuel Manning Todd, P. G. M.

MEMBERSH IP.

For several years past each successive Grand Master in his
Annual Address has alluded to the general prosperity of this Institution and its phenomenal growth in numerical strength, each ·one
showing a marked increase over the other, but the year just closed
has witnessed a gain not quite as large as was made last year.
llllght cllapensatlons to form new Lodges have been granted, and
there hns been 11 net gain of two thou.s and one hundred and five
memller11, maklnK the total number of Lodges within this Jurisdiction two l111111l n•il 1111<1 ninety-nine, with a membership at the present
t I11111 of thirty 011<1 I houaand, slx hundred and nineteen.
Thia 1·11plc1 h11·rc1U1e Is worthy of reflection. We trust that it was
not <•au1ecl by a desire to make Masonry popular, and a resort to
methods that are not sanctioned by the best usages of the Fraternity.
It may be attributed in a large· measure, I believe, to the general
prosperity which continues to prevail in our State; by the attractions it has in the way o~ natural resources, climatic ~onditions,
educational advantages, business opportunities, and generally as a
State most suitable for homes, all of which has drawn the attention
of the people 9f the East in our direction and resulted in a large
immigration to California.
We must rememl.i er also that the na.tural Increase in population
is considerable, and it will be observed that of those who are now
becoming identified with this Fraternity, the great majority of them
are young men. They are young men of promise, a credit to the
Lodge to which they belong, and no doubt will be greatly benefited
by their Masonic associations.

1905.]

GRAND LODGE OF 0ALIFOHNIA.

u

There is something in Masonry which attracts men; it should be
left to them, however, to say whether they wish to join or not.
There should be 110 solicitation whatever. Let them come in of their
own free will. No man, however humble, should be kept out whose
life is clean, and no man should be admitted whose character will
not bear the closest scrutiny.
There is a feeling among some of the older heads that Masonry
is becomiqg too common, and that sufficient care is not exercised in
the selection of material. Our constant aim should be to have
within our ranks good and true men, and none of questionable
standing.
In every community Masons should be easily recognized by all
as men of character and honor, and this high standard can only
be maintained by caution as to the admission of applicants. No
member of a Lodge should be actuated by bad motives In the use of
the ballot. Petty spite, personal jealousy, and little business diffl·
culties should not be permitted to influence a Brother in considering the fitness of an appllcant for membership. There are seasons in some Lodges when, because of some disagreement or disturbance, it becomes impossible for even the best men In the community to gain admission thereto. This ls all wrong, but It is
unavoidable. It has always been so. My belief is that conditions In
this respect are constantly improving, and there is no reason to be
discouraged if once in a great while an epidemic of that nature
breaks out in certain locallties.
Very few dispensations to re-ballot have been requested this year.
Most, if not all, were from Lodges In the cities, and In several cases
they were occasioned by reason of a similarity of names and a mistake as to the identity of the person. On the whole I believe the
affairs of the subordinate Lodges have worked smoothly, and the
Inspectors, as a general rule, speak only in terms of praise of tli.e
conditions prevalllng in their respective districts.
·This has been a year of material growth; cornerstones have been
laid, several Temples are now fo course of construction, some have
been dedicated and others are being planned. Generally speaking,
the financial condition of the Lodges is all that could be desired.
MASONIC HOME.

In the month of April I visited the Masonic Home and spent a
night there. The Brothers and Sisters and the children were Invited
to the assembly hall during the evening and we all passed a couple
of hours very pleasantly. We had some very good playing by the
band, some selections upon the piano, songs by the little ones, and

12

'

I

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 10,

there was a short talk by myself, in an· endeavor to speak a few
words of comfort and cheer to the older ones, and of advice and encouragement to the children.
I was struck most forcibly by the advanced age of the grown
people. It seemed to me that nine out of ten were over seventy and a
number of them over eighty years of age. There are to be seen the
two extremes ·of childhood and old age, and it is hard to tell what infiuence association with the very old will have upon the very young,
under such circumstances, but it is evident that if it were ~ot for the
presence of the children the Home would be cheerless indeed, and
the discontent of the older people much more manifest than it is
now. Some allowance must be made for the misfortunes and infirmities of old age. No complaints were made to me, and I made it
a point to visit most of the Brothers there. They are feeble and not
a.ble to work. Some of the founders of the Home, in their enthusiasm, declared that in time it would become mainly self-supporting. I do not believe that time will ever come. If it were to do over
again, it may be that it would have been better not to have built the
Home but to have created a fund of some sort which could have been
used to help subordinate Lodges when necessary to support their
aged and unfortunate members, their widows .and orphans, they to
remain· among their friends in the places where the Lodges were
located, and the associations were dear to them.
But.the Home has been established; it is splendidly located, it
will have to be maintained and it should be the pride of the Masons
of California. It is too much to expect the men who are there, owing
to their enfeebled condition, to labor upon the farm or in -the orchard
or vineyard, and it will not pay to employ help to carry on such
work with the expectation that any profit will come from il:. While
there is more ground than is ac.t ually needed, it is good property,
with a prospect of large increase 'in value, and in my judgment it
would not be wise to dispose of any considerable ;iortion of it now
but to endeavor to preserve it as it is for some years hence and leave
it for those who compose some fut.ure Grand Lodge to determine
what shall be done with the surplus land, if any, or whether it shall
be extensively cultivated or not. The cost of maintaining the Home
is quite a tax upon the Lodges and to some of them an actual
burden. Wherever it can be .don-a to advantage the expense should
be reduced. In purchasing supplies, quality considered, the very
best bargains should be obtained; While it is the desire of every one
that everything reasonably required for the support and comfort of
the inmates should be furnished, we have a right to expect and exact
caution in the expenditures and economy in the management of its

l!:J05. J

GRAND l;ODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

affairs. In my judgment the Superintendent, Dr. Rucker and his
~stimable wife, are just the right persons to be in charge of the
Home, and they feel the responsibility and are endeavoring to conduct it as they would if it were a private institution of which they
were the owners. It does not take one who has a household of his·
own very long to see that Mrs. Rucker is not only a. good manager
but a superior woman in every respect. It is indeed fortunate for
us that w~ were able to induce. them to accept the position, and although there are many things to try their patience ln 'the discharg~
of their duties, I hope they will be content to remain and administer affairs for a Jong time to come.
While in the south last May visiting Lodges, the Southern California Masonic Home Association had just purchased the old San
Gabriel Hotel for a Masonic Home, and I was taken out to see the
property. It comprises ten acres, is situated in the beautiful San
Gabri.el Valley, with a fine view of the surrounding country, is only
eleven miles· from the City of Los Angeles, upon the line of an
electric road, and i doubt if a more desirable location for the purpose
could have been found in that section anywhere, and I am sure such
a property could not have been purchased elsewhere for eighteen
thousand dollars, the price paid for it, or for anything like that
sum. It had been used as a hotel in boom times, but larger and
more expensive ones had been constructed in towns near it and this
one had to close for want of patronage. The grounds are nicely
laid out and well shaded. When I was there the building was being
renovated and would soon be ready for occupancy. It is sightly,
large and commodious, with .s pacious rooms, which were partly furnished, broad corridors and wide porches, and although it was built
for a hotel, it could not have been much better planned had it been
designed for a Masonic Home, intended to accommodate from one
.hundred
one hundred and fitty people; and I am confident if one
should begin now to undertake to duplicate this or to buy a site and
construct a building in every respect suitable for a Home, but not
more so than this, It could not be done for Jess than three or four
times the purchase price of this property.

PHILIPPINES.

The Master of " Manila" Lodge sent me a copy of Section 62 or
the new Penal Code being prepared by the Commission for the government of the Philippine Islands, which Section was as follows:
"Section 62: All persons who shall meet together for the purpose of forming, or who have formed any society whose meetings
~re held in secret, or whose purposes and operations are not openly
published, or whose members are required not to disclose any of the
details of Its organization or operation, not authorized in writing
by the government of the Philippine Islands, or who shall after the
passage of this Act continue membership in any such society not so
authorized, sha,ll be punished by a fine of not more than two
thousand pesos or by Imprisonment for not more than one year or
both;. providing that any such persons who shall after a complete
disclosure of all the details of the organization and operation of such
society prove that the objects and ends of the society are legal, shall
be relieved of the penalty herelnabove provided.'' .
While It was evident that It was not the Intention of the lawmakers to have the provisions of this Section apply to worthy fraternal or benevolent societies, still they would come within its
letter, and It was thought and feared that if In the course of time
its enforcement should fall into the hands of prejudiced persons, it
might work a hardship on those of the Masonic Fraternity belonging
to Lodges In those Islands under charter from this Jurisdiction.
Accordingly a communication was addressed by me to the War
Department calling attention to the provisions of this law and the
trouble that might come from It, and within the last month I received
a reply stating that the original Section bad been struck out and the
following substituted:
" Section 62: All persons who shall meet together for the purpose of forming or who shall form any secret society, or who shall
after the passage of this Act continue membership In a society
already formed, havi ng for its object In whole or In part the promotion of treason, rebellion or sedition, or the promulgation of any
political opinion or policy, shall be punished" by fine not exceeding

16

PROCEEDINGS m' THE

[Oct. 10,

two thousand pesos, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year or
b<ith."
To this law there could be no objection whatever.

DECISIONS.

With about three hundred Lodges and more than thirty thousand
Masons in this Jurisdiction, it is to be expected that in the course
of a year a good many questions will be submlttted to the Grand
Master. Of the .many presented to me, it is li~ely that some· In
principle had been previously decided, but at least a few were new,
and I have selected and herewith submit for the considel'ation of the
Grand Lodge, the following decisions:
1. The Constitution provides that no Lodge shall admit a visitor
without due inquiry or examination. The term, " due inquiry," is
not satisfied by the consideration of letters ~r written statements
only, given by the Master or Secretary of the Lodge of which he
claims to be a member, to the effect that he is a Master Mason in
good standing. Documentary e.vidence alone, no matter of . what
character, is not sufficient to admit him, but he must prove himself
by a personal examination. Where, however, he has a statement
from the Secretary of a Lodge, under seal, that he is a Master Mason
in good standing, and is unable fo pass a rigid test, very slight
evidence by examination should be sufficient to admit him.
2. The Master of a: Lodge asked the following question: "Where
there are nine candidates to be voted for at the same meeting, can
:Ne have them all voted for at the same time, and then if the first
ballot is unfavorable, order a separate ballot as to each?"

1905. l

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

17

MY. answer was "No." Such a procedure would hardly be a fair
expression of the will of the Lodge, and it would give an objectionable applicant a better opportunity to come in.· In speaking of balloting for a candidate, the Constitution uses the singular number.
There is no provision for grouping candidates, and there can be no
reb;lloting when two or more bl.ack balls appear.
3. Charges may be brought against a Fellow Craft Mason for a
Ma3o::iic o:!l'ense, just as if he were a Master Mason. The procedure
ie the same In all cases and like penalties may be imposed.
4. . A. B., a Master Mason, was charged with unmasonlc conduct;
the charges being presented by the Master of his Lodge. By ~equest
the case was transferred by the Grand Master to another Lodge for
trial. The accused was found guilty and sentenced by the Lodge
which tried him, to be suspended. He some time later petitioned
the Lodge of which he was a member to be'reinstated and restored
to all his rights and privileges, and the question for decision is,
which Lodge should act in the matter-his own Lodge or the Lodge
which tried him. I held that It should be the Lodge that pronounced the judgment of suspension, which sentence was for an
indefinite period. Section 3 of Article V of Part VI of the Constitution, provides that a Lodge may annul any such sentence of suspension promulgated by itself; and In Section 5 It is declared that
when any suspended Mason desires to petition thf Grand Lodge for
restoration, he shall first make application to the Lvdge by which he
was suspended, and there is no provision by which a sentence pronounced by one Lodge may be annulled by another. It cannot be
maintained that the applicant was In fact tried and sentenced by his
own Lodge, and that the other was merely the instrument to carry
out its will 11.nd purposes. The Lodge to which the case was trans·
ferred obtained complete jurisdiction to try it, and either to acquit
or convict, according to the evidence; and if found guilty to impose
a penalty, and it alone can wipe out the sentence if so disposed.
5. On March 5th, 1883, C. D. was suspended from member::Jhlp by
his Lodge for non-payment of dues. He was then owing ~36. On
November 7th, 1904, at a stated meeting, It was reported t<;> his
Lodge that he wished to be restored to membership ul!on paying
$36 and having his dues since suspension remitted, and on motion 1t
was unanimously accepted, but no ballot was had thereon. At the
stated meeting on December 5th, 1904, the minutes of the meeting
ot November 7th were read and approved, and upon discussion as to.
the validity of the restoration it was resolved to have C. D. sign a
petition for restoration and to have it Ile over for one month, which
was done. At the stated meeting or. January 2d, 1905, the petition

6. The daughter of a Master Mason in good standing when he
died, married to a man who has been a Mason, but dimitted, and who
has been out of standing for many years, and who has attempted
suicide and is sick in a hospital, the wife Being destitute, is entitled to consideration at the hands of the Lodge to which her father
belonged at the time of his de_a th. The right to relief depends upon
the fact that she is the daughter of a Master Mason, and if worthy
herself she did not forfeit any right by reason of an unfortunate
marriage or the misfortunes of matrimony.
7. Th~ minutes of a Lodge show that E. F. received the E. A.
Degree therein, September 9th, 1862, petitioned for advancement
J'!ovember 26th, 1887, was balloted for on December 24th, 1887, and
declared rejected. At the stated meeting in May, 1905_, he sent to the

he be advanced, and filed an affidavit to the effect that he did not
petition the Lodge for advancement on November 26th, 1887, nor
authorize any one to present his name a t that time, nor give his
consent thereto. The question asked by the Lodge was, should it
be governed by its own record of the matter, or should it receive and
act upon evidence from the. outside. The ruling was that the Lodge
should be governed by its own record; the ballot taken on December
24th, 1887, should be treated as a denial of advancement by the
Lodge, and that he could only proceed now by petition, reference and
clean ballot the same as if he had not received the first Degree.

service there in a body on Easter Sunday, I do not see that any harm
to ' Masonry can come from It, and know of nothing to prevent it.
No dlspensation could be granted to wear regalia on such an occasion.

12. In August, 1904, a petition for the Degrees was flied, and at
the time the petitioner was a resident within the jurisdiction of the
Lodge, and In every respect eligible to membership. Before the committee could interview him and because of unforeseen circumstances
be was obliged to remove and change his residence to an Eastern
State. No report was made by the committee and nearly a year
after the matter was referred to them, the petitioner asked to withdraw his petition and have the money refunded. It seems like a
hardship to deny the request under the circumstances, but I felt
constrained to hold that the application could not be withdrawn.
Section 3 of Article III of Part III of the Constitution provides
that, "No application shall be withdrawn after reference to committee except as hereinafter provided in this Section." The only
exceptions are that " If the committee find the applicant disqualified
in consequence of insufficient residence or physical disablllty and
find no other objection to him, they shall make a special report
thereupon In which case the Master may direct the withdrawal of
the application without further action."
This applicant had been a r esident within the Jurisdiction of the
Lodge during six months next preceding the date of his application

[Oct. 10,

and was such at the time of applying; therefore his request for
w.ithdrawal did not come within either of the· exceptions provided
by the Constitution.
13. After a petition was received and referred to a committee,
but the day before the stated meeting at which it was to report, a
member of the Lodge went to the Master and made a verbal objection
to the candidate. The committee reported favorably, but Its report
was not permitted to come before the Lodge.
The Master inquires: "Whether he should order a ballot, or
should the objection hold good, and if no ballot is taken, how long a
time should e_lapse before he should declare the petition rejected? "
The Constitution gives a member an undoubted right to object,
and a fair construction of the .provision Is, that the objection may
be made at any time after the petition has been received and referred, provided it be interposed before his Initiation. Its language ·
is: "No Lodge shall have m'o re than one ballot for the Degrees;
but, though an applicant may be elected to teceive them, if, at any
time before his initiation, objection be made by any member, he
shall not receive the Degree until such objection shall have been
withdrawn," etc. If a member may object and prevent initiation
after election, certainly he should have the right and power to do so
before election, and it should be treated in ·an respects as one interposed afterwards, and unless withdrawn would hold good for sixty
days from the time it was made, and finally result in a rejection. ·
14. On June 10th, 1904, G. H. was elected to receive the Degrees,
and on the 21st of the same month the Entered Apprentice Degree was
conferred upon him. In December, 1904, he was indicted for steal-'
ing mail matter, and on being arraigned confessed his guilt. The
Federal Judge before whom he was tried found from the evidence
that he was insane at the time of the trial, and that he had been
insane for fourteen months, which period would not only cover the
period when the offense was committed, but would go back to a time
prior to his presenting his petition for membership in the Lodge.
He was committed to a hospital for the insane and is now confined
therein. The question submitted to me was: "Was not the action
of the Lodge in accepting the petition of G. H. irregular and its
proceedings null and ·void, for the reason that he was found to be
insane?"
My answer was in the negative. In the first place neither he nor
the ·Lodge is bound by the finding of the Court as to his being
insane at the time he joined the Lodge, or the commission of the
offense, in any action by the Lodge to cancel his membership because

1905.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

21

of his insanity or to try him for a Masonic offense. His petition was
presumably presented in the regular way; a committee appointed to
investigate his fitness to be a member; .the committee reported
favorably; he was elected and rec~lved the First Degree, before any
discovery was made. It does not appear that he made any fraudulent
representations either in his petition or to the committee, or did anything to deceive them or the Lodge. While every man seeking to
join. a Masonic Lodge should be of sound mind, if the Lodge was
deceived as to his mental condition and desires to get rid of him or
cancel his membership because of his insanity, and this can be
done, he has a right to be heard upon the question, and of course
it cannot be tried and determined while he remains insane.

The_ resolution was made necessary because some members had

case of an adverse report whether one or more reported unfavorably
and the responsibility would be shared by all. If wrong in my construction of the resolution in question, the Committee on Jurisprudence will set me right. If right, and the members of this Grand

resolution can be changed so as to cover the ground.

This letter was dated September 2d, 1904, and the Masons who

•
The sovereignty of the Hawaiian Islands was transferred t<;> tl:)e
United States on the 12th day of August," 1898..
On September 22d, 1904, there was established the organization
named " Maul " Lodge, and which obtained Its charter or dispensation from the Grand Lodge of Scotiand long after Hawaii became
American territory. Our Grand Lodge has never claimed exclusive
Jurisdiction anywhere, except within the boundaries of the StatE\ of
California, and it has always recognized the fact that prior to the
annexation of Hawaii Its Jurisdiction over the Lodges it established
there was but temp.o rary, and as to territory exercised· In common with other Grand Lodges of the world, and liable to be lost
whenever three ar more Lodges were established there and they saw
fit to organize a Grand Lodge of their own, which they could now do,
and if done, their Lodges would become immediately released from
all obligations to any other Grand Body. So long as Hawaii remained a Republic, or while it was a Kingdom, it was recognized as
common ground, and all Masonic Grand Bodies had concurrent Jurisdiction therein. When it became a part of the United States, then,
under Masonic law of this country, the subordinate Lodges that were
there, still belonged to the Jurisdictions where they obtained their
charters, respectively, but when it came to the formation of new
Lodges, no Grand Lodge, except those within the United States had
the right to grant a dispensation for such a purpose. Prior to the

1905.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA..

27

Revolution the Grand Lodges of England, Ireland, Scotland, France
and Hamburg, issued charters for Lodges within the Colonies.
Since that time they have undertaken to do so but seldom, and
whenever any of them bas at tempted it, It has been resented by the
Grand BOdies of America. So far as I know no Grand Lodge within
t he United States has ever sought to establish a subordinate within
the dominion of the Kingdom of Great Britain or any of her de·
pendencles, and we believe that whenever any country comes under
the American fiag and becomes American soil, that thereafter no
foreign Grand Body should grant dispensations or seek t o establish
Lodges therein. If the Grand Lodge of Scotland can charter a J,odge
on the Island of Maui, which belongs to the United St ates, It can
charter other Lodges in Honolulu and elsewhere in the Haw~iian
Islands, and with equal propriety, it could be done in t he Terntory
of Alaska.
This has never been allowed or attempted without protest.
While the facts were not exactly the same and probably no .case can
be found exactly similar to this, as the Territory of Hawaii, owing
to Its sit uation in mid-ocean, is, in many respects unique, still it is
American territory, and the Masonic law which would apply to any
other American territory wi!J apply to it; and in reference to a case
which arose in New York in the early fifties, where the Grand Lodge
of Hamburg was seeking to invade the rights of the Grand Lodge of
New York by establishing Lodges there, our own Grand Lodge In
1851 at its second Communication in sympathy with the Grand
Lod~e of New York, expressed itself by resolution on this subject as
follows :
"•Resolv ed, That this Grand Lodge can give no countenance or
support to the pret ention of the Grand Lodge of Hamburg or any
other foreign Grand Lodge, to a right to grant charter~ for Lodges
in any of the territory of the United St ates of America.

So far as I can find this resolution has never been changed
or modified, and Its language Is just as applicable to territory sub·
sequently ac:,1ulred, as that which then existed.
With the law thus declared, or at least the sentiment of our
Grand Lodge thus expressed in its ear ly h istory and never altered,
I feel it t o be my duty to hold that •Hawaiian ' Lodge, No. 21,
should n ot request • Maul • Lodge to confer the Degrees, or eit her ot
them on Bro. Smiddy, nor should it render a similar service tor
•Maul ' Lodge at its request.
It Is not necessary for me to go full length in deciding your
questions. r have no desire to interrupt the pleasant personal rela·

LODGE " LE PBOGRES."

At the last Annual Communication, Lodge "Le Progres de
L'Oceanle," No. 124, A. and A. S. R. of Honolulu, . petitioned this
Grand Lodge for a charter or dispensation. It was chartered in
1842 by the Supreme Council of France. The reasons for making
this request are given very fully in the petition which Is found on
page 872 of the proceedings of last year. It had the recommendation
of "Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, and also of the Inspector of the 49th
Masonic District. It was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence,
their report is found on page 1080, and I quote from it the following:
" We are of the _opinion that it would be inexpedient to finally act
upon this pe~n at this Communication of the Grand Lodge. • • •
Were w~tlsfled as to the legality of the method suggested, we are
of t!J..e' opinion that no dispensation or charter should be ordered
wlille this Lodge ls a subordinate of another Grand Body, and
further that no such action should be taken until after full I»·
vestlgatlon as to the origin of the Lodge, Its history, work and
membership. If twelve or more Masons in Honolulu wish to organize a new Lodge therein under our Jurisdiction, they may proceed under Section 2. of Article I, P~rt III, of our Constitution, and
apply at any time to the Grand Master for a dispensation. We
recommend that final action upon this petition be defe,rred until the
next Annual Communication; that In the meantime such Investigation as the Grani:l. Master deems advisable to make as to the merits
of the case (be made), and that the incoming Committee on Juris·
prudence report at such Communication as to the legality of the
method proposed."
Several months after adjournment it was again called t o my
attention and since that time I have had a good deal of cor·
respondence In relation to It, mostly with Bro. Joshua D. Tucker of
Honolulu, who Is the present Inspector of the 49th Masonic District.
In May, replying to a letter received from the Master of "Le
Progres " Lodge upon the subject, I expressed myself as follows:
" Let me assure you that It Is a mistake for any of the members
of • Le Progres ' to think for a moment that there was any opposition in our Grand Lodge to ' Le Progres ' comtng under our Juris·
diction. If there was I have not heard of it. It Is plain to be seen
that we are in a delicate position and we do not desire to have it
berome embarrassing and be regarded as treating the Supreme Coun-

cil of France in a way similar to what we have been treated by the
Grand Lodge of Scotland in the 'Maui• Lodge matter. We want
you to be free to deal with the Supreme Council as you deem best
for your own interests. If the relation should be severed we would
not be compromised in any manner and ' Le Progres ' could act as

Asking Bro. Tucker for information as to the origin, history,
work and membership of " Le Progres " Lodge as suggE>sted by the
report of the Committee, he wrote me as follows: ·
" This Lodge was erected under a dispensation from the Supreme
Council of France 33d in the year 1843 by one Capt. Le Tellier, who
held a roving commission from that Body. Their charter was received in the year 1850. In the year 1852 a number of its m~rnbers
dimitted and formed -''Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, under charter from
the Grand Lodge of California. 'Le Progres ' has had many ups
and downs during its existence and now numbers about 130 members. They are a progressive body of men, most of them being young ·
men, and they would be a credit to any Body. The second section
of the Third Degree is the same as the old work in the California
Jurisdiction, with a few additions as to admonitjon and ~xplana­

the California work as it was before it was changed by the present

Deg-ree is very different in some particulars, and It is In this part
that they desire to retain. In fact the ceremony is very Impressive
and in no way detracts from the beauty of the work."
In one of his letters Bro. Tucker says; "The members of the
Lodge want to come under the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of ·
California and so expressed themselves at their last meeting, not by
vote, but to me individually."
Still later be said: " The members of • Le Progres' inform me
that they have received a communication from their Representative
in Paris, who informed them that their request for a severance of
relations is about to be consummated."
After this and a like assurance from the Master of "Le Progres "
Lodge not being disposed to take any steps until fully assured that
their relations with France were in a fair way of amicable adjust·
ment, and believing that their reiease was reasonably certain; I advised Bro. Tucker that in my judgment the best plan to pursue

The leases will all expire in June, 1909. The rental per month
last year was $3,170. This year it is $3,780, or more than $600 per
month more than it was a year ago.
There is a feeling quite prevalent, as shown by the debate wben.
this question was being considered at the last session, that this
building is no longer adequate or adapted to the purposes for which
it was designed. The corner-stone of this Temple was laid by Grand
Master Curtis in the presence of a vast assemblage of representative
Masons on the 24th of June, 1860, and this Hall was first occupied
by the Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in May, 1863.
The building was not then finished, and it took several years to
complete it. In his address to the Grand Lodge on the occasion of
first occupying it, Grand Master Belcher said: " This is the finest

1905.J

GRAXD LODGE OF UALlFORNIA.

33

and most perfect building upon the Pacific Coast, and when finished
will be the most beautiful, if not the most expensive Masonic Temple
in America."
And Grand Secretary Abell, who was also secretary of the H11ll
Association, in making his report, and an appeal for funds to complete the structure, made at the same session, uses this language:
"When finished it will be by far the most imposing, most commodious and most convenient edifice for Masonic purposes in the world."
There may be a few here to-day who were present on both occasions, but if so they are but few indeed.
It is more than forty-five years since the corner-stone was laid,
and more than forty-two years since the Grand Lodge held its first
Communication in this Hall.
Evidently it was thought then that this building would stand for
ages. It was built during the most trying years of the great Civil
Wat', when times were hard and money scarce, even in the Golden
State of California. It cost in the neighborhood of $.250,000, and
there was an indebtedness upon it of $100,000, bearing interest at the
rate of one and one-eighth per cent. per month. It was built mainly
by the efforts and energy and the capital of the Masons of San Francisco. But things have changed since that time. In 1860 California.
had a population of less than four hundred thousand, to-day It has
nearly two millions. In 1860 San Francisco had less than sixty thousand population, while to-day it has nearly five hundred thousand,
or more than· as many as were in the entire State of California at the.
former period. In 1860 there were only one hundred and thirty·
Masonic Lodges in California, with a membership of five thousand'.
and fifty-five, while to-day there are 299 lodges with a membership of:
31,619.
At that time there were only eleven Lodges in San Francisco-,_
with a total membership of eight hundred and forty-seven, while at
the present time there are nineteen chartered Lodges and one Lodge
under dispensation, with a total membership of six thousand tw()
hundred and sixty-one.
Comparatively speaking, San Francisco was then a village-now
it is a great city with a magniftcent future. The old landmarks are
disappearing, splendid buildings are being erected· to take the place
of those that have outlived their usefulnf'ts. While we venerate age
and appreciate what our predecessors ha'\-.! done for us, yet If th&.
present Temple is no longer suitable for the purposes for which it
was intended, it is not sacreligious to tear it down, and the Masons
of San Francisco, with a little help, perhaps, from others within the
Jurisdiction, are able to build one that is suitable.

3

34

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 10,

It would not be wise, however, in my judgment, to dispose of this
property and seek to acquire another site.
To the average man from the country or city it would seem that
the present location is most admirable. It is centrally located, readily accessible, easily found by strangers, surrounded by magnificent
structures, and more likely to increase than depreciate in value. If
this property were sold the purchasers would be apt to remove the
building and erect another, as this could not be worked over or used
to advantage for business purposes. And where in San Francisco
can be found a lot seventy-five by one hundred and sixty feet with
light on three sides, in every way ·a s desirable as this?
And if such a lot can be found, what would have to be paid for
it. It rests largely with the Masons of San Francisco to say what shall
be· done. We should deal fairly with the private individuals who are
the owners of stock, but the Masons will have to do what is for the
best interests of all concerned.· The stock could be increased and
the increase sold, or if a debt is to be incurred instead of paying one
and one-eighth per cent. per month, as was done forty-five years ago,
money could now probably be obtained at four per cent. per annum,
on such security as could be · given, if a new building were constructed, and it would probably yield an income of more than six per
cent. per annum on the investment.
If this building is not suitable it seems to me the best thing to do
would be to begin to plan now to erect on this lot a modern Temple
twelve to fourteen stories high, for bll"\liness and lodge purposes, and
be ready to begin operations when the present leases expire, and let
it again be said that "when finished it will be far the most imposing,
most commodious and most convenient edifice for Masonic purposes
in the world."
MASONRY.

We, the representatives of the various Lodges in this Jurisdiction,
certainly take pride in such an assemblage as this. We know something of what has been accomplished by Masonry in California; a few
have watched its growth from the beginning, and many are familiar
with its history.
Without effort it has steadily advanced, and it has placed its impress upon the civilization and institutions of our commonwealth.
Its teachings are salutary and ennobling. No man can long be identified with it without having high.er aspirations and a nicer conception of his duties to his fellow-man. It awakens noble impulses and
incites and encourages an ambition to be helpful and to do good.
Every one of us can bear testimony to the benefits we have derived
from it, and we -have- ·frequently witnessed the blessings it has

1905.]

GnA!\D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

3.5

showered upon others. Its charities are unbounded and yet without
ostentation. It inculcates morality, improves citizenship, and uplifts
humanity. As a character-builder it has no superior; it makes men
more considerate of the rights of others, more affectionate toward
their families, and more fraternal in their intercourse with their
fellow-men.
· By the profane, Masonry is usually judged by the acts of its indi·
vidual members. This being so, let us strive to so llve that we will
not bring disgrace upon it; let us bear in mind the lessons taught
in the lodge-room, -and may our thoughts and aims raise us to a still
higher standard of manhood. Masonry develops the best traits in
man's character. It · tends to make him benevolent, kind hearted,
sympathetic, charitable. We should remember that in the practice
of charity we should not confine it simply to financial aid to one in
need, but we should have charity in the broader sense, of looking
with compassion ·upon the frallties of our brother, of speaking kindly
of his infirmities, if he has them, and of using1our best endeavors to
reclaim him if going astray.
It ls a pleasure as well as a duty to speak a word of cheer and
lend a helping hand to those in sickness or distress, and to do what
can be done to better the condition of mankind, and the thousands
of men belonging to this institution and practicing these principles,
cannot but command the respect and admiration of the world.
CONCLUSION.

At the last Communication there was appropriated " For the con·
tingent expenses of the Grand Master, and for actual expenses incurred,'' the sum of $1,200, and as is customary a draft for the same
was given me at the beginning of the term. While I have kept no
itemized account of expenditures, the expenses of myself and others
a:cting for me, such a's I have been permitted to repay; have been met,
and I have found that the sum appropriated was more than sufficient
for the purpose, and of the amount I have turned over to the Masonic
ttome Fund the sum of $400.
·
Situated as I have been, it was not possible for me to spare the
time, make the visits and look after the welfare of the Craft as many
of my predecessors have done.
Residing as I do in the City of Eureka, with the most available
means of reaching San Francisco by steamer, . it was fortunate for
me, and as much so for others, that the home of the Deputy Grand
Master was in Los Angeles, and that of the Senior Grand Warden in
Berkeley, and I am under lasting obligations to those officers for their
_assistance during my term.
In December I attended the banquet given by "Durant" Lodge in
Berkeley, installed the officers of the several Lodges in the city of

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 10,

Sacramento, took part in the observance of the fiftieth anniversary
of "Morning Star" Lodge of Stockton, and was present at the installa·
tion of officers and banquet gjven by "Fidelity" Lodge of this city. In
the spring I made a flying trip through the State, visiting Lodges in
the principal towns and cities, from San Diego to Yreka, but it was
hurriedly done, and the smaller places and those not upon the main
lines of travel by rail were overlooked, and In the performance of my
duty in this respect I feel like offering an apology, and am sure I
have not done what was reasonably expected of me.
Wherever I have been I have met with generous treatment, and
the meetings were a source of pleasure to me and I trust of profit to
the Fraternity. My only regret is that I have not been able to do
more for Masonry, which I regard as not only the most ancient, but
as the noblest fraternal organization in existence.
With the conclusion of this session my official duties terminate •.
I am profoundly grateful for the honor which has been conferyed
upon me, and highly appreciate the uniform courtesy and open·
hearted hospitality received by me at the hands of the Brethren.
Whatever credit, if any, is due to my administration ls to be
shared by all the Grand Officers, and I wish to express my thanks to
the Grand Secretary for favors bestowed, and to our Deputy Grand
Master, Bro. Flint, and our Senior Grand Warden, Bro. Hart, for thel-r
many acts of kindness and valuable assistance In aiding and representing me on many occasions during my term.
May we all be deeply Impressed with the responsibility resting
upon us; and may all our ·deliberations be conducted in a spirit of
harmony and brotherly love. May the legislation to be enacted at
this session be inspired by wisdom, and prove to be beneficial In its
results; may our lives become better by reason of our association,
a_n d may the Influences for good which are certain to be manifested
here not be confined to ourselves individually, but reach out and be
felt in every community in the great State of California, of which
we are all so justly proud.
GEORGE W. HUNTER,
Grand Master.

The R. '. W.-. MOTLEY H. FLINT, Deputy Grand Master, presented the following : WHEREAS, The Masonic brethren residing near Sawtelle, Los Angeles
County, California-among the twenty-three hundred "Boys in Blue of 186165," assigned to the National Military Home for disabled volunteer soldiers
in this State-have long felt the necessity for a Masonic Lodge, particularly

WHEREAS, Thirty;nine Master Masons have presented a petition for a
dispensation for said Lodge, all of said thirty-nine Master Masons having pre·
sented certificates of withdrawal from the Lodges of which they were last a
member-less than six months ago-together with a recommendation from
"Santa Monica" Lodge, No. 307, the nearest or most convenient Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Deputy Grand Master FLYNT, accompanied by Bro. GEORGE
N. BLACK, Inspector of the Forty.second Masonic District, visited Sawtelle
on the evening of September twenty-seventh, and met with the ·brethren of
the proposed new Masonic Lodge, and which is to be known as "Veteran's"
Lodge, and at their request the work was exemplified, and it can be safely
stated that the brethren are enthusiastic and look forward with much pleasure to the fact that a portion of their last days may be spent in true Masonic
jntercoure!", u.nd in a Lodge-room furnished by them at a sacrifice, .but for their
love of the Fraternity. The work was almost letter-perfect, and there is no
good reason why a charter should not be granted ;
BE TT THEREFORE RESOLVED, That so much as may be necessary of Part
III. Article I·, ~ections 1, 2 and 3, of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge
be suspended, and that the books and records of proposed ' ' Veterans ''
Lodge be brought up to the requirements of a Lodge under dispensation ; that
said Lodge be not required to work under dispensation, but simply to submit copy of By·laws, prope1-ly signed, and record books, and; when so sub.
mitted, the Grand Master is hereby authorized to issue a charter · to said
L odge, and that the fee for a dispensation and charter be waived by this Grand
Lodge; and
B& l'l' FURTHER RESOLVED, That, provided the records required are sub.
mitted to the Grand Lodge within thirty days after the close of this Grand
Lodge, that the Grand Secret.u y be, and he is hereby authorized, to include
in his annual report, the membership of the proposed " Veteran's" Lodge,
without expense to that Locl11e. It ia the intention and desire of the mem·
hers of proposed "Veteran's" Lodge that, provided a charter be granted, to
hereafter p1<y all Grand Lodge dues, per capita tax, etc., the same as any
other chartered Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction.

[Oct. 11,

Upon investigating the foreioing, it will be 1hown · that this M aaonic
Board of Relief can be operated under ordinary conditions with a much
smallH appropriation from the Grand Lodge than it has heretofore 1·eceived.
In Pll:l>t years, under different circumetances. the fonds of the Bonrd were
not adequate to the demands made upon them and in consequence it. was
deemecl necessary to fix the per capita tax of the subordinate Lodges for the
Masonic Board of Relief, at eight cents per month per member, and a resolu·
tion wo.s pas11ed by the Grand Lodge (which we believe to be still in force)
tnaking it compulsory for the Lodges of this Jul'isdiction to pay that sum
into the Board of Relief.
We believe, however, that this resolution should be expunged autl subordinate Lodges called upon to pay only such sum as will be sufficient to
meet the operating expenses of the Board, and the Board given to understand
that the funds of the Grand Lodge are at all times available for the making
good of shortages consequent upon all subordinllte Lodges within this Jurisdiction, being unable to meet demands which may be made upon them for
the p1·oper carrying out of the Masonia obligation•, and also for relief furnished to sojcrurniog dimitted Brethren who have dimitted from this or
outside jurisdilltleins, but who have kept themselves in standing with the
Fraternity.
The matter of reimbursement has, during the past year, been well canvaased throughout the United States and foreign jurisdiction• and the
Fraternity generally concede our position that a Board of Relief .acta in the
capacity as the agent of Lodges, whithersoever located, and that Charity
disbursed to the individual ha.s been so disbursed for the account of the
Lodge, which Lodge, if financially unable to meet its just.obligations, should
be cared for by the Grand Lodge of the Jurisdiction under which it is chartered .
The foregoing tends in no way to withhold proper relief to the worthy, a11
the preceding statement will indicate. Notwithstanding that the Board this
year presents its report ebowing a surplus of funds on hand pr&ctically equal
to the full amount the Grand Lodge intrusted it with a year ago, it will be
noted that fully as much money has been disbursed for Charity and the
-burial of the dea.d as has beeu done in prior years.
·
We trust tha.t thi11 yer.r~s report will be ea.tiafactory and the mode of pro·
cedure which ha.a governed the Board during the pa.et year, will meet with
the approval of the Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
H . E. PKNNBLL, Chairman.
J. B. RUF.BEi' , Secretlxry.

BRo. REUBEN H. LLOYD, from the Special Committee on New
Temple, presented the following report:To the M.·. W.'. Grand Lodge ofCalif11rnia:Your Special Committee, appointed at the last Communication of this
Grand Body for the purpose of in,·estigating the question as to whether or
not it would be well to sell the present Ma.sonic Temple and purchase a lot
elsewhere and construct a new temple, or whether it would be advisable to
erect a new temple upon the present site, or retain the old temple in its
preeen t condition, respectfully report :
They met with the Representatives from other Grand and Subordinate
Bodies of this Order, who represent some lS,000 out of the 25,000 sharea of
the capital stock of the Masonic Hall Association, the remaining 7,000 shares
being held by outsiders. After full consideration, the consensus of opinion of
the Committee was that the present site, which has a frontage of 75 feet on
Montgomery street, 160 feet on Post street, and 75 feet on Lick etre.,t, is the
moat available, and perhaps the best, which could be selected in San Francisco,
and it would be very bad policy indeed to dispose of it.
The present· Temple, constructed half a century ago, was designed when
a large portion of the population was not yet certain about the growth or
future of 8a.n Francisco-then more than sufficient to supply all the lodge and
other room required. Now the Order ha.s outgrown its capacity, and many
of the bodies have been compelled to seek quarters elsewhere. The elevator
• and steel construction systems have made it possible to replace our ·present
Temple with a magnificent landmark of our Order, amply sufficient to supply
all our wants for the next century, and bring a handsome income besidee.
Your Committee, for the purpose of ascertaining the feasibility of erecting
a new Temple on the old site, sought the advice of D. H. BuRNHA~, Esq.,
who desip;ned and superintended the construction of the famous Masonic
Temple of Chicago, and also a number of large modern steel buildings of San
Francisco, and who has just finished an elaborate plan to beautify this city.
After giving the matter a full consideration, he said he was heartily in
accord with the opinion of the Committee that the present site should not be
changed, and it would be a, wise thing for the Association to erect a modern
twelve-story Clase "A" Building in place of the present Temple. At our

We have carefully gone over the prospect of oonstructing a building on
the present Masonic Temple site, northwest corner of Montgomery and Post
streets, and can consistently sa,v that a twelve story steel Class " A" structure
on this property would yield a re\•enue approximately of $200,000 per annum.
Deduction for maintenance would show a net revenue of about $175,000,
which, valuing the land at $1,000,000 and a building at $600,000, or $1,600000 in all, providing the building were fully occupied, over a ten per cent net
revenue per annum upon said amount.
We arrh-e at this revenue in the following method:
The ground floor, including the basement, whir.h can be utilized for Safe
Deposit Vaults, also shops, the rental of same about ~6,000 per month;

It will be seen that Mr. Burnham figured on a building costing $1,000·
000. and Mr. Rich on one for $600,000; but Mr. Burnham estimated the
value of the lot at $800,000,.and Rich at $1,000,000; so the real difference
between them on total value is $200,000, which still leaves a large net revenue
<10 the undertaking.
The Temple stores are under leases running for four years from last June.
The present rent, $3, 772 per month, is quite inadequate to the value of the
property. The ooostruction of the lower floor making it undesirable for corn·
mercial purposes, a larger rent cannot be had. With a proper building, the
first 11.oor and basement would yield enough to pay the interest on the ontlay.
• We believe the best interests of the Order would be subserved by the
erection of a new modern Temple; and steps should be taken looking to the
()omraencement of the work four yenrs hence on the expiration of the present
leases.

In aoco1·dauce with the expresseJ wishes of the Grand· Lodge I am
pleased to say that with the assistance of Bro. Max Goldman and R. S. Allen
I have prepared and will submit to the Grand Lodge a uniform lecture for
the coaching of candidates in the lectures of the First and Second Degrees,
which I hope will meet with the approval of this Grand Lodge.

But, brethren, iu my journeyings as Grand Lecturer, it has been my
experience t111~t ma11y who apply for examination in order to visit are so
poorly prepared that it is only by the exercise of the greatest latitude on the
part of the committee that the visitor can gain admission. Many would.be
visitors know absolutely nothing of what took place during their initiation,
passing and rising, and I am more than ever convinced that this Grand
Lodge should m11ke it obliga.tory upon all candidates to pa.ss a satisfactory
examina.tion in the Lecture of the Third Degree before being permitted tO go
forth as full.fledged Master Masons. It would reflect more credit upon the
Lodges in which they received their degrees, and it would he of great benefit
to the individual brother who might wish to visit where he is not known.
I wish here to emphasize the great importance of being exceedingly careful
to select for the various officers of the Lodge those whose reputation for
unswerving honesty of purpose, for square dealing between man Rnd man, for

The institution of Masonry in California has attained a most exalted position among the fraternal organizations of the world. Situated, as we are, in
" l'ltate of s118h broad dimensions, such wonderful resources, euch varied
mdustries, such exhilirating climate, such inviting ha.rbors, with a population
tha.t is ever· increasing and alive to progress, and ever seeking the highest
idea.le, the most advanced possibilities, does it not behoove this Grand Loclge,
more even than it does the subordinate Lodges, to exert its utmost caution in
the selection of those who shall stand forth to the world·as the representatiYes
of the thirty-two thousands of Masons in this Commonwealth? Should they
uot be men who bear unsullied, spotless reputations in the communities
whence they hail ; shall they not be men whoso hearts· are filled with gentle
tLnd generous sympathy for those whom fortune 's frowns have driven to penury
1111d dispair, and should they not be men who have shown their associations
At home and a.broad that they are willing and c:i.pable to portray in public and
111 private the great underlying principles of this greatest of all fraternal
1ocieties ?
\Ve cannot take chances. Those whom we select should be those whum
wo know, those whose pa.st life bears uo blemish, those who, upon the floor of
t.he Grand Lodge, ha,ve demonstrateJ the fact that they have ideas and can
voice them in a manner that will reflect credit upon themselves and the great
fraternity that they, as officers, will represent when they wear the toga of
this Grand Lodge.

Your committee again congratulates this GrlUld Body Oil the work being
done and the progress being made by its subordinate Lodges ; and while the
gain of 2, 151 members for the year 1905 is :i;ot as great as in 1903, which was
2,343, or in 1904, which was 2,!!90, it has been sufficiently large to convince
us all that we are experiencing a wonderful gro,vth.
The returns this year show marked improvEment over those of 1903 and
1904; the rating of Lotlges for the last three years is as follows: The numbei:
of Lodges marked perfect in WO!! and 1904 were 224; , while those marked
p11rfeot in 1905 are 250, showing an increase of 26 Lodges with perfeot reports.
The number of Lodges whose returns were sent back for correction were,
in 1003, !13; in 1904, :n ; and in W05 only 2:t The number of Lodges whose
returns were transmitted later than the time required by the Constitution
was, in 1903, 20 ; 1904, 17, and 1905, l!J. 'l'he number of Lodges whose
returns were not transmitted within the proper time, and which had to be
returned for correction w:i.s i in l !JU!{ and 1904, and 5 in 1905.
From the above showing. it wiU be seen that t~~ returns .have come ~at;~
the Grand Secretary's office 10 much better cond1t10n than m any prev1om1
year, and your committee believes that the Secretaries of the various Lodges
are subject to congratulation for this excellent ehowing.

proper consideration, that this custom is as useless as the 'appendix
vermiformis' Is to the human body. It seems to us that the custom

Your committee to whom was referred the resolution relative to
expenses Incurred by Lodges In the burial of deceased brethren at
the Masonic Home have had the same under consideration and report .
as follows:
It Is the duty of Masonic Lodges to pay the expenses of their
deceased members and the widows and orphans who are dependent
upon them. It would be inequitable and unjust to require one Lodge
in the vicinity of the Masonic Home to bury all who may die there,
at an expense to them. Such expenses as are necessary In performing
t~ls duty should be paid by the Lodge to whom the deceased belonged
or under whose care he or she may have been.
The Lodge incurring the expense should send its claim to the
Lodge of the deceased and It should be settled by such Lodge.
The Grand Lodge should not be required to pay these amounts;
the burden ls on the Lodge and should be met by it.
We therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopted.

M.'. W.'. FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI, Chairman of the Com·
mittee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :
To the M.'. w:. Grana Lodge of Oalifornta :

Your committee has had under consideration the decisions rendered by the M.'. W.'. Grand Master during the year upon a question
of Masonic Law. We are pleased to be able to state that the report
of the Grand Master upon this matter shows that he has given to this
branch of his duties the same careful and conscientious attention that
has characterized all of his Masonic Work, and that his decisions
upon many somewhat novel and difficult questions are generally cor:
rect expositions of our law.

,lt~o. ]

GRAND LoDGE OF CALIFORNIA.

lll

The first decision or the Gran_d Master was as follows, viz:
1. . The Constitution provides that no Lodge shall admit a visitor
without due Inquiry or examination. · The term •due Inquiry t ls
not satisfied by the consideration of letters or written statements
·only, given by the Master or Secretary of the Lodge of which he
claims to be a member, to the etrect that he Is a Master Mason in
good standing. Documentary evidence alone, no matter .of what
character, Is not sufficient to admit him, but he must prove himself
by a personal examination. Where, however, he has a statement
from the Secretary of a Lodge, under seal, that he is a Master Mason
In good ·standing, and ls unable to pass a rigid test, Very sllght
evidence by examination should be sufficient to admit him.

The _gist of this decision Is that documentary evidence alone is
not sufficient to entitle a visitor to admission without examination.
This appears to be the settled law of the jurisdiction. It was said
some years ago when Bno. BELCHER was chairman of this committee
that one on asking to be received as a visitor must, unless vouched
for by some one present, prove himself to be a Mason, to the satisfaction of the Master of the Lodge, on a personal examination, and a Grand Lodge diploma or certificate or other documentary evidence can never be received as sufficient to entitle the appllcant to admission without examination. The present decision Is but
a re-affirmation of this. It is of course necessary that the Master
should, in all cases, be satisfied that the visitor ls a Mason.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
2. The Master of a Lodge asked the following quesuon: " Where
there are nine candidates to be voted for at the same meeting, can
we have them all voted for at the same time, and then if the first
ballot ls unfavorable, order a separate ballot as to each?"
The Grand Master answered "No," and In this we entirely concur. Our regulations provide an orderly and dignified method ot
voting upon the appllcatlon of one who desires admission to our
mysteries, and this method must be followed.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
The Grand Master decided that3. .Charges may be brought against a Fellow Craft Mason for a
Masonic offense, just as if he were a Master Mason. The procedure
is the same in all cases and llke penalties may be Imposed.
This decision Is In strict accord with our law (See Vol. XXI, proc.
l'P· 11 , 218). We recommend that It be approved.

The Grand Master reported the following decision:4. A. B., a Master Mason, was charged with unmasonic conduct,
the charges being presented by the Master of his Lodge. By request
the case was transferred by the Grand Master to another Lodge fol'
trial. The accused was found guilty and sentenced by the Lodge
which tried him, to be suspended. He some time later petitioned
the Lodge of which he was a member to be reinstated and restored
to all his . rights and privileges, and the question for decision is,
which Lodge should act in the matter-his own Lodge or the. Lodge
which tried him. I held that it should be the Lodge that pronounced
the judgment of suspension, which sentence was for an lndefl.nlte
period. Section 3, Article V of Part VI of the Constitution, provides
that a Lodge may annul any such sentence of suspension pronounced
by Itself; and in Section 5 it is declared that when any suspended
Mason desires to petition the Grand Lodge for restoration he shall
first make application to the Lodge by which he wa~ suspe~ded, and
there Is no provision by which a sentence pronounced by one Lodge
may be annulled by another. It cannot be maintained that· the
applicant was in fact tried and sentenced by his own Lodge, and that
the o_ther was merely the Instrument to carry out Its will and
purposes. The Lodge to which the case was transferred 6btalne<1
complete jurisdiction to try It, and either to acquit or convict, according to the evidence; and if found guilty to impose a penalty, and It
alone can wipe out the sentence If so disposed.
·
Although we have grave doubts as to whether the framers of our
Constitution ever contemplated the result here reached, viz: that a
subordinate Lodge of which ~he suspended Mason was never a member should have tl).e right to restore him to his Masonic rights simply by reason of the fact that it had adjudged his suspension upon a
transfer of the case from the Lodge to which he belonged. We are
satisfied that under the law as it Is written, there can be no escape
from the conclusion reached by the Grand Master. The framers
of the constitutional provisions in this behalf probably had In mind
only cases of suspension by a Lodge of its own members, and overlooked the contingencies of an absolute transfer of the case from
one Lodge to another, or a proceeding Instituted in some other Lodge
than that of the membership of the accused, by reason ot his residence within the te~ritorial jurisdiction of another Lodge. We,
however, must take the law as it is written, where, as in this case,
it Is plain and unambiguous.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
The Grand Master reported as follows:-

1905.]

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

6. On Mai'ch 5th, 1883, C. D. was suspended from member.ship by
his Lodge for non-payment of dues, He was then owing $36. · On
November 7th, 1904, at a stated meeting, It was reported to his
Lodge that he wished to be restored to membership upon paying
$36 and having his dues since suspension remitted, and on motion it
was unanimously accepted, but no ballot was had thereon. At the
stated meeting on December 'iith, 1904, the minutes of the meeting of
November 7th were read and approved, and upon discussion as to the
validity of the restoration it was resolved to have C. D. sign a
petition tor restoration and to have it lie over for one month, which
was. done. At tlle stated meeting on January 2nd, 1905, the petition
for restoration was rejected by ballot, it failing to receive the support of three-fourths of the members present and on motion the resolution of November 7th, restoring him to membership and accepting
the $36 was rescinded. Upon 'this state of facts it was decided that
the vote taken on .November 7th, restoring him to membership, was
void for two reasohs mainly: First, because the application was not
laid over for one month; and second, because a vote thereon was
not taken by ball-ballot, and that the approval of the minu_tes of
November 7th, at the meeting held on December 6th, 1904, did ·not
affect the matter.
This decision Is in accord with the provisions of Sec. 11, Art. III,
Part III of our Constitution, which requires with the laying over of
the application for one month, and the approval of the application
by a three-fourths vote "by ballot." We recommend that the decision be approved.
The Grand Master decided as follows, viz:6. The daughter of a MasteT Mason 1n good standing when he
died, married to a man who has been a Mason, but dimitted, and who
has been out of standing for many years, and who has attempted
suicide and is sick in a hospital, the wife being destitute, is entitled to consideration at the hands of the Lodge to which her father
belonged at the time of his death. The right to relief depends upon
the fact that she is the daughter of a Master Ma.son, and if worthy
herself she did not forfeit any right by reason of an unfortunate
marriage or the misfortunes of matrimony.
This decision was correct, and should be approved, and we recammend accordingly,

degrees, and it therefore followed as stated by the Grand Master,
that the applicant could obtain the remaining degrees only by petition, reference and ballot in the ordinary way,
We recommend that the decision be approved.

8. While Masonry is not a religious institution and should not
mix up with religious matters, or favor any creed or sect, yet if the
memb'ers of a Lodge or any considerable number of them, see flt
to assemble in the hall, and walk together to church, and attend
service there in a body on Easter Sunday, I do not see that any
h a rm to Masonry can come from It, and know of nothing to prevent
it. No dispensation could be granted to wear regalia on s uch an
occasion.
Of course this decision is correct. We know of no l~w or reguJa'.
tion· of Masonry that precludes two or more Masons from going to
church together, even if they go directly from the hall of the Lodge,
instead of from the house of one of them.

. The Grand Master reported as follows_:12. In August, 1904, a petition for the Degrees was tiled, and at.
the time the petitioner was a resident withm the jurisdiction of the
,Lodge, and in every res~ct eligible to membership. Before the com:mittee could interview him and because of unforeseen circumstances
1le was obliged to remove and change his residence to an Eastern
;State. No report was made by the committee and nearly a year
:after the matter was referred to them, the pet.itioner asked to withdraw his petition and have the money refunded. It seems like a
hardship to deny the request under the circumstances, but I felt
constrained to hold that the application could not be withdrawn.
Section 3 of Article III of Part III of the Constitution provides
that,· "No application shall be withdrawn after reference to committee except as hereinafter provided in this Section." The only
exceptions are that " If the committee find the applicant disqualified
in consequence of insufficient residence or physical disability and
find no other objection to him, they shall make a special report
thereupon in which case the Master may direct the withdrawal of
the application without further action."
This applicant had been a resident within the Jurisdiction of the
Lodge durinf? six months next preceding the date of his application
and was such at the time of applying; therefore his request for
withdrawal did not come within either of the exceptions provided
by the Constitution.
The decision of the Grand Master was correct for the reason
stated by him. The Lodge should, however, proceed to consider the
application just as if the applicant had not left the state. The residence of the applicant at the time of the making of the application
gave the Lodge jurisdiction to proceed. The applicant is entitled to
a determination of the matter. If he be finally rejected, his money
can be returned to him, and if he be elected, the Degree can be conferred upon him by some Lodge in the state to which he bas gone,
at the request of the Lodge electing him.
We recommend that the decision be approved.
The Grand Master reported as follows:
After a petition was received and referred to a committee,
but the day before the stated meeting at which it was to report, a
13.

117

member of the Lodge went to the Master and made a verbal objection
to the candidate. The committee reported favorably, but its report
w11s not permitted to come berore the Lodge.
The Master inquires: "Whether he should order a ballot, or
tihould the objection hold good, and if no oallot is taken, how long a
time should elapse before he should declare the petition rejected?"
The Constitution gives a member an undoubted right to object,
and a fair construction of the provision is, that the objection may
be made at any time after the petition has been received and referrect , provided it be interposed before his initiation. Its language
ls: "No Lodge shall have more than one b;1Jlot for the Degrees;
but, though ari applicant may be elected to receiye them, if, at any
t i me before his initiation, objection be made by any member, he shall
not receive the Degree until such objection shall have been withdrawn," etc. If a member may object and prevent initlatlon after
ele ction, certainly he should have the right and power to do so before
election, and it should be treated in all respects as one interposed afterward, and unless withdrawn would hold good for sixty days from
the time it was made, and finally result in a rejection.
The main point decided by the above is that the objection to
initiation that may be made by a member to the Master, may be made
before as well as after election, and when made before should be
treated as if made subsequent to the election, and unless withdrawn
within sixty days shall constitute a rejection of the candidate. In
this we are disposed to agree with the Grand Master. It may
often happen that one having good and · Jegal reason to prevent the
admission of an applicant may know in advance that he will be
unable to be present at the election and unable to acquaint the
Master with his objection after election and before initiation, and a liberal construction of the Constitutional provision in the interests of Masonry and for the protection of the
craft against unworthy material, would warrant the conclusion that
he should be aHowed to make his objection in advance, so that the
same would assist in the event of a subsequent election of the candi·
date. But when so made we are satisfied, that the objection ought
to be treated solely as one made subsequent to election. The Constitutional provision was plainly intended solely to enable a member
to prevent the initiation of an applicant who had been elected to
receive the Degrees. Its language is "though an applicant may be
elected to receive them, (the Degrees), if, at any ttme before his
initiation, objection be made by any member" etc. It was never intended to interfere with the orderly course prescribed by the Consti- .

tution up to and including the election. The Constitution provides
for the reference <!f an application for the degrees to a committee,
requires that committee to report, and further provides in terms that
"If the report be favorable, a ballot shall be had" (Sec. 3, Art. III,
Part II I). The objectiou to be made by a member to the Master is
available for any purpose only in the event of an election, and cannot ·
bar the report of the committee or the ballot.
We therefore are of the opinion that notwithstanding the objection, the report of the committee should have been received, and a
ballot thereupon had, and if the ballot was favorable, the candidate
should have been declared elected. The objection made by the member should have been treated as effectual only in the event of the
election of the candidate and as dating therefrom, and if the same
was not withdrawn within sixty days thereafter, it would constitute
a rejection.

Investigate his fitness to be a member; the committee reported
1avorably; he was elected and received the First Degree before any
<llscovery was made. It does not appear that he made any fraudulent
1·epresentations either in his petition or to the committee, or did anything to deceive them or the Lodge. While every man seeking to
join a Masonic Lodge should be of sound mind, if the Lodge was
deceived as to his mental condition and desires to get rid of him or
nancel his membership because of his insanity, and this can be done,
he has a right to be heard upon the question, and of course it cannot be tried and determined while he remains insane.
This decision was undoubtedly correct for the reasons stated.
therein, and we recommend that it be approved.

We recommend that the decision of the Grand Master be approved
except in so far as it intimates that the objection made would constitute a rejection if not withdrawn within sixty days from the time
it was actual1y made, and that in so far as it thus intimates it be
modified by making the sixty days commence to run only at the date
of the election.

and on the 21st of the ·same month the Entered Apprentice Degree
was conferred upon him. In December, 1904, he was Indicted for stealing mail matter, and on being arraigned confessed his guilt. The
Federal Judge before whom he was tried found from tile evidence
that he was insane at the time of the 'trial, and that he had been
insane for fourteen months, which period would not only cover the
period when the offense was committed, but would go back to a time
prior to his presenting his petition for membership in the Lodge.
He was committed to a hospital for the insane and is now confined
therein. The question submitted to me was: "Was not the action
of the Lodge in accepting the petition of G. H. irregular and its
proceedings null and void, for the reason that he was found to be
insane?"
My answer was In the negative. In the first place neither he nor
the Lodge is bound by the finding of the Court as to his being
insane at the time he joined the Lodge, or the commission of the
offense, in any .action by the Lodge to cancel his membership because
of his insanity or to try him for a Masonic offense. His petition was
presumably presented in the regular way; a committee appointed to

In . support of the charge, the only testimony that was introduced
that was not hearsay was a certificate of the Master and Secretary
of " Hill's Ferry " Lodge, No. 236, under the seal of the Lodge, that
the accused had lived in t.he neighborhood of Newman, California,
for several months, and while there he was accompanied by a woman
whom he represented to be his wife. Objection w·as made at the
trial to this document. While it was made by Masons, the accused
had no opportunity to ask any questions regarding its contents, and
upon Its admission was concluded by its terms. An ex parte affidavit
is not admissible as evidence. (Anderson's Manual, Decisions 684,
748.) And an ex parte certificate of the Master and Secretary as t<>
facts within their knowledge can have no greater weight, especially
when objection is made to its introduction. If the presence of a witness is not obtainable before a commission, authority is given for
taking his testimony upon giving notice to the accused, which wm
enable him to attend in person, or by counsel, and question the wltr,ess as to his testimony. (Constitution, Part VI, Art. IV, Sec. 5.)
The accused has appealed from the judgment of suspension rendered against him, and we are of the opinion that the action of the
I .odge should be reversed.
