To the M:. w:. GrWN.d Lodge of Oalifornia:
Your committee appointed to consider the matter of the establishment in Lodges of this Jurisdiction of a system of life membership respectfully rePQrt that they have considered the same, and recommend the adoption o! the following General Regulation:
Any Lodge having a Board of Trustees may avail itself of the
benefits of life membership upon the following conditions:
First-At the annual meeting of the Lodge there shall be elected
three Trustees-one to hold office for one year, one to hold office tor
two years, and one to hold office for three years. At each annual
election thereafter one Trustee shall be elected to take the place of
the one whose term ls about to expire. The Trustees first elected,
and every Trustees subsequently elected, before entering upon the
rlischarge of his duties shall execute a bond for the faithful performance of said duties, in such sum and in such security company as the
Lodge may designate. Said bond shall be made payable to the Master of the Lodge, and all expenses incident to the execution of the
bond shall be paid by the Lodge.
Second-'l'he Trustees shall take charge of the Life Membership
Fund, and of all bonds, stocks and permanently invested moneys belonging to the Life Fund. They shall keep said moneys safely invested as directed by the Lodge. They shall from time to time pay
to the Secretary of the Lodge the earnings of all bonds, stocks and
o~her investments, to be paid by the Secretary to the Treasurer of
the Lodge. The Treasurer shall place said earnings to the credit of
the General Fund of the Lodge.
Third- The Trustees shall keep a correct record of tile Life Membership Fund, and of all bonds, stocks, investments and moneys
placed in their charge. They shall keep all invested moneys under
their charge deposited in such reputable savings banks as may be
directed by the Lodge. They shall at the stated meetings in June
and December of each year make a full report in writing of all business transacted by them during the intervening period, together with
ri particular statement of all bonds, stocks, investments and deposits
in their charge belonging to the Lodge.
Fourth-All moneys belonging to the Life Fund and all moneys
received for life memberships shall constitute the principal of said
Life Fund, and shall in no case be withdrawn from said fund except
ty consent of the Grand Lodge, upon a recommendation adopted by

Bro. JoHN D. MURPHY, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following report:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee, to whom was referred the case of FRANK ELMER
GRAHAM, suspended by " Oak Grove" Lodge, No. 215, September 1st,
1905, and from which judgment an appeal was taken by the accused,
have had the same under consideration, and report:
The record shows that the accused, in June, 1899, applied to
Brother L. SIMON for a loan of a considerable sum of money; and,
it appears from the record and the admissions of the accused before
this committee, that the Joan was consummated upon the direct
understanding that the parties were Masons, and that the obligor
pledged his Masonic honor to the liquidation of the indebtedness.
A note was given, payable in ten years, but no payment of either
principal or interest has ever been made. There is some dispute as

1905.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

133

to the terms of the agreement, the accused claiming that in consideration of certain services to be performed for a member of the
accuser's family no interest was to be charged. This is denied, and
it is admitted that no such services were performed; and on this
point it is sufficient to say that the contention of the accused was
determmed adversely to him both by the Trial Commission and also
by a judgment of the Superior Court of this State, which the accused
permitted to be entered by default against him for the full amount
of principal and interest claimed.
The case is not without its difficulties, being on the border line
of that class of legal transactions between brothers regarding their
business aft'.airs, concerning which it has been repeatedly and firmly
beld that Masonic Bodies will not take cognizance unless there is
present the element of fraud, breach of trust, misrepresentation or
bad faith.
In this case, notwithstanding his solemn promises, the record
shows that the accused failed to make any payment whatever during
the life of the note, originally given, or since the obligation has
assumed the sanctity of a judgment. One five dollar payment was
·offered on condition that the accused's theory that no Interest be
charged was agreed to. It ls admitted that the accused has worked
the greater part of the time since the note was given at a rate of
wages which, in the opinion of your committee, was sufficient to
have enabled him to have made substantial payments on his obligation, had he entertained any honest desire to do so.
The record Is bristling with fair promises and good intentions,
but nothing more substantial has materialized; and when, in order
to defeat the running of the Statute of Limitations against his
claim, the accuser was compelled to apply to the courts for a judgment, the accused neglected to offer any defense to the action, but
promptly protected himself by filing a petition in bankruptcy, and in
the opinion of this committee, for the sole purpose of defeating the
possible collection of tbls very claim, to the payment of which he
had pledged his Masonic honor.
Out of liabilities aggregating over $500 less than $101) was represented by claims other than the one under consideration.
We deem it unnecessary to further discuss the facts of the case,
being of the opinion that from all the facts and circumstances the
Subordinate Lodge properly took cognizance of the oft'.ense, and that
the Inhibition of this Grand Lodge against the sentiment of pecuni·
·ary controversies of Its members In the tribunal of the Lodge should
not be used as a shield to avoid the just consequences of dis-

134

[Oct. 13,

honest acUI. We are of the opinion that the action of the Lodge
should be affirmed, and therefore offer the following resolution, and
recommend its adoption:
Resoived, That the action of "Oak Grove" Lodge, No. 215, suspending FRANK ELMER GRAHAM from all the rights and pr! vlleges of
Masonry be and the same Is hereby approved.
All which is respectfully submitted.
JOHN A. HosMER,}
J. D. MURPHY,
Committee.

Bro. ALONZO J. MONROE, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following report:
To the M.'.

w:. Grand Lodge of CaU.fornta:

Your committee, to whom was referred the appealed case of
ARTHUR LEROY PIPER, a Master Mason of "Pacific" Lodge, No. 130,
who was expelled from that Lodge September 1, 1905, for unmasonic
conduct, viz.: deserting his wife and child and refusing to maintain
or support them when in a destitute condition, although importuned
so to do by the Master and other members of his Lodge, have duly
considered the same and report as follows:
We find the proceedings at the trial and the record to be in all
respects regular. No objections were or are now made to the same·
or any part thereof. From the record It appears that the decision
of the Commissioners and vote of expulsion were concurred in by all.
A hearing was had in the matter before the Grievance Committee,
at which time the accused appeared in person, as well as by his.
attorney. "Pacific" Lodge wa~ represented by Bro. F. L. HANSEN,
its Master. The accused was given the fullest opportunity to present his appeal and statements, and argument on his behalf were·
then made by himself and his counsel, and also a · statement by
Bro. HANSEN on behalf of the prosecution .
The record shows some conflict of evidence, but in the main the
facts are admitted.
The principal contentions of the accused were that the punishment was unduly severe; that he had not willfully refused to support his wife and offspring, and that he should be given a chance.
His able couµsel urged with great earnestness that the door of hope

1905. J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOUNI.~.

135

should not be closed against him, that he was trying to redeem his
past, and quoted that "there is a future left for all men ·who have
the virtue to repent and the energy to atone."
It was claimed that accused was out of work and earning nothing,
and for that reason could not provide for his family. And on these
considerations we were asked to recommend in our report the granting of a new trial in this case.
The matter being submitted and duly considered, two questions
on appeal arise, viz.:
Did the evidence justify the conviction of the accused?
2. Was the penalty imposed unduly severe under the circumstances of this case?
1.

As to t he first point, we believe the decision of a Lodge on questions of fact should be affirmed, unless it is very clear that such
decision is not wa.rranted by the evidence.
We find that .the evidence in the record and that taken by this
committee entirely sustain the decision of guilt. Indeed, most of
the facts are undisputed. The accused claims he left his wife a few
minutes after marriage and has not since lived with her.
The marriage occurred about four years ago. She testified that
he lived with her a few months after marriage. He admitted that
when his relations with her commenced she was undeflled, and no
claim is made that there is any shadow on her character, except
through her relations with him. He testifies that the marriage was
to give the child, born four months after his marriage, a name, and
they agreed that they would never live together. This she denies.
She appealed to the Superior Court and obtained an order requiring
him to pay $100 ·per month for her maintenance. Refusing to do
this, he was adjudged guilty of contempt and Imprisoned. Thus
the question of his ability to provide for his wife and offspring was
found against him by the court. While he has paid a comparatively
small sum, his wife and child have been left destitute. She was for
a time In the hospital, and during the year past received the
necessaries of life In part from the Master of " P.aclfic " Lodge. The
accused utterly fail ed to show a good or sufficient excuse for his
neglect.
The desertion and neglect of wife and child is a Masonic offense.
The law imposes the legal duty of providing for wife and offspring. On the threshold of Masonry the novitiate Is taught that
justice Is a cardinal virtue and demands that we render unto every
man his just due.

136

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

[Oct. 13,

The Entered Apprentice is charged to be obedient to his country's
laws and to practice the domestic virtues. The offense here, having
its beginning in an Immoral act which destroyed a young woman's
virtue, and culminating in desertion of her as his wife, allowing her
and their child to live In destitution and bringing himself to be
found guilty of disobedience to the court and lmprlsone.d for contempt, has made him unworthy to sit with Masons and invites the
severest penalty. Nor Is i.t true that the door of hope is closed by
his expulsion.
One of the objects of punishment is to make the accused and
convicted brother see the error of his ways and truly have the
virtue to repent and the energy to atone. The Lodge is ever open
for his reinstatement when he comes back and walks In the path
of truth and honor.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of " Pacific" Lodge, No. 136, in expelling ARTHUR LEROY PIPER from all the rights and privileges of Masonry be and the same is hereby affirmed.
Respectfully submitted.
JOHN A. HOSMER,}
J . D. MuRPHF.Y,
C mmittee.
ALBERT NORRIS,
o
H. J, MoNROE.

M:'. W. '. FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports :
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee has had under consideration the report of the
Grand Master as to his correspondence with the Master of our
"Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, of Honolulu, Territory of Hawaii, relative to the Masonic standing of " Maui " Lodge at Wailuku, H . T.,
a Subordinate Lodge of the Grand Lodge of Scotland. The question
arose because of the desire of a candidate who had been elected to
receive the Degrees In our "Hawallan" Lodge, and who had there

1905.J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOllNIA.

137

received his First Degree, to have the other tw·o Degrees conferred
by "Maul" LodS"e, at the request of and for "Hawaiian" · Lodge.
This, of course, could only be done . In the event that "Maui " Lodge
was a regularly constituted Lodge, lawfully existing in the Hawaiian
Islands.
The sovereignty of the Hawaiian Islands was transferred to the
United States of America on August 12th, 1898, and they have ever
since constituted territory of this country, ·At the time of such
transfer, no Masonic Grand Lodge ever having been organized
therein, there were in such territory two Subordinate Lodges holding charters from our own Grand Lodge: One, "Pacific," holding
a charter from the Grand Lodge of Scotland, and one " La Progress,"
holding a charter from the Supreme Council of France. All of these
Lodges continue to exist therein, holding their allegiance to their
respective Grand Lodges, and no Grand Lodge has ever been organized therein ..
On September 22d, 1904, "Maul" Lodge was granted a charter
or dispensation by the Grand Lodge of Scotland, and has continued
to act thereunder. No question appears to be made as to Its legitimacy and regularity other than the single one raised by the contention that by reason of the fact that the Hawaiian Islands constitute
American territory, nci foreign Grand Lodge, and by " foreign Grand
Lodge" Is meant any Grand Lodge outside of the United States of
America, has now the right to charter any Lodge therein, that we
must regard the establishment of any new Lodge therein by any foreign Grand Lodge as an invasion of the jurisdiction of each of our
American Grand Lodges, and, regarding the Lodge so established as
illegitimate, not allow any Masonic intercourse on the part of the
members of our Lodges with those of the Lodge so established.
It will readily be seen that the question thus pi;esented is a most
important one, but fortunately, in view of the interests involved,
it is not, in our judgment, difficult to determinne.

The Hawaiian Islands have always, by reason or the fact that no
Grand Lodge was ever organized therein, constituted, Masonically,
open territory. By open territory, we mean territory not within the
exclusive territorial jurisdiction of any existing Grand Lodge, and
therefore territory. within which any Grand Lodge may charter
Subordinate Lodges.
It Is elementary Masonic law that a Grand Lodge has not only
an exclusive territorial jurisdiction over the State or country within
which it may ·exist, but also jurisdiction to constitute and maintain

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

LOct. 13~

Lodges in any State or country not included in the territory of any
other Grand Lodge.
We ourselves recognized and enforced this right more than fifty
years ago by chartering" Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, in the Hawaiian
Islands, then foreign territory, and more recently, but prfor to the·
acquisition of that territory by the United States, by chartering
"Kilauea" Lodge, No. 330, in the same territory, and have maintained said Lodges ever since they were so chartered.
Our Constitution to-day provides that the executive powers of
this Grand Lodge include the granting of dispensations and charters
to establish and perpetuate Lodges within this State "and in other
territory where no Grand Lodge exists." (Sec. 3, Art. III, Part I.)
In so providing, we but assert a right always recognized to exist
in any Grand Lodge. It is only when a Grand Lodge attempts to
establish a Lodge within the territorial jurisdiction of another
Grand Lodge, that the establishment of such Lodge constitutes an
invasion of the jurisdiction of any Grand Lodge.
It is not claimed that the Hawaiian Islands were not open Masonic·
territory up to the time of the transfer thereof to the United States·
of America. The only question then, Is as to whether that transfer
brought them within the territorial jurisdiction of any Grand Lodge.
It is plain that it did not. We have no Grand Lodge of the United.
States of America-no body exercising Masonic control over all
territory of the United States. Each State and each Territory with
the exception of one or two, has its own Grand Lodge, exercising
supreme control and having exclusive territorial jur~sdiction within
the limits of said State or Territory. The Hawaiian Islands are
not within the territorial jurisdiction of any Grand Lodge of any of
our States or Territories, and no such Grand Lodge claims exclusive
territorial jurisdiction over them. How, then, can it be contei;i.ded
that the establishment of a Lodge therein by any foreign Grand
Lodge is an Invasion of the jurisdiction of any American Grand
Lodge.
It is suggested that such an act would be an invasion of the jurisdiction of each of the American Grand Lodges, which alone should
have power to charter Lodges on American soil. We have not been
able to ascertain that such a doctrine has ever been asserted by any
American Grand Lodge, and so long as we ma'\ntaln our system of
separate and independent State and Territorial Grand Lodges, such
a doctrine would not appear to be In consonance with well established Masonic principles. Our American Grand Lodges have no
collective territorial jurisdiction.

1905. J

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

139

The regu~ation adopted by the Grand Lodge in 1851, referred to
by the Grand Master, had reference solely to an invasion of the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of New York by the Grand
Lodge of Hamburg, by the establishment of a Lodge within the State
of New York, and cannot be properly construed as having reference
to any territory not within the territorial jurisdiction of some
Grand Lodge. The somewhat broad language there used wa~ modified in May, 1854 (Vol. I, Proc. p, 318), by a resolution stating the
doctrine as follows, viz: "It is the sense of this Grand Lodge that
all persons claiming to hold Masonic Lodges In the United States or
Its Territories, within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of any
State or Territory, without authority from such Grand Lodge, are
Illegal and clandestine."
According to our decision, what Is known as the American doctrine goes no further than this, viz: Only one Grand Lodge shall be
established In any State or Territory. Whenever one ls established
It has the absolute control and government of all Masons and of all
Lodges of the first three Degrees, and no other Grand Lodge or
Grand Body can in any way Interfere with Its jurisdiction by estab11shing new Lodges therein, or even by maintaining those already
established. The territory Is absolutely, exclusively and perpetually
the territ<?rY of the Grand Lodge established over It. From the moment of the organization of the new Grand Lodge, Its jurisdiction
becomes absolute over the entire territory, and all Lodges and all
Masons there must acknowledge it and yield obedience to It and
their allegiance elsewhere ceases. (Vol. X, Proc. pp. 547, 553: 579.
Vol. XII, Proc. p. 112.)
This Is the American doctrine, declared by Mackay, and many if
not all of our Grand Lodges and Is the only American doctrine as
we understand, and It has no application to the case in hand for' the
reason that no Grand Lodge has ever been organized in Hawaiian
Territory.
We are therefore of the opinion that the action of the Grand
Lodge of Scotland In chartering " Maui " Lodge In the Hawaiian
Islands cannot be regarded by us as such an Invasion of the jurisdiction of an.y American Grand Lodge as would warrant us In holding the Lodge to be an Illegal body. If we are correct In this conclusion, there would appear to be no reason why said Lodge could
not under our Constitutional provision, at the request of our Hawaiian Lodge, confer Degrees for " Hawaiian " Lodge upon persons
elected therein to receive such Degrees, provided that the work of
said Lodge in conferring the Degrees is In all material respects the
same as ours.

1905.)

GRAND LoDGE OF CALIFORNIA.

141

We regret that this matter was not brought to our attention in
time to enable us to make a more careful presentation of our view
in regard thereto.
It is so important for the interests of Masonry In the Hawaiian
Islands that a speedy determination of the question be had, that we
have cho.sen to thus hastily express our conclusions, rather than to
let the matter lie over for another- year.
We recommend that this report be adopted as embodying the
view of this Grand Lodge upon the subject under discussion.

The resolution as offered, we are confident, does not cover the
entire subject as contemplated; it is defective; no method is provided for the appointment of the committee, the notification, or the
receipt of and action on the report. If it Is the desire of the Grand
J,odge to adopt a plan whereby the names of the committee shall be
kept secret, then a careful examination of the Constitution and
IJnlform Code of By-Laws should be first made, and all necessary
legislation had to accomplish the purpose. We recommend that the
resolution be 'not adopted, and would propose, without recommendation, the following resolution:

The petition of our "Hawaiian" Lodge, No. 21, _to the effect that
our Grand Lodge use its utmost influence to the end that no . further Masonic Lodges be hereafter established in the Territory of
Hawaii under authority of any foreign jurisdiction, has received our
consideration.
In view of what we have said in our report upon the general subject, just adopted by the Grand Lodge, it is apparent that there is
no way in which we can properly act in the direction desired.

Resolved, That this Grand Lodge is in favor of some action by
which the names of the Committee of Investigation on petition for
<legrees or membership shall be kept secret, and the matter is
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence to report at the next
Annual Communication some legislation on the subject.

In regard to Decision No. 15 of the Grand Master, relative to the
action of the Lodges of Sacramento in the matter of forming a corporation for the management and sale, under contract for perpetual
care, of their cemetery property, your Committee on Jurisprudence has
been unable in the brief time allowed to ascertain the real facts and
give proper consideration to the question presented.
We therefore recommend that consideration of the matter be deferred until the next Annual Communication.
Respectfully submitted.

Your committee have had under consideration the resolution rela"tlve to reports of Committees on Investigation, and report as follows:

Your committee, to whom was referred the report of the Special
Committee on Life Membership, have had the same under consideration, and report as follows:
The report of the committee provides for a scheme for life
membership In the form of a General Regulation. This cannot be
done, as has been heretofore held, the only means of accomplishing
such purpose being by amendment to Section 1 of Article IX of the
Uniform Code of By-Lawe. The plan suggested is, we think, too
complicated, many of the provisions being unnecessary and matters
of policy to be left largely with the individual Lodges.
We therefore recommend that the report of the Special Committee be not adopted.
As has been said before, "the question of life membership has
been before this Grand Lodge many times, and appears to be a
difficult . one to arrange in any satisfactory manner."
·
At the Annual Communication of 1903 a full and exhaustive
report, together with a proposed plan, was presented by this committee. The same was discussed at great length In this Grand
Lodge, with the result that the following resolution was almost
unanimously adopted:
"Resolved, That this Grand Lodge does not approve of life membership in Subordinate Lodges."

It would seem that such action would have settled the question
for some time to come; but at the Annual Communication of 1904

BOARD OF RELIEF.
(a) In all cities where two or more Lodges have concurrent
jurisdiction, there may be a Board of Relief, to be composed of the
Masters of all such Lbdges, or in case of their inability, absence or
declination to serve, then one of the Wardens, or a Representative
to be elected by the members of the Lodge in such manner and at
such times as may be provided by the compact.
( b) Such Boards of Relief shall make such provision as may
be necessary for the temporary care of worthy Masons, members of
Lodges or Jurisdictions outside of the jurisdiction of the Lodges
composing such Board of Relief, as may be in need or distress, and
may be then ·in their respective Jurisdictions, and also afford such
members in need or in distress such permanent care as the Lodge
to which such member may belong may provide for; and shall also
provide such temporary relief for dimitted Masons in good standing
within their respective Jurisdictions, and in need or In distress, as
they may deem necessary, and shall also make provision for the
relief of widows or orphans of such Masons In distress under like
conditions as would be given to the brothers themselves.
Said Boards of Relief shall also provide for proper funeral
services and interment or cremation ·of Masons, members of Lodges
outside of their respective Jurisdictions, and of dlmitted Masons,
and of the deceased widows and orphans of such members, any of
whom may die in their respective Jurisdictions.
( c) The expenses incurre\l by any such Boards of Relief in any
of the matters. provided for in the preceding section shall, except
as to dimitted Masons, be charged against the Lodge to which the
member belongs; and in the event of the inability of any such Lodge
to pay the same, the Grand Lodge under whose jurisdiction su ch
Lodge is chartered shall be r equested to assist such Lodge in the
reimbursement of any such expenses.
( d) For the purposes of defraying the expenses of conducting
such Boards of Relief, said Boards shall have the power to levy upon
the Lodges within their respective Jurisdictions such per capita tax
as may be necessary to pay such expenses and carry out their objects; but such tax shall not exceed in any Masonic year the r ate
or sum of 10 ·cents per month per capita of the members comprising
such Lodges, except by the consent of two-thirds of the Lodges comprising any such Board of Relief, such consent to be given by
majority· vote of the members present at a stated meeting, or a
special meeting called for such purpose.

w:. Bro. CARU:TON C. CASE:, from the Committee on
Charters, presented the following report:
To the M. •• W. •. G;rand Lodge of California:

Your committee, to whom was referred the request of "Hayward" Lodge, No. 226, to change its name to ~hat of "San Mateo"
Lodge, No. 226, have had the same under consideration, and report:
The communication from "Hayward" Lodge to the Grand Lodge
Is as follows: (See letter.)
The printed proceedings of the last Communication of the Grand
Lodge show that " Hayward " Lodge meets on Thursday of or
next succeeding the full moon. The weather bureau department
of San Francisco Informs your committee that the full moon for
October came at 6 o'clock and 3 minutes this morning, hence "Hayward" Lodge could not have legally met In stated meeting last
night, the date of their communication and request to the Grand
Lodge. The communication does not state that the vote to change
the name was taken at a stated meeting, and we are unable to find
the representative of "Hayward" Lodge.

presented to the incoll,!ing Grand Master that " Hayward " Lodge at

same be permitted, and that the name of " Hayward" Lodge, No.
226, be changed to "San Mateo" Lodge, No. 226.
Respectfully submitted.

M.". W.". FRANK M. ANGE:LLoTTI, chair111an of the Committee, presented the following report:
Tp the M.°.

w:. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia:

Your committee reports as follows :
The following proposed General Regulation was referred to us:
Resolved, That the following be adopted by the Grand Lodge of
California, to be known as General Regulation No. 82:
No. 82. No Junior Warden of a Lodge shall be installed until he
shall have produced to the installing officer the certificate of the .
Grand Lecturer or of the Inspector of the district in which his
Lodge is situated, certifying that he has personally examined such
Junior Warden-elect and that he is qualified to give the work and
lecture of the First Degree; and no Senior Warden shall be installed
until he shall have produced a like certificate of his qualification to
give the work and lectures of the First and Second Degrees. Such
certificates shall be sent to the Grand Secretary and filed in his
office.
We find that the pronosed Regulation in no way confiicts with
any constitutional l>rovision, and report it back to the Grand Lodge
without any recommendation as to whether it be adopted or rejected.
As it involves quite a radical change in existing methods, we however, are of the opinion that consideration of the same be deferred to
the next Annual Communication, and recommend accordingly.
Respectfully submitted.
FRANK M. ANGELLOTI'I, )

Past Grand Master, the M:. W.-. CHARLES L. PAT roN, presented
the following : WHEREAS, It is the sense of this Grand Lodge that the intimate relationship which has always existed between it and the entire Masonic world· should
continue in its fullest vigor;
AND WHEREAS, The present system of exchanging Representati\'es with
other Grand Lodges, while accomplishing nothing towards this purpose, seems
by the report of the Committee on Correspondence to commit the Grand
Lodge to views as to Masonic Law and other matters :without the direct action
of the body itself, because many Masons suppose that the report of the Com·
mittee on Correspondence ha~ been adopted by this Grand Lodge
THEREFORE RESOLVED, That the incoming Committee on Jurisprudence·
is requested during the ensuing year to examine into the system of representa.
tion between Grand Lodges, consider the matter carefully, and if any change
be desira~le, the committee is requested to formulate a plan by which the
appointment of Representatives by this Grand Lodge shall be discontinued, and
report the same to the next session of the Grand Lodge for its action.

Which was referred to the incoming Committee on Jurisprudence.

ALABAMA.
413 Lodges.

15,393 Members.
The Grand Lodge of Alabama held its Eighty.fourth Annual Communication In Masonic Temple, Montgomery, commencing December
6, 1904, at 7:30 P. M.,-M.". W." . Robert J . Redden, Grand Master;
R.". VV:. George A. Beauchamp, Grand Secretary. Three hundred
thirty-three Lodges were represented, together with thirty-six other
Grand Jurisdictions. Four Past Grand Masters were in attendance.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master then proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
He alluded to the passage of time and its changes. From the
organization of the Grand Lodge, in 1821, with its seven weak but
hopeful petitioners for a charter, to the more than three hundred
Lo4ges whose representatives were assembled to-day in its E!ghtyfourth Annual Communication.

REPORT ON CORRE~PONDENCE.

5

He had granted dispensations for the forming and opening of
seventeen new Lodges and the reorganization of two old Lodges
during the year.
He placed five corner·stones with the usual Masonic ceremonies,
and dedicated the new Masonic Hall of. "Greeno" Lodge, No. 598.
He had the satisfaction of reporting that no Grand or Paet Grand ·
Officer had been stricken from their official roll during the year
now closing, and he E\Xtended the fraternal sympathy of the Grand
Lodge of Alabama to sister Jurisdictions who were clothed in mourn·
ing for brethren who had been summoned to the Great Beyond.
We note nothing in the decisions of the Grand Master to question,
although the Committee on Jurisprudence object, in one instance, to
his evasion of the local law.
The election of officers being in order, the following Brethren
were choEen to serve for the ensuing year, and with the appointed
Grand Officers were installed by Past Grand Master Russell M. Cunningham, R. ·. VV. ·. Bro. David VV. Mc!ver acting as Master of the
Ceremonies:
M.". w:. Bro. Henry H. Matthews, Grand Master; Ben M. Jacobs,
Deputy Grand Master; Hugh S. D. Mallory, Senior Grand VVarden;
Lawrence H . Lee, Junior Grand Warden; VVilliam H. Dingley, Grand
Treasurer; George A. Beauchamp, Grand Secretary; Charles A.
Allen, Grand Tyler.
The time of Grand Lodge was occupied in the transaction of its
regular routine of business, until the reception of the R epresentatives of other Grand Jurisdictions. The roll was called, and among
the responses we note that of Hon. VVilliam Y. Titcomb, of Anniston,
Representative of California, and Alabama's distinguished Chairman
of Correspondence.
HONORS TO THE MEMORY OF BENJAMIN FRANKLIN.
The following Preamble and Resolutions were submitted by
"Franklin" Lodge, No. 587, and adopted:
" WHEUEAS, The two·hundredth anniversary of Benjamin Franklin's birth occurs on ·the 17th of January, 1906; and
"VVHEREAS, Benjamin Franklin immortalized his name in the
history of the early days of our American colonies as well as in
the advent of Free Masonry therein; and
" WHEREAS, Benjamin Franklin, as a. Brother of the Craft and
as Grand Master, was an honor to the Masonic Fraternity during
his life; therefore, be it
"Resolved, 'l' hat we, the VV. M., VVardens and Brethren of" Franklin" Lodge, No. 587, A. F . & A. M. of Alabama, in regular communl-

11ystem has been most effective for promoting harmony between the
Masonic Jurisdictions of the world by directing the attention of lead·
Ing active Masons to their different construction of fundamental
laws governing the usage and customs of the Craft, controlled, primarily, by a genuine desire, above all else, for a united Masonic sentiment among all Masonic Jurisdictions; and we know, further, from
observation ancl experience, that "!nharmony" has, perhaps, been
caused by the neglect of Representatives who have accepted the
honorable position only to discredit it by neglecting its duties and,
in some cases within our knowledge, by belittling the importance of
the appointment.
We hardly think Grand Master Henderson meant to say that the
Representative system was promotive of "inharmony " ; yet the
action of the Committee on Grand Master's Address, at the ensuing
session, might warrant the assertion; for, in that, although the
subject was not mentiop.ed by the Grand Master, the committee
appointed to segregate and r efer matters mentioned in the address
to the appropriate committees, "volunteered " the following:
" It will be patent to any one who will gfve the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Bodies
proper consideration, that this custom Is as useless as the " appendix
vermi form!s" is to the human body. It seems to us that the custom
must have originated In the desire to decorate members with a mere
title. The only proper way for one Grand Lodge to communicate
with another is through the Grand Masters. Your committee can
see no necessity for the continuance of the custom, and therefore
r ecommend that it be abolished. Many of the Grand Lodges are dispensing therewith, and we think the Grand Lodge of California
should do likewise."
The report was approved, as the committee supposed, and thus
was wiped out the Representative system of this Grand Lodge ; in
other wor ds, it was doing by indirection that which probably could
not have been done directly-a bad kind of legislation. Of course,
t here was a colored gentleman around somewhere, but where was he
housed? We shall probably learn more of the matter at the ensuing
session.

REPORT ON CORRESPON DENCE.

The present report is by Chairman Titcomb, our representative,
and like all his work, is " good and square." He gives us a review
of sixty-one Grand Masonic Bodies, in a great part constituting our
Masonic world.
In his notice of the Grand Lodge of California he quotes from the
address of Grand Master Henderson his recommendation in the
matter of Grand Representatives in the following words :
" T hat the matter of appointing Representatives of the Grand
Lodge residing at or near other Grand Lodges, be abolished, as
all business is transacted between the. Grand Masters or other
Gr and Officers in t hese days. It is a useless, cumbersome custom,
and promotive of inharmony."
And Comp. Titcomb requests us to enlighten him, as set forth in
the following enquiry :
"How the custom is ' promotive of inha rmony,' we signally fail
to discover. Brother Davies, please enlighten us on that point. Is
it to be expected that other Grand Lodges will contin'ue to accredit
Representa tives to the Gra nd Lodge of California after being informed that the latter has abolished the system so far as she is
concerned ? This matter touches us in a t ender spot, for, doubtless,
it will be inc:umbent on us to sur render a commission we have
been proud to hold, as emanating from so great and influential a
Jurisdiction as that of California. For the recommendation was
concurred in."
As to wherein the appointment of Representatives is "promotive
of inharmony,'' Bro. Titcomb, we can only give you the dull schoolboy's answer-" Please, sir, we don't know." On the contrary, we
do believe and have the experience of mor e tha n ha lf a century of
active Masoni c life to back up the assertion, that the Representative

ARIZONA.

of the J urisdiction represented by him, the earnest wishes of the
Grand Lodge of Arizona for the continuance of the present healthy
and prosperous condition of Freemasonry at home and abroad.

19 Lodges.

1,191 Members.
The Grand Lodge of Arizona held its Twenty-third Annual Communication in Tucson, commencing on the 15th day of November,
1904, at 10 o'clock A. M.,-the M.'. W.'. James Sommerville Cromb,
Grand Master; the V. ·. W. ·. George James Roskruge, Grand Secretary. Sixteen Lodges were represented, together with twenty-seven
other Grand Jurisdictions.
Ten Past Grand Masters were in attendance. An excellent portrait
of the retiring Grand Master appears on the opening page.
The Grand Master named the regular and filled the vacancies in
the standing committees, and proceeded to deliver his Annual
Address. He opened with thanks to the Great Creator for the
privilege ·of the present meeting, and a cordial welcome to the
assembled Representatives of the Craft in Arizona.
Referring to roll call he noted the absence of familiar names
of Brethren who had served with them during the early years of
their organization, but whose kindly faces would greet them no
more in Grand Lodge. He reported the names of twenty of their
own tribes and families who had passed to rest, and he recommended that the necessary pages in the journal of the year be devoted to their remembrance in connection ·With the · many eminent
Brethren of sister Jurisdictions who had been stricken from the
rolls of the living during the past year.
In mentioning their relations with other Jurisdictions, he reported all apprehended difficulty with the Grand Lodge "vane de
Mexico," as settled to the satisfaction of all parties. Of the condition of their own organization, he said:
"Nearly all the Lodges are in a strong, healthy condition-our
net gain for the year being sixty-eight."
Among his recommendations was the prohibition by Grand Lodge
of the use of intoxicants at Lodge banquets. He closed with good
words for Bro. Roskruge whom he earnestly recommended to the
mercy of the Grand Lodge.
The report of the Grand Secretary was, as usual, full and comprehensive.
A charter was granted " Mount Moriah " Lodge, U. D., and numbered 19 upon the Grand Lodge· registry.
The Representatives of other Grand Jurisdictions were introduced by W. ·. Frederick G. Brecht, Representative of Colorado, and
greeted by the Grand Master who extended to them a hearty welcome with the request that each would convey to the Grand Master

Appropriate response was made. by Bro. Fletcher M. Doan, the
Representative of the Grand Lodge of Egypt.
Bro. Francis A. Shaw, P. G. M. and Chairman of the Committee
on Necrology, made an eloquent and feeling report devoted to the
loss of Friends and Brethren, which was adopted.
Chairman Goldwater, of the Committee on Jurisprudence, re·
ported on the recommendation of the Grand Master concerning the
use of intoxicants at banquets, as follows:
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred that
portion of the Grand Master's Address, recommending 'that action
be taken prohibiting the use of intoxicating liquors at Lodge banquets,' begs to report that it has given the matter careful consideration. It can find no ·indication that the Masons of Arizona
are unable to control their appetites, and does not bel!eve that the
use of intoxicants by the Brethren ls of an alarming nature.
" It is the duty of each Master to guard his Lodge, and if any
member thereof conducts himself in such a manner as to reflect un·
favorably upon the Fraternity, the Master should admonish him of
his errors, and, if unable to bring about a reformation, the offend·
ing Brother should be disciplined by the Lodge.
"Masonry is not a prohibition society, nor is it its province to
reform the world. Temperance is defined by us as a domestic and
public virtue, whereby we are taught to avoid excess; but one may
be intemperate in his views on the 'liquor question ' as well as in
other ~ays.
"Your committee commends th~ motives of the Most Worshipful
Grand Master, but finds no reason at this time for any action by
this Grand Lodge."
The report was adopted.
The Finance Committee recommended the discontinuance of the
appropriation for the publication of the Report on Correspondence,
which was concurred in.
The election of officers being in order, tellers were appointed,
and the M.·. W. ·. George Shand, of Tucson, was chosen Grand
Master, and the V.'. W.'. George James Roskruge was re·elected
Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master, having made his appointments, all were installed by the Grand Master, Past Grand Master Martin W. Kales
acting as Master of the Ceremonies.

11

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

.REPORT ON ConRE.SPONDESCE .

Thanks were extended to the members of Tucson Lodge and the
citizens generally for their courtesy and hospitality, to the officers
and members of "Tucson " Lodge, No. 4, for their excellent exemplification of the work before Grand Lodge, and to the several railroad
companies for excellent service and kind attention.
Th.:i ritiring Grand Master was presented with a Past Grand
Master's gavel, which brought from· him a few eloquent and ·appreciative remarks.
The Grand Master appointed the standing committees, and the
Grand Lodge was closed in Ample Form.

in accordance with Ancient Masonic Usage, including a stirring
oration by Bro. Hugh A. Dinsmore, Grand Orator.
The Grand Master named the committees and then proceeded to
deliver his Annual Address. After a few words of cordial greeting,
he gave the Grand Commandery the following elP.gant salutation:
"The year now fast drawing to a close is one of unusual historic
Importance. While the spirit of thanksgiving and praise has been
manifest throughout that vast portion of our national domain over
which, a century age, waved the flag of the Castilian, and has found
expression in the most magnificent display of art, science and industrial development ever conceived by mortal mind, our own Grand
Jurisdiction has kept pace with the times, and the Year of Light
5904 has become the first of a new period when Arkansas Masons
enter new fields of labor, and strive for higher achievements. It is
in this good year 5904 that the Grand Lodge of Arkansas is lifted
from the thralldom of debt. It has been reserved for you, my
Brethren, constituting the Sixty-second Grand Lodge of Arkansas,
to look with mingled feelings of pride and praise upon this magnificent Temple, and realize that it is your very own. With what
measure of wisdom and success it shall be utilized, let the deliberations and decisions of your present meeting bear witness."
He reported the placing of thirteen corner-stones of public school,
church and county buildings.
The decisions of the Grand Master were approved by the Committee on Law and Usage, most of them being determined by the
iocal law.
Past Grand Master George A. Donnelly, being prevented by age
and infirmity from meeting his Brethren at the present session,
Grand Lodge, by telegraph expressed sincere regret at his enforced
absence, and extended its profound sympathy with him in his
affliction.
Grand Secretary Hempstead submitted his usual full and comprehensive report-in fact, a complete history of the finan cial condition
ancl prospects of the Grand Lodge. He says, speaking for the Board
of Control, that as a result of the heroic plan for the improvement of
Grand Lodge finances: "The wisdom of the biennial sessions ls
manifest, and demonstrated by the fact that we are to-day free of
debt, with a surplus in hand for the first time since the erection
of the Temple, and the prospect for the future seems very bright
indeed to your Board."
The Grand Orator. R.". W.'. Bro. F. 0. Butt, delivered an impressive oration for which he received the thanks of Grand
Lodge, and it was ordered published in the journal of proceedings.

REPORT O.N COURESPO:'<DENCE.

Bro. Charles D. Belden, Chairman, submits an elaborate report
in which he r eviews the proceedings of sixty-two Grand Jurisdic-.
tions in a paper 'o f 254 pages, but through some combination of
circumstances, the California journal failed to reach his temporary
workshop in Pittsburg. We think Bro. Belden was fortunate in
being denied the privilege of extending his report another page.
George Shand, Grand Master; George James Roskruge, Grand
Secretary.

The Grand Lodge of Canada held an Especial Communication in
the village of Auburn, May 30, 1904, for the purpose of placing the
corner-stone of the Knox Presbyterian Church in that village.-The
M.'. W.'. Bro. J. E . Harding, Grand Master, presiding ; the M.' . W.'.
Bro. Hugh Murray, Grand Secretary.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form.
The ceremonies were performed in accordance with ancient
usage and ceremony. The stone was inscribed:
'l'his Corner-stone of Knox Presbyterian Church was
laid by M. ·. W. ·. Bro. J. E. Harding, K. C., Grand Master,
assisted by the Grand Officers, in the presence of a large
t·oncourse of inhabitants of the Village of Auburn.
Thos. Straughan, W. T. Ridell, John Fingland-Trustees.
The Acting Grand Secretary then deposited the scroll in the
cavity of the stone, t ogether with a box containing certain newspapers, records a nd coins.
The Grand Wardens and the Deputy Grand Master applied the
implements of their office to t he stone after it had been placed in
position, and announced that the Craftsmen had done their duty.
The Grand Master then consecrated the stone with corn, wine and
oil, and pronounced it well made, truly laid, well proved, t rue and
trusty.
The Grand Master then gave a short address, and the procession
was reformed, the Brethren returned to the Hall, and Grand Lodge
was closed in Ample Form.

The Forty-ninth 'Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Canada, in the Province of Ontario, was held in the town of Rockville, commencing on the 20th day of July, 1904,-the M.". W.". J. E .
. Harding, Grand Master, on the Throne; R.". W.". Bro. Benjamin
Allen, Deputy Grand Master; M.". W.". Bro. Hugh Murray, Grand
Secretary. Three hundred thirty-five Lodges were represented, together with thirty other Grand Jurisdictions-California by V.". W.".
G. S. Rynerson, M. D.
Nine Past Grand Masters, twenty District Deputy Grand Masters,
and a large number of Past Grand Wardens, Chaplains, Registrars,
Organists and Stewards, with many visitors, were in attendance.
Many letters and telegrams of regret for non-attendance were
received and read by the Grand Secretary.
The Mayor and officers of the Town Council were introduced
and welcomed the Grand Lodge to Brockvllle, as did also a deputation from the Masters and Past Masters of the Brockville Lodges.
A fine steel-engraved portrait of the Grand Master-elect, M...". W.".
Benjamin Allen, ornaments the present number of the Journal.
The Grand Lodge was then opened in Ample Form with prayer
by the Grand Chaplain. The Committee on Credentials reported,
and the Grand Master proceeded to deliver his Address. We excerpt
the opening lines of his Address because the admonition is applicable
to every Grand Lodge on our National Roster. He said:
" I greet you and welcome you to the good town of Brockville,
and to the Forty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Canada, in the Province of Ontario. Let each Brother present
feel the full responsibility of his position as a Representative, and
whilst he is renewing old associations and making new acquaintances,' let him not forget the claims of duty, but attend the sessions
of Grand Lodge and assist in the management of the Craft and in
legislating for the 32,000 Craftsmen of this Grand Lodge. It is essential for him to remember that the Brethren of his Lodge expect
him to give his attention to this, rather than to spend the term of
Grand Lodge in having what is popularly termed " the time of his
life."
The Grand Master reported the placing of the corner-stones
already referred to, his 'visitations, dispensations issued, and the

ftnancial condition of the Grand Lodge. Of the Fraternal Dead,
he said:
"The Craft in this and the sister Grand Lodges have been called
upon to mourn the removal of many useful and eminent Brethren
whose loss will long be felt. Full particulars will be found in the
Report of the Committee on the Fraternal Dead."
The Deputy Grand Master, in reporting the condition of the Jurisoliction in connection with an account of his visitations, refers to his
Neighbors on the other side of the river-the Grand Lodge of New
York-in these words:
"In conjunction with the Most Worshipful Grand Master and
Senator Gibson, I had the honor of being the guest of M. ·. W. ·. Bro.
W. A. Sntherland, P. G. M. of the Grand Lodge of New York, and
Hon. P. G. Master, of this Grand Lodge, in the city of Rochester, on
November 6th, when the ceremony of dedicating the Masonic Temple was conducted by the Most Worshipful the Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of New York, and his officers. I desire to express my
thanks to M. ·. W. ·. Bro. Sutherland for his princely hospitality,
and also to the Brethren of Rochester for their kind reception of ns,
as well as to the quartette for their beautiful rendition of our
National anthem, ' The Maple Leaf.' And by no means the least
interesting part of the Deputy Grand Master's Report Is the following: "By no means the least pleasant visit made by me outside
the Jurisdiction was that to 'Holland' Lodge, No. 8, in the city of
New York, on May 10th, when I was received and welcomed by ·w:.
Bro. Freeman and his officers and members. The work of the Second
Degree was the best I have ever seen in any Lodge in the United
States. The toast of the Grand Lodge of Canada and its Deputy
Grand Master was enthusiastically received, and what pleased me
most was the honor done to our Most Gracious Sovereign, His Imperial Majesty Edward VII, the Brethren of 'Holland' Lodge singing 'God Save the King' twice. I trust the spirit of brotherhood
which has done so much to bind together the two great nations
on this continent may be still more in evidence as the years roll
by, and that peace and harmony may reign until time shall be
no more.''
The foregoing interests us and for another reason: We
think it was in May; at any rate It was at the annual meeting of the Grand Lodge of New York in 1850, at
which the M.". W.". Oscar Coles was chosen Grand Master, we were a
delegate looking for a charter for "Little Falls" Lodge, numbered,
we think, 386, under the old dispensation " before the war.'' Doctor
James W. Powell, Grand Secretary, took us in charge and in his

He opened with a glowing tribute to Freemasonry and the pleasure and satisfaction of its votaries derived from the observance of
its anniversaries, and h e ornamented his tribute with a glowing
eulogy of the land of all lands, Fair Virgin Colorado, than which,
the Grand Master says: "No fairer land lifts its faC'e to kindly
skies."
Under Necrology, he paid affectionate tribute to his late friend
a nd co-worker, Deputy Grand Master Cooper. He also reported the

Armstrong.

Colorado to sister Jurisdictions in mourning for the unusual number
of Frlencts and Brethren called home during the year.
He reported the Constitution of three new Lodges during the
year, and issued his Dispensations for the forming and opening of
four new L&dges at Steamboat Springs, at Fort Lupton, at Fruita
and at Lyons.
His reported decisions refer only to the construction of the law
of Colorado, and were approved by the Committee on Jurisprudence.

COSTA RICA.
190 Members.
6 Lodges.
Our latest return from the Grand Lodge of ·costa Rica is of the
special Communications of January and February, 1904,-John l\'L
-Keith, M. ·. W. ·. Grand Master.
The most interesting event of the year was the effecting of a
reconciliation between the Grand Lodge and the Supreme Council
of Central America (Guatemala). This is the body from which the
Charters of the Lodges which organized the Grand Lodge of Costa
Rica were originally received. We have reported before the protest
of the Supreme Council.
Matters were brought to a crisis by the chartering by the Supreme Council of another Lodge in Costa Rica. The Grand Lodge
of Costa Rica promptly declared this Lodge and its members "clandestine." Negotiations were at once opened between the Grand
Lodge and the Supreme Council resulting in the recognition by the
Supreme Council of the Grand Lodge of Costa Rica and the interchange of Grand Representatives. This removes all apparent local
antagonism and cause of friction. The newly chartered Lodge will
probably apply for a new Charter from Costa Rica.
During the year the Grand Lodges of Alabama and the District
of Columbia extended fraternal recognition. At one of the Quarterlies our Grand Representative, Bro. Cipriano Soto, presented his
credentials and was cordially received. At the Annual he was
elected Grand Senior Warden, although he was not present. We
noticed that he was also absent at the adjourned meeting when the
Grand Officers were installed, whereupon the office was declared
vacant.
Next Annual at San Jose, January 27, 1905.
Gustavo Pradilla H., elected Grand Master; Edmund A. Osborne,
P. 0. Box 429, San Jose, re-elected Grand Secretary.

We have received the "Anuario" for 1903-04. Quarterly sessions

Brethren, a 'gain of 204 over last year.
·
By a circular of April 20, 1904, the Grand Lodge of Cuba an- .
nounced to the Masonic World that, at the instigation of the Grand
Lodge of Louisiana, it had its Annual session in the preceding
month resolved to suspend relations with the Grand Orient de
France for the reason that this body had violated the Ancient
Landmarks of the Craft in not demanding a profession of faith in a
Supreme Being from its candidates.
The Grand Master's address at the Annual Communication foreshauowed this action. He told the Cuban Craft in substance either
to eultivate the friendship of America and English Grand Lodges
which are as bodies opposed to the Grand Orient de France, or to give
up relations with these bodies and seek closer connection with France
and the Franco-Spanish Masonic influences. At that time !<'ranee
and Cuba still exchanged mutual Representatives. He clteu the
action of a deputy in the Cortes of Spain, Grand Master of a French
Grand Orient in Sp::iin, who participated in a debate on the conflicts
between Masons ~.nd the Catholic Church. In closing this portion
of his remarks Bro. Pellon said:
"If as is done in Cuba in Anglo:saxon countries and in others
that i~itate them, Mason~ would limit their efforts to the attainment of ideal morality and human perfection, we should not see
the strange spectacle of a minister, who years ago proposed reforms
for the colonies, declaring in the Cortes of Spain that the Masons
and not the friars were the cause of the insurrection in the Philippines."
Among the decisions made by the Grand Master the following are
of interest:
A person having only one hand cannot be initiated.
No Lodge can refuse admission to a visiting Brother in good
standing.
The son of a Mason cannot become a candidate for initiation
until he has reached the age of twenty-one years.

by warrant, or reorganized during the year. An exchange of Repre-

The following interesting record of recent events in Queensland
was submitted by the V.' . W.'. John Strachan, Grand Registrar:
V.'. W.'. Bro. John Strachan. K. C., Grand Registra r , said : Most
Worshipful Grand Master i n the Chair, by command of His Royal
Highness, the Grand Master, I have the honor to report to Grand
Lodge with reference to certain Masonic events in the State of
Queensland. As is probably known to all here, the Grand Lodges
of England, Ireland unrl Scotland have equal, though independent,
Masoni.c jurisdiction in certain colonies of the Empire, and in other
territories, including India; and it having been represented to the
Grand Mastet of England that some uniformity of practice with regard to certain matters should prevail, His Royal Highness some
months ago communicated with the Grand Masters of Ireland and
Sr otland, in order that joint a ction might be taken respecting- .
(1) The recognition in each jurisdiction of the decrees of
suspension, exclusion, or expulsion, pronounced respectively by
the Masonic authorities of the other Jurisdictions when acting
judicially;
( 2) The status in each such Jurisdiction of Worshipful
Masters and Past Masters of the ot her Jurisdi ctions or Constitutions, and their eligibility in certain events to take t he Chair;
( 3) The recognition of new Grand Lodges, where there are
Lodges under the several Constitutions in the colony or territory
of the proposed new Grand Lodge.
Before any joint understanding coulcl be arrived at, events had
moved with singular rapidity in Queens land, where there has been
for many years a number of Lodges, formed respectively into a
District Grand Lodge under the Grand Lodge of England, a Provincial Grand Lodge under the Grand Lodge of Ireland, and a Dl,strict
Oran<! Lodge under the Grand Lodge of Scotland. About a year ago,
th e Provincial Grand Master under the Irish Constitution addressed

32

REPORT ON ConHESPONDENCE.

HEPORT oN CoRRESPONDEr;cE.

a letter to the M.'. W.'. Grand Master of Ireland, announcing that
·' there is a determination to establish a Sovereign Grand Lodge of
Queensland, no matter at what cost," and, forthwith, overtures were
made to the English and Scottish Lodges to join the movement.
Our District Grand Master (the Hon. Augustus C. Gregory, C. M. G.)
thereupon caused a circular to be issued to all Lodges under his
l·are, pointing out what steps were necessary, under Rule 218A, for
obtaining a dispensation to hold a meeting at which the question
l'Ould be considered. But so far, I believe, there has been no desire
expressed on the part of the English Lodges to join in the movement or even to discuss the question. In April, of this year, however,
certain Brethren of the other Constitutions met and resolved to
form a Grand Lodge of Queensland; but the value of such a resolution may be properly estimated when we find that out of the 152
Lodges in Queensland, only thirty-nine identified themselves with
the movement, leaving 113 which decline to do so. Of the twentysix Irish Lodges, twenty-five were in favor, and one against; of the
sixty-four Scottish Lodges, fourteen were in favor, and fifty against;
while, of the sixty-two English Lodges, not one was in favor. Thus,
the English District Gi·and Lodge remains intact, with its sixty-two
Lodges; the Scottish District Grand Lodge remains with fifty Lodges,
while fourteen have apparently allied themselves with the twentyfive Irish Lodges, to constitute an irregular assembly of about onefourth of the total Lodges in the State. This minority has sent out
to the several Granil Lodges of the world a circular letter claiming
recognition rn the following words: "The action taken by the
Brethren in this State will, ·it is trusted, be approved by your Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge, and I am instructed to respectfully request
Fraternal recognition and co-operation for the Grand Lodge of
Queensland, in the full hope and confidence that such recognition
wlll be cordially and promptly given, thus tending to insure to this
Grand Lodge sole jurisdiction within the territory." The application
having been carefully considered by the Most Worshipful Grand Master of England and his Masonic Advisers, I am commanded to Intimate that His Royal Highness does not propose to ask Grand Lodge
to acknowledge the so-called Grand Lodge of Queensland. It only
remains, therefore, for me to move the following resolution :
The Most Worshipful Grand Master, having received a communication from the secretary of a body in Brisbane styling
itself "The Grand Lodge of Queensland," requesting recognition
of such body as having sole Masonic jurisdiction within that
territory, and His Royal Highness having intimated that he
does not propose to ask Grand Lodge to accord such recognition,

33

it is hereby RESOLVED, That the United Grand Lodge of England
refuses to acknowledge the aforesaid body in Brisbane as a
Grand Lod~e, or as having any Masonic jurisdiction in the State
of Queensland.

l~aplain, and Acting Deputy Gra~d Master, seconded the resolution,
which was carried unanimously.

Lodges dining at Freemasons' Tavern, to provide th eir own wines,
paying a corkage in respect of what was consumed. The Board
has received from Spiers and Pond an intimation that the company

the Holborn and Frascati.
Both .J. Lyons & Co. and Bro. Oddenino have expressed a desire
to become tenants of the property, and have intimated their readiness to meet the wishes of the Board in regard to the purchase of
wines and the payment of corkage.
It ls estimated that in order to meet the reasonable requirements
of the Craft an expenditure of probably not less than £30,000 would
be necessary on the reconstruction and decoration of the Tavern ;
and, in view of that expenditure by Grand Lodge, Lyons & Co., Ltd.,
are prepared to take a lease of the property for fourteen years from
Michaelmas. 190G. at t he rental of £3,000 a year.
The Board. in vjew of the fact that the rent offered by Lyons &

Tavern, a snm not exceeding £30,000, and to enter Into such agreements with Lrons & Co. and other necessary parties as may be

their souls gone to their eternal abiding place. Over their graves
Jet us keep the acacia green and, while we treasure their memory in
our hearts, let us hope that we may all meet again and partake of
a blessed Immortality that will never end.
"What is the existence of man's l!fe
But open war or slumbered strife?
Where sickness to his sense presents
The combat of the elements;
And never feels a perfect peace
Till Death's cold hand signs his release."

A handsome photogravure of the Georgia Masonic Home, located,
we presume, at Macon, is noticed on the opening page.

No reporter can do justice to the eloquent words of the Grand
Master of Georgia, but by excerpting his sentences as he uttered
them. We. therefore, devote a page to the opening of his Annual
Address, that his well-chosen words may be preserved in our Hbrarv
to be drawn upon when " living words a r e needed ":
" MY BHE'l'IInEN : In far off Eastern lands, where the crescent or
Mahomet is the emblem of his followers, It is the custom, at stated
intervals, to call the faithful to prayer.
" From the time when th e sun in splendor rises in the East, to the
hour when it sinks to rest behind a sea of gold, the Muezzin calls five
times to the followers of the prophet to lift up their hearts In prayer.
And whenever that sonnd Is heard, the faithful believer, wherever he
may be, in mosque or mart, with his face toward the East, prostrates
himself upon the ground , and exclaims: •Great Is Allah! Great is
Allah! ' Followers of a false prophet they are; but the custom is a
noble and an Inspiring one.

HEPORT 0N CORRESPONDENCE.

"In the Talmud is found a beautiful legend, relating how God
selected an angel-Sandalphon-to stand at the outermost gates of
the Celestial City, listening to the prayers that ascend t.o the Throne
of Grace. And as he stood thus, he gathered the prayers and changed
them into beautiful flowers, ancl the fragrance they shed was wafted
through the streets of the City Immortal, until It reached the very
throne of God.
"Masonry, founded, as it Is, upon the Book of books, the Holy
Bible, inculcates and enforces the duty of prayer. On bended knee,
with our faces turned toward the East-the source of light and glory
-we are taught to hold communion with Him, the Architect Supreme; who holds the universe in the hollow of His hand.
"Pr~yer is indeed the golden link that binds the creature to his
Creator; that rolls away the bu.rdens of the soul; that uplifts the
spirit; that changes the gloom and darkness of despair into the glory .
and splendor of an uudying faith.
" Men may revile us, tyrants may persecute us, bnt while Masonry
stands upon the mighty rock of prayer, neither powers nor principalities nor the hosts of darkness shall prevail against her.
"And so to·day, "with prayer and praise upon onr lips, with deep
t)lanksgivlng in our hearts, we enter upon the duties of this, our One
Hundred and Eighteenth Annual Communication. Never before in
all her splendid history has Masonry enjoyed snch abounding prosperity as during the year just past. A substantial inC'rease in numbers; peace and harmony prevailing; the moral standard raised
high; a full treasury; many new Lodges instituted; and, above all,
the Home. for which we have labored so long and so earnestly, fully
completeu, and soon to open its hospitable doors to the worthy wards
of Georgia Masoury. Surely our hearts shonld glow with fervent
gratitude to the God of our fathers who has showered so bonntifully
npon us His rlrhest blessings and His choicest benedictions."
. Directing their attention to absent Brethren who had long been
wlth them in the goou work of re-bulllling the city and house of the
Lord, he paid a most eloquent tribute to the lives and characters
of Comp. Wm. A. Graham and Charles Wessolowsky, Past Grand
High Priests of the Grand Chapter of Georgia, and to the many
"bright lights" which have been extinguished in other Jurisdictions.
He said : "We can but offer the consolation of our deepest and
sincerest sympathy."
At the close of his presentation of the financial condition of the
Jurisdi ction, he says : "Once more I must congratulate the Grand
Lodge upon the splendid condition of its finances, and at the same

time again urge that at the pr.esent Communication we shoul{l be
very careful with our appropriations, in view of the maintenance
of the Masonic Home, which we all regard as the pride an·d glory
of Georgia Masonry."

39

The Grand Master had a busy year. Besides the three dispensations for the forming and opening of new Lodges, he issued one hundred and fifty for the placing of corner-stones and all other purposes.
£Tnder the bead of Decisions, he said:
"During the past year I have received not less than two thousand
letters containing inquiries as to Masonk law and usage. I have endeavored to reply to this vast correspondence promptly and in detail,
a lthough with but very few exceptions, the questions propounded
were fully covered by the Masonic Code."
As his decisions were approved by the able Committee on Jurispruden ce, we have no romment to make. He made many visitations• in fa,ct, all that time and his other duties would permit. Before
closing his address " under personal," he said:
"Standing within this sacred temple and In this august presence,
I here consecrate myself anew to the cause of Masonry and humanity, to the service of God, to the welfare and happiness of my beloved Brethren. In the words of the sweet Moabitess of old, I declare
to you with all my heart and all my strength,.' Entreat me not to
leave thee or to return from following after thee ; for whither thou
goest I will go, and where thou lodgest I will lodge. Thy people
shall be my people, and thy God my God. Where thou dlest will I
die. and there will I be burled. The Lord do so to me, and more
also, if aught but death part thee and me'."
The Grand Master appointed the committees, and Grand Lodge
was " called off " to prepare for the dedication of the Home.
At the appointed. hour Grand Lodge assembled in front of the
Temple,, where conveyances were in waiting to convey officers and
members to the building site. It goes without saying that on this
occasion "there was music in the air," and eloquence was at a discount. With Grand Master Meyerhardt, Past Grand Masters w. A.
Davis, James W . Taylor, Grand Wardens Henry Banks and George
M. Napier, and Deputy Grand Master Thomas H. Jeff~ies on the
rostrum, there was certainly no room for ordinary talk.
The Gra.nd Lodge was "called on " for the •resumption of its
routine business at 7:30 I'. M., when matters concerning the Home,
the reports of the several committees a nd the introduction of new
hnsiness was considered.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Past Grand Master Joseph Robbins submits another of his
brilliant reports furnlsJ:iing to the enquiring Masons the condition
of the Ma.sonic World in a paper ·of three hundred and twenty-five
pages. It goes without saying that Bro. Robbins Is to-day easily at
the head of the class whose bu.slness it is to gather In and comment
upon the transaction of Masonic bodies, " wheresoever dispersed
around the globe." His knowledge of the organization of the Ancient
Craft and from " whence they came." In short he Is a correspondent
fit to represent the great big Jurisdiction he honors with his pen.
He notices California during the administration of Grand Master
Henderson; he followed closely ~he business transacted at the session and never hesitates .to notice a departure from ancient usage
and customs. He notes the suggestion of our Grand Lecturer concerning " The Sprig of Acacia " In connection with the burial service
and comments as follows:
"And as to the Sprig of Acacia, when the Master t3,kes it in his
hand, and after the Master has recited that portion of the service
already prescribed, let him say, placing the evergreen upon his left
breast, • we cherish· his memory here,' then raising it upwards, 'we
commend his spirit to God,' and then dropping the sprig into the
grave, •and his body to the earth.' The Brethren should follow
the Master In these movements, except that when he deposits the
evergreen into the grave they should simply let their hand fall by
their side. Then let the Marshal form the Brethren in procession
and march slowly one by one past the head of the grave, and when
there arrived, let each in depositing bis evergreen first press it to
bis left breast, then point it upward and lastly deposit it in the
grave. The adoption of these suggestions would in my opinion
add much to the solemnity and impressiveness of the occasion.
And Bro. Robbins comments :
"This is very pretty, and it caught the favor of the Grand Lodge
and was adopted. To our mind, however, it is open to the fatal
objection that it merges into one two distinct ·ceremonies each of
which bas existed by its own right ever since the Masonic burial service had an existence. If the grand honors are to be retained as a
feature of the· ceremonies, they should not be anticipated on the one

REPOUT ON Comu;;sPoNDEKCE.

4·9

hand, or diluted by repetition on the other. It is true that the
burial servlc_e as a whole, as It is variously given to different Juris(1ictions, is a thing of shreds and patches-bearing too often the
impress of minds ambitious of Immortality for their gushing rhetoric, getting further with each addition from the terse simplicity of
:Masonry, but through all these mutations has survived a framework
of distinct! ve features which cannot be spared without destroying
its Identity.''

The Grand Lodge of Indiana held Its Eighty-fourth Annual Communication in the City of Indianapolis, May 23d, 1905, commencing
at 10 o'clock A. M.,-M.'. W.'. George E. Grimes, Grand Master; R.'.
W.'. Calvin W. Prather, Grand Secretary. Five hundred and seventeen Lodges were represented.
Past Grand Master Henry S. Orme of Los Angeles represents the
Grand Lodge of Indiana near the Grand Lodge of California. Our
Representative near Indiana, Past Grand Frank S. Devol, was not
present. Fifteen Past Grand Masters were In attendance.
A fine portrait of Grand Master Alfred W. Emery graces this
number of the Journal.
Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by foe
W. ·. Henry C. Weston, Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master named the committees and pr0ceeded t,o deliver his Annual Address.
He commenceci· his Address by congratulating the Brethren upon
the full representation present to honor the eighty-fourth Anniversary of the Grand Lodge of Indiana, he said: "One needs but
to glance at your beaming countenances and witness the hearty
greetings of the Brethren as they meet each other face to face, hand
to hand, heart to heart, hearts that beat In unison In a common
cause and a Brother's welfare to know that Brotherly love prevails.''
He said the past year had been a busy one,-" prosperity, peace and
harmony pr!\vaillng." But amid the sunshine and rejoicing there

REPOR'r ON ComtlSPONDENOE.

The Grand Master-elect made his appointments and all were
installed, but according to Bro. Murrow the work was not finished
in "Ample Form." We quote:
" The installation ceremonies were a farce. The business of the
body was over. The election was over. It was late. Many Brethren
were anxious to catch a train soon due. The Grand Secretary was
requested to perform the Installation Service in "short order." No
book was furnished. Brethren were constantly leaving the hall.
Ther e was confusion, noise, haste and entire lack of interest.
" The Grand Secretary did the best he could under the circumstances. He will never do the like again. The installation of the
new officers of a Grand Lodge should be made impressive. This requires sufficient time. It should have the earnest attention and
interest of all the Brethren."
The Grand Lodge closed with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.

56

REPORT ON COHRES:POND.l!:NCE;

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"Some time sin<:e Brother Joseph E. Morcombe, Committee on
Correspondence of this Grand Lodge, proposed through the Masonic
press that the Craft of the entire world should take steps toward
properly celebrating its bl-centennary. The present Grand Lodge
system had its beginning In London, June 24, 1717. It Is thus proposed that in the English metropolis In 1917 the Masons of the
world shall gather to review the two centuries of history, to estimate
present tendencies, and judge of the future. It is with pleasure
I endorse the suggestion, believing that as an Iowa Brother has
been first to propose the same, the Iowa Grand Lodge should also
be first to accord such endorsement. It may appear that this is looking far into the future, but twelve years wl!l be necessary to properly bring out and perfect the details of such a meeting."
The committee on the address said of Brother Morcombe:
" In like manner the committee would especially commend the
action of your Grand Master in the matter of the appointment of the
skillful Masonic writer, Brother Morcombe, to the position of Grand
Lodge Historian, a position provided for by this Grand Body at its
last annual communication."

Bro. J. R. Lindsay, Chairman, presented the report of the Committee on Fraternal Dead In a fraternal and feeling report devoted to
the remembran ce of the lives and .characters of the 459 Brethren
named on the pages of Iowa's death roll, and t he eight-page report
was adopted by a rising vote.

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form and the Grand
Master proceeded to deliver his Annual Address. He commenced by
tendering, for Grand Lodge,· its thankfulness to God for the prosperity and harmony with which they had been blessed for the preceding years. and after a brief reference to the principles of Freemasonry he closed his introduction in the following words:
"In this, the One Hundred and Fourth Annual Communication
of the Grand Lodge_ of Kentucky, may our deliberations be conducted
with a mind to the responsibility that is upon us. May they be consonant with the high ethical purposes of our noble Order. May the
glory of an honored past be an effectual inspiration to us, so that
we may turn, from a brilliant retrospect, to see, with a prophetic
eye, a no less brilliant prospect."
And then referring to the "vacant places" in Grand Lodge he
mentioned among the workers who were missed among the brethren
the names of Past Grand Master J. Soule Smith and James Andrew
McKenzie and Grand Pursuivant Charles M. Hobson.
In speaking of Constitutional Amendments to recognize the fitness of things as they are at present, he remarked: Which we "second the motion."
" In regard to the " Reporter of Foreign Affairs," the affairs of
other Grand Lodges in the United States can hardly, in my opinion,
be styled "Foreign" with propriety. I submit that a more appropriate title would be "Reporter of the Doings of Other Grand
Lodges."
Among his reported Decisions, we note but one that may be
of practical value in the present run of current events. We quote
question and answer:
"Question 7. One, who was once a member of a clandestine Lodge,
but states when he joined this Lodge he was under the impression
that he was joining a regular Masonic Lodge, and as soon as he discovered that it was not he withdrew, and has never had anything
to do with it since, petitions. Can we confer the degree?
" Held. If the Lodge is more than ordinarily careful in the investigation, and finds that the petitioner is in every way worthy
and sincere in his statement his petition can be received, referred to
a committee and balloted on as in other cases of petition for degrees; but, of course, the degrees must be conferred as they would
be on any other profane."

REPORT ON ConnEi;PoNDENCE.

"The apron is worn: First degree, bib up; second degree, bit
down, apron ftowing freely; third degree, bib down, ftowing freelyexcept when worn as a mark of distinction the left lower corner is
tucked up. This is in conformity with the teachings of the oldest
charts, and is consistent with the progressiveness of our degrees and
the analogy of the operative Craft. It is also the teachings of the
oldest Jurisdictions of the United States. And (the wearing as
stated) is to be obeyed by subordinate Lodges."
