In the reception of the Representatives of other Jurisdictions we
notice California was left out, but the Grand Master addressed the
:Representatives present, thirty Grand Jurisdictions, they were
saluted with the "private Grand Honors" and addressed by Past
Grand Master Edwin Marks, Reprej\entatlve of New Brunswick, who
after a feeling address was succeeded by Past Grand Master Buck
who In the course of his remarks said:
"But an incident has transpired which arouses my interest and
stimulates my devoted energies to a defense of the system of Grand
Lodge representation. Several Grand Jurisdictions have discol'I·
tinued and much has lately been said about it, ofticially and unoft\.eially, it ls referred to by many in terms of ridicule and derisionas useless, purposeless, unmeaning.
" I beg to take issue with our esteemed sister Grand Jurisdiction
on the subject:-not directly, for it is her own atrair throughout,
and I do not venture to criticize-merely as a member of the gFeat
Brotherhood. I use the incident to express my views on the custom
of Grand representation with such reasons as I may be able to suggest on my feet, without special preparation, why it should be continued and preserved.
" I concede that it serves no practical purpose as a rule-al·
though I have at least one case of practical experience in my mind
when the Representatives of two foreign Grand Jurisdictions had
important work to present to this Grand Lodge in the interest of
their respective principals, who were Involved in a very serious
controversy. I admit they serve no business purpose, and If any
such arise the respective Grand Masters are the persons to transact
them.
,
"The Grand Representative is not appointed for business purposes;-he· merely rises, if you will, as an evidence, a tangible
symbol expressive of the friendship and fraternal relations which
exist between the bodies-a link in the chain of unity- <meness,tdentlty of being and purpose of all the Masonic Bodies on earth.

flEPOnT o.s CoRRESPONDEN.C E.

69

" Every Masonic Grand Lodge has its own specific affairs of administration, of discipline, of finan ce, of property, as a business
concern, so to speak, that is its own exclusive province, In which
no one can properly interfere by criticism or comment.
"But as a Representative-an exponent of the Body of Freemasonry--every Grand Lodge Is the distinct co-worker of every
other Grand Lodge-all equal and all supreme-yet all bound by
the same obligations and ties to guard the landmarks of Masonry
and transflts them unimpaired to posterity. Each sitting In judgment on all the others--each subject to that judgment-to see that
Masonry remains the one-immutable-universal unity which
nothing can change or destroy. A universality in fact and in
philosophy;-going around all the earth with the rays of the sun,
holding the heart-beats of humanity in the unison of brotherhood of
man.
" Each Grand Lodge is the keeper-the custQdian-in its domain
--<>f indivisible a part of this ideal unity and to strike ~t the system
of Interchange of Grand Lodge representation-ls to deny the existence of common sympathy, the ideal of universal aspiration.
"In this Mo~t Worshipful and historic Grand Lodge the Representatives of other Jurisdictions have always been received In the
spirit of true brotherhood, and we are glad to be able to testify that
the present occasion Is bnt a new chord in the woof and web or
fraternal concourse and collaboration which should hold together all
the Masonic Bodies of the World, that we may truly cherish the very
cllmax of our being-the universality, in fact and in spirit of 1',reemasonry."

The Grand Lodge of Montana held four Special Communications

sad tribute of respect and affection to a Past Grand Master, viz., at

·word, Grand Master in 1886-7; at Townsend, August 17, '04, for

Sept 2, '04, for the burial of James W. Hathaway, Grand Master in
1887-8; and at Deer Lodge, Sept. 6, '04, for the burial of James
Hamilton Mills, Grand Master in 1895.
The Annual Communication was held in Masonic Temple,
Helena, October 5th, 1904, commencing at 9:30 A. M.,-M:. w:. H.
S. Hepner, Grand Master; R.". W.". Cornelius Hedges, Grand Secretary. Fifty Lodges were represented, together with thirty-three

Lodges were represented.

The Grand Master appointed the Committees on Conference, on
Grievance, Correspondence, A~ounts, and Unfinished Business. He
then delivered his address, stating his pleasure at the privilege of
extending a welcome to so many active and enthusiastic gentlemen
in the great cause of Masonry.
He referred to the great conflagration of February 7th, and what
seemed a dispensation of Providence, the saving of the Temple
in the midst of the great disaster. He reported the particulars of
the several ceremonial observances in the placing of the cornerstones of public buildings In course of erection, and that the monument authorized to be erected by the Grand Lodge to the memory
of the Grand Secretary Emeritus R.'. w:. Bro. Jacob H. Meda!ry,
was in course of construction.
The Committee on Accounts presented its report, which was
accepted.

examined and approved.

There is but one Cornelius Hedges, and the present report assures
us that he will "tarry with us yet awhile," if there's anything in
signs. We feel from bis cheerful expressions in the present report
that he is well again, and will be present or accounted for at roll
call. He reviews California under the administration of Grand Master· Henderson. He compliments the Grand Master on his activity
in the discharge of official duty, praises and quotes from Grand Orator Hart's oration, speaks of the unusual gain In membership, and

MICHIGAN.
51,871 Mem~rs.
388 Lodges.
The Grand Lodge of Michigan held its Sixty-first Annual Communication in Masonic Temple, Detroit, May 23, 1905, commencing
at high twelve,-M.'. W:. Fletcher E. Turrell, Grand Master; R.' ·
w:. Lou B. Winsor, Grand Secretary. Three hundred and eighty-six
Lodges were represented, together with thirty-eight other Grand
Jurisdictions. Eighteen Past Grand Masters were in attendance,
and all the Grand omcers answered roll call.
Handsome portraits of the retiring Grand Master, and also of
the Grand Master-elect, are noted in the opening pages of this
number of the journal.
We note the presence among the Past Grand Masters of the
veteran, Hugh Mccurdy.
The Grand Lodge of Michigan was opened in Ample Form with
prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
Hon. George P . Codd, Mayor of the city of Detroit, delivered an
eloquent and cordial address of welcome to the Grand Lodge, which,
by request of Grand Master Turrell, was responded to on behalf of
the Grand Lodge, by Past Grand Master Lou B. Winsor.
Grand Lodge "called o!T" until 2: 30, when it re-assembled, the
Grand Master presiding. The Grand Secretary called the "roll
of honor," to which there had been no additions during the late

has caused to be inscribed upon the death roll the names of 783
members of the Masonic family of the Grand Lodge of Michigan.
He also reported the death of many eminent Masons of other
Jurisdictions, and extended the sympathy of the Grand Lodge of
Michigan to the mourners.
He reported the issuance of dispensations for the forming and
opening of new Lodges, the dedication of twenty-two Halls and
Temples to the uses and purposes of Masonry, and the placing of
t:even corner-stones of public buildings.
He reported his visitations and the enthusiasm with which he
was greeted. We excerpt the following as the correct practice
which should be followed by all Secretaries in the discharge of their
important duties:
" The Secretary of ' Crystal • Lodge has also been very lax in
the performance of his duties. He should have been sure that the
fee accompanied the petition, for no petition should be presented to
the Lodge which ie: not accompanied by the fee. When the fee is
received by the Secretary, he should charge himself with it upon
his financial record, and the same should in all cases be turned over
to the Treasurer and become a part of the Lodge funds. Should
the petition be rejected, a warrant should be drawn upon the Treasurer for the return of the fee, and all the details of the entire t ransaction will thereby be permanently recorded. The Secretary was
unable to find the petition when I requested it. This should in all
rases be permanently preserved."
The Grand Secretary reports the following communication, received from Grand Secretary George Johnson of the Grand Lodge
of California:
"R.'. W.'. Sm AND DEAR BHOTHER:
"At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California,
1904, the following recommendation was unanimously adopted:
" ' It will be patent to any one who will give the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges
proper consideration, that this custom is as useless as the appendix
vermi formis in the human body. It seems to us that the custom
must have originated in a desire to decorate members with a mere
title. The only proper way for one Grand Lodge to communicate
with another is through the Grand Masters. Your committee can see
no necessity for the continuance of the custom, and therefore recommend that it be abolished.'
"Truly and Fraternally,

recess.
The Grand Master proceeded to deliver the Annual Address.
A change In the time of assembling the Grand Lodge from January to May so lengthened the term of the Grand Master, as he says,
as to give him the privilege of reporting to the Grand Lodge the
" busiest Masonic year the Grand Lodge of Michigan has ever experienced." He commenced his report by giving a Fraternal greeting
to the Representatives of more than 50,000 Free and Accepted
Masons, assembled for the purpose of reviewing the past and legislating for the future welfare of the Fraternity.
"But," he said, "before considering the business of the session,
let us invoke the Divine blessing upon our labors and · then devote
a brief period to the ·remembrance of the Brethren and friends who
have passed to rest within the year."
He called up the Grand Lodge, and the R.'. W.'. Grand Chapla~n
invoked the blessing of the Deity.
He was pleased to report that, although their official circle remained unbroken, yet the repeated visit of the Winged Messenger

But for the certificate of Grand Secretary Johnson, we should
have believed it impossible for a radical change to have been made
in the usages and customs of the Grand Lodge of California, without
our knowledge, we being present when the report referred to was
made.
We were present in the Grand Lodge during the reading of the
report of the Committee on Grand Master's Address-a committee
of division and reference of the several matters presented and recommendations made by the Grand Master.
The Grand Master made no reference to the subject of Representatives to and from Grand Lodges, and no one seated on the opposite
side of the hall from the reader of the report had the remotest idea
of the voluntary recommendation of that committee, or the response
would have made a different record. Our first knowledge of the
matter was the publication of the circular under date of about
February 1st, three and a half months after the close of the session.
Legislation °bY indirection is bad policy. In the present attempt to
amend the Constitution by resolution, there can be but one resultfailure.
From the reports of the officers of the Michigan Masonic Home,
we learn the Home Is caring for fifty-two inmates-forty-four males,
and eight females, the average age of the Brethren being 71 years,
and of the women 76 years.
Bro. Frank H. Williams, Chairman of · the Committee on Obituaries, made an eloquent and feeling report, which was adopted, and
the Funeral Grand Honors given.
· The Committees on Charities and on Appeals reported, and their
reports were approved. The general routine of business having been
completed, and the election of officers for the ensuing year being
in order, the following-named Brethren were chosen to fill the stations for the ensuing year: John Rowson, Grand Master ; Charles
L. Stevens; Deputy Grand Master, Charles E. Sweet, Senior Grand
Warden; Erastus E. Stone, Junior Grand Warden; William Wente,
Grand Treasurer; Lou B. Winsor, P. G. M., Grand Secretary; Frank
T. Lodge, P. G. M., Grand Lecturer; Rev. A. A. Knappen, Grand
Chaplain; Thomas Reardon, Senior Grand Deacon; Arthur M.
Hume, Junior Grand Deacon ; G. Roscoe Swift, Grand Marshal;
James F. McGregor, Grand Tyler.
The Grand Master made his appointments, and all were installed
by Past Grand Master Lou B. Winsor, Past Grand Master John J.
Carton acting as Master of tli.e· Ceremonies.

to sister Jurisdictions bereaved by the loss of friends and Brethren.
Bro. Thomas Montgomery, Grand Secretary, makes his usual interesting and valuable report, the closing words of which we quote
as a deserved tribute to a veteran Mason:
" 1 have assisted in laying corner-stones at Windom, Duluth and
Anoka, and last month attended the funeral of Past Grand ~aste~
Kiester, at Blue Earth. I was particularly attached to . Bro. Kiester,
as to him I was indebted for the appointment of Grand Secretary in
November, 1889, to succeed Bro. Pierson. I might note here that
I have been present at the burial of all of our eleven deceased Past
Grand Masters, except that of Bro. Sherburne, the first to die, in 1868
and of ten other Past Grand Officers.
" 1 also was privileged to constitute " Montgomery " Lodge, No.
258, February 22d last, to install one of my sons Master of "Midway"
Lodge, No. 185, for the third time, and to visit quite a number of
Lodges. during the year.
"As a Grand Lodge we continue in terms of amity with every
other English-speaking Grand Lodge in the world, sixty-five in number and exchange our proceedings with theirs., We also receive circul~rs and periodicals from Grand Lodge officials of Cuba, Porto Rico,
Mexico, Brazil, Belgium, Switzerland and several other Foreign
Jurisdictions, and send them our proceedings when requested.
1

"In closing my report I am happy to say that my relations with
the Grand Master and other Grand Officers, as well as with all other
Brethren with whom I have come into official or personal contact,
have been of the most cordial character. Profoundly thankful to one
and all for the confidence reposed in me in the past, and actuated by
one great object, the honor and glory of Minnesota Free Masonry, I
hope to continue to maintain that confidence and to earnestly work
with my co-laborers for the growth and prosperity Of Our beloved
Fraternity as long as life shall last."

of Jackson, February 23, 1905,-M. ·. W. ·. Thomas Upton Sisson,

In addition to the Grand Officers, twenty Past Grand Officers
and permanent members were in attendance. Two hundred and

The portrait of Grand Master Sisson appears on the opening page;
that of Past Grand Master H. H. Folk, who died in Paxton, Florida;
that of Senior Grand Warden W. H. Howard, who was buried
October 29, 1904, at Meriden, and of Henry Strauss, Grand Tyler
from 1887 to 1900, at intervals in different ·parts of the journal.
The Grand Lodge was welcomed to Jackson by the Hon. Garland
C, Syle on behalf of the citizens, and the welcome was responded to
by the Grand Master. The Grand Lodge was opei;ied in Ample Form
with prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
·
The Grand Secretary announced that a great sorrow had come
upon M.'. W.'. Bro. Phineas M. Savery, Past Grand Master, on the
previous Thursday night, when death took from him the partner of
his joys and sorrows for more than fifty years, and that he, himself,
was prostrate upon a bed of sickness. On motion it was ordered
that the Grand Secretary should immediately telegraph to Bro.
Saver:y its warmest sympathy and heartfelt condolence, and the
following telegram was sent at once:
·
"CAPT. P. M. SAVERY, Past Grand Master of Masons, Tupelo, Miss." The Grand Lodge sends loving sympathy in your illness, and
condolence in your affliction, and it earnestly prays for your restoration to health ·and strength.
"FREDERICK SPEED, Grand Secretary."
'l'he Grand Master then proceeded to deliver his Address. The
unique opening of the addres::; is our warrant for its excerpt. He
said:
"You will pardon your Grand Master for a moment's digression
from the ordinary address of this occasion, because it is with specially great pride and pleasure that he calls this Grand Lodge to
order. On April the 17th, 1834, a dispensation was granted to
"Pearl" Lodge, No. 23, of Jackson, Hinds County, Mississippi, and
the first Master of that Lodge was Upton Miller; and now, after
nearly seventy-one stormy, eventful and historic nineteenth-century
years have passed, his grandson, as Grand Master, calls the Grand
Lodge to order, being entertained by "Pearl" Lodge, No. 23. Breth·
ren, I am not only your brother, but I am your grandson, and permit

tne to say to you in the language of the Psalmist of Old, ' If I forget
thee, 0 Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning; if I do not
remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth.'"
He continued his eloquent dissertation, illustrated by reference
to the " Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man," " King
John and Magna Charter," "Joseph Warren and Bunker Hill,"
"George Washington," "Thomas Jetrerson," and "The Declaration of
Independence," until apparently impressed with the duties of the
hour. Under the head of Necrology:
"The sweetest of all the Canticles is ' Nunc dimittis,' or t he ' Song
of Simeon.' When he beld the infant Jesus in the Temple, he took
the child in his arms and burst forth into a song of thanksgiving,
commencing: 'Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace,
according to Thy word. For mine eyes have seen Thy salvation.'
This is the outburst of a heart that is filled with peace and contentment. One upon whose soul this great flood of light is shed, faces the
Doleful Messenger, Death, with calm resignation and
" ' Sustain'd and sooth'd
By an unfaltering trust,' approaches his grave,
' Like one that wraps the drapery of his couch
About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams.'"
And then, in most eloquent words, he pays affectionate tribute
to the late Senior Grand Warden Howard, James M. Hitt, W. F.
Stephens, H. H. Folk and Mississippi's death roll of 1904.
He reported the constitution of seven Lodges and reported the
issuance of three dispensations for the forming and opening of three
still newer ones.
He did not make a general visitation of his constituent Lodges,
but says he would like to have visited but for the pressure of business.
The District Deputies reported the condition of the Lodges in
their several districts, and the Grand Lecturer made a full report
of his work.
Grand Secretary Speed's report is an exhaustive statement of the
financial condition and prospects of the Grand Lodge ot Mississippi.
The Grand Lodge resolved, on motion of the Committee on Correspondence, "That the Grand Lodge of Mississippi welcome the
Grand Lodge of Queensland into the sisterhood of Grand Lodges,
which she enters of right by virtue of the regularity of her formation, and wm· gladly cultivate closer relationship with that Grand
Body by an exchange of Grand Representatives."

The opening page of the journal presents to us a faithful likeness
of M.'. W.'. Bro. John Davis Vinci!, Past Grand Master and Grand
Secretary of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Andent, Free and
Accepted Masons of Missouri, who died at his home in St. Louis,
October i2, 1904, and whose remains were interred with Fraternal
honors in his family burial Jot In the cemetery at Columbia, Mo.,
October lo, 1904.
Doctor Vinci!, as he was lovingly called, was born in Tazewell
County, Virginia, August 24, 1830, and from a record of his Masonic
history published in the Biographies of the Grand Lodge Officers in
1901, first appeared in the Grand Lodge of Missouri at the Annual
Communication, May 23, 1859, as the Representative from " Spring
Hill " Lodge, No. 155, of Livingston County, Missouri. He served as
Grand Chaplain until 1863, when he was elected Senior Grand Warden. In 1864 and 1865 he was elected Deputy Grand Master, and in
1866 was chosen as Most Worshipful Grand Master, serving what
was then known as the " long term," lasting nearly eighteen months,
which was on account of the change made in holding the Annual
Sessions from May to October. At the close of his term he retired,
but for one year only, as in 1868 he was again called to the
Grand East.
The Golden J ubilee of this veteran Mason was celebrated August
13, 1904, on which anniversary he was presented by his, Masonic

William Frederick Kuhn, with a biographic sketch of this eloquent
expounder of Masonry. The M.'. W.'. Brother's residence Is in
Kansas City.
The Grand Lodge of Missouri held its Eighty-fourth Annual
Communication In Scottish Rite Cathedral, St. Louis, September
27, 1904,-M.'. W.'. Wiiliam F. Kuhn, Grand Master; R.'. W.'. F. W.
Mott, Grand Secretary. Three hundred and eighty-nine Lodges were
represented. All the Grand Officers, forty District Deputies, and one
hundred and forty Past Masters were In attendanct..
The Grand Master expressed the appreciation of the Grand Lodge
o! the courtesies .of the Brethren of the Scottish Rite in placing at
their disposal, without cost, their beautiful cathedral.
The R. ·. W. •. Bro. A. C. Stewart, executive head anu spokesman
for the Cathedral Association, addressed the Grand Lodge in a most
eloquent Address of Welcome, to which the Grand Master responded.
The Committee on Credentials reported, and the Grand Master
proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
It goes without' saying that the address was an eloquent dissertation in Its opening upon the aims and purposes of Masonry, under
the head of Necrology, he paid affectionate tribute to the Brethren
who had been called home during the recess of the Grand Lodge.
He reported the issuance of dispensations for the forming and
opening of ten new Lodges, and the placing of eleven corner-stones
of public buildings.

He appointed a number of Representatives of Missouri near other
Grand Jurisdictions.
He reported· a number of decisions, nearly all of which were
governed by the local law of Missouri, and were approved by the
Committee on Jurisprudence.
He spoke earnestly In approval of the management of the Home,
and of the abiding interest In Its success by the good women of the
Eastern Star.
He appointed a committee of Past Grand Masters to determine
and report to the Grand Lodge " The Foreign Grand Bodies not in
Fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge of Missouri, that should
have recognition."

His report of the condition of Masonry in Missouri was enthusiastic. He said: "In my visitations I have come in contact with the
best, the truest, the noblest men in Missouri-men who stand for the
ideals of life that humanity may be better."
M.". W.". Grand Master Kuhn reported that the growth of the
Grand Lodge during the past year had been very saUsfactory, as well
as prosperous. There were over 3,000 Entered Apprentices, 2,000
Master Masons, and 1,000 Affiliated, while 700 have joined the silent
throng during the year. This brings our total membership to nearly
40,000, the increase during the year, so far as be could ascertain,
beginning back seven or eight years, was the largest in our Jurisdiction that he was able to discover.
To enliven the usual dull routine of business, consisting of the
reports of several committees, the business of the Home, etc., the
following bit of refreshment was indulged in. The report says:
"The Grand Master entrapped R.".
Bro. Allan McDowell by
calling him to the platform, ostensibly to make a report. Bro. McDowell innocently started to say that the report of his committee
was not quite ready, whereupon the Grand Master suddenly · presented him with a very handsome gold-headed cane, suitably inscribed, and spoke touchingly of the life-long and faithful services
that Bro. McDowell had rendered to the Grand Lodge.
" Bro. McDowell was overwhelmed with surprise, and as soon
as he could overcome bis emotion, responded in his usual happy
manner, and gave a brief review of his work as Grand Lecturer."
The R ." . W." . Grand Orator, Bro. Will jam R. Gentry, delivered a
fine oration, and Bro. Allan McDowell made his report as Grand
Lecturer.

Every member of the Grand Lodge present arose to his feet
without a moment's hesitation, thus manifesting their great love
and sympathy for him.

REPOR'f ON CORRESPONDENCE.

This report. is the last work of the lamented Vincil-a review of
196 pages in which he reviews the doings of forty-three American
and thirteen Foreign Grand Bodies. He reviews California unue1·
the administration of Grand Master Henderson. The report is a
pleasant one, impressing one, as he always did, with his kind feeling
and good wishes for California. In Fraternal remembrance of good
Bro. Vinci!, we excer.pt his last notice of our work:
"The report of the committee on this important branch of Masonic work covers 175 pages, embracing notices of forty-seven American and eleven Foreign Grand Lodges, making a total of fifty-eight
proceedings reviewed. The work was performed 'by M. ·. W. ·. Bro.
William A. Davies, Chairman of the Committee. It is, as heretofore,
a strong and practical review of Grand' Lodge transactions. The
Missouri proceedings for 1902 received courteous attention, covering
three pages, embracing a review of all the business done .at our
Kans11;s City session. Brief attention was paid to the report of this
Committee on Correspondence. Carrying out a purpose formed before this r eport was commenced, I must make my review of California brief, as will be the case with all others."
And this last cheering message proved to be, in truth, as in fact,
the conclusion of his work on earth. God give him rest.
CONCLUSION.

First, however, to examine the rolls and ascertain those among the

pages in the journal of the year be set apart and. devoted to the

He referred to a case of the invasion of the Jurisdiction of the

generall y known as the French Lodge-the Brothers receiving th e
degrees in that Lodge being claimed as a resident of Reno, Nevada.
Comment is unnecessary, as the Grand Masters of California and
Nevada are fully advised in the matter, and' neither desire nor will
imbmit to sharp practice in considering Jurisdictional rights.

pathy. Official notification has reached me of the death of the followi.ng Eminent Masons; and the · Brethren rose to their feet and
heard In silence the lengthy death roll read."
The condition of this Grand Jurisdiction is best given in the
closing words of his Address:
" When I accepted the office to which you kindly elected me three
years ago, I did so with a full appreciation of the duties and great
responsibilities that fall upon one who presides over this Grand
Lodge, and also with a feeling of diffidence when I considered how
many well-tried and prominent Masons had been my predecessors,
who, when building the edifice of Freemasonry In this Providence,
tiad well laid its foundations. I felt, however, that the very success
of the former Grand Masters was a guarantee to me that the true
Masonic spirit prevailed, and that I would receive the co-operation
of every member in the discharge of those duties and in meeting
those responsibilities. In this I made no mistake, for at the end of

97

a term of three years I have to make acknowledgement of a genuine
and loyal support from nearly every officer and Individual of this
body. The position has been one of pleasant associations and
memories. Let us then, Brethren, cultivate and cherish a spirit of
devotion to those principles of religion and morality which our institution teaches, and let us hand over to those who follow us not
only our robes of office pure and untarnished, but an institution free
from the promotion of ends personal to ourselves, and Inspired by
but a single purpose, the promotion throughout the world of the
essential qualities of true manhood.

He referred to the occas ion of the coming together of the brethren
of the faternity, of their responsibilities and duty, not only to preserve inviolate the heritage entrusted to them but in turn to pass it
over to their successors. He gave them a cordial greeting and congratulated them on the present condition of the Jurisdiction.
" As our first business," he said : " Let us hear who among our
brethren have died during the year, with a brief summary of the

inscribed thereon.
He reported the placing of the corner-stone of the new Masonic
Temple in Laconia.
We find nothing requiring comment in the r eported Decisions of
the Grand Master ; but he makes a fe w remarks concerning "Per-petual J urisdiction over rejected applicants" that we would "keep
standing " before the members of the fraternity, that all Masons
may be informed of the injustice of this wicked requirement.
When two years ago, I assumed the duties of the office of Grand
Master, I counted myself a firm believer in tl;le principle of perpetual Jurisdiction over rejected mat erial. I was satisfied with the
reasonableuess of the theory for such perpetuity, and confess that I
was prejudiced in that direction. It was almost a tenet of my Masonic profession. But during the Incumbency of the offi ce of Grand
Master I have had to deal with the theory and with the practice.
as held here and as held elsewhere, in an official capacity, and my
faith in it has been transformed into a personal belief that it is unreasonable, and sooner or la ter is destined to be discarded by this
Grand Jurisdiction, as being unreasonable, and because it is - not in.
conformity with the law .and -J;Jracti ce ..of the majority of other Grand

ioo

REPORT ON ConREBPONDBNCE.

Jurisdictions, with whom, without surrendering too much, we
should strenuously endeavor to be in happy concord. My ex·
perience as Grand Master has been that the matter of Jurisdictiondisputes concerning it, and the requests for waivers of Jurisdiction
-is the most perplexing and annoying of any that are presented for
()fficial consideration and direction. Take an example, for .instance,
that has come within my knowledge : Twenty-five years ago a New
Hampshire Lodge_rejected the petition of· an applicant. Many years
since, he removed to another Grand Jurisdiction, whNe, I understand, the principle of perpetuity is not recognized. He still desires
to be a member of our fraternity; but notwitstanding his long ab:
sence from our State, a request for a waiver of Jurisdiction, presented here in full compliance with our requirements, is .refused,
and the Grand Master is compelled so to report. There is embarrassment, there is injustice, there is great unreasonableness in
such an instance of the length to which our position leads. Still
other requests for waivers come to your Grand Master from Jurisdictions which assert in plain terms to him that they do not believe
in the theory of perpetuity, do not practice it, but go through
the formaUty of . making the request to comply with our requirements, so that they may live in peace with us. The resulting em·
barrassments are unpleasant, not alone to us of New Hampshire,
but to others. We are holding to that which is certainly becoming
obsolete when we strive to maintain perpetual Jurisdiction. Some
day we shall cease to insist that we, almost alone, are right and
that the great majority is wrong. The time limit in this particular
is sure to bl' adopted by our Grand Body before many years elapse,
and the men ll\'ho accomplish this reform will wonder how and why
it was persistP-d in so many years. It may not be in my time-yet
I hope to see t!:at day-but I desire to be on record in our proceed·
ings as advocating a recession from our present position, that w:
may be in accord, as I understand it, with the greater part of the
Masonic world. I endeavor to suppress the zeal of the convert, but
speak plainly and feelingly with every confidence of · ultimate approval. I recommend that this matter referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence.
The Committee on Address of 'the Grand Master recommended
the reference of his comments on Perpetual Jurisdiction to the
_C ommittee on Jurisprudence, and it was so' ordered.
The Grand Master gave notice that dinner had been provided and
invited all to attend.
Grand Lodge was called off until 2 o'clock, when it was called
<>n and business proceeded.

He referred to the year as an eventful one. Masonry has prospered as never before in its history, the outer door has been well
guarded but our membership has grown without sacrificing quality or
character In his enthusiasm he said: " 1 am proud of you and
may a ki~d Providence ever keep you united in the good and noble

REPOHT ON Comrns1•0NDENCE.

111

work to which yon have devoted so much of your time, talents and
1111hstance. When referring to the Fraternal Dead he said:
"Death casts its dark shadows across every pathway, across
every life and ove r every living thing. It ls a melancholy truth that
the strong and the weak must fall alike before the remorseless
scythe of Time. Neither fame nor fortune, neither rank nor power,
can avert the swift Messenger that calls all men to account. When
his touch is laid upon man, the sunshine of day is changed to the
darkness of night, the stars disappear in the firmament, dust returns
to dust, and the spirit departs to the realm of Eternal day."
And after quoting the beautiful poem, " Oh, a wonderful stream
is the river of time," he added: "Recalling the lives of those who
met with us a year ago, have passed on to the higher life, let us,
at the very threshold of our Assembly, pay a tribute to their
memory."
After presenting the lengthy death roll and paying a tribute of
respect and affection to the names inscribed thereon under Necrology,
he nnmeu the dead of sister Jurisdictions and of Eminent Masons
wher esoever dispersed, and extended the sympathy of the Masons of
New York to the bereaved Jurisdictions.

Under Questions and Decisions, his r eported opinion concerning
r.n election would not be good law in California, as our Constitution
ueclares that " Blanks shall not be counted as votes." We have always considered the opinion quoted as sound, believing that the voter
has the right to cast a blank and that it should be counted as a vote.
•
" My attention has been called to the difference of opinion with
referen ce to blank ballots at an annual election for the officers of a
Lodge. In some localities blank ballots are not counted in the
whole numbe r of ballots cast. To the end that there niay be no
further misunderstanding in this matter, I desire to call the attention of the Masters of the several Lodges here represented, that
a Brother to be legally elected must have a majority of all the bal·
lots cast, notwithstanding the fact that some of the ballots so cast
may be blanks."
He expressed his grateful thanks to the Knights Templar of New
York for their "practical" aid and assistance in support of the
Home. and of two eminent Brethren one of whom has since taid
himself down to rest. He says these-good, kind and .c pe_e ring words :

In the great volume of business reported by the Board of Genera.I
Purposes there is little of direct interest to our readers. We excerpt
the committee's report concerning t he Grand Lodge of Costa Rica,
and pass the bulk of matters considered to the choice of the officera
for the ensuing year. The committee said :
"That the Craft Lodges that united to form the so-called Grand
Lodge of Costa Rica were undoubtedly irregular in their origin; but
that they .have fulfilled all the purposes of Craft Masonry in that
territory for many years, and the er~ction of a Grand Lodge seelillJ
to be the best way to bring them into line with more regular Lodges.
and to institute the best and most regular method of Masonic government. The committee, therefore, begs leave to recommend that the
Grand Lodge of Costa Rica be recognized by this Grand Lodge as
the sovereign Masonic body of Costa Rica."

M:. w:. W. ·s. Liddell, Grand Master; R:. w:. John C. Drewry,

The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, and the Grand Master proceeded to deliver his annual address.
.He greeted the Grand Lodge with a hearty welcome to the duties
and pleasures of the Annual Communication, which had brought
them together to review the past and under the guidance of the
Supreme Ruler to legislate for the upbuilding of Free Masonry.
He had issued eight dispensations for the forming and opening of
n~w Lodges.
I
He referred with affectionate and loving tribute to the Brethren
who had passed to rest during the year. In sympathy also with Sister Jurisdictions stricken by the visits of the Grim Reaper, he ex·
tended the condolence of the Brethren bound together by the ties of
friendship and brotherly affection. He commended to the care of the
Grand Lodge their kind attention to the needs of the Oxford Asylum.
. The Grand Lodge restored the Charter of "Eno" Lodge, No. 210,
at Durham, Durham County.

Collins of Enfield, and is a good, fair review of the Masonic world
"as it is to-day," but his introduction speaks for itself so fully and
yet so briefly that we will let him tell it himself:
"Your Committee on Correspondence begs leave to present. its
ninth annual report upon the condition of the Craft as disclosed by
the transactions of English-speaking-Grand Lodges which have come
to hand. An inspection of the proceeding of fifty-nine Grand Jurisdictions gives evidence of unparalleled prosperity, complete harmony and a noble emulation In good works.
"It Is believed that an occasional glance at this report, brief and
incomplete as it is, will be a revelation and inspiration to the North
Carolina Mason, for whose service it Is prepared."

The Grand Lodge of North Dakota held its Fifteenth Annual
Communication in Masonic Temple, Fargo, June 28 and 29, 1904,
commencing at High Twelve,-M.". W.". J~mes T. Blacklock, Grand
·Ma:;ter ; R.". W." . Frank J. Thompson, Grand Secretary. Sixty-five
Lodges were represented, together with thirty-seven other Grand
Jurisdictions. Thirteen Past Grand OfHcers were in attendance.
A portrait of Grand Master Blacklock appears on the opening
page.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form, and the Grand
Master proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
With a cordial greeting to the assembled Brethren, he referred
to the history of Grand Lodge, its organization, growth and present
coudition, during the fifteen years of its existence its original roll
had increased from thirty to seventy-two Lodges, and its membership from 1,322 to 4,847 Master Masons, among whom "there is no
contention," save only as Lodges, "as to who can be·s t work -and best
agree."
He made at!ectionate mention of the " Fraternal Dead" of other
sister Jurisdictions, as well as the bereaved of their own "tribes and
families" of North Dakota.
Among his ofH·cial acts, he dedicated a Masonic 1'emple to the
uses and purposes of Masonry at Bottineau, and constituted " Leeds "
Lodge, No. 67. During the recess he had granted dispensations for
the forming and opening of five new Lodges, and another coming
so late that he thought best to· refer it to the Grand Body now In
session.
· No important decisions were reported; at least, none not fully
governed by the local law and regulations.

He also paid the following tribute to the lamented Bro. Jacob H.
Medairy, Grand Secretary Emeritus, of Maryland:
"But one Grand Secretary has passed away during the year, and
it was with regret that the Guild learned of the death of Bro. Jacob
H. Medalry, which occurred at his home In Baltimore, February 3,
1904. Bro. Medairy had served his Grand Lodge as Grand Secretary for forty years. The infirmities of age coming upon him, the
Grand Lodge of Marylan.d, a few short months before his death,
created him Grand Secretary Emeritus, with full rank and pay.
for life. The Grim Reaper, however, came before the brother could
reap much of the enjoyment from relief from official duty, and took
him hence.''
The Grand Secretary read a nice note of thanks received from
R.'. W.'. Bro. Thomas Klelnogel, in which he acknowledged receipt
of a Past Junior Grand Warden's apron, presented to him by this
Grand Lodge, at the hands of Chris Diehl, Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge A. F. & A. M. of Utah.
The Grand Master announced the appointment of the committees.
'l'hc routine of business included amendments to By-Laws and the
.incorporation of Lodges.
The Committee on Necrology made a feeling report. In referring
to the distinguished dead of other Jurisdictions, the committee said:
" Early in our Masonic career we are taught that the best and
wisest men of all ages have· been promoters and encouragers of our.
noble art. We, therefore, find among our Illustrious Fraternal Dead
those who were great not only in Masonry in their particular Jurisdiction, but, also, were great in the affairs of the throbbing world,
who were truly beacon lights during their lives, and who will continue to be such in the years and centuries to come. The Grim
Tyrant, Death, has visited many of our sister Grand Masonic Jurisdictions, and the list of his victims is dire and long."
They closed their report with the beautiful and appropriate words
of Albert Pike :

For the weak are heavier crosses,
Every year,
Last spring with sobs replying
Unto weary autumn's sighing,
While those we love are dying
Every year.
To the past go more dead faces,
Every year.
As the loved ones leave vacant places
Every year,
Everywhere the sad eyes meet us,
In the evening's dusk they greet us
And to come to them entreat us,
Every year.''

The Grand Lodge of Ohio held its Ninety-fifth Annual Communication in the Valentine Theater, Toledo, October 19, 1904, commencing at 10 o'clock A . :M:.,-M:. W:. 0. P . Sperra, Grand Master;
R : . w:. J. H. Bromwell, Grand Secretary. Four hundred and
eighty-nine Lodges were represented, ,together with forty other Grand
.Jurisdictions. Fourteen Past Grand Masters and two Past Deputy
Gri.ind Masters were in attendance, with twenty-three District Lecturers.

Portraits of the Grand Master and the lamented veteran Grand
Master S. Stacker Williams appear on the opening pages of this number of the journal.
·
In conformity with Ohio usage, the Grand Master opened a Lodge
of Master Masons in Due Form and appointed the Committee on
Credentials, and upon the report of that committee of a proper
representation, he declared the Grand Lodge of Ohio open in its
Ninety-fifth Annual Communication, the Grand Chaplain invoking
the Divine favor upon the session.
The Grand Master introduced His Honor, the Mayor o.f the city,
who gave the Grand Lodge a cordial welcome to the city of Toledo.
The several departments of Legitimate Masonry were represented by
their officers, and were invited to seats in the Grand East.
The Grand Master then proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
With a cordial welcome he extended his greetings to the Representatives of. the Masonic family of Ohio, with its sixty thousand
members. He congratulated them upon the condition of the Craft,
and invoked the spirit of harmony in all their deliberations. After
reporting the names of many Eminent Masons, members of sister
Jurisdictions, who had been " called home," and of whose departure
he had been officially informed during the recess, he said:
" While at this time we rejoice in our strength and are buoyant
with hope of future greatness, let us pause in memory of the
eight hundred and seventy Masons of this Jurisdiction, tried and

128

REPORT ON CoRR:t:SPONDENCE.

true,. who have crossed the dark river to serve their better Master,
paying loving tribute to their memory. This large number of deaths
from our ranks is almost appalling, being the greatest in our
history. And thus, my Brethren, while the sun will continue to
shine as bright, and the birds will s!ng as sweetly, anticipated joy
is turned to sadness by the absence of familiar forms and faces
we had expected to meet.
" Darker, darker, and more wan,
In my breast the shadows fall;
Upwards steals the life of man,
As the sunshine from the wall.
From the wall into the sky,
From the ;roof along the spire;
Ah, the souls of those that die,
Are but sunbeams lifted higher."
His announcement of the death of that Exemplar of Freemasonry,
S. Stacker Williams, was an eloquent tribute to a " Mason of force
and power that was almost a: necessity in the Masonic history of
Ohio."
He issued dispensations for the forming and opening of four new
Lodges, and made a large number of visitations.
The Deputy Grand Master reported his acts and, in his brief
report, paid the following tribute to one of Ohio's most Illustrious
Masons:
" If I were inclined to amplify my report on any of the numerous
occasions at which I have been present, it would be the occasion.
of performing · the last sad offices to our Illustrious Brother and
esteemed ,Past Grand Master, S. Stacker Williams. Indeed, the
occasion seemed to me to be particularly impressive, because, as a
young man, I entered the Grand Lodge when S. Stacker Williams, as
Grand Master, was guiding the Craft over the tempestuous sea of
troubles of Cerneauism. The picture of Stacker Williams as Grand
Master, presiding over that body of men, was stamped indelibly upon.
my mind, and from that day to this I have always admired this
man whom we all have delighted to honor."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Report on Correspondence is the feature of the Proceedings
of the Grand Lodge of Ohio, and in the present number consists of
the review of sixty-four Grand ·Jurisdictions of the Masonic world,
of which thirty-nine are American, and sixteen foreign, making a
book of 323 pages. The author is Bro. William M. Cunningham, who
was Grand Master of Ohio In 1877, and of whom Ohio's Masonic
poet, M.". W:. Nelson Williams, wrote, in 1895:
... For forty long, success! ve years,
Upon our Grand Lodge roll,
Your name has had an honored place,
And honored well the scroll.
For forty years, almost the length
Of life's uncertain span,
No name has been more honored
Than the name of Cunningham."
.
And in 1905 he is yet with us at the head of the roll of Past Grand
Masters in attendance at the session of 1904, and " long may he
wave." Bro. Cunningham reviews California for the administration
of Gra:nd Master Henderson, and notices approvingly the routine
business of the session.

The Grand Master's Address was read by the Deputy Grand
Master. Perhaps we hadn't ought to say it but, when we re-read
the results of his administration, we feel strong enough to say that
we are not surprised that It made Grand Master Matthews sick to
think of facing the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma, where, if anywhere
in organized Masonry, a firm a·n d strong administration of the law,
in the interest of the uses and purposes of Masonry, was needed.
His weak apology shows it to have been the Jurisdiction committed
to his charge as Grand Master.
We note in his report of the discharge of his arduous duties as
Grand Master, twenty-two Lodges were constituted, and every one by
the Grand Master's proxy, and he issued dispensations for the forming and opening of fourteen (14) new ones.
What an opportunity for an active Grand Master to inscribe his
name at or near the head of the Grand Masters' column in Oklahoma.
Among his " duties in other fields " his time was so occupied
that t~e Grand Lodge Treasury got Itself mixed up in sundry business speculations, and the funds gathered in with much enthusiasm
for "lo! these many years," took to themselves wings and are no
more counted among the assets of the .G rand Lodge of Oklahoma.
But amid all his explanations, we think the following "presses the
button" and establishes his · reputation as the Grand Master that
didn't know what he was made for. We excerpt the following from
the closing llnes of his address:
" I have made no official visitations, but have always, when
convenient, called at the Lodge Hall and met witli the Brethren,
when I happened to be in town on their meeting night, and have in
every Instance been received with the honor which the high office
of Grand Master entitled me to; and at this time I wish to call
special attention to the condition in which I found some of the
Lodges. While most of them were kept in a very tidy, presentable
condition, showing that the Brethren believe that the meeting place
of Masonry should be something more t han a place where all may
gat her together indiscriminately, yet I am sorry to say that l found
many others in an unkept, unswept condition, the doors without lock
and key, the furniture broken and dilapidated, the paraphernalia
rarelessly laid around for the public inspection, and the Lodge room
open to all at all hours, and used for every conceivable kind of
meeting."
We note the following report of the Grand Secretary concerning
"Work by the Grand Lodge." Query- Whence came he and wb.ere is
his home ?

" R:. w:. Srn AND DEAR BROTHER: At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, the following
recommendation was unanimously adopted:
" 'It wlll be patent to any one who wlll give the appointment
of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges proper consideration, that the custom ls as useless as the " appendix vermi formls"
in t he human body. It seems to us that the custom must have
originated in a desire to decorate members with a mere title. The
only proper way for one Grand Lodge· to communicate with another
is through the Grand Master. Your committee can see no necessity
for the continuance of the custom, and therefore recommends that
It be abollshed.
Truly and Fraternally,
"' GEo. JOHNSON, Grand Secretary.'"
Certainly a most extraordinary document, and when we- think
that we were present when that committee reported, with not the
remotest idea of what the report was loaded with, and learned f or

the first ti me, nearly four months thereafter, what the Grand Secretary certifies to as the unanimous action of the Grand LoLlge was a

other recognized Grand Lodges and to receive and accredit Representatives from them." Further comment upon this matter will be r eserved for our conclusion.

R. ·. w. ·. Grand Master Brother James W. Brown addressed the
Grand Lodge as follows:
"We are assembled once more
the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania to pay the last sad tribute to a Past Grand Master.
" Death has laid a heavy hand upon the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania during the past two years. In that time we have mourned
for Past Grand Master Bro. Michael Arnold, Past Grand Master Bro.
Samuel C. Perkins, Past Grand Master Bro. Conrad B. Day, and
Junior Grand Warden Bro. Charles M. Swain, and to-day we mourn
Past Grand Master Bro. George E. Wagner.

as

138

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

" Succeeding Grand Master Bro. Henry W. Williams upon his
death, he acted as Grand Master for the remainder of the year,
eleven months. The two succeeding years he was elected and served
as Grand Master of Masons in Pennsylvania.
" It was my privilege to serve as an officer of the Grand Lodge
during those three years, and to be brought into close contact and
relationship with Bro. Wagner during that period, when my feelings
for him ripened from Fraternal regard to personal affection and
admiration. I was deeply impressed with his courtesy and kindness and consideration for every one with whom his duties as
Grand Master brought him in contact. Wise and just, lenient and
considerate, he never forgot the dignity and· responsibility of his
office.
"Could I as ably fulfil the duties of the office during my term,
I would be satisfied.
"He died Saturday, September 30, 1904, at low twelve. He leaves
only a memory, but it is the memory of a just and upright man, a
conscientious citizen, a brave soldier, and a loyal and faithful servant of Freemasonry."

A. Tennis, and several Brethren.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

" In former years it was not found necessary to have anything
but the plain work of the Lodge, beautiful in its simplicity and teachings, and nothing can be added to make it more effective,
" I therefore dlrect that the use of vocal and instrumental music
shall cease in the Lodges during the Work of the Degrees.
"If the brethren of the Lodge desire music, they can have it
when no Work is being done, and provided it does not delay the
business, or the conferring of the Degrees.
" This Edict must be audibly read in your Lodge, at its next
stated meeting, and copied in full in the Minutes.
"Yours fraternally,

the river, always in touch with the main Body concerning its principles and policy. The present review is of the administration of

The Committee on the 'Vebb Monument and Grounds reported as
follows:
"The undersigned Committee on the Webb Monument and
Grounds in the North Burial Ground, beg leave to state that there
is nothing new to state in regard to their condition.
"The ground is kept in perfect order, and the monument to that
illustrious Mason, Thomas Smith Webb, being constructed of marble,
shows some signs of deterioration, which is only natural, after having been exposed to the elements for so many years·; but it is looking
well, nevertheless, and will probably continue to do so for many
years, or until the 'Webb Monument Fund' amounts to a sufficient
sum to provide a new monument of the more durable granite."

TENNESSEE.
19,420 Members.
430 Lodges.
The Grand Lodge of Tennessee held its Ninety-first Annual Communication in Freemasons' Hall, Nashville, January 25, 1905, commencing at 10 o;clock A. M.,-M. ". W.'. James Lloyd Sloan, Grand
Master; R.'. W.'. John Berry Garrett, Grand Secretary. Four hundred and fifteen Lodges were represented. Twenty-one Past Grand
Masters, one hundred and eight Past Masters and five District Lee•
turers were in attendance.
A portrait of M.'. W.'. James W. Irwin, Grand Master-elect, appears on the opening page of this number of the Journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form after prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master named the standing corµmittees and proceeded
to deliver his Annual Address.
He expressed thanks to God for His goodness in permitting them
to meet again in Annual Comunication. A year has passed since our
last meeting. Did It bring you joy or sadness? Perhaps both; but
it has gone forever, we cannot recall it but may draw wisdom from
the errors and mistakes we have learned later.
He mentioned his observations made while visiting Lodges and
called attention to the lack of business methods he found in many
of them. He referred to and paid affectionate tribute to the fraternal
dead of the year, one of whom we remember as California's Representative in the Grand Chapter, Brother Angel S. Myers. He also
expressed the sympathy of the Grand Lodge of 'l'ennessee with sister
Jurisdictions in mourning for Eminent Sons and Brethren.
Four cornerstones were placed in accordance with the usages and
customs of the fraternity.
In matters of visitation, although prevented from carrying out
his plans in full by sickness in the family, he made the following
splendid record. He says:
"I attended the meetings of my home Lodge many times during
the year, but I did not do so officially, and therefore do not enumerate them as Tisits.
"To 'summarize what the visits mean, and to make them, let me
state that I met over 6,000 Masons in the Lodge rooms, not counting those met at public addresses. I traveled 1,670 miles by private
conveyances. I delivered forty-eight public addresses on Masonry,
all these at the request of the several Lodges asking it. I made 182
visits. I visited every Lodge in twenty-one counties and some in
twenty-four other counties."

Most of the Rulings and Decisions reported by him grew out of
or were dependent upon the local law upon the liquor question, the
following declaration, made by him, which answering many of the
questions, is a good indication of his purposes and rulings upon all
matters affecting the integrity of the Grand Lodge of Tennessee:
, " It became known tci me that some other Orders had rented a
Masonic hall in which to hold their meetings, and that some members of said orders met in the hall on Sundays and played cards,
using the altar as a table. I Immediately ordered the Masonic
Lodge to cancel the contracts as soon as possible, and forbid the
renting to those Orders again which desecrated, or permitted the
desecration of the Masonic altar.
"In my ruling on the liquor question I have endeavored to carry
out the clear meaning of edict 61 and the purpose of this Grand
Lodge as I understand It. I feel certain that this Grand Lodge
will never take any backward steps on this question."
Among the incidents remembered by Grand Master Sloan connected with the record of his administration, the following excerpt
is abundant proof that he was the examplar of one of the cardinal vlr·
tues and one seldom met with in this wicked world, or there would
have been more funerals in Tennessee last year:
" Notice was mailed to 'Friendship' Lodge, No. 229, of the pro·
posed visit of the Grand Master. After a drive of twenty miles
through rain and over muddy roads, I arrived at the Lodge building
and found no one to greet me. I finally found the Secretary of the
Lodge and ascertained he had not received any notice of my coming.
Upon investigation at the post-office the letter was found where it
had beeri two weeks. The Secretary said that he remembered seeing
the letter, but as It was addressed to him as Secretary of the Lodge,
he supposed It was a call for aid to some Lodge or somebody and he
had put it In the Lodge box to await the Lodge meeting. It had not
been opened.
"Notice was malled to the Secretary of 'Flatwoods' Lodge, No.
428. After a ride of fourteen miles, I found no one informed of the
visit. The Secretary's excuse was that the notice said the vislt
would be in the evening or night-he did not know which it would
be, and hence did nothing toward notifying the Brethren. He did
not know the difference, It seems, between afternoon and evening.
" Notice was malled to the Master of ' Hohenwal.d' Lodge, No. 607,
and after a ride of sixteen miles by buggy and ten miles by rail,)
found on arrival that no one knew of the visit. · Next day I accidentally met the Master who c.a ndldly said he got the notice and put
tt in his pocket and forgot it afterwards."

The W. ·. Herbert R. MacMillan, Master or'" Weber" Lodge, No.
6, welcomed the Grand Lodge to Ogden, extending to the members
the freedom and hospitality o! the city.
The Grand Master named the Committee on Credentials, and the
Grand Lodge was "called oft" until 2 o'clock P . M.
The Grand Lodge was "called on," pursuant to adjournment.
The Committee on Credentials reported. The Grand Master named
the other committees and proceeded to deliver his Annual Address.
He referred to history of the Grand Lodge, its progress and present prosperity; he gave a cordial welcome to the Representatives
of the Lodges who had come up to review the past and devise means
for the future advancement of Freemasonry in Utah.
He mentioned the names inscribed on the death roll of the year,
and tend~red to the affiicted ones, the widows and the fatherless,
the sincere sympathy of the Grand Lodge.

He constituted, by prdxy, " Hiram " Lodge, No. 12, and installed
Its officers duiing the recess.
No decisions were reported because none had been asked forcertainly a good reason.
We ·sincerely regret to learn of the misfortune conveyed in the
following brief extract, and shall hope to hear In the very near future of Bro. Dlehl's complete recovery. Meanwhile may the good
Lord comfort and console . him.
"While 'most of us have been enjoying the best of health during
the past year, there has been one who has not been so fortunate. I
refer to our Grand Secretary, .Bro. Christopher Diehl. Shortly
after the last session of the Grand Lodge he was taken down with
la grippe, which confined him to his home for several weeks. A
short time ago he had the misfortune to break his ankle. It is not
necessary to say that he has had the sympathy of all the Brethren,
and the officers and members of the Grand Lodge rejoice that he
has so far recovered as to be able to meet with us on this occasion."
Bro. Diehl's report Is, as usual, a complete record, In brief, of
the working and financial condition of the Grand Lodge of Utah.
The Grand Master received and addressed the Representatives
of other Grand Jurisdictions present, and the Grand Lodge welcomed
them with the Grand Honors.
R.". W.". Senior Grand Warden and Past Master of "Weber"
Lodge, Bro. Sidney Watson Badcon, reminded the assembled Brethren of the reception tendered by "Weber" Lodge this evening, and
cordially requested them and their ladles to be present and participate
in' the festivities.
The Grand Master called the Brethren to their feet to listen to
the report of 'the Committee on Obituaries, Bro. Henry Simon,
chairman. The report was a mournfully eloquent paper devoted to
the remembrance of the good Brethren who had passed to rest.
After the reading, the Grand Honors were given and the report
adopted. The Grand Lodge, upon the recommendation of the Committee on Jurispru.,dence, declined to amend the laws concerning the
vote of Past Masters, giving each a single vote, in lieu of the present
collective vote. That simple question came near destroying the
New York Grand Lodge Oorganlzation some sixty years ago, h ence
we say the Grand Lodge acted wisely.

"At the Annual Communicatiou, held in the City of Mexico,
January 8, 1904, twenty-three Lodges were represented ..
" The Grand Master reported that 'with each year which passes,
the stability of the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico becomes more and
more marked, in, spite of the many obstacles which impede the
growth of true Masonry here.' Regret was expressed that ·this
Grand Lodge had been represented at the Masonic Congress, which
met in Genoa, September, 1902, and we infer that with a clearer
knowledge of the component parts assembled at those meetings, this
Grand Lodge will not furth~r give its countenance thereto.
" In the consideration of several complaints for invasion of
jurisdiction, by the acceptance of material belonging to sister Grand
Jurisdictions, there was evinced a disposition to make amplP. amends.
The Grand Master also recommended :
" ' That the border Lodges exercise the greatest care when receiving applications from those who have come from the Un.i ted
States to fully assure themselves of the actual residence and previ·
ous good character of such applicants.'

the number of deaths to have been one hundred and ninety during

pages be set apart to their memory in our printed proceedings."
He reported no important decisions. He earnestly advocated the
importance of the Past Masters' Degree, and deprecated its too-frequent omission as part of ·the installation ceremonies. There is a
touch of warmth in his closing words. We quote:
"We are told by travelers that amidst the Arabian hills is a
valley given up t o the culture of odorous shrubs and spices, where
the air is redolent with fragrance. Going away, the visitor finds
that the perfume clings to the hair and garments for days. May
this Annual ·communication of the Grand Lodge of Vermont be so
harmonious, uplifting and soul-inspiring that we · shall go away
charmed with, and strengthened by, the spirit of brotherly love,
and our lives made fragrant with nobler and more earnest desires
to bless and uplift mankind."

REPORT ON ConnESPONDENCE.

Telegraphic congratulations were exchanged with the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin.
Past Grand Master Kittredge Haskins, Chairman of Committee
on Grievances,. reported none in sight.
Referring to the Grand Master's mention of the Past Masters'
Degree, the Committee on Jurisprudence reported in accordance
with the usage and custom of legitimate Masonry, as follows: .
"From information which your committee has received, as well
as from personal knowledge, we believe that practically all, if not all,
Masters in this Jurisdiction have had the Past Master's Degree either
conferred upon or communicated to them, and to infer that such
is not the case from the mere. fact that no report has been made to
the Grand Secretary, would, we think, be hardly warranted; and, if
a Master who had not had the Past Master's Degree were to preside
in a Lodge and confer degrees, Masons so made would not be, in our
opinion, clandestine, but such a course should never be permitted or
tolerated by the Grand Lodge.
" Our law upon this subject is plain, and any violation of it in
the future by a Subordinate Lodge, should be considered cause for
citing such Lodge to show cause why its charter should not be forfeited."
T UE R ECOUD OF A VETERAN.

The annual election of officers being in order, the Grand Master
called to the East, with the request that he would preside during
the election, Past Grand Master Nathan P. Bowman, which request
drew from the M. ·. W. ·. Past Grand Master the following remarkable
record. Bro. Bowman, addressing the Grand Lodge, said:
" I appreciate the honor of having been called upon once more to
preside at the e lection of officers of the Grand Lodge, and I wish to
make a few remarks.
"There have been since I was made a Mason, fifty-five executive
session s of this Grand Body, fifty-one of which I have attended, my
a bsence during the other four being caused one year by reason of
serving as a soldier in the Civil War, and three years by sickness and
death in my family.
"A large number of years I have presided at t he. election of t he
officers of this Gra nd Lodge, but with the weight of eighty-three
years resting upon me, with poor eye-sight and rather feeble health,
I feel my inabiUty to participate in the a ctive duties of this Grand
Lodge, and must r espectfully ask to be excused from presiding at
this election.

IlEPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

159

" I thank you, Sir, for the honor of being invited, but must respectfully decline.
"As I realize that the infirmities of age are creeping on, and that
life at all times is uncertain, and that it is possible I may not meet
with you again in Grand Lodge, it would be, and is, my reques t that
when the time of earthly dissolution comes, the Grand Lodge may
perform for me the last sad rites.
"Most Worshipful Grand Master and Bret hren, I thank you for
your innumerable Fraternal courtesies."

.
After a brief introduction reverting to the early days of his
forty years' active experience in the Fraternity, he reported the
routine of business transacted during the ~ecess; first, however,
referring to the Brethren who had passed to rest since the last
Annual Communication. He referred with much feeling to his

Communication of this Grand Body, his hearty hand of congratula-

" His last rites were attended with Masonic honors by the Grand
Lodge under charge of Bros. K. Kemper and J. W. Eggleston, respectively Deputy Grand Master and Grand Junior Warden, as it was almost impossible for me to attend personally.''
He made several visitations, placed several corner-stones of
public buildings and monuments.
Among his rulings under the head of "Decisions," we note one
that would put an end to some of the radical legislation on the
liquor question; for instance,
" That a By-Law stating that no petition for initiation can be
entertained from a person engaged in the liquor business, either as
proprietor, manager, or salesman, is illegal."
He expresses himself decidedly on the question of the duty of
the Grand Master to keep in touch with the Craft by visiting his
constituent Lodges, in the following:
" I believe in personal visitation in response to invitations from
the Craft. Each response takes time and money. The first . item is
mine, and for which I make no charge, and the second is yours.
Kindly accept this in explanation of my expense account, which I
have been informed is, comparatively, largely in excess of th,e aggregate expenditures of the two preceding Grand Masters."
His address was referred to the Past Grand Masters present for
division and reference.

address.

clearly dependent upon the law of Washington for decision.

" Exemplar" of a good Grand Secretary, Bro. Thomas M. Reed, and
here in California we respond: So say we all.

A DESERVED TRIBUTE.
M.' . W.'. Bro. Joseph Kuhn presented the following resolution,
which, on motion, was referred to the Committee on Finance:
" WHEREAS: Our Venerable Brother, Thomas M. Reed, having
served this Grand Lodge faithfully since its organization in 1858,
and as its Grand Secretary for forty·two years; and,
"WHEREAS:. Owing to his physical condition and the growing In·
firmities of age he finds it almost impossible, not only to perform the
requisite labor· of his office, but to endure the mental strain con·

165

nected therewith; and, having expressed a desire to be relieved in
some way by this Grand Lodge from its heavy responsibilities; and,
"WHEREAS: The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Washington
recognizes his unusual ability and untiring service· in its behalf
during the past half-century, feels that it is not only due him, but
that the Grand Lodge is honoring itself by continuing him as a
permaneni officer of this Grand Body; therefore, be it
"Resolved, That the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of Washington hereby
elects and appoints M.'. W.'. Bro. Thomas Milburne Reed as its
Emeritus 'Grand Secretary, with a salary of one hundred dollars a
month during the remainder of his natural life."
The following resolution was presented by M.'. W.' . Bro. Y. C.
Blalock, and, on motion, adopted:
"WHEREAS: Our W.'. and Rev. Bro. William Pelan, Grand Chaplain, unable to be present at this Annual Communication owing to
his enfeebled condition and advanced age; therefore, be it
"Resolved, That the R. ·. w. ·. Grand Secretary extend the sympathies of this Grand Lodge to our Venerable Brother under the seal
of the Grand Lodge."
The Committee on Finance submitted the following report, which,
on motion, was adopted:
"We, your Finance Committee, to whom was referred the resolution introduced by P. G. M. Joseph A. Kuhn, in regard to electing
P. G. M. Thomas M. Reed as Grand Secretary Emeritus, respectfully
report as follows :
"We have consulted with Bro. Reed a11d have gone over the
entire matter and we believe that it would be to the best interst of
the Grand L~dge that he be continued as Grand Secretary; and we,
therefore, recommend that the resolution be not adopted."
Although it was thought best at this time not to adopt the preamble and resolution, yet the tribute remains "of record."

WESTERN AUSTRALIA.
69 Lodges.

3,348 Members.
The Grand Lodge of Western Australia held a Quarterly Communication at Fi:e-emasons' Hall, Perth, January 27, 1905-M.'. W.'.
the Rt. Rev. C. 0 . L. Riley, D. D., Grand Master; the V.'. W.'. Bro.
J. D. Stevenson, Gra~d Secretary. Twenty Lodges were represented,
and there was a full attendance of Grand Officers, Past Grand Offlcers
and Past Masters.
Beautiful portraits of the M.'. W.'. Michael Sanson Pro Grand
Master, and the R.'. W.'. Arthur McMullen, Past Deputy Grand Master, in full ceremonial dress, appear In this number of the journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form.
The proceeuings of this meeting are almost wholly devoted to a
special report on the correspondence which had passed between the
Grand Secretaries of the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland re·
garding the sovereign rights of Scotland In the province of Western
Australia, and other matters relating thereto.
The concensus of testimony is In favor of the Grand Lodge of
Wester-n Australia, and its position in refusing to recognize Lodges
instituted within its territory by the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
subsequent to the organization of this Grand Lodge, is fully warranted. This Grand Lodge is also to be commended for the course

IlEPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

167

adopted with reference to the old Lodges of the Scottish Constitution and their members.
"When the Grand Lodge of Western Australia was inaugurated
In February, 1900, thirty-three private· Lodges acknowledged allegiance. There are to-day sixty-nine Lodges owing fealty to the
Sovereign Grand Lodge of Western Australia, being an increase of
thirty-six-more than doubling the original body. The increase is
made up by twenty-five new Lodges consecra~ed, and eleven Lodges
that have sJnce affiliated from the other Constitutions. Last year
the numi:Jer of financial members on the books amounted to 2,980,
while this year the number is 3,348, showing an increase of 368. No
less a number than 411 have been initiated during the twelve months
ending December 31st last. Owing to the large number of Free·
masons that have made Western Australia their place of residence
during the last few years, I have prepared a return of affiliating
members, showing the Constitutions they have joined from. During
the last four years our ranks have been increased by no less than
734 joining members."
The Grand Lodge of Costa Rica was recognized as a just and legal
Grand Lodge.
The Grand Officers were installed and the Grand Anniversary
Festival held on thP- evening of April 28th.
The first toast, " Our King and Patron," was proposed by the
Grand Master, and the "Tyler's Toast" and "Auld Lang Syne," followed by "God Save the King," closed the ceremonies of the Communication.

WISCONSIN.
Zl,261 Members.
The Grand Lodge of Wisconsin held its Sixty-first Annual Communication in the Masonic Building, M!lwaukee, June 13th, ll}06,
commencing at 2 o'clock P. M.,-the M.'. W.'. David H. Wright,
Grand Master; R.'. W.'. William W. Perry, Grand Secretary. Two
hundred and thirty-nine Lodges were represented, together with
forty-two other Grand Jurisdictions. Fourteen Past Grand Masters,
two Past Grand Deputies and twelve Past Grand Wardens were in
attendance.
" In Memoriam " portraits of Past Grand Master E. E. Chapin,
who was Grand Master in 1880-81, and Past Grand Master Oliver
Libbey, who was Grand Master in 1884-85, appear in this number
of the Journal.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form. The Grand
Master named the Committee on Credentials and proceeded to de·
liver his Annual Address. He gave the Brethren a cordial welcome
and said ."The . Grand Chaplain has Invoked the Divine Blessing"
and we are ready for the Work before us.
Before reporting his official Acts he directed the attention of the
Brethrlln to the death roll of the year, closing with the assembling
of the present Annual Communication with the names of 338

The reports of several committees having been considered and
disposed of the motion of Past Grand Master Aldro Jenks, Grand
Lodge adopted the following:
"WHEREAS, Brother David H . Wright having for many years
endeared himself to the Craft in Wisconsin, by reason of his loving
service and manly qualities, and having during the past year discharged the arduous duties pertaining to the office of Grand Master
of Masons of. this Grand Jurisdiction, with marked ability, zeal and
fldelity; therefore, be it
"Resolved, That in token of our veneration and fraternal regard
for him, he be presented with a suitable Past Grand Master's Jewel."
The election of officers for the ensuing year was held and the
following Brethren were chosen:
Jesse C. Bradley, Milwaukee, Grand Master; Edwin J. Farr, Eau
Claire, Deputy Grand Master; Spencer M. Marsh, Neillsville, Senior
Grand Warden; Wesley J. Cochrane, Fox Lake, Junior Grand
Warden ; James M. Pereles, Milwaukee, Grand Treasurer; William
W. Perry, Milwaukee, Grand Secretary,
The Grand Master-elect having made his appointments, all were
installed by Past Grand Master Nathan C. Giffin, Past Grand Master
Aldro Jenks acting as Master of the ceremonies.
The Grand Secretary in his report says:
" It has been the custom from time immemorial, of the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin, to wait one year after the Brother is out of
office before presenting a Past Grand Master's Jewel. It is a custom
which the dignified Grand Body has not departed from, and it can
be safely said that only such an occasion as the present one, perhaps, w!ll ever cause the Brethren to change the custom, but owing

WYOMING.
1,649 Members.
23 Lodges.
The Grand Lodge of Wyoming held its Thirtieth Annual Communication in Evanston, August 17th, 1904,-M.'. W.'. T. S. Taliaferro, Grand Master; R.'. W.'. W. L. Kuy Kendall, Grand Secretary.
Sixteen Lodges were represented. Five Past Grand Masters and
twenty-five Past Masters were present.
A portrait of the Grand Master-elect, F. A. Luckfield, appears on
the opening page.
The Grand Lodge was opened in Ample Form with prayer by the
Grand Chaplain.
The Grand _Master named the Committee on Credentials and then ~
presented to Grand Lodge a welcome visitor in the person of the
R.'. W .'. Bro. Christopher Diehl, the Veteran Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge of Utah. Needless to say he was welcomed and saluted
with the Grand Honors.
The Grand Master delivered his Annual Address. He said the
rapid flight of time had so absorbed the recess of Grand Lodge that

He had visited many of the Lodges and was everywhere received
with the kindness and coutesy universal among Masons. He paid
affectionate tribute to the Brethren who had passed to rest during
the recess, as also to those of other Jurisdictions who had been
called Home.
No important decisions were reported. He issued Dispensations
for the forming and opening of two new Lodges, one at Glenrock
and the second at Chugwater.
The Deputy Grand Master submitted his report of his duties during the absence of the Grand Master from the Jurisdiction.
The Grand Secretary made his report, from which we excerpt the
following abstract of Work:

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

A most excellent report Is the present, being his nineteenth, by
Brother W. L. Kuy Kendall. To say that simply it Is a good review
does not do justice to the author of this excellent review of the Masonic world. He notices California for the administration of Grand
Master Henderson, and gives It the benefit of his good opinion as he
do.is also the Oration of Grand Orator Hart. He pronounces· Bro.
Hart's application of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity to Masonry
to be "very good." In his conclusion he refers to a paper of Bro.
Speeds that we hope to find room for somewhere:
" In concluding this, our Nineteenth Report, we Incorporate the
following from the pen of that able Masonic jurist, Brother Frederick Speed of Mississippi, as the same was printed in the Shibboleth, with the statement that it is in accord with our contention
for years past regarding every point treated therein. It Is time that
the cloak of mystery claims, having no foundation in fact, and so·
called Masonic histories, based upon assumed theories for which
there is not the slightest foundation, should be ignored and completely discarded."
M.'. W.'. Frank A. Luckfleld, Grand Master ; R.'. W.'. William L.
Kuy Kendall, Grand Secretary. Correspondent, Bro. Wm. L. Kuy
Kendall, Saratoga.

neau Grand Lodge of Ohio." At the same time we remind our
Brethren and call their attention to the difference between "clandestine" and "Irregular Masons" ~ "A clandestine Mason Is one
who received the degrees In a lodge unlawfully existing." "An Irregular Mason is one who 'received the degrees In an irregular manner in a lawfully constituted Lodge."
A clandestine Mason has no Masonic standing, and cannot be
healed.
An irregular Mason has Masonic standing, and It is only necessary to correct the irregularlt.y in his making to enable him to enter
himself on the Tyler's register as a just and upright Mason.

additional Report covering each and every item of this work, which
