Afternoon Session,
Tuesday, October 9th, A. L. 5906.
The Grand Lodge was called on at two o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to
the Grand Lodge, as follows:Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
One year ago, as we gathered together in this b eautiful city, the
metropolis of the Pacific Coast, teeming with industry and prosperity, we little thought of the change which would be effected in so
short a time; but we can all give thanks to Him who does all things
well, that in our hour of need the Grand Jurisdictions of the world
poured forth their relief quickly and generously, and that in our
State we had the necessary men of courage, honesty and ability to
handle the relief matters in a most satisfactory manner, but, better
still, they had the tenacity and unity of purpose to determine to
rebuild our demolished and burned sections of the State better and
more substantial than before.
Brethren, you who have not visited the stricken sections of our
State prior to the convening of our Grand Lodge can have no conception of the bravery of our citizens, when, immediately following the
disaster and fire of April 18th, last, the men of California, with the
pioneer spirit of '49, determined that the California of the future
should be far better, more solid and substantial than before. What
has been accomplished to date speaks volumes for these men of courage, a nd from my observations I believe, and I am sure you will agree
with me that in a short period of time our metropolis and other
injured ~ities near by will soon be a credit and joy to all Californians.
The r elief work incident to the disaster of April 18th last having
been such an important matter, and involving so many different
points, I have deemed it best to submit to the Grand Lodge an

Our Grand Jurisdiction has suffered severely during the past year
in the loss of two of our Past Grand Masters: M. :. W. :. William
Johnston, who was Grand Master in 1891, entered into rest November
14, 1905. The Grand Lodge was specially convened at Sacramento,
November 18th, and the last and solemn duties to our dead Brother
were performed by the Grand Lodge, with Past Grand Master Edmund C. Atkinson in charge of the ceremonies.

M:. w:. Hiram N. Rucker, who was Grand Master in 1887,
passed to the Great Beyond December 13, 1905. The Grand Lodge
was specially convened at Merced, December 16th, a nd before the
largest concourse of citizens ever gathered in that city the beautiful
ceremonies of our Order were conducted by R. :. W. '.. Edward H. Hart,
Deputy Grand Master.
Both of t hese Brethren will be greatly missed at our Grand Lodge,
but their kindly faces, their genial words of greeting and their able
advice on all important questions will live in our memories until time
shall be no more. The very sudden and unfortunate accident which
befell Brother Past Grand Master Rucker and caused his untimely
death was a decided loss to our Widows 1 and Orphans 1 Home, over
which institution he was Superintendent, and the able and entirely
satisfactory manner i.n which our Brother performed his duties
makes the loss to our Fraternity doubly hard.
·
I have take:fl. the liberty to appoint as a Special Memorial Committee on the death of Past Grand Masters Johnston and Rucker
Brothers Past Grand Masters E dmund C. Atkinson, }'rank M. Angellotti and James A. Foshay, and recommend that a s.l'ecial hour be set
apart for the r eading of the Report of this Committee.
Owing to the destruction of our entire Grand Lodge records, and,
in fact, all papers connected with the Grand Secretary's office, it is
not possible to give t he full list of deaths of t,he Grand Officers o.f
other Grand Jurisdictions, except those received subsequent to April
18th last. It is greatly to be regretted that proper tribute and respect
cannot be shown in this Address to the honored dead of other Grand
Jurisdictions, but probably that can be corrected next year, when
notifications from our other bodies have been received. We mourn
with our Sister Jurisdictions the loss of the following Brethren:

New Lodges.

Condition of Our Jurisdiction.
It is with pleasure that I am able to report to you that, notwithstanding the unfortunate casualties of a few months since, ·the
general condition of Masonry within our Jurisdiction is most satisfactory in every respect. The returns for last year show a member·
ship, on July 31, 1905, o"f 31,561; the returns for this year show a
· membership of 33,769, a net gain of 2,208.
Lodges located at points most seriously injured have undoubtedly
felt the effect of the disaster, and I have in a number of caseB
authorized Lodges to return the fees of petitioners where the appli·
cants had presented their petitions for degrees prior to April 18th,
last, and which petitions were to be acted upon at the meeting subsequent to April 18th, and where it further appeared that the petitioners
or applicants required the amount of the fees for the support of
themselves or their families, and were in no financial condition to
lose the cost of the fees or to take tlle degrees. While ,I acted without
legal authority in these cases, it was in the interest of charity and
humanity.

Lodges Constituted.
Lodges for which charters were issued at the last Annual Communication wer e regularly constituted as follows:

Hart, Deputy Grand Master;
"Oceanic" Lodge, No. 371, by Worshipful Joshua D. Tucker;
"South Pasadena" Lodge, No. 367, "Unity" Lodge, No. 368, and
"Ocean Park" Lodge, No. 369, by the Grand Master in person;
" Amity" Lodge, No. 370, by Right Worshipful Edward H. Hart,
Deputy Grand Master.

Under the Resolution, · adopted at the last Annual Communication, reading as follows:
"Resolved, That the Grand Master issue a Dispensation to 'Veteran' Lodge, located at Sawtelle, Los Angeles county, California, if
upon examination he finds that all the provisions of our Masonic law
have been complied with; that no fee be charged for such Dispensation, and t he same be remitted by this Grand Lodge; that when
such Lodge shall have complied with our law and this Grand Lodge
orders a Charter issued to it, that no charge be made for such Charter,
and all fees therefor be remitted,"
Dispensation was issued to "Veteran" Lodge, at Sawt.elle, Los An·
geles county. It is with pleasure that I report that the old soldiers
deeply and sincerely appreciate the action of this Grand Body, and
I find from personal visits that the L odge is doing a great and noble
work. They have at this time seventy members on the roll, and I
trust that, in accordance with the Resolution of the Grand Lodge, a
Charter will be issued, and no charge be made for t he same.

Immediately following the disaster of April 18th last I called upon
the Master of each Lodge in the district which suffered on that fateful morning, asking for full and complete reports of their condition.
I found that in ·a large number of instances Masonic Temples and
places of meeting had been badly injured to such an extent that meetings could not be held therein. I issued instructions for the Masters
to make the best po,ssible arrangements under the circumstances, following as closely as possible to our Constitution and General Regulations, and if necessary temporarily change the meeting nights until
such time as the normal conditions would be resumed. It was a matter
that required immediate action; hence I acted promptly in every case
and was naturally compelled in a large extent to rely upon the wisdom
and the judgment o~ the Masters of the various Lodges.

Amendments to By-Laws.
Amendments to By-Laws have been presented in a number of cases
for approval, and of such amendments which have been approved by
me I presume have been lost with the records of the Grand Secretary's
office, but no amendment has been approved until said amendment
conformed in every respect to the uniform Code of By-Laws. It is
certainly to be regretted that many of our Secretaries are not familiar
with our regulations. It has been necessary for me to return, sometimes two and three times, these proposed amendments for correction.
Charters.

October 8th, corner-stone, Masonic Temple, Santa Rosa, Grand
Master officiating.
Special Dispensations.
During the year quite a large number of requests have been made
upon me for special dispensations to reballot on petitions of rejected
candidates. I presume the major portion of these records were
burned; hence I can only state that no dispensation has been granted
by me to reballot on rejected candidates without the fullest investigation, and in practically every case it has been shown that the
rejection was caused by mistaken identity. I have kept a record of
the reballoting on all rejected candidates for which dispensations
were issued, and am pleased to state that in each and every case the
candidate was elected. In several cases I have refused dispensations
to reballot on rejected candidates for the reason that I did not believe
that the facts as stated justified the issuing or granting of such dispensations.

Many Charters were burned or destroyed in April last, and it has
not been possible as yet to renew them. I have therefore authorized
all Lodges which did not have charters at this time to continue to act
and work as if the charters were in their possession. Just as soon as
the Lithographing company can renew our Charters duplicates should
be issued to all the Lodges requiring the same.
Regalia.
I will state for the benefit of the m'e mbers of the Grand Lodge
that this body owned two sets of regalia; one of which was used for
ceremonies taking place outside of San Francisco and the other being
the new regalia recently purchased for use at our Annuil.l Communications. Both of these magnificent sets of regalia were consumed in
the :fire of April last, but fortunately the Grand Secretary in his wisdom had one thousand dollars insurance on the same and by my direction he has undertaken to replace one of the sets which the manufacturer has promised for use at this Annual Communication.

Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles.

tions arrive here without funds, and frequently with families entirely
dependent, but with the hope of securing employment; and in hun·

refused to accept financial assistance, and, in fact, declined charity.
All they desired was an opportunity to secure honest employment.

Brother C. W. Bush, a member of the Fraternity residing in Los
Angeles, California, died some eighteen months since, leaving a portion of his estate h> the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles.
Owing to the peculiar laws of. this State, it was thought at one time
that the Board of Relief of Los Angeles would not be able to secure
this property, but by the active and energetic efforts of Brother
Samuel Prager, President of the Board, and Brother August Wackerbarth, executor of the estate, said Masonic Board of Relief, to thoroughly protect itself and to protect the interests of the l!'raternity,
duly incorporated under the laws of the State of California, and on
August 1st came into possession of the property, consisting of. a
two-story brick building at the corner of Los Angeles and Market
streets, in Los Angeles City, of the appraised value of $33,000.00;
also, two unimproved pieces of property in Los Angeles City of the
appraised value of $12,196.99, making the total appraised value of
the estate turned over to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles
$45,196.99.
The present income of this property is two hundred and twenty
dollars per month. Unfortunately, a few days after the Board came
into possession of the property a fire occurred in the building at Los
Angeles and Market streets, causing a damage of several hundred
dollars. This, however, was covered by insurance, which will probably
fully protect the Board. In order that the Fraternity will be pro·
tected in years to come, it will be necessary for this Board to place
the property on an income basis, which will undoubtedly necessitate
the selling of the unimproved property and the making of further
improvements in the building at Los Angeles and Market streets, the
balance to be invested in other income-bearing property or securities.
Consequently, this Grand Body will probably be called upon to make
its usual contribution to the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles
for the coming year, and after that, when their property is placed
upon an income-producing basis, or within one year, the necessary
contribution to said Masonic Board of Relief can be materially reduced.
Masonic Employment Bureau of Los Angeles.
After a connection of nearly ten years with the Masonic Board of
Relief of Los Angeles, and a thorough study of the situation, I felt
that, as California is the Mecca of thousands of people from the
East, who visit our Golden State by reason of its mild climate or in
search of health, many of our Brethren from the Eastern Jurisdic-

Believing that our Fraternity could set a good example in this
way, I prevailed upon the Scottish Rite Bodies, Chapters and Com·
mandery of Los Angeles to make monthly donations for one year to
open a Masonic Employment Bureau. This Bureau was opened for
business November 15, 1905. A regular office is maintained in the
Masonic Temple in Los Angeles, which is open from 9 · a. m. to 12,
noon, and is in charge of a competent Secretary, whose duty it is to
secure written applications from worthy Masons and their dependent s
desiring employment, and then each afternoon to visit all employers
and endeavor to place our deserving Brethren in positions. The
results have been more than satisfactory, and I am pleased to state
that the Masonic Employment Bureau of Los Angeles, during the te~
~onths of its operation, has made a most magnificent showing, as the
following Report from the Secretary of said Bureau will show:

Wit.bin the past sixty days Brother Reuben H. Lloyd secured a

been a splendid and magnificent monument to Masonry to erect a

the fire changed the situation very materially ·in San Francisco, and
it is my judgment that the action in selling the property at the price
W.ven was a decided advantage to the Fraternity. The Committee in

requested by me to hold the money intact as long as possible, or until
after this Grand Body should meet, in order that i =ediate action
could be taken whereby a Temple, a credit to Masonry and to this
Grand Body, should be erected.

Printing List of Members.

As the membership of this Grand Jurisdiction increases the work
of the Grand Master necessarily increases in proportion; consequently
it is a serious question as to the amount of time the Grand ]\faster
can devote to the correspondence and questions brought up for decision, which time might be saved had the Masters and Secretaries
followed the plain rules and instructions laid down by our Constitution and in Anderson's Manual.

At our last Annual Communication a Special Committee on the
publication of the proceedings of this Grand Body recommended that
the rosters of Lodges formerly published in the proceedings of this
Grand Body be so modified that only the name, number and address
of the Lodge, name and address of the Master, name and address of
the Secretary, and the time of the stated meeting be published. The
Committee on Finance in their Report, which was adopted by the
Grand Lodge, recommended as follows:
''Omit therefrom the rosters of the various Lodges, and insert in
lieu thereof tabulated statement showing the number and name of each
Lodge, together with the names of the Master and Secretary thereof
and the date and place· of meeting.''
In my judgment, after careful and mature deliberation and_ after
investigation of the work of the various Relief Boards incident to the
disaster of April 18th last, it is a serious mistake not to publish the
names of the members of our Grand Jurisdiction in good standing. I
do not maintain that it is necessary that the same should be in the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge, but it is my idea that at the annual
meetings of the various Lodges of this Jurisdiction held during December of each year there is a general overhauling of the records and
delinquent members are suspended; hence, on January 1st of each year
practically all of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction have accurate and
complete rolls of their members, and as the election takes place in all
Lodges during December it is my judgment that it is wise and expedient to publish early in January a complete roster of each and every
Lodge of this Grand Jurisdiction showing newly elected and appointive officers and members in good standing, and have the same properly
distributed to each constituent Lodge of this Grand Jurisdiction.
During our relief work of last April hun~reds of applications were
made by Masons of this jurisdiction and. we had no data to work
upon except the proceedings of 1904, the last published that gave the
list of members, and it was a real necessity that a later and more
correct list of members be secured. I am sure that any member of
this Grand Body who was in active participation in the relief work
will coincide with my views and agree that it is essential for the

Decisions.

I find from experience that many questions are asked which could
have bee'n readily detetmined by a little thought or perhaps a careful
study of the books which should be in every Lodge room. However,
there have been more or less important questions which I deemed
best to present to you for determination as to whether they involved
points which should be finally decided by this Grand Body. Perhaps I
may be criticised for making my explanations too lengthy, but I find
on reviewing my correspondence that a lengthy answer fully explaining all points is better understood than a short decision; hence all of
my questions and my decisions are given herewith in detail.
Written complaint having been made to me by three Past Masters
of "Hermann" Lodge, No. 127, that one Brother M. S., a member
of said Lodge, forwarded a letter under date of May 1, 1905, to
''Hermann'' Lodge, requesting a dimit, and at the stated. meeting,
held on the same day, said dimit was granted to him by resolution of the
Lodge, his dues having been paid in full at that time. The same
brother, in a communication dated June 30, 1905, forwarded his dues
for the months of May, June and July, and requested to be placed in
good standing in "Hermann" Lodge, advising that his actfon was
hasty on his part and that he desired to be reinstated in said Lodge
after a membership of twenty-three years.
At the stated meeting of said Lodge, held July 3, 1905, said communication was read, and, on motion, it was unanimously resolved to
grant the prayer of Brother S., take back his dimit and regard him as
a member of said "Hermann" Lodge in good standing.
The three Past Masters before referred to made objections to this
procedure, claiming it was contrary to the regulations of the Grand
Lodge, but no action was taken and the matter was, in due course of
time, referred to me :in a communication dated September 20, 1905.

to advise the Master and members of "Hermann" Lodge that their

Brother could not be considered a member of said Lodge, for the reason that a similar case had been fully decided by the Grand Lodge
at the Session of 1864, set forth in Section 91 of Anderson's Manual,
reading as follows:

diction and joins another Lodge in this ·Jurisdiction he carries with

''When a member of a Lodge has paid his dues, and at a stated
meeting announces his intention to withdraw, his membership ceases,
and he can become a member again of that Lodge only by petition
and ballot, as in the case of any other non-affiliated Mason. It is not
competent for the Lodge by vote to reinstate him.''

authorized to expend, ~n each Masonic year, a sum not exceeding five

by the Lodge for the Entered Apprentice degree.''
Which, to my mind, answered the question propounded, and that was
that the entered Apprentice is still an Entered Apprentice and should
be carried on the Rolls as such, unless he has committed some act, or
in the future commits some act which requires that charges be preferred against him in the regular manner. The approval of the Grand
Lodge showing that the fee should be returned, less the amount
charged by the Lodge for the Entered Apprentice degrees shows
clearly that the applicant continues in the Lodge as an Entered Apprentice, even if denied advancement.

And also instructed them to note that the wording of the regulation
is ''total r evenue for the preceding Masonic year,'' consequently the
rental derived from the local Order of the Eastern Star was in that
case part of the revenue of their Lodge, and said funds could not be
diverted for the purpose of refreshments.

Certificate of Membership.

"Has a Lodge, or the Worshipful Master thereof, the right to
create a salaried office not mentioned or enumerated in the By-Laws of
the Lodgef Is such an appointment lawfulf"
This question was brought out by a resolution adopted by "Doric"
Lodge as follows:
''That the Master be empowered to appoint an instructor, said in·
structor must be a member of ''Doric'' Lodge, for the purpose of
assisting candidates in the lectures of the first and second degrees.
Said instructor to ·receive a compensation of five dollars for each
candidate instructed by him.''
In the Uniform Code of By-Laws adopted by this Grand Lodge
there is no provision for the appointment of such an officer as an
Inst:i:uctor. Under our Constitution it is provided that no Lodge shall
advance an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft to a higher degree
until after a strict examination in open Lodge he shall have given
satisfactory evidence that he is entirely proficient and well qualified
in that or those he has already taken; thus being clearly noted that it
is the duty of the candidate to be properly prepared. There is no
doubt as to the right of the Master, without the consent of the Lodge,
to appoint a brother to instruct a candidate; the real question is as
to the right to pay for such service from the Lodge funds. It appears
that when the resolution was adopted by "Doric" Lodge many can·
didates were appearing for examination, and hardly two had the same
work. It is undoubtedly at times a hardship on the Master of a
Lodge and on the Brethren to be required to teach a candidate the
lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees. After
a thorough and mature deliberation it is my opinion, as our laws now
exist, that Lodge funds cannot be used for the purpose of paying an
instructor, but the question as to whether or not it would be a ma·
terial advantage to our Fraternity if all candidates were taught the
work uniformly and might not materially reduce the work imposed
upon some of our Brethren in Lodges which are increasing rapidly in
membership by having a paid instructor should be given careful con·
sideration. Hence, I have not decided the question, but refer it to the
Grand Lodge for a decision as to the expediency of creating such an
office and having it paid by the Lodge if deemed best by any Lodge
of this Jurisdiction to do so, or to amend our uniform Code of B.y·
Laws to cover all points involved in the question presented.

Complaint was made to me by a member of "Palo Alto" Lodge,
No. 346, that on March 1st he preferred charges against a member of
that Lodge. On March 31st, at 9:30 p. m., the :first stated meeting
following the trial, the Master announced the result of the trial, the
penalty being found to be a reprimand.
On April 30th, at 4:30 p. m., complainant alleges that he personally
gave the Master written notice of appeal, the Master, however, noti·
fied him that his notice of appeal did not come within the limit
specified by the Constitution. I advised the Master of the Lodge and
the complainant that according to the Constitution an appeal may be
taken to the Grand Lodge by either party at its next succeeding
annual communication, but not unless notice of such intended appeal
shall be- given to the Master in writing within thirty days after his
announcement of the result of the trial, and it was my judgment that
this appeal should have been received any time on April 30th up to
midnight of that day, the first of the thirty days being April 1st,
and the last day being April 30th.

My answer to this letter was dated December 9th, and was as
follows:
''Referring to your favor of the 4th regarding life membership in
your Lodge, also referring to the copy of By-Laws of your Lodge and
calling m;y attention to Article VIII, Sec. 3, which provides how life
memberships may be established in your Lodge, permit me to call
your attention to the fact that the copy of By-Laws as submitted was
apparently revised November 12, 1903. If that be a fact, I can not
understand why this Section regarding life memberships should be
in your by-Laws. Please note Section 928, Anderson's Manual, reading as follows:
" 'Sec. 928. No Lodge under the Jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California can establish life memberships by resolution or
in any other manner.'
''This was approved by the Grand Lodge in Session of 1901. Same
was not apparently understood by all Lodges, as you will note by
reading Sections 936 and 937, which are as follows:
" 'Sec. 936. Several Lodges in the Jurisdiction have contended
that the decision of the Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication of
1900, relative to Life Membership, did not prevent them from issuing life memberships where a standing resolution or by-law passed
prior to and in force at the time of the decision so provided. I have
decided that a life membership is not established by the mere passing
of a resolution providing for it, but that the act of receiving the
money and issuing the certificate constitutes or establishes the life
membership, and that, since said decision, it is improper and illegal
to issue or grant any life membersb,ip or receive any money therefor,
and any and all resolutions or by-laws providing therefor should be
immediately repealed by the Lodge.
" 'Sec. 937. Where a Lodge, prior ta the decision of 1900, has,
by resolution or otherwise, granted a life membership, agreed that
a Brother should be a life member, and enrolled him as such in
accordance with the·agreement, or in any manner created and granted
such life membership, it is then an executed contract between him
and the Lodge, and ~an not be set aside or rescinded without the
consent of both, and ~uch life memberships must stand.'
''This was adopted and approved by the Grand Lodge in Session
of 1902, consequently why should the revised copy of your By-Laws

It was my intention when I assumed the position as Grand Master
to give the Masonic Home considerable attention, but, unfortunately,
other matters of serious importance have prevented, but recently I
had an opportunity of visiting our splendid institution and going
over it very carefully. In my judgment, the Home is well and economically conducted; the Brethren, their wives and the widows who are
domiciled there are certainly well taken care of in every particular.
It was very pleasing to note the neat and healthy appearance of all
the children, and I cannot speak too highly of the excellent care and
motherly devotion of our Matron, Mrs. Rucker, whose heart is undoubtedly wrapped up in the welfare of the children, young and old,
under her c.h arge. It is my opinion that the Trustees are handling
the business of the Home in the best possible manner, and I cannot
see how any great saving can be made. We have erected this magnificent institution, and must conduct it so that it will be a credit to
our Fraternity, and I feel positive that our Trustees are doing everything in their power to follow the teachings of our beloved Order
and looking carefully after the interests of the Grand Lodge. It has
been suggested that it would be more satisfactory to some of the
Lodges if we followed the method adopted by the Southern California Home; that is, to require each Lodge which may place an
adult or a child in the Home to pay for their maintenance, and for
the Grand L0·lge to provide for the fixed charges, suelh as expenditures
for help, Superintendent, Matron, taxes and other charges that must be
maintained to keep .ip the institution, but the cost of food and
supplies given to each inmate shall be paid by the respective Lodges
whom they are charged against. This question was brought up in
Los Angeles, where one Lodge of three hundred and forty members
pays annually three hundred and forty dollars towards the Masonic
Home, and has never had any direct benefits from it, whereas another
Lodge of equal size has had a Brother and his wife as inmates for
several years; hence, as a suggestion, it might be well ·to investigate
the propriety of changing the system, following the lines, as before
stated, of the California Masonic Home Association at San Gabriel.

Dispensation for New Lodge in the Philippine Islands.
During the past few months I have received considerable ·correspondence relat ive. to the establishment of another Lodge in Manila,
Philippine Islands. Papers were in proper form, with the exception
that Certificate of Qualification from a Master of a Lodge was not
transmitted. In view of the fact that this is a .constitutional requirement, I transmitted all papers to our Grand Secretary, with
instructions that it would not be possible for me to sign the Dispensation for this new Lod.ge until this very necessary requirement had
been complied with. At my last interview with our Grand Secretary
I find that this certificate has not as yet b een received, hence there is
no necessity for issuing a Dispensation prior to the meeting of this
Grand Body.
Among the papers asking for this Dispensation .is the approval
of "Manila" Lodge, No. 342; yet by the same mail I r eceived a
let ter from the Master of tha t Lodge, in which he submits certain
arguments showing that it is not altogether advisable to establish
another Lodge at Manila at this time. It might b e well, therefore,
that all correspondence in connection with a new Lodge and papers
.asking for Dispensation be referred to a Committee for investigation
and report to this Grand Body at this Session.
Necessity of a New Lodge at Dinuba.

now recall several cases where certain Lodges have arbitrarily refused

Conclusion.
Finally, my. Brethren, in c.losing my Report, I desire to thank you
one and all for the kindness and courtesy extended to me during the
past Masonic year. I commenced my year's work with the best
intentions in the world, intending it to be one long to be remembereq
in Masonic history, for I anticipated visiting practically all the Lodges
in the State, but my personal business, my health, and the relief work
has prevented. I have, however, been enabled to visit a large number
of our Lodges and have been received with fraternal kindness,
and I assure you that the memory of the cordial greeting, the hearty
hand-clasp, and the words of welcome :from our Brethren will never
be forgotten. Not being gifted with the flow of words required by
our orators, I have not attempted to make speeches during my numerous visits, but have endeavored to impress upon all the Fraternity that
this was to have been a business administration, and if I have succeeded to your satisfaction it will be a source of great pleasure to me.
In visiting different portions of the State I have observed a great
deal o:f discussion regarding "Superior California,'' "Northern California,'' ''Central California,'' and ''Southern California.'' My
.t:!rethrcn, we have in this great State but one California, and that is
the whole and the entire State. If there is any time in our history
when we require united effort it is now, and by this united effort we
can rebuild and make the portion of our State requiring our assistance
far better than before, and I ask you now, one and all, to forget
eve.rything but that one great word, ''California.'' It will require
the highest type of .!itizenship to continue California's reputation
and steady advancement, and nothing can do more in up-building this
great State than to have each and every Lodge in California assisting
in the splendid work.
Respectfully and fraternally submitted,
MOTLEY HEWES FLINT,

Condition of Masonry in the Philippine Islands.
Brother Amos G. Bellis, representative from "Manila" Lodge,
No. 342, called upon me the past few days, at my office in Los Angeles, and brought up for serious consideration the condition of
Masonry in the Philippine Islands, more particularly as to the recognition of certain Grand Jurisdictions, and on the advisability of the
establishment of a Grand Lodge in . the Philippine Islands. Inasmuch as the conversation brought up several matters of vital importan(l•, to Masonry in general, I r equested Brother Bellis to set forth
all of the facts in a communication which would be presented to this
Grand Body. Said communication is as follows:
"Los Angeles, Cal., October 3, 1906.
"Motley H. Flint, EBq., M.·. W.-. Grand Master,
Grand Lodge of California, F. and A. M.,
Los Angeles, Cal.
"Most Worshipful Sir: In reply to your request for a statement
regarding the Spanish-Filipino Lodge -in Manila, working under
cha1ter from the Grand Orient of Spain, I desire to submit the following:
''In Manila at the present time there are three active Lollges,
reoularly chartered by the Grand Orient of Spain, viz.: "Dalisay"
L;dge, No. 177; "Modesto" Lodge, No. 199; and "Sinu~uan."
Lodge, No. 272. Another Lodge, "Mabini,'' No. - , worki.ng in
Aparri, Cagaayan (the northern part of Luzon)', rec~ntly rec~ived a
charter from the Grand Orient. These Lodges were not recognized by
"Manila" Lodge, No. 342, Jurisdiction of California, until the latter
part of 1904, when in response to an inquiry, our W.:. M.-. Brother
H. G. Squier receiven a communication from M.:. W .: . P.ast Gr~nd
M·ister Nutting inferring that these Lodges were regular, since which
tir•.e. Masonic intercourse has been exchanged between ''Manila''
Lodge and the three f:panish-Filipino Lodges above metttioned.
''There are also about seventeen other Lodges in the Philippines,
all claiming to hold charters from the Grann Orient of Spain, that

The Grand Orient of Spain is composed of the Supreme Council
33d degree; the Grand ·council of the Order, members of which are
elected by a General Assembly consisting of representatives from all
Lodges, Chapters, etc., up to the 33d degree; and the various Subordinate Bodies dependent upon the above. The Supreme Council exerci~es juris.diction over all the degrees from the fourth to the thirtythird, while the first three . d egrees are the special charge of the
Grand Council of the Order. The Grand Orient of Spain claims to
work in Scottish Rite Masonry only.
''There were also Revera! Lodges in tlie Philippines holding charters from the Grand Orient of France, but these Lodges were not
recognized by ''Manila'' Lodge. I understand that the party at the
he<1•~ of these Lodges has recently returned his charter to the Grand
Orient of France, and has petitioned the Grand Council of France to
be healed.
''I have recently been informed that there are several Masonic
G.-and Bodies in Spain, each claiming to be regular, and as there has
beeu some doubt expressed as to whether or not the Grand Orient of
Sp~in, which controls the three native Lodges in Manila recognized
by ''Manila'' Lodge, is a regular Masonic Body recognized as such
by . other regular Masonic Jurisdictions, I would fraternally request
that this matter be looked intp and that "Manila" Lodge be informed in the premises._ I b elieve tl\at this qu13stion .should be settled
in view of the large numbers of dormant Lodges claiming to hold
charters from the Grand Orient of Spain, and which may become
active at any time, au,d also of the fact that new Lodges are being
chartered. Two of these native Lodges have an American member
raised since the American occupation, and when I left Manila o~e of
them had received and balloted upon petitions from three Americans
for the degrees of Masonry.
"I might state here that there is a Spaniard residing in Cavite,
P. I., who claims to be a regular Mason, and who states that the
Grand Orient of Spain is not a regular Masonic Body. I also know
that this Spaniard has been refused admittance to the three native
Lodges in Manila, as 'they claim that he is under a ban of the Grand
Orient of Spain, and on their objection he was also denied admittance
into "Manila" Lodge. However, I a m informed that this Spaniard
visits "Cavite" Lodge frequently.

the ·G eneral Masonic Relief Fund i,i.s follows :

GRF\ND Mf\STER'S RELIEF
REF ORT
Los ANGELES, CAL.
·
October I, 1906.
Brethren of the Grand Lodge
On the morning of April 18th last as I was about to leave my home toattend
to my business engagements the telephone operator at my office called ml' up
and stated that she had just received a message from the train dispatcher
of the Southern Pacific Railway informing her that there had been a severe
earthquake in San Francisco and a number of people had been killed. Of
course I little realized that the dfsaster would prove so serious, but on reaching the center of the city I ascertained that the newspapers were preparing
to issue extras and then it dawned upon me that the casualty was much more
serious than first appeared. I immediately called upon the telegraph companies and the railway auth~rities for full information but unfortunately
the wires out of San Francisco were either seriously damaged or not working
satisfactorily and but little information could be secured more than the fact
that the loss of life had been appalling and the city of San Francisco was
burning. Notwithstanding the fact that my physical condition was not all
that could be desired I deemed it my duty to go to San Francisco at once
and within a short time Brother Oscar Lawler, Grand Orator, telephoned and
volunteered his assistance and agreed to go with me by first train. We left
Los Angeles at the first opportunity and on reaching Oakland the next morning found the streets crowded with panic stricken people from San Francisco
practically all of whom had lost all their earthly possessions and were simply
striving for an opportunity to get away from the scene of the terrible disaster
and the conflagration which was fast destroying the metropolis of the Pacific coast. After inquiries I ascertained that a meeting of Masons had been
called for April 20th at the Masonic Temple and I attended this meeting
and found that it had been called by Doctor R. W. Meek, he acting as tern.

.

226

PROCEEDINGS QF THE

porary Chairman. It was found that the first matter of importance :was the
securing of funds to meet the immediate necessities. Every bank m Oakland and surrounding points was closed. I finally, by giving proper guarantees was accommodated by Brother Samuel J . Taylor, Secretary of the Realty
Syndicate, with a loan of one thousand dollars in gold, and at t~s ~ime I d~­
sire to express to Brother Taylor my deep and sincere apprec1at10n of his
kindness in our hour of need: Finding that it was not possible to secure further
funds I telegraphed to Los Angeles and instructed that three thousand dollars
in postal money orders be sent me from I,llY personal funds iis I was satisfied
that I could secure the necessary amount through thepost-office. I will add
that for many days all the available funds I secured was through post-office
money orders sent me from Los Angeles which were promptly cashed through
the courtesy of the Postmasters of Oakland and San Francisco. This method
immediately relieved the financial situation. Dr. R. W. Mee~ was elected
President of the Masonic Relief Bureau and appointed the followmg brethren
members of the Executive Committee. Alfred William Burrell, ·David
Rutherford, George Roeth; Adam Francis GunnandJosephFountainChi..ndler.
The Masonic Temple at Oakland was immediately opened and lodging given
hundreds in the different rooms in the building. Hot meals were prepared
and no person- was refused lod11:ing or meals. A splendid organization was
effected and to our beloved brethren of Oakland Masonry is surely greatly
indebted. While I do not know the names of many of the volunteers who
gave up their time for the splendid work, still I have their li~e~esses i~ m.y
heart and I can but express in this feeble manner the appremat10n whwh IS
due to them from all the Masons of the world. Eighteen large wagons were
secured and through the efforts of the General Relief Committee at Oakland
and the Oakland Board of Trade, both of which organizations were most
kind and generous at all times, sufficient provisions were secured to fill the
eighteen wagons and they started the next morning by first boat for San
Francisco. I personally used a carriage which we loaded with bread and
canned beef, and on arriving in the stricken city food stations were established at many points, Brother Lawler and myself distributing the pr~visions
we had to the people on the streets whom we met as we drove to the different
refugee camps.
Certainly one of the Saddest sights I have ever seen was during the first
day of our relief work in San Francisco. Mothers calle~ to us as w~ drove. through
the streets begging for bread for their children and milk for theu babies, but
I am very glad to state that it was only on the first day of our work that we
found the conditions to be so serious 'for on the following day the food had
arrived in such quantities thatall cases of serious distress could be promptly
relieved.
For your information let me detail in a few words the work of one day
in connection with the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau and that of your
Grand Master and Grand Orator who spent the entire day for fourteen consecutive days in the stricken city. In Oakland each night the eighteen wag-

GRAND LODGE OF CALI~ORNIA.

227

ons would be loaded with such provisions as were obtainable· at six o'clock
the next morning bread and other provisions were loaded ~ntil all of the
teams had their capacity. Doctor Meek and his able executive foroe detailed from the splendid committee of volunteers certain of our Masonic
brethren to accompany each team and look after the distribution of food in
San Francisco. At six o'clock each morning, as before stated, after the teams
were all loaded with fresh bread and the balance of the ·provisions I loaded
my own carriage with bread, condensed milk for the babies, and cases of
corned .beef; we reached the ferry at the foot of Broadway, Oakland,as early
as possible to be sure and catch the early boat. On the arrival of the teams
in San Francisco they were driven to points where food stations had been
opened. ~mbers of the Oakland executive committee had been sent to
these food stations and also to the Oakland ferry where food was distributed
for se~eral .days. Any person, be.he Mason, Christian or pagan, was promptly
supplied with the needed food. milk and coffee; in fact every person applying
was promptly fed. This same condition prevailed at every food station
opened under charge of the Masonic Fraternity. The wagons were sent to
all points where refugee camps had been opened and after the food had been
distributed these large wagons were loaded with old men and women and little
children with their personal belongings and taken many miles to the Oakland
Ferry and sent across by boat to places of safety. The value of teams at
that time may be appreciated when I state that some few hard hearted perdons who owned horses and wagons who desired to make money out of the unfortunate charged as high as twenty-five dollars to take a family from the
district outside the burned section to the ferry; conaequently it will be clearly
noted that the teams sent from Oakland did a great and splendid work. After
the teams reached the ferry with the old men, women and children additional
food supplies were secured from the United States Government and relief
bureaus and again distributed to the different supply depots and another
load of old men, women and children and their belongings taken to the ferry
to ~ transferred to Oakland and places of safety. This continued each day
until dark and we were compelled to cease work then as the city was without
lights, the power plants having been destroyed.
The difficulties of getting through the streets of San Francisco after the
awful conflagration cannot be described, but it took heroic action on the part
of brave men to accomplish the splendid work.
.
During each day I drove through all parts of the city as I had received
many .telegrams and letters asking my assistance to locate missing relatives
and fnends, and I am pleased to state that I wa.s enabled in many dozens of
cases to send telegrams advising that. relatives and friends were safe. For
days I kept advertisements in every paper published calling for information
concerning missing people; this list, of course, was secured from the telegrams
and letters I had received from the anxious people throughout this Union.
One ?ase in particular which I call up at this time is of an old gentleman and
his wife who were quite feeble who desired to be sent to Cleveland, Ohio. The

228

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

gentleman was a member of all the Masonic bodies in Chicago and was destitute, further he was paralyzed from the waist dqwn. I finally secured a good
Masonic brother who was strong and rugged and who carried on his shoulders
this paralyzed and destitute brother several miles from the district outside
the burned section to the ferry and placed him and his wife on the train and
started them safely for Cleveland.
After my inspection of all the food stations and endeavoring to relieve
the distressed at every point and search for lost and missing relatives and
friends I returned to Oakland each night where I found Doctor Meek and his
splendid committee hard and actively at wock. During the night hundreds
of telegrams and letters were received which required"attention; eastern jurisdictions were telegraphing funds and asking what assistance they could give,
and these letters and telegrams demanded answers. This work required many
hours of each night and it finally became necessary for me to wire to Los Angeles for my private secretary; the only expense for clerical assistance in this
great work that I endeavored to perform to the best of my ability was for
railway fare and hotel expeiises of my private secretary while in Oakland
attending to my correspondence and telegrams.
I had made an engagement as Grand Master to lay the corner stone of
the Golden Gate Commandry Asylum on April 21st, the Grand Lodge to meet
at King Solomon's Temple, San Francisco. I reached King Solomon's Temple,
located outside the burned section, exactly on time on that day but illiltead
of opening the Grand Lodge I endeavored to open the doors of that Temple
and start another food station. The next morning in King Solomon's Temple
Grand Orator Lawler and myself spent many hours, he cutting slices of bread·
and I opening cans of corned beef preparing sandwiches to feed the hundreds
of hungry people surrounding the Temple.
I desire to commend at this time Brother E . M. Percy one of our volunteers at the first meeting held in Oakland. Brother Percy resides at 3570
Clay Street, San Francisco, outside the burned district, and he turned over
to us his residence for use as a food station and supply point and also as a hospital in taking care of the sick. Further than that he was on duty day and
night looking after the distressed.
To Brother H. M. Owens, Past Master of California Lodge No. 1, we are
greatly indebted for looking after the detailsand introducing to me Brother
M. Hennings of Mount Moriah Lodge No. 44. Brother Owens learned from
Brother Hennings that he had a bakery that could be used; he conferred with
me and I advis!ld that all expenses would be borne out of the funds in my possession, and with that understanding Brother Owens arranged to have the Board
of Public Works approve the oven for baking bread, notwithstanding the
fact that there :were no fires permitted in the city. Flour was secured
and on the third day after the disaster the bakery was open and two
thousand loaves distributed from it daily as follows· Five hundred
loaves to the Board of Relief at King Solomons' Hall; five hundred

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

229

loaves to Mission Masonic Hall,and the balance divided up between the Hebrew
Orphan Asylum and St. Mary's Hospital. Bakers were secured through the
Masonic Relief Bure~u at King Solomon's Temple and the only expense involved for which I was compelled to pay out of my funds was two.hundred
and fifty dollars. This bakery continued actively for eight days and it is
needless to state that during that period the good accomplished was of inestimable value. I have personally advised Brother Hennings of the gratitude
of myself as Grand Master and that of this Grand jurisdiction and now desire
to publically commend both his action and that of Brother Owens.
It is probably unnecessary to detail the work of the Oakland Relief Bureau for the reason that the full and complete review of the work of said Bureau will be found in full as a portion of this report, but I can only state that
I personally appreciate more than words can tell the work of the executive
committee and the many volunteers who assisted in the splendid Masonic
relief work. Many of our brethren on that executive committee and the
volunteers gave up their own business for days simply to relieve the distressed
and I assure you that they have literally followed their obligations and the
Masonic teachings.

Brother John Thompson, Master of Mission Lodge No. 169 and the corps
of volunteers at Mission Masonic Temple are entitled also to my sincere thanks
for the splendid work they performed during the trying hours immediately
following April 18th. There can be no question but that they accomplished
a wonderful amount of good and relieved hundreds of cases of distress. While
it is not possible to enter into elaborate details of the work of the brethren of
Mission Lodge still I feel that in justice to them their work is entitled to great
credit and also the commendation of this Grand Lodge.
It took some few hours for our brethren in San Francisco to fully realize
their position. Many were dazed by the disaster but it was not many hours
before they came bravely to the front and determined that the Masonic relief
should stand out boldly. A meeting was promptly called at King Solomon's
Temple, presided over by Worshipful W. Frank Pierce, details of organization
perfected and Worshipful Brother Harry J. Lask placed in charge as Secretary.
After discussion the following were elected permanent officers of the organization: Worshipful Brother William Frank Pierce, President; Worshipful
Brother Harry Joseph Lask, Secretary; Worshipful Brother Harry Davis
Loveland, Vice-President, (Brother Loveland, on account of illness, soon after
resigned and his place was filled by the appointment of Worshipful Brother
Brilsford Pease Flint.) Worshipful Brother Otto Frank Westphal, Treasurer.
This organization developed into what I consider one of the most substantial
and satisfactory relief boards ever gotten together. I have several times examined the business methods adopted and have the highest praise for the
manner in which the work has been carried on from its inception. Complaint
was made to me that the Masters of the lodges of San Francisco were not giving the attention necessary to relieve the distressed and I therefore issued

mandatory instructions to the Masters to at once issue summons for every
member of their lodge to attend a meeting and check up the membership
carefully and if any members were not accounted for to .go to the refugee
camps, visit each one, and ascertain if there were any Masonic brethren in
distress and if so to relieve them at once. Perhaps the officers and members ·
of the lodges in San Francisco may feel that my letters were sharp and peremptory. It was not my desire in any way to criticise them but it was with the desire
that every Me.son, and in fact every person connected with the Masonic organization directly or indirectly, receive the benefits of the relief that was required at that time. I felt that there were many who before April 18th had
ample funds and resources to take care of them the rest of their days, but after
that were penniless and who were so modest and despondent that they
would not ask for relief and it was our duty to assist them above all others.
There was no particular danger from the brother or members of his family
who applied for relief but there was danger that those who through modesty
and losses occasioned by the fire were destitute and were suffering in some
tent or unprotected place in or around the refugee camps. My reports fr<:>m
the San Francisco lodges were very satisfactory and I now desire to "commend
the Masters and officers of those lodges for their strict compliance with my instructions.

ceived information that a family residing in San Francisco-a woman with
five little children-had applied to the General Relief Board, not Masonic,
for assistance and the same had not been secured. I requested Brother Lask
to carefully and promptly investigate the case and he found that the family
were without clothing and were sleeping on the floor. ·As I had funds in my
charge given me by different jurisdictions to relieve the distressed be they
Masonic or otherwiiie, I deemed it my duty to grant the required relief although the family had no Masonic connections. Proper clothing, furniture
and provisions were supplied, and while throughout this relief work I have
endeavored to be guided by Masonic rules and regulations I have as yet to
refuse one worthy case where it proved to be a Ma.son out of standing or some
one of Me.sonic connection that required some assistance. I am very thankful
to some of our jurisdictions that in entrusting relief funds to me instructions
were given to dispose of it as I deemed best and proper, consequently in
every worthy case of a suspended Mason I have granted immediate relief.
In submitting this report I can state that no case of any kind, Masonic or
otherwise, brought to my attention where relief was desired was refused by
me and I am indebted for the opportunities of extending relief to those outside of the Fraternity and those out of standing to some of our sister jurisdictions who issued instructions that. I should relieve the distressed be they
Masons or not.
·

The General Masonic Relief Boe.rd of San Francisco have submitted a
full and complete review of the vast work performed by their perfect organization, and as this review is a portion of this report and will be in the hands of
every member of the Grand Lodge it is unnecessary probably for me to recapitulate the work accomplished, but I feel it my duty to state that the
President, Worshipful Brother W. Frank Pierce and his good wife have both
given up their time and personal possessions simply to aid the distressed and
to comfort the affiicted and that since the disaster Brother Pierce has done
nothing but give the General Masonic Relief Board his entire time and attention.
For the other members of the executive committee and the
officers ·of said committee who have so loyally and devotedly
ministered to the wants of those of our Fraternity requiring it I
uce.n only report that from my investigation they have accomplished all that
cold be desired. In times of trouble such as we have experienced in thisgreat
state dm:ing the past few months it brings forth men and we
should give thanks that men of courage and determination were found in
San Francisco wh~ were willing to give up their time for those who required
relief and advice. ·For Brother Harry J. Lask, the efficient Secretary of the

He is thorough, systematic, painstaking and reliable, and his books and

months I have had a great deal of correspondence with Brother Lask, particularly jn connection with inquiries from other jurisdictions concerning
neceSSl!.ry relief and in every case the investigation has been thorough and

been severely afflicted, the most impQl'tant points where damagewruireported
to be severe were San Jose and Santa Rosa. I made prompt inquiries and
ascertained that relief was required at once. Telegralllil were promptly sent
by me to both cities instructing them to extend any relief required and funds
would be promptly sent. Relief bureaus were established at both San Jq{l0
and Santa Rose. and I have kept in touch with the situation at all times and
am glad to state that relief has been granted promptly in every case and ample
funds have been kept on hand in both cities to provide for all. The brethren
of Santa Ro!'ll. made a most u!gent appeal that I visit that city and look
over the situe.ton and I was exceedingly glad that I did for I believe that I
brought new courage to our discouraged brethren of that little city. Of course
our brethren of San Francisco were severely smitten but they were not, in
my judgment, a comparison to that prosperous little city of. Santa Rosa where
every business house was gone and the merchants stared at the ruins of their
once prosperous business, and many who were independent on the night of
Aprilj7th were bankrupt the next day. To give some idea of the situation
I had a number of photographs prepared showing the condition of the city
at the time of my visit, the same being submitted herewith:

a lung time. The brethren had sold their old property and had practice.Uy

one which should receive assistance and felt they should assist in the rebuilding of the Temple I would be glad to be advised. Personally I am strongly
against the Grand Lodge favoring subscriptions for the rebuilding of Temples
and would oppose such a project at any other time but the situation in portions of our state was entirely different and if relief was ever 'required it· was
at Santa Rosa. Some of our sister jurisdictions advised that they believed
as I did but in this case the situation was different and they would assist
if their Grand Lodge would consent, but in many other jurisdictions immediate
response was sent and one of the great.Grand Jurisdictions. of this country
telegraphed authorizing me to draw for five thousand dollars for the benefit of
Santa Rosa. I have received large subscriptions for this city and have thus
far advanced them but ten thousand dollars towards the rebuilding of the
Temple.
Immediately upon my return to my home in Los Angeles after completing
the details of the organization of relief bureaus at different point(! addressed

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

235

a letter to the Master and Secretary of every lodge' located in or near the
etricken district asking as to the condition of the brethren of their lodges
and Masons of other jurisdictions, advising that immediate relief should be
given in every case and that it was my desire that careful and immediate
investigation be made so that all distress should be relieved promptly. Furthermore that in a case of doubt whether a brother might be in standing
it were better to err and grant ·relief rather than to stand on strict Masonic
rules and regulations. Through this vast correspondence received in reply
I have been in close touch with the situation throughout the entire district,
covering some two hundred miles in length; each and every case has received
my serious and thoughtful consideration and where I deemed it necessary
request has been made for some brother in whom I had absolute confidence
to make a careful investigation and submit the facts to me. This rendered
it possible for me to assist every Lodge and every worthy case throughout
the entire district and I know of no request made upon me that has not
received immediate attention. Many of our sister jurisdictions have written
or. telegraphed me asking that relief be extended to certain brethren of their
jurisdiction, which requests have had' attention by telegram or by first mail.
Throughout Lake and Sonoma Counties the loss was very serious, consequently
a great deal of my time has been taken up in investigating worthy cases
throughout both of these Counties, but I feel at this time that there is no
reason why there should be any suffering at any point provided the Masters
and members of the Lodges have performed their duty as true Masons.
The fire in San Francisco was so very disastrous that it left hundreds
of thousands homeless, the consequence being that former residents of San
Francisco have scattered throughout the state and many lodges have been
called upon to assist. Where information has been given to me I have immediately reimbursed every Lodge. In Los Angeles a relief bureau was promptly
started and every member in good standing of all the lodges in the city called
upon to donate one dollar towards the fund; this resulted in the accumulation of something between three and four thousand dollars which has been
used to splendid advantage and is being used daily for the relief of the distressed Masons, their wives, wide>ws and orphans, who formerly lived in
San Francisco but are now residing in Los Angeles. As before stated a review
of the work performed by the San Francisco and Oakland relief bureaus has
been made a part of this report, and in addition I have requested the Secretaries of the relief boards at Sacramento, San Jose, Santa Rosa, Alameda and
Los Angeles to sub~it reports and the same are included with this document.
I feel that the work performed by all the Boards has been conducive of a geat
amount of good and it is my earnest desire that at the next stated meeting
of the lodges in this state the great work of relief be explained fully to our
brethren of this Grand Jurisdiction. Probably there has never been a disaster in our time that has covered such a scope of territory. Of course the
loss of life as compared to the property value was infinitesimally small, but
undoubtedly no such loss ·has ev.01 0een sustained in the United States as was

that incident to the disaster of last April. During my recent official visits
to lodges of this jurisdiction it seemed to bethe general opinion of our brethren
that the work of relief had ceased, but I assure you that the work has really
just commenced and it has been my fear that the coming winter would show
that more actual relief will be required than at any time since the disaster.
Not a day passes but some serious case is brought to my attention; destitute
widows and. brethren require clothing, food and general supplies. Many
families have no furniture whatever and they must be provided with some
few comforts for the coming winter. After mature and thoughtful deliberation I have investigated the situation throughout all the districts of the state
and have apportioned the funds at my disposal to every relief bureau that I
believe will require additional funds during the coming winter, and it is with
great pleasure that I inform you that thereisnota relief bureau in this state
that has not ample funds on hand to meet fully the needs of our distressed·
during the winter months. While I have provided for every case called to
my attention I have harvested my resources to some extent for the coming
winter and it is certainly a satisfaction to be able to report that each relief
bureau has been apportioned sufficient funds so that they can see that our
brethren will be well and. satisfactorily provided for months to come.
This report has been brought down to as near the date of the meeting
of the Grand Lodge as possible. As my term of office a11 Grand Master is
about to expire I assure you that the work of relief has not ceased and will
not cease for many months to come, but it was necessary for me to submit to
you a full and complete statement of the work performed and particularly
a correct and complete financial statement showing every dollar received by
me and the matter of its expenditure.
During the early days of the relief work it became apparent that clothing
of all kinds would be required, particularly in view of the fact that a great
quantity of the old olothing shipped by different relief committees in this
and other states was unfit for use. On my return to Los Angeles I purchased
at. ,the lowest cash prices large quantities of boots, shoes, underclothing and
outside clothing for men, women and children, to the amount of five thousand,
three hundred twenty-seven and 83-100 Dollars; the suppliesbeingshipped to
San Francisco whenever necessities demanded it or until the committee there
was enabled by the reopening of the wholesale houses of that city to purchase
in open market at reduced rates the required clothing to conduct their supply
bureau in a proper and systematic manner. I might add for your information
that the General Masonic Relief Board under the supervision of Worshipful
Brother W. Frank Pierce conducts a full clothing bureau, and every article of any
kind or character needed by members of the Fraternity is promptly supplied
on demand.
And now my brethren I have submitted to some slight extent the details
of this great work of relief and I realize full well the great responsibility that
was thrown upon me and it has been my sincere regret that my health was

not of the best, notwithstanding this fact I have endeavored in every way
to faithfully carry out the trust imposed. On reviewing the entire situation
I feel that the work of the Masonic Fraternity will stand out boldly as being
well and ably performed. There may be criticisms but in my judgment there
can be no just criticism for among the many committees at work they were
all able, willing and anxious to serve our brethren. While mistakes have been
made I am sure they were not intentional but occurred through some misunderstanding.
During the past five months fully one-half of my time has · been devoted
to relief work, the correspondence and telegrams received and sent being as
follows: Telegrams received, 179; telegrams sent, 115; letters received, 922;
letters sent, 1123; total telegrams and letters received and sent, 2339. Some
cases required great thought, study and determination as to the best procedure. but I am sure that I have endeavored to bestow the charity given and intrusted to me to the best of my ability. I little thought when I assumed
the position of Grand Maste.r that such a responsibility would be forced upon
my shoulders but I am glad that my physical ability was sufficient to do the
work and if I have performed my duties satisfactorily to the brethren of the
Grand jurisdictions of this world who have contributed so nobly, then I am
satisfied. As reports of the various bureaus of relief have reached my hands
it has been thought necessary to send additional funds in order that each may

$5647.17 making a total of $100,000.00 in cash and supplies furnished the

shape to provide for the relief required for many months to come.

a:ridnations wasalwaysthe first to send relief andthiswasthefirstopportumty

San Francico, Cal., Sept. 1906.
" To relieve the distressed is a duty incumbent on all men, and particulary on Masons. who are linked together by an indissoluble chain of sincere,
affection. To soothe the unhappy, to sympathize with their misfortunes
to compassionate their miseries, and to restore peace to their troubled minds,
is the great aim we have in view. On this basis we form our friendships
and establish our connections.
Hon. Motley Hewes Flint
M. W. Grand Master of Masons, California
Most Worshipful Sir and Brother:
Complying with your will and pleasure contained in letter of the 16th
ult., and following a custom. long in vogue of printing a report of stewardship
of important affairs entrusted to the care of those on whom devolve such
matters, we herewith beg leave according to such usage, to submit to you the
workings of this particular Board, together with a short history of its inception,
the cause for such, together with financial and statistical exhibits, which
we trust will meet with your approval as well as bring to the
attention of the members of the Craft whithersoever dispersed, the work
accomplished by this board and its endeavor to carry out the tenets of our
ancient and beloved fraternity

! 9th-20th last, and recognizing the importance and necessity of concerted

action for those who were sufferers by the earthquake and fire, a number of
Craftsmen in this city assembled and determined on at least, distributing
food to those who might be in want of it. To this end the directors of King
Solomon's Temple, 1745 Fillmore St., lent assistance and gratuitously placed
their main rotunda at the disposal of a few zealous Craftsmen, who started
out immediately to procure eatables. Stores from the general commissary
department of the United States Government were obtained. Chairs, tables,
cutting knives, axes and other implements necessary to work with were borrowed, and thus equipped, the iron gates were thrown open and the task o
feeding the hungry began. At first it was only intended that the Masons and
their kindred should be supplied, but as supplication after supplication was

266

267

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

made, almost begging for food, the portals were opened wide, and the distributing station started by Masons for Masons was in reality a veritable
"Gates Ajar".On the first day of the voluntary giving out food, upwards of
seven-thousand persons of both sexes, of all ages, of every nationality and
irrespective of creed or religion were supplied. From that on, and for nearly
nine days thereafter, at least six-thousand rations a day were given out, and
the fervent "God bless you", the silent thanks and the humble gratitude of
all was more than payment for the trying and strenuous work of the little band of Master Masons who worked day and night, early and late The
good, big-hearted Craftsmen of Oakland and Alameda County, hearing of the
work that was being done, came to the aid of those in charge by supplying
food in such quantities that at times it was a puzzle where it could be stored.
In the whole world's history covering calamities which have befel cities,
countries and nations, (and none have been handed down in any equalling
that which overcame our cherished city) , is there any record of the feeding
sans cost to any one, as was the case on the many days succeeding the second
and third days of the disaster. In a population of over 500,000 persons, and
allowing that 100,000 of them fled the city, there is yet to be heard of one
single instance where anyone went hungry. Arrangement had been made,
and was made for everyone, and it will always be a remembrance, never to
be forgotten, of the millionare standing in front or behind the poorest soul in
the "Bread-line" (Prince and Pauper) awaiting his chance to obtain something, no matter how little or what he might be given, to appease his and his
family's hunger. Conditions were unalterably changed, and "one touch of
nature made the whole world kin". As disasterous and sorrowful as was the
calamity, it had its good effect in maliing all as one family and binding the
tie of brotherly love and fraternity stronger. It knew no station in life,
all, like the teachings of Masonry, were of an equality; they met upon the level
and parted on the square - such a square as had never before dawned on
men - not even Craftsmen who suffered, to realize the full meaning and
intent of that teaching, Moreover, it brought an old and sacred Order
to the front rank of respect and esteem. The profane opened their eyes in
wonderment, and their very looks indicated that Masonry amounted to something after all, )lnless how could they who were members of it, succor those
who had belittled and defiled it, and treat all as if of their own fold. The
parable of the good Samaritan was brought home to them, as it never was
before; and while our Craft needs no commendation, no thanks, nor testimonial, it is gratifying to know that its principles and teachings have found favor
with many who heretofore have abhorred what they term "Secret Societies".
Willingly day after day, with joyful mien, the little band of workers - the
gleaners in the Lord's vineyard of help and assistance,- toiled without murmur, and it was only when it was found that storage for food became the
question, that it was decided to limit the distribution to Masons and their
families only. As previously stated, our good brethren of Oakland and Ala·
meda County were supplying us with untold quantities of food of every

description, even to thousands of loaves of bread, as well as appetizing boxes
of cooked foods made up in a generous way, and tons of fruit. Not to be
out done, and feeling assured that a Masonic distributing station had been
established (the telegraph lines up to this time being broken, and
even mail facilities and telephone communication dis-established) our loyal
and ever ready brethren of the beautiful Southland - Los Angeles - and
contiguous places - started food relief trains to this city, via Alameda county,
which trains were supplemented by others from Fresno, Tulare, Sacramento,
Marysville, Chico, Red Bluff, Redding and every portion of the state - places
untouched by shake or fire - and in this way, food, carloads of clothing
bedding and other comforts and necessities were delivered to the station in
this city as quickly as steamer and other modes of traffic could bring them.
We, ourselves, Californians as we are, used to prodigious liberality, were even
dazzled by the quantities of provender showered upon us. As grateful as
were the poor profane who were receiving bounty at our hand, so much more
grateful were we, and pen nor tongue cannot find words to say what we would
have said, could we have reached any and all of God's thoughtful angels those remembering our sad plight and with bounteous offerings caring for
our then necessary and instant welfare. Our gratitude was silent, but our
prayers for their every success in life made amends for what we did not publicly proclaim. Kindly and fraternal acts such as these do not a little to draw
together in the bonds of peace, harmony and lasting friendship all of the human
race, and is hastening the time when
"Man to man the world o'er
Shall brothers be for a'that."
The distribution of food and clothing was continued right along, and on monday, April the 23rd, at your solicitation, as also Will and Pleasure, Most
Worshipful Sir, a preliminary meeting was called at ten o'clock in the morning,
at the temporary office of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction, in King Solomon's Temple, No. 1745 Fillmore St., at which there
were present nine brethren, including your honored self, who after listening
to your more than fervent appeal to organize, so that together,- as in union
there is strength, - the best and most effective work could be done, a preliminary organization was effected at which the following temporary officers
were elected:W. Bro. William Frank Pierce, President.
W. Bro. Harry Joseph Lask, Secretary.
W. Bro. Harvey Davis Loveland, Vice-President.
(W. Bro. Loveland, on account of illness, soon after resigned, and his place
was filled by the appointment of W. Bro. Brilsford Pease Flint).
W. Bro. Otto Frank Westphal, Treasurer.
A plan of action was immediately mapped out llnd the work began .

268
