"CALLED TO LABOR"
Sub-stations were established, committees were appointed, and the real
work of the Board commenced. The name chosen was:

GENERAL MASONIC RELIEF BOARD
As a compliment to you (moreover deserved) you were induced to
accept the Honorary Chairmanship.
At date of Thursday, April 26th, due and timely notice having been
given, a meeting was held at 9.30 o'clock in the morning, at which there were
present the officers as before named and a majority of the elective officers of
the several branches of Masonry in this city. At this meeting, the officers
elected at the preliminary meeting of April 23rd were made permanent; and
words of commendation for what had already been done, was the key-note of
all who spoke. Further and more amplified means of extending relief was
discussed and determined upon, and with every assurance by yourself that
ample funds were at the command of the Board, for any and all calls, it" was
ordered that a general assemblage of all Master Masons be requested to meet
and confer with the Board on Monday, April 30th, at which time it was hoped
every Master Mason in this city would lend a hand to aid the distressed and
those requiring relief.
"Blest be the tie that binds."
On that date, at 9.30 o'clock in the morning, the meeting took place, and a
more enthusiastic gathering of Masons never assembled. All seemed to be
imbued with the one thought of helping those who were in need of assistance,
and the attendance was so large, that many had to·content the.m selves with
remaining int.he lobby, and catching here and there a word of what was taking ·
place in the meeting room. Volunteers were called for to take charge of
districts in the unburned portions of the city, and in less time than it takes
to record this, over two hundred brethren had offered their services to assist
the Board in its work. Districts were outlined, all points were covered, and
a general plan adopted whereby none should be overlooked who needed help.
It was also resolved that the Masters and Wardens of all the blue lodges,
as well as the first three officers of every branch of Masonry, the women relatives of members of the fraternity, should form an advisory committee to
this Board, and that meetings should be held every morning, at which time
the general work of the day should be determined upon, and ways and means
adopted for carrying into effect .and the best methods of caring for and aiding
the distressed and homeless. This advisory committee met for several weeks
and ·did much to carry O\lt the noble work outlined by yourself. During all
this time, the officers held frequent meetings and enlarged the scope of its
labors.
It was believed that the addition of two well known Craftsmen as officers
of this Board, and to serve with it in an advisory capacity, would extend its

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

269

sphere of usefullness, and in consonance with this, R. W. Bro. Jacob Hart
Neff, Past Junior Grand Warden and Bro. Charles Lord Field were made a
part of its executive. The question of employment being brought to the
attention of the Board, it was decided to call a general meeting of the Craft
for Sunday morning, May 13th, and on that date ·at 10 o'clock, a monster
meeting was held when the immediate necessity of providing situations for
those of our brethren who had lost their employment was brought up, and
sub-committees were appointed to report to the Board any employment that
could be had for those in need of places, and more especially to visit those
members of the Craft requiring help, and acquaint them with the fact that
many of the brethren were in need of employment, and if possible, to give
Masons a preference in engaging help. That meeting was the means of
placing many a Craftsman on his feet, and giving him an opportunity of supporting himself and family, as well as relieveing this Board of much of its
work. Hundreds of positions were found for our brethren, and while scores
of the places accepted were not equal to those held by them previously, still
there was not a murmur of discontent from any one, but on the contrary,
words of thanks for being able to earn a living, were heard on all sides. All
this time, food was being distributed three times a day, and clothing, blankets
and other necessaries and comforts of life bountifully given. The best of
feeling prevailed, and happy·, smiling countena.Ilces, not withstanding the
terrible ordeal through which they had passed, were the rule and not the
exception.
"And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor
and though I give my body to be burned,
And have not charity, it profiteth me nothing." . .
The Board also from its inception was furnishing transportation to all
parts of the world to those who solicited it. It was the policy of the Board not
to give transportation to any able bodied man whose home was in this city
who desired the chance of going to some distant state or country, either for
recreation or to get'away. The need of our men remaining here became more
apparent daily, and it was oniy to those who had been sojourning here that
such free transportation was given, but no objection to granting it was made
women and children, as they were better off out of the city t han in it. The
several railroad and steamship companies gave this Board half-rate fares,
and to them our thanks are more than due
The quarters of the provision depart~ent proving inadequate on
account of the great amount of food being distributed it became necessary
to move to a larger place, as well~as ask for more volunteers to help in distributing the food. As time wore on, a better system of food distribution
was put into effect. Regular hours of giving out supplies were established
and orders were required from each person applying for the food, an apportionment on the lines of government rations being applied, thereby giving to each
person enough, and still not that over-abundance which might create waste.

271

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

.GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Our brethren in charge of this· department worked with a will, sometimes
remaining on duty as long as eighteen hours a day, still putting in their time
cheerfully and with never a murmur of discontent. They wanted to please
as well as help their brethren and famili~ and succeeded so well as to earn the
gratitude of all.

During the first number of weeks of the inception of the Board, many
thousands of dollars were advanced both to lodges and individuals, who did
not desire our offering, but only asked for an accomodation in the shape of
a loan until such a time as the banks should reopen, or their business so
arranged as to permit them to obtain what was really and justly theirs.
Bank accounts were cashed, cheques paid, money advanced on insurance
policies, the stii)endiaries of lodges and the local Board of Relief taken care
of and the bills and other urgent accounts d:ue by lodges paid. All advances
were made at their face value, no discounts were taken and no profit attempted, as it was the policy of the Board to assist all of the Craft needing help to
the fullest extent of the meaning of the word "ASSIST". Nearly every loan
or advance so made has been repaid, and in many cases the Board was asked
to accept a profit, but in each case the proffer was declined with thanks.

The general offices of the Board were also found to be too small and
cramped to efficiently conduct the relief business, which was growing instead
of lessening, and accepting the generous offer of R. W. Bro. Jacob Hart Neff
to occupy the splendidly arranged and fitted lower floor of his home, on
Monday, May 7th, the headquarters of the Board were moved to 1154 O'Farrell Street, where it has remained ever since. The word "generous" is used
above in speaking of the offer from Bro. Neff. It is but a mild adjective, as
R. W. Bro. Neff has steadily declined to accept remuneration of any kind, and
has even when extra necessities were needed, paid for the same himself, and
positively declined reimbursement. The provision department was also
moved, notwithstanding the fact that the location was away from the "maddening crowd", the demands upon us were even greater than ever. Our helpers
were equal to the occasion and no matter how large the number, or pressing
the demand, all were served, and bountifully at that. Carloads of omoked
and canned meats were sent to us; tons of California's most luscious and
succulent fruit, flour, coffee, canned goods and thousands of loaves of bread
handled, and everything that heart could wish for was donated by our thoughtful and beloved brethren in all parts of our country and state. Dainty boxes
of cooked meats and eggs, together with fruits and canned goods were sent by
the wholesale.
As many of our brethren were destitute of clothing and bedding (including their families) and as it became apparent that the external as well
as the internal part of their body must be cared for, the women relatives of
our brethren were pressed into service and by courtesy of Pastor J . Fuendeling of St. Mark's German · Evangelical Lutheran Church, the spacious basement of his "House of the Lord" was given for our use, and in it was stocked
a plentiful supply of every kind of clothing, including outer and underclothing,
not excepting warm comforters and necessities for the baby, as well as the
aged. The Red Cross Society donated upwards of fifteen hundred dollars
worth of government shoes, besides tents, mattresses, blankets and woolens.
The women were placed in full charge of the clothing 'tlepartment and the
requirements of all of our fraternity who applied were supplied. This establishment was maintained until August 1st, when it was deemed best to concentrate the entire work of the Board under the direct supervision of its
officers, and the department was moved to a large storeroom near our offices
and managed directly from this office
"Never sitting down contented while our fellow creatures
around us are in want, especially when it is in our power
to relieve them."

"Renew our hope, inspire our faith."
Telegrams of offers of help in the shape of money came in daily and before
a reply could be sent accepting the same, package after package of coin and
currency was being delivered into our Treasurer's hands. Our distant brethren were not slow in showing and proving the metal of their great big-heartedness. Action followed ·words, and tangible action at that, and at no time from
t he commencement 'of the work of relief was there a moment but what ample
funds were at hand to meet any and all exigencies that might arise. The
Board received inspi.ration at all times from you, Most Worshipful Sir and
Brother, as every letter and telegram sent by you gave us to understand
that your heart and influence was with us in our work, and you desired the
broadest and most liberal charity shown. Such words as those kept us
filled with a love for the labor we·were engaged in, and while we heard nothing ·
but pitiful stories and saw nothing but sorrow and helplessness, we were
imbued with a spirit to keep on and work the harder for our poor distressed
brethren who had suffered so keenly from the calamity that had befallen us.
In this we were nobly aided by hundreds of our brethren, each of whom
volunteered to share part of our work at any and all t~es, day or night.
We were in the midst of most trying times, but never undaunted, and our
motto was Nil desperandum. Our only thoughts were to try and alleviate
suffering. and how well we succeeded remains for those assisted to say.
"Charity extends beyond the grave through the
boundless realms of eternity.'
Besides the work of feeding the hungry, clothing those bereft of almost
everything, supplying beds and bedding, furniture, stoves, cooking utensils,
crockery and cutlery, and temporarily assisting others by finding employment for them, and a hundred and one other things to lighten the burden of
their woes, we have cared for and visited the sick, administered to the dying,
buried the dead, traced and recovered lost ones, returned children to their
parents, effected reconciliations, and have thrown the strong protecting arm
of Masonry around many, some of whom.would have had injustice done them

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

and what little they had taken from them if not for our intercession.
Through our influence the amounts due from fire insurance companies on
losses have been obtained, appraisements on losses have been increased at
least twenty per cent, and as high as fifty, and proportionate payments made
on fire insurance matters, and proofs of loss have been prepared. We have
. cashed claims due from the City Relief Finance Committee and Red Cross
Fµnds, and have drawn legal documents, including agreements, leases,
powers of attorney and other papers. In fact, this Board has performed
and accomplished more than is known, and has even conducted women and
children to the steamers and railroad trains, moved their personal effects
and belongings, assisted them in leaving the city, and attending to their_
every want, so that their departure might not only be safe, but so guarded
as to prevent any confusion or accident arising. We have assisted in repairing dwellings and chimneys, and making houses habitable, as well as renting
houses and rooms for many and finding places of abode. The members of
the Board have been at the call of any and every unfortunate, night and
day, even at "low twelve", and every case requiring attention has been given .
immediate help, our motto being " Quick action and needful assistance".
Many have been the hurried and wild automobile rides in the dead of night,
to care for the sick or dying. Physicians have been ·called, nurses engaged
and hospital service attended to as quickly as vehicles could carry, and often
it has been an all night watch of care and solicitude, but in the end a labor of
love - errands of mercy - with results which fully repaid~.

<lonations, that is, so far as could be applied. To this end it was decided
that true charity comists in helping people to help themselves. From experience it was known that to give an applicant any sum of money at one time
amd not try to help him so that he could help himself would be no.charity
or assistance to him whatever, but would rather make him a dependent, and
as our Craftsmen hesitate:i to accept anything that might be termed "Charity",
we gave all to understand that they were only receiving what was their
rights as pledged by each and all by every tie which binds us together as
li'ree-masons. To make this RIGHT more effective and pronounced, we
decided on restoring people so far as we could, to the position occupied by
them prior to the calamity and we have given sewing machines, irons, pressing boards, shears, etc. to those who were tailors, so that they again might
resume their usual avocation. Instruments have been furnished to dentists,
together with dental chairs and machinery necessary to' resume their profession; instruments and books to physicians and surgeons; tools to carpenters,
machinists and all kinds of mechanics; sewing machines to women who are
dressmakers and for household purposes; wagons and horses to laundry
wagon drivers; and to other tradesmen; instruments and charts to seafaring
men; pianos and other musical instruments to music teachers, performers ·
and vocalists; photographic supplies and cameras to artists and· photographers ; electrical appliances to those engaged in the electrical business and to
apprentices learning that, as well as other trades. No profession, art or
calling has been neglected and while as previously noted, we did not attempt
to overdo it, we have given good and plenty and to use a common term
" have endeavored to put them on their feet again". Even to attorneys and
counselors-at-law have legal books been given, and it may be surprising 'to
many, when it is known that of all who have suffere:i the most through fosses
from the fire, professional men and women take the the front rank. Not
only did many of them lose their valuable instruments, reference books and
electro-machinery, but their clients and patients scattered, and their business
since then has been such as to barely give them a living.
"Acting with our neighbor upon the square, rendering
him every kind office which justice or mercy may
require, and relieve his distress and soothe his affiiction."
Our influence - the strength of Masonry - has been used in more than
one way. It has been successfully carried out in intercessions with the civil
and military authorities. Our letters have been honored in nearly every
instance, and much good has come to many of our brethren and ·t heir families through the influence of letters sent by this board to those high in authroity, oft-times not members of the Fraternity, but who recognizing its strength
and well defined principles which are known to the profane as well as to those
initiated into its mysteries.
Nothing that could be thought of for the welfare of our brethren has been
left undone, and our every thought has been to devise means to make all ali
happy as could be under the trying times and to give them all the succor, help

It has been the endeavor of the Board to keep the expense account as
low as possible. No money has been squandered or frittered away; nothing
has been purchased in the way of office or other supplies not essentially necessary, and the salaries have been fair but not exorbitant. At the beginning
of our labors and for some weeks thereafter. it was imperative that some of
our helpers be paid, as they had families to support, and having themselves
lost everything by fire and being in the same unfortunate position as thousands of other sufferers and their loved ones having to be fed, clothed and
housed, it was no more than right that some small return be given them. Had it
not been that we were able to employ them, we must of n ecessity have relieved them out of the funds at our command, and by giving them something
to do and reasonably compensating them, we saved an amount of money
which otherwise we would have had to donate, and at the same time, made
them independent. They earned all they recived, in fact they did not receive
enough, but considering what we were constituted for, we did not deem it
fair to give them their full worth in pay and they felt as well that it was
incumbent· on themselves to give part of their time and services for those who
were in a more u_n fortunate position than they.
It was decided by the Board after it had been in existence but a short
while, to conduct its affairs as practicable as possible and in aiding those who
might seek our assistance, to apply what is known as practical charity to our

274

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and aid possible. Our only regret at times has been that ·we may not have
done enough for some, but when second thoughts of that kind came upon
us, we P.ave hunted them up and made amends for any little shortcomings
that may have occured as an error on our part.
"Stop a minute and say Hello"
As down life's road
smoothly go,
For a pleasant word an a cheery s~le
Will shorten the road by many a mile
For some poor brother who is going slow,
So stop a minute and say - Hello"
The funds which constitute the capital of this Board were derived from
donations received from yourself, Most Worshipful Sir and Brother in your
official capacity as Grand Master of Masons of this jurisdiction; from nearly
every Grand Commandry of Knights Templar in the United States; from
several Blue Lodges of different jurisdictions;· from Grand Chapters, Royal
Arch Masons and the Ancient and Accepted Scottish llite Freemasonry, who
forwarded their contril:rotions to this Board direct, instead of to and through
you, not forgetting a number of lodges in our state which we believe should
have their donations returned, as said lodges have enough to contend with
at present in caring for their own, for not only has the City of San Francisco
suffered financially and in other ways, but the whole State has had its share,
therefore, we believe that with the funds already received from jurisdictions
other than our own, we have ample means, (at least for the present) and
intend to return to our own brethren of this jurisdiction that which they have
sent us. Part of our funds have also come from Chapters of Royal Arch
Masons; from Scottish Rite Bodies of the ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite
of Free-Masonry 9f both Northern and Southern Jurisdictions; from individuals too modest to have their names made known; from the Great Priory
of England and Wales; from Havana, Cuba; from the City of Mexico and from
Manila, Philippine Islands. Surely we have not been forgotten or overlooked
anywhere, and from letters which we constantly receive, we are assured that
if we need more, the donations already made will be doubled, yea tripled, if
we ask, and what is more that the treasuries of the Masonic bodies are at
our disposal for the assistance and aid of California brethren. The funds
received by permission of every contributor have been turned into one common fund- that is consolidated-and Masons, whether Blue Lodge, Chapter,
Templar or Scottish Rite, have been assisted from this one grand fund, irrespective of degree, place or nationality. One fund for all, the only qualification being worthiness and Masonic standing, and not any height of Masonry
which they may have attained. The spirit of this Fraternity, one of its
strongest landmarks - Equality -;---- has been observed, and we have no
doubt that the course pursued by us will be met with favor by every Craftsman who may read or hear of our actions through this report. To our more
than generous donors, our brethren near and far from us, although ever in
our remembrance, let us quote the old Latin Maxim, which we believe justly
applies to them :-

lou

GRAND LODGE OF· CALIFORNIA.

275

"He gives twice, who gives quickly."
Our gratitude is extended for the thoughtful and prodigal amounts sent to
us by those brethren.
The business of the office of the Board has been enormous. When it
is realized what it means to receive thousands of communications, telegram~
and inquiries, and every communication, letter, telegram, postal card and
inquiry answered without delay, then some little idea may be form_ed of
a small part of our work. We have endeavored to conduct our affairs on
strict business lines, not forgetting that Fraternity was coupled with the
business in hand, and to each and all, whether by" written or verbal communcation, it has been our endeavor to answer every communication, not alone
expeditiously, but in an intelligent manner, and to give as fully as possible
the informat.ion desired. Our accounts, d11-ta and vouchers are in perfect
shape, and although an audit has been had and everything found to be correct,
the intent of Masonry, one of its most saCJ"ed tenets that its
charities must be unostentatious and that the left hand must not know
what th) right hand doeth - has been more than strictly adhered to, and
as will b&, further seen by examining the schedules of. relief exten.ded, neither
the name of the person assisted nor the lodges of which they claim membership are given, and none outside of yourRelf and the members of this Board
are cognizant of who as individuals have been relieved, or as to whether this
lodge or that lodge or other body of Masonry has received more or less than
the other. While it has been essentially necessary for the Board to have the
names of applicants and lodges, their numbers and locations, in order to keep
its records straight, and its finances clear so that the Board of Audit, (a Committee of the Grand Lodge of this jurisdiction), can intelligently pass on all
vouchers of expenditures; no one but tho~ebefore mentioned have any definite
information of those aided, and under your instructions, never will. The
vouchers after approval, will have been destroyed and thus an effectual
silence of Masonic law and custom faithfully adhered to.
We believe that with the foregoing a synopsis of our labor has been
reported, and we now present to you statistical, financial and other tables
which will show in detail the full workings of the Board.
STATISTICAL.
Secretary's Office.
At the commencement of the work, the office force consisted of an assistant secretary, an accountant, two stenographers and twenty messengers.
This number was retained for nearly six weeks and until it was found that it
could be reduced. At the present writing, and for the past three months,
the office is conducted by a bookkeeper, a stenographer and one messenger.
At the outset, as many as seven buggies, automobiles, wagons, carri~ges and
other kinds of vehicles were used and hired in order that distant cases for

276

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

relief could be immediately given attention. Since then, the number has
been reduced, and at present, one buggy is in daily use, and is kept constantly
at work. It is not amiss here to say that our subordinate employees have
proved true and loyal in our cause. The immense amount of work performed
by them speaks volumes for their efficiency and faithfulness, and not only
our own, but. the thanks of the fraternity are due them.

Provision Department.
All told when this branch of our work was at the highest point, there
were fully forty of our brethren who assisted in the distribution of food.
This number finally gave way to six, who had all they could attend to for
many days. They worked \irelessly and without complaint, and were the
means of bringing comfort to the hungry and needy. Connected with this
department were four ~rays and six wagons, each of which made innumerable
trips daily, obtaining cases of food , clothing and bedding at depots, etc., and
distributing orders to those unable to come to us, by reason of infirmity and
old age. When we discontinued our provision department (June 2nd) we
turned over to the Salvation Army about six tons of provisions, consisting
of hams, bacon, canned meats, canned fruits, cereals, etc

Clothing Department.

11715

This part of our work was placed in charge of the women relatives of
members of the Fraternity, who were given full charge and who arranged up to
and including August 1st, for a number of themselves each day to take charge.
T his gave all an opportunity to assist in the distribution of clothing, shoes,

278

etc. Since the last named date the department has been under the immediate
control and charge of the Secretary's office and all distributions are made on
order. The department at present is giving complete satisfaction and our
storeroom has all the articles necessary to make the applicant comfortable
and happy. Prior to date of August 1st, fully fifteen hundred persons,
(estimated) were supplied with clothing, consisting of shoes, underclothing,
outer wearing apparel etc., the major portion of which was received as donations. Since August 1st, we have supplied at least three hundred and
seventy-five persons with clothing, shoes, underwear etc., also with blankets
and comforters, sheets, pillow cases and towels.
Supplies to the amount of $4961 . 92 have been purchased for this department, same consisting of suits, wrappers, petticoats, skirts, night dresses,
ladies' mens' and children,s underwear, shoes, hosiery, blankets, comforters,
sheets, pillow cases, towels and table clothes.

Employment.
While no regular employment bureau has been established, we have been
able by individual effort and our influence to supply our brethren or their
kin with a few positions, as are more fully enumerated in the following excerpt
from our records. We could have accomplished more in this particular line
had those of our brethren in affluent circumstances requiring help come to
our assistance and informed us of their wants, giving us the preference in
supplying them with those of our applicants who wanted postions. We
trust that ere long such brethren will affiliate with us and make this Board
the nucleus of an employment bureau which will prove far better for those
needing our care, than the mere giving of alms and other assistance. It will
make many of our applicants self-supporting and be more compatable with
their own self respect and the dignity of the Craft
·

Conclusion.
"He looketh on the earth, and it trembleth,
He toucheth the hills, and they smoke."
Psalm civ, 32.
And now Most Worshipful Sir and Brother, we have placed before you
the record of our labors. We appreciate, as officer~of this Board, the great honor
you have conferred upon us by confiding to our care the noble work which we
have endeavored to carry out.. It is a distinction to be proud of, in trying
to help huma.llity and our brethren. St. James declared that true and undefiled religion before God and the Father is in visiting the widows and orphans
in their affliction and keeping one's self unspotted from the world. Surely
to relieve the distressed and aid all in affliction and to cheer them with sympathy is the divinest work in which man can be engaged. Our obligations
of gratitude to all our brethreen who have in any way assisted· us, whether
financially .or by their help, or by their good and kind suggestions and ready
response to our appeal for their advice and assistance can never be expressed
and much less recompensed. Words in such a case are but empty thoughts,
their reward must come hereafter, and from a higher power. ·
This report would indeed be incomplete without some little recognitio n
by name of several of our brethren who have given so freely of their time and
labor and have so unselfishly devoted the best efforts ·of their hearts to ai
us and our unfortunate in the severest and most urgent cases. To our Bro.
George Henry Boskowitz, M. D., of Doric Lodge No. 216, modest and unostentatious, no words are adequate to render tO him our gratitude and that o
all the Fraternity for his many acts of professional kindness. Day and night,
always at our command, leaving his large practice to be of service to our
sick and dying, he has gratuitously given his skill, and we would be truly
ungrateful did we not here mention him as an example of all that is Masonic
and noble.
Our Bro. Roland English Hartley, M. D.,. Past Master of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260, is also here placed on our roll of ·honour, for always and ever
ready to visit and care for the sick, following his every obligation to aid his
brethren whenever and wherever in distress .
To Bro. James William Ward, M. D., of Crockett Lodge No. 139, we are
under the deepest obligation. .Occupying the position of President of
the board of Health of this City and County, it has been our good fortune ·
to have him as a member of the Fraternity and to personally know him as
a man and physician. · All the influence at his command has been free)
granted to us. Position after position has he given those of our brethren
qualified to fill the same. In such places where he needed men, and the
hospitals under his control have been the haven of many a poor unfortunate
demanding his attention, with the best of care and skill given them to restore
health and happiness.
Others too numerous to ·mention, of the same profession, have served tis
or offered their services and to all we can truly say THANKS.

Alaska, Australia, and to points in Europe.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

We also extend our thanks to Bro. Arthur William Foster of Oriental
Lodge No. 144, President of the California Northwestern Railway Company
and the North Shore Railroad Company, for furnishing transportation
without cost, to many of our brethren. . Although importuned many times
to accept remuneration, Bro. Foster has at all times refused, saying that it
was as little as he could do. to assist this Board in that manner. To Bro.
Lollis Glass, Past Master of California Lodge No. 1, Vice-President and General
Manager of the Pacific States Telephone and Telegraph Company we are
indebted for free telephone service, a matter of considerable import and saving
to us, and one duly appreciated.
To Bros. Abraham Isaac Bloch and Louis Bloch of Fidelity Lodge No.
120, we also extend thanks for many courteous acts in furnishing us with
supplies for our office, for which although strongly importuned to accept pay,
have refused, each time saying that what they or either of them could do for
the welfare of their afflicted brethren they were only too happy to do so and
were glad of the opportunity to give their mite.

well meant intentions for the rebuilding of our beloved 9ity, still there are
conditions which seem to us will bring on an era of dull times, and how far
that will affect those of our brethren who. have lost their all, remains to be
seen. One cannot but admire the joyful, smiling and contented faces met
every day; a universal cheerfulness and. thankfulness; no one seems to be
discouraged, although many have gone through enough misfortune to make
them anything but hopeful; but in every case and especially those cases
with which we have directly dealt, it is to be said that the first one has to
be met who has looked dt1Spondent, and was not bright and cheerful, with
hope for the future. We have heard them utter thanks to God for their and
their family's lives being spared, and. that it was no worse. All seemingly
cheerful and happy under the worst conditions. Among the many, temporarily
housed in tents in our parks and vacant building lots, are some of our own
Fraternity. Whether they will procure permanent abodes for the winterremains
to be seen, and those who clerk for a living whether they will be retained in
their positions, or if so, whether the compensation will be enough to ke~p
them and their famiJ.y (if they have one ) in fairly good circumstances. These
are conditions that confront us, as well as some of our brethren who up
to this time have weathered· the storm, and have not applied to us for assistance, as they have been able thus far to care for themselves witheut requiring'
the aid of us or from any other source. We hope and pray for the best, but
if we are correct in our conclusions as to the future, we desire to so husband
our funds so as to be able to relieve any and all who may require Masonic
aid and assistance. It is true, notwithstanding a denial in some quarters,
that living and other expenses have increased beyond measure or reason, and
a person who has to earn his daily bread, and whose earnings are limited, will
need and require our help and we want to be prepared for that contingency, if
it should arise. While we do not desire to continue the existence of this
Board a day longer than is actually necessary we feel that its life should be
prolonged for a reasonable time, and until the last one of our brethren who
needs help is firmly placed in a position to help himself. We believe in going to
the limit and extent of our obligations taken as Master Masons, and we fully
realize that in so doing we are sacrificing many of our own interests, but so .
long as we are helping our fellows, we are more than willing to make such
sacrifice. We can here quote' with due regard to its truth the following excerpt
from the writings of a most Worshipful Grand Master of a sister jurisdiction.
"No longer are men banded together in our Fraternity to erect physical
structures or overcome physical foes. The LIGHT that we follow leads to
a keener insignt, a better understanding, and a nobler expression of the
human faculties. The materials with which we labor are constituent elements of
every human being and our purpose is to learn how to use the materials to
construct temples of the MIND and SOUL which will be pleasing in the eyes
of the Great Architect of the Universe."

To the Very Worshipful Grand Secretaries of every English Speaking
Jurisdiction and to the subordinate officers of Blue Lodgesweareindebted for
many courtesies, always ready to answer our telegrams and correspondence,
as well as to perform any anil all favors we have requested from them,we appreciate their efforts for us and so record it.
To the · various transportation companies, both rail and steamship in
this city, to the daily newspapers, to tradesmen with whom we have doolt,
and to countless others in many and devious occupations and positions, we
extend our gratitude for many acts of kindness, only hoping that we may be •
able to show our better appreciation for what they have done for us than by
the simple word THANKS.
We cannot conclude this report without mentioning what in our opinion
is the present condition of unfortunate and distressed members of the Craft
and their families in this City. At the 'present time we firmly believe that
all who suffered either physically or financially, or both, from the earthquake
and fire, to be in fairly good condition, that is so far as immediate wants and
n~cessities are concerned. All their wants have been met as fully and as to
their needs as has been possible, and while we admit that there may be some
"whose wants may not have been made known to us, those who have applied
or been sought, have had everything done for them that could be, and
that all of these are comfortably situated at present a~d are nearly above want
of anything. That, for the past and present, but the future is ~hat is troubling us, We grieve to say that we fear for the future. We are fearfol of the
approaching winter. This may seem pessimistic, but to be truthful, we must
say so, although we should have preferred to have taken the other view, and
would have done so, had we the slightest belief in the roseate word -optimistic.. While the people of this city are to be given every credit, and which is
no more than deserving, for their fortitude in the hour of affliction, and their

The mystery of Masonry, the craft of Freemasons, has from the inception of the order been discussed freely by those without its ranks. No conclusion, however, has ever been arrived at other than that to know the secrets
of the lodge, one must become a member.
But that Masonry has done an enormous amount of good in different
ways and directions has long been agreed upon. One of its most noteworthyacts of charity and relief in the history of the organization, was that following the earthquake and fire in San Francisco on the memorable morning of
April 18th, when the greater pdttion of that city was reduced to a heap of
smoking ashes and ruins.
It is of these affairs that we now have to deal, and following a description
in general of the disaster in both San Fran~isco and Oakland, the many acts
of self denial on the part of the members of the Masonic fraternity on the Oakland side of the bay; the numerous worthy deeds done.and the countless steps
taken to alleviate much suffering and to provide for the destitute, will be told
in detail. . For although the thousands of charitable deeds of Masonry rarely
€ach the ears of the general public-it being a rule of the order to act in an

300

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

unostentatious manner-the acts of the Masons in this particular seems justly
public property and the occasion demands and has demanded from the beginning, a public record of the work done and the good accomplished.
Before going into the history of the disaster itself, it will be well to state
that among the most willlng workers with the Masonic lodges was Mayor
Frank Mott. He was tireless at his task and did much to aid the Masonic
fraternity. Each night between the hours of 10 and 12 o'clock he was in close
consultation with Dr. R. W. Meek,.chairman of the Executive Committee
and president of the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau. And another worthy
of the highest praise and consideration is Most Worshipful Motley H. Flint,
Grand Master of Masons of California. he was an enthusiastic worker for the
relief of the refugees and provided the Oakland Relief Bureau with ample
funds, the same having been sent to him from all o~er the United States. The
future work of the Oakland Bureau will be continued along the same lines
until all of those who were in distress by the disaster of April 18th, have been
relieved.
Toward the end of this report, it will be noticed that the expenses and
general relief work are bunched in figures, it being ahnost impossible to determine just where the money went or into which channel it was forced without going through the entire list of vouchers which are in the hands of the
Chairman of the executive committee and the President of the Masonic Relief Bureau.
It is with great pleasure for this committee to make special mention of
the names of Mrs. Mary M. Van Court, Miss Kate Clarisse Morris and Mrs.
Caroline W. Emery who were most obliging and who worked for the relief of
total strangers just as though they had been of their own flesh and blood.
Treasurer George. Roeth is also one who is deserving of special mention. He
worked day and night and was ever of uncomplaining disposition. Without
his assistance the Relief work of the Masonic Bureau, would have found con
ditions much worse than they were.
On the morning of April 18th., last, a day and days to follow.long to be
remembered, it seemed that the world had run its course. There were few
inhabitants of San Francisco who were of an opinion other than that their
last day had come. The dp.y had dawned as calm and peaceful as a summer's
dream. Yet there was an oppresion, a feeling of unrest, a horror of something
that was about to happen but could not be foretold. Many tell of an uneasiness that seemed like the approach of unwelcome death. Others felt the
nervousness which precedes an illness; and the rest of the city slept.
Those who have taken notice of the husb and indescribable Eiilence of the
woods; who have heard the mournful soughing of the winds through the pines
just at the break of morn; have heard the wierd cries of the birds and beasts
of the forests as nature frowns and.takes on a darkened aspect; have listened
to the creaking and groaning of the trees like one in pain; have seen and heard
a flash and crash of lightning, a r0ar of thunde~ followed by a sudden hush as

GRAND LODGE OF CALiFORNIA.

301

though all nature were at rest, can picturein the minds eye to aslight extent
the first fierce rockings and wrenchings of the earth. and subsequent happenings which threw the minds and hearts of the inhabitants of the doomed city
into a state of alarm and desperation.
The darkness had hardly faded from the sky when the first shock came.
It was terrific in its intellBity; It seemed to wish to blot all things from the
coast. There was a crash of chimneys, falling walls, and buildingw,-gyrating
round in fantastic dances,-leaned far toward each other in the streets and
all but tumbled wrecks of their former "selves.' For a moment there was a
lull, a breathing spell. Then apparently froin the bowels of the earth there
came up a roaring as from a den of wild beasts followed by jar after jar which
shook the city to its foundations. The quake was terrifying, absolutely hideous, a monstrosity in its acts. . It seemed that there would be no end to the
thing. People ran screaming from their homes only to locate in even more
dangerous places. Domestic animals such as cats and dogs, were bewildered
and hurried and scurried about with their masters i~ search of a place of safety,
a somewhere that quiet could be found. But it was useless. In every direction there was ruin and desolation. Everywhere the conditions were the
same.
The earth's crust was· shaking, guivering, wrenching to the right and left
and in other opposite directions and it seemed that nothing could survive the
shock. Then all at once things seemed to find their equilibrium. The groans
of the wounded and dying ceased, those who had escaped unharmed stood
amazed and the most hideous and mind-wrecking character of it all, was the
ghastly, unearthly silence that followed.
It seemed like a tomb in the open streets. Not a thin'g of life seemed to
move or breathe. The seriousness of the situation ~ould not at first be grasped.
From all sections of San Francisco there could be plainly seen the glare of
light on the leaden sky cast by the fires which had sprung up in a hundred
different directiollB almost simultaneously. The dread cry that water was
not a.v ailable with which to fight the flames was passed from lip to lip and not
unlike N.e ro at the destruction. of .the beautiful city of Rome, the homeless
settled down to witnE)Ss the scenes of desolation and ruin.
·
It was not for long, however, for soon every available able-bodied man
was pressed into service in the attempt to stay the flames which were fast devouring buildings and property which had survived the tremblor. As the
men fought fast and hard, the women and children were hurriedly carrying
away the belongings from their doomed homes. Many pitiful sights .were
witnessed, many acts of charity were done and through it all the residents
showed a spirit of bravery and unconcern matchless in every particular.

Hardly had the last severe shock subsided before Mayor Schmitz and
other officials of San Francisco were at work attempting to· quiet a bewildered
ulmtitude, and the soldiery-the men of blue who know not what fear is-the mell" of blue of both the ·army and the police force-were soon patrolling

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

the streets to prevent looting and the wanton destruction of property. The
commanders located at the Presidio on that verge of land kissed by the first
waters which flow and ebb from the yawning mouth of the Golden Gate, did
wondrous things on behalf of the sufferers. They brought order out of chaos,
stilled the fear which seemed to close the throats of strong men and dependent
women and in tens of thousands of ways assisted in the work of caring for
those who had lost their all in the earthquake and fire.

peared to them, could have visited so fair a city and they feel that it was far
more an act of God than of human effort, that any part of the city was left
standing in which many of the thousands of strick.en men and women and
children found at least temporary homes.

302

Some of the scenes enacted during the first hours of the burning of the
city beggar description. The hospitals and homes for the wretched were
turned into mad houses. Patients w.ho were unable to care for themselves
groaned and cried out with feelings of helplessness, and, the stronger ones,those on the way to recovery-ran about like one possessed. · Fainting women,
praying men and bewildered children could be seen on evety hand and the
work of removing the sick, the crippled and the otherwise afflicted to the general hospital at the Presidio was by no means a small undertaking. There
were many nurses, who, from a feeling of duty had worked themselves beyoI].d
the power of human endurance and fell fainting to the floor. This added to
the already !Ong list of sufferers and for a time confusion reigned supreme.
As the flames, stealthily at times, then noisily and with a roar of defiance
swept their way along the principal streets, many lives were snuffed out'. The
dead and dying were tenderly cared for, but those who were in positions td
know agree that San Francisco's death roll would be long in calling provided
everybody had been recovered. The flames and resulting ruins have carefully and completely hidden from human sight all that remains of many who
were once prosperous citizens and beloved members of now grieving families.
For a time it appeared that there would be much illness in the city by
the Golden Gate and that there would be a famine, but these things happily
did not occur owing to the liberality and promptness of the outside cities providing food and clothing and Oakland was by no means the last to come to
the aid of her sister city which was so sorely stricken. In fact it was through
the efforts of the generous citizens, worthy officials and lodges and churches of
Oakland that San Francisco was not left to suffer and hold out her scorched
and withered hands for succor one moment longer than was absolutely necessary.
After days and nights of bitter strife with the flames which had greedily
consumed millions of dollars worth of property, it appeared that they were
under control, and hundreds, yes thousands of workers, both civilian and of
the army, who had kept the city in a roar with exploding dynamite, the use
of axes and wrecking paraphernalia, sank from utter exhaustion and in their
turn needed the care of those for whom they had risked their lives .that a portion at least of the city's homes might be spared.
Those who took part in the attempt to stay the flames have stated that
it all seemed like a dream; that nothing so overwhelmingly disastrous, it ap-

It was not long after the excitement had somewhat subsided that tented
cities filled with the destitute sprang up in many quarters and within an incredibly short space of time a regular system of relief had been adopted and
put into operation by those in authority. True'it was that the "green-eyed
monster, jealousy" crept in to make affairs disagreeable regarding the care
of certain camps, but taken as a whole the affair was most admirably handled.
And among the hardest workers in the field of desolation, care and want were
the members of the Masonic fraternity on the Oakland side of the bay who
were truly Masons from a lodge standpoint and who looked like masons by
trade as they struggled and wended their way about the smoky and grime! aden city in their work of relief.

San Francisco was indeed unfortunate. From exalted heights among
the world's greatest cities, she was suddenly stricken with earthquake and
fire and cast down so low that she became an object of chp,rity. Her parks
were dotted with the tente of refugees and her citizens were left struggling
in the throes of recovery and rehabilitation. For a considerable period of time ·
her situation was as an orchestra with every instrument out of tune with every
other instrument, and noise and dissatisfaction, not harmony resulted.
That any man or set of men could solve the problem of peace and regularity at such a time seems almost beyond comprehension, but it was done
and done well. The stones and bare bleak walls of San Francisco appealed
as eloquent advocates of harmony and decided effort on behalf of her dwellers
and officials and there were few who refused to join in the effort to lift their
city from the position which she occupied. Love of home was never more
thoroughly exemplified and debris filled streets, wrecked structures and ashes
did not deter many from at least making an attempt toward the reconstruction
and rehabilitation of the city by the Golden Gate.
Through all this terrible disaster by which every hotel, bank, every large
store and nearly every storeroom and wareroom in the city had been destroyed,
the conduct of the three hundred thousand people who were homelessand
thousands more who were left without the means of livelihood, was admirable. There was very little panic p,nd no serious disorder. The rations, tents,
and blankets on hand at the army posts adjacent to the city were dealt out
to the sufferers with no account of the responsibility involved; and within
two days, relief supplies from nl'lighboring states and cities and army supplies
from various army posts had begun to arrive and were being distributed.
It is almost useless to attempt to .go into detailed accounts of the events
of the days and nights of horror. Four square miles of the city were soon on
fire. The night was as light as day, and the roar of the conflagration, the
crash of falling walls, and the continuous explosions made a pande mnium

simply indescribable. It was .shortly after this that the members of the Masonic fraternity began to cross the bay for San Francisco to lend a helping

and others who had suffered through the disaster.

strongest terms and pledged the support of the Grand Lodge and the entire
order of the state. At this first meeting Brother Meek was elected perman-·
ent chairman and his endeavors during theentire relief work are worthy of more
than passing recognition. He, like many others of the order, worked day and

And it is advisable to say just at this time that the Masons were not holding meetings exclusive of everything else. It was necessary that they should
get together for the purpose of appointing their cominittees, directing the

work that wa.s being done on the outside and attending to other most importantmatters in cominittee meetings, but there was as much being done in the field
all the time and the Masons were the first in line to attend to t h!'! business
required.
Within a few hours after the disaster, there was not a member of the
Masonic organization on either side of the ba.y who had not been cared for
in one way or another. This refers to those in want. All those who had
escaped without loss in any direction, gladly joined with the working forces
and gave their aid in relieving the suffering which had existed in every direction.
As a first step in the direction of relief, the Masonic Relief Bureau on the
second day following the disaster sent eighteen wagons drawn by two horse"
each, filled with provisions to the stricken city. At a low estimate one hundred
and fifty tons of provisions were sent to San Francisco, the most of it being
furnished at the expense of the Masons. True it is that a p ortion of this
amount was given. by the Oakland Chamber of Commerce.
For over a week the brethren worked like slaves in Sa.n Francisco and
did not c9mplete all their work in Oakland for months after the disaster.
The headquarters in Oakland were in the Masonic Temple at Twelfth and
Washington streets and there were stations established in San Francisco at
Twenty-third and Mission streets, at the Stanya.n street entrance to the Park,
one in King Solomon's Ha.II on Fillmore street, one at North Beach and another
one at 3584 Clay street. Besides these there was a head. distributing point
and office in the ferry building. The amount of business transacted in these
quarters was enormous. At the ferry station there was a force of men constantly preparing sandwiches which were carried off in teams for distribution.
At least $15 a day was paid out for ea.ch of these wagons by the Masons and
after t hey had distributed the food, they picked up refugees' trunks and baggage
on their return trip. 1\ regular checking system was established and many
articles were carried to headquarters for the refugees regardless of sex, race,
color or to which fraternal organization, if any, they~belonged. And besides
the food which was freely distributed to the needy in San Francisco, over
35,000 meals were supplied the refugees in the Oakland Temple. Money
was sent in liberally from all quarters of the United States and this, with what
had been given locally, resulted in an immense relief fund at the disposal of
the Masonic fraternity.
The executive committee of the order was most generously treated by
the Santa Fe and Southern Pacific Railroad companies. · In many instances,
money was advanced for transportation and besides this t he companies never
refused any transportation to worthy and deserving people. In all the relief
work done in the city of Oakland and surrounding communities the railroad
organizations aided materially, and had it not· been for their conscientious
effort on behalf of those doing relief Work, but little headway could have been
mad~. The Ma.sonic fraternity are particularly t hankful to the companies

for the aid granted them by these corporations. The heads of the transportation companies on both sides of the bay were more than accommodating
and set a good example to others in a position to help in the relief work and a
general straightening of the tangled situation. Wherever a case was reported
by the Masonic executive committee as being worthy of assistance, there was
no disputing the report and the destitute soon found themselves speeding
over the rails on their way to home and friends. It would take a book of
large dimensions to place all the names of refugees who were carried over
the lines of the companies to all sections of the United States. It is stated
that refugees were carried to every point where the roads were run. This
in eludes the roads in the east which opened their lines to the local companies.
At the time of the arrival of the advance guard of the Masonic fraternity,
Market street was full of excited, anxious people who were gazing horrified
at the mins as the result of the various fires which had been merged into one
great conflagration. The presence of the members of this order with flying
badges had an instantly reassuring effect on all awe-inspired persons. They
knew the quality of the men wearing the badges and not in one ins.tance did
anyone of those in the streets apply for aid that it was not granted.
The thing that at this time ·made the greatest impression on the working lodge men was the strange and unearthly silence. There was no talking,
no apparent excitement among the near-by spectators; while from the great
and dying city lying at their feet there came not a single unusual sound.' No
one seemed to be greatly concerned over material possessions and each was
to the other as a brother. San Francisco had indeed been taught a hard lesson
and a lesson that softened in some distinct manner the instincts of the sufferers or their more fortunate brothers and sisters. Not that charity and
self-denialhadnoeager followers before that memorable time, but the terrific
disaster set more people to thinking of the bible's teachings than could all
the sermons ever preached from the pulpits of high or lowly houses of worship.
And the disaster which had changed San Francisco from a condition of
opulence 'to mendicant, came swiftly. Just a few short hours before, the
beautiful city by the sea had been a thing of beauteous life. It was the beginning
of the grand opera season and the star singers from all over the world had gathered together to give San Francisco music lovers one of the treats of the season. That light and refreshing "Carmen," was sung on Tuesday nightfatal Tuesday night. A few hours later there was no opera house, no places of
amusement, no safe place to go. The beautiful women who the night beore- had been brilliantly attractive in diamonds and ermine were rushing
hither and thither, caring not for dress, for jewels, for nothing but safety.
There was flame everywhere, smoke everywhere, and a feeling of hopeless
dread, filled the hearts of poor and rich alike. In a few short hours there
was a scene of desolation and destruction sufficient in its enormity to turn the
minds of even the strong~st men. Thit shock was a never-to-be-forgotten
sensation. It seemed that the devilish forces of destruction had centered

beneath the sandy crust of San Francisco peninsula. There was a rocking
motion north or south, followed by an upheaval that twisted buildings as
though they were builded of the most flimsy material. There was a panic
in many of the larger hostelries but numbers were collected in mind although
gazing at scenes of horror that were to sweep the city and fill the parks with
refugees.
It was some time before the people awoke to a full realization of the fact
that nature, with the combination of untoward circumstances, was not playing entirely fair. The men who were tmdging toward the city found crowds
already in the streets and in the squares watching the widespread destruction
and desolation. And these very refugees were being slowly but surely driven
further westward by the spread of the flames as they were fanned by the April
breezes. The action on the part of all the authorities was most commendable
and they have been the only ones to receive words of praise for their acts.
Many brave deeds, many acts of self-sacrifice, were done by others and the
Masonic brethren were by no means the last to give a helping hand to the
needy and wretched. They, as well as everyone else were for a considerable
time helpless in the face of the wail of fire which leaped block after block in
its work of destruction. In the first wild rush for a place of safety it was no
more than natural that the thoughts of the homeless thousands should turn
to a desire to leave the doomed city. Many there were who gaye up all hope
that even one building would remain standing and it is agreed that the changing of the wind to the east just at a critical time was all that prevented a further spreaJ of the fire into the Western addition. Had the flames once gained
headway on the west side of Van Ness avenue, it would most probably have
burned itself out along the shores of the Pacific.
It was 11.t this time that the railroad companies were prompt with their
most necessary aid, crowding their ferries and carrying refugees to all points
of the compass without charge. The,day of the greatest outgo was that folfowing the first shock and the movement was continuously heavy for the next
week or more. Simultaneously with the movement providing for carrying
people to places of refuge outside the city was the prompt effort to transport
supplies from all:directions, and the runs of relief trains from all quarters of
the globe broke .i,ll the transcontinental freight train records.
The fire swept in all over 455 blocks or squares, but fortunately all or
most of the waterfront was spared. This made it possible for the removal
of the refugees from San Francisco to Oakland and then to other outside
point~. It was felt by those who first jumped to .the steering gear in the
enormous work of caring for the destitute and arranging for the rebuilding '
of the great city, that the most searching test of efficiency in this world is
the sudden strain of emergency. Those who bore the supreme strain of unexpected emergency are those who are now considered the "men of the hour."
And there has not been a soul who denies that those in charge of railways
dotting this coast, saved, by most heroic measures, the city of San Francisco
from the terrible -consequences of panic and stampede.

It has been stated that in all the overwhelming calamity that befell San
Francisco during the three days' and nights' conflagration that followed the
earthquake, one of the supreme tragic moments was reached that Wednesday morning when the firemen, rushing with their engines and hose carts to
the various points of alarm, found themselves standing helpless before the
spreading flames beside empty hydrants. But there were more tragic moments than that. One of them was when Chief of the Firemen Sullivan was at
death's door by an injury sustained at the time of the earthquake. Bµt the
supreme tragic moment, the one that appealed to everyone in San Francisco
and outside points was, "what can be done with the hundreds of thousands
who are homeless and penniless?" The earthquake and fire were the acts
of God. The care for the poor, bewildered and destitute were the aets of
humanity. And from where was the first step toward relief to come? The
officials and the soldiery were active, but what of them in the case of those
who were flocking into the city of Oakland by the thousands-yes-tens of
thousands? They came unclothed-they came hungry, destitute, weary and
with hearts and minds heavy and numb because of the ordeal through which
they had just passed. This was the supreme moment and it is fortunate that
there were men in the city of Oakland who were equal to the emergency and
a goodly number of them wore the insignia of the Masonic fraternity.
On the <?akland side of San Francisco bay, it was like taking command
of a battle after it had been turned into a rout. The effectual fire fighting
in San Francisco was on the part of brave men who had the endurance or
permission to stay in threatened buildings, in fact it was of their own choice,
but the care of the wanderers, the putting of life into the stomachs and minds
of the wretched and depressed, the clothing of the naked, the feeding of the
destitute, fell into the hands of just as brave men as those who had risked
their lives in the attempt with dynamite and battering rams to stop the spread
of the flames. For is it not an act of bravery and stout-heartedness to feed
and clothe restless thousands when it took determined effort to find either
clothing or food, to find places in which the wretched could lay their heads,
to find blankets with which to cover their shivering forms? Is it not an act
of bravery to abandon one's business, to go without necessary sleep and to
labor by the light of the sun and throughout the darkest hours on behalf of
those unfortunates with whom you have no acquaintance or ties of relationship? Is it not bravery to risk your own lives to save those who hold
out hands of want to you for assistance? And these things and more were
done by the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau.
Before going into detail as to work done in the city of Oakland by the
Masonic Relief Bureau after the arrival of the refugees here, it may be well
to give some reasons as to the necessity for such a chaotic condition of affairs from the scientific side of it. Alexander G. McAdie of the United States
Weather Bureau situated in San Francisco has said, "that not the least interesting feature of the great earthquake was the record made at various
points on the earth's surface, showing the displacement of the earth particle,

or in other words, the indication of the passing earth tremors and waves.
The instrument by which earthquake motion is determined is called a seismograph, and the particular type of instrument most favored today is the
Bosch-Omori horizontal pendulum seismograph. The instrument obtains
its name from an eminent investigator Bosch; and an equally eminent Japanese investigator-Dr. F. Omori, Professor of Seismology in the Tokyo Imperial University and member of the Imperial Earthquake Investigation
committee. Ten or more of these instruments are installed at different points
around the globe, and doubtless very full records have been attained, the discussion of which will materially increase our knowledge of the way in which
the earth's surface transmits the jar occasioned by any great slip or dislocation of strata, comll!only called an earthquake.
"Europe seems far away from the Pacific Coast ·and yet within twenty
minutes from the time the earthquake began in San Francisco these horizontal and vertical Micro-Seismographs were busy recording, as best they could,
the different sets of wave motions traversing the United States, speeding
across the Atlantic and hurrying throughout Europe. Japan is our neighbor
to the West. but not a close neighbor. Within eleven and one-half minutes
the seismographs in Tokyo were recording the beginning of the shock in San
Francisco. It was then about 10:30 Wednesday night in Japan-Japan
standard time. Without delay Prof. Omori could tell by means of the record
given on the seismograph that a severe earthquake had occurred on the American side of the Pacific at 5:13:05 A. M.-our time. The record of the earthquake at Washington, D. C., in the weather bureau laboratory obtained by
Prof. Charles Marvin, with a large Omori seismograph, told him before the
news had yet arrived from San Francisco that a severe dislocation of the
earth's crust had occurred about 2450 miles away from Washington. It was
then 8:19 in the morning, Washington time. The actual displacement of
the ground at Washington, D. C., was nearly one-half inch each side of a point
of rest. The movement was so slow, however, that only a seismograph could
detect it.
"At Tokyo the movement was a little less and equally slow. In San
Francisco if a record of the movement could have been obtained, perhaps an
inch or more each side of the neutral point would have been recorded; but
executed in an extremely short time. These displacements, continuing for
about forty seconds, from west to east and back again, and up and down,
constitute the heavy, racking and twisting motions known to nil of us.
"One of the most interesting features of the seismograph record is the
duration of the so-called preliminary tremors. These small waves travel
through the body of the earth at the rate of about six or seven miles a second. They precede the larger waves, which apparently move on the earth's
surface and travel at a rate of about two miles a second. Knowing the interval between the beginning of the preliminary tremors and the beginning
of the surface waves, we can determine approximately the point or line of

312

313

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

origin of the earthquake. Thus at Washington the preliminary tremor lasted
six minutes. At Tokyo, mne minutes and forty-nine seconds. At Birmingham, Engiand, they lasted twenty-live minutes. Sometime in the future
when seismographs will be in use in San Francisco, we will be able to note
the beginning of a small earthquake, and by comparing our seismograph
with those made elsewhere, determine the center or line of origin.
"At a point exactly midway around the world from San Francisco the
tremors would have lasted twenty-eight minutes. It is not merely to satisfy
scientific curiosity that such records are made. Far from it. The welfare
of mankind is the objective. Judging from the history of disturbances in
this kindly land, the present generation will probably not be called upon to
again undergo such experiences as those of April 18th.. Mankind fortunately
recovers quickly and as quickly forgets. A certain few, however, more devoted than ever to their labors, will follow the trail with a doggedness and
persistence that can only spell achievement, measuring earth movements
for the welfare of all men."
No sooner had the refugees and Masonic lodge members commenced to
arrive in Oakland, than those who had taken up the relief work realized that
there was an enormous amount of work to do. While the various members
of the order had done all that humans could do in the way of relief in San Francisco, there was a heavy strain on this side of the bay. In order that there
might be no confusion in arranging for transportation, food, clothing or money
for the really needy, the Masonic Executive Committee went at once to work
in the preparation of blanks which when properly filled out and signed, were
all that were needed by those in search of employment or anything else in
the way of assistance. That the simplicity of the form and yet its thoroughness might be determined, it is here reproduced :

The brothers . sent to San Francisco received much praise at the hands
of their superiors for .the splendid results they obtained and the general good
work done there. It was no easy task to climb about the brick-filled streets
and through hot debris to reach the side of those in trouble; it was no easy
task to convince many that it would be safe to cross San Francisco bay to
Oakland as they had been informed that Oakland was as bad off as San Francisco if not worse. As soon as they were prevailed to come to Oaklan d, how
ever, they were glad of the chance to get somewhere where they knew that
they would be provided for in every way. They were clothed, fed, housed,
given money, provided with transportation and sympathy at the hands of
the Masonic Relief Bureau and many of those so aided had no connection
. whatever with the Masons or any member of the Masonic fraternity. Yet
this had no effect on the attention given them. The Masonic records of the
greatandoverwhelmingdisaster show that numerous utter strangers to Masonryorthe crafth Ld the best ofatt.ention and at no cost to themselves. Hundreds of women nnrl likewise men who had no place to go and who were in need of
food, were taken in by the committees and properly attended. No worthy
subject, and in fact many unworthy ones were lifted upon their feet by those
who had willingly given their time and attention to the helpless who came
to Oakland in droves.

A slight idea of the enormous amount of work and good done by the Masonic Relief Bureau can be gleaned from minutes held by the members of
the bureau and of the Executive Committee. The first meeting, as has been
told, was held on ,t he twentieth day of April, a time when it was seen that every
organization, church and individual must put forth their best efforts toicare
for the thousands of refugees who were flocking to the Oakland side of the
bay. At that meeting, necessary committees were appointed and steps were
taken for obtaining and distributing information badges that there should
be no hitch in efficient service. It was at this meeting that the Grand Lodge
and the entire order of the state promised their support in the work. During the evening of the same day the wives of the members of the·various lodges
were called in to take a hand and right well did they do the work laid down
for them. The executive committee was appointed during this meeting
and many brothers volunteered their services in any capacity. In fact there
were so many wishing to give their aid, that no work could be found for them
to do. There was not a member of the order found who was not willing and
even anxious to get in line with the workers.
On a called meeting for April 28th, it being called to order by Chairman
R. W. Meek, it was agreed to transfer the .work of the committee to the secretary. In consequence the chairman was empowered to employ a competent
person who gave his entire time to the relief work. This was a great saving
of time to the committee which was working night and day to keep things
running smoothly and to see that all the wants of the refugees were attended
td. It was agreed at this meeting that the Executive Committee should
rneet nightly, until the stress of trouble was over, and it was also agreed that

During the meeting of May 14, Brother Robert E. Evans was directed to
issue supplies from the Masonic Temple only on Mondays and Thursdays.
Prior to this time a vast amount of clothing and food stuffs had been issued
every day from the Temple but by this time there was less rail for aid, many
of the refugees having secured work or taken their departure for other pa:r:ts,
so the daily issuance of supplies was considered not necessary. As the demands were fewer the members of the executive committee decided at this
meeting to have sessions only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays instead
of every night in the week. This was agreed to by every member of the executive committee and despite the decrease of the number of sessions in a week,
all relief work was most thoroughly attended fo. At the meeting on May
18th, the first case of one's mind being effected through the horrors of the
earthquake, was brought to the attention of the mem.b ers of the executive
committee. A member of· the lodge visited the house where the unfortunate was located and he and his wife were furnished with necessaries and given
transportation to their home in Los Angeles county where they could be given
proper attention. Another member was given transportation to Fresno,
he having lost everything in the disaster.
Up to and including May 25th, much general business was transacted
and at a meeting on the latter date, Chairman Meek notified those present
that he was in receipt of $5000 from Most Worshipful Motley H. Flint for
relief purposes.
This willgive but a slight impression of the actual work that was done
by those in charge as well as the regular relief workers of the Masonic Relief
Bureau. Hundreds and thousands of cases were attended to; transportation
was given out with a lavish hand, hundreds. were clothed and a countless
army of the needy were given food and shelter. It would be most difficult
to call to mind just the number of cases attended to. There are records of
a number of them, but in many instances not even a pencil mark was kept
as a record of most charitable a.ct~, but those who aided the needy were of
large hearts and carry in their being the souls of men which cannot stand
idly by and see humanity suffer. ·
That which has been told heretofore was largely attended to by the executive committee. While their actions were all that could be desired and that
they directed the general relief work, goes without saying, but the labor of
the members of the other committees was far from being anything but most

And then there is the printing committee which consisted of Thomas
Miller, Roy Farish and J . H. Taylor. They were tireless at their task and
their efforts greatly assisted every other committee in the relief work. Then
there was the auditing committee-the committee which has more to look
after possibly than any other committee other than the executive committee.
But the auditing of bills, the straightening out of many tangled matters is
of no small consequence. Their work must be conscientiously and thoroughly
done and this was so in regard to this committee. One of the best committees
of the Oakland Relief Committees, was the Auditing Committee with James
P. Edoff at its head. Both that committee and the Auditing Committee of
the Masonic Relief Bureau are worthy of the utmost praise.
Then there was the Bedding and Cots Committee. They are obliged to
work hard and those who believe that relief work from standpoint of this committee is not difficult and trying work, he or she try it. Here and there and
there and here for something for the needy to rest a weary head. A hunt
fora cot, a search for a bed and when the day is done and although hundreds have
been provided for in this direction, there are hundreds more waiting for a
repetition of the work that has gone before. And the Train Committee.
Those who have fought their way through large crowds i'!st for the purpose
of finding a relative or friend, can realize what the members of such a committee must have to contend with. At the time just following the earthquake there were thousands hurrying to Oakland. It was the duty of the
members of this committee to locate the deserving refugees and see to it that
they were properly cared for, and it was a gigantic undertaking.
Then we have the ,H ousing committee. The members of this committee
were obliged to go from place to place in search of rooms and other accommodations for those who were arriving in Oakland faBter than they could be
provided for by all the relief committees, lodges, churches and other like associations. The Housing committee worked day and night in Oakland to get
rooms for those who depended upon them in this direction. Every house
in Oakland was visited with the hopes that a vacant room could be found.
They were successful in many instances but in a great majority of cases, the
wanderers were sent to the refugee camps or to tents provided for them.
Every cot available to the Masons was pressed into service regardless of race,
