These first one hundred applications are included in this report with the
object in view of showing the various requirements of the refugees and . to
illustrate how many different lodges had members who were rendered entirely destitute by flame a~d earthquake.
Some wanted one thing and some another. There were petitions for
transportation, food, clothing, cooking utensils, tents, cots and bedding and
numerous other articles needless to mention. The largest number probably
asked for transportation as they were anxious to get near friends or relatives.
But hundreds were clothed and fed during the days of stress and discontent
following the disaster. In the Masonic Temple there was a n unusually busy
scene. Those without places to sleep and those without food or shelter were
all provided for and it is safe to say that the members of the Masonic fraternities were as heavy losers as those connected with any like organization.
And the members of the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau did not stop
to look into their own losses when they saw the thousands or homeless flocking in Oakland. They at once prepared to meet the emergency and most
well did they do the work. They worked hand in hand with the Oakland
Relief Committee and outside lodges and also did much individual and collective relief work. Had it not been for the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau
in Oakland, there would have been much unnecessary suffering and want.
The Masons, as has been said before, did not only care for Masons, but out
of the generosity of their own hearts and pockets, prepared most generously
and aided greatly in the general relief work which was going on. In fact
the Oakland Masonic Bureau considered itself a part of a great organization
of relief committees, lodges and churches which were working toward one
end-the care of the de9titute and the protection of the helpless.
The exact details of the work can never be tabulated. So much good
was done and quickly forgotten because of something else to do, that no record
was kept of every act, but the general aid given and the charity extended,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

321

will not be forgotten long after the city of San Francisco has cleared away
her debris and risen anew 1 one of the grandest cities of our United States.
And she will not forget that Oakland willingly and unselfishly held out a helping hand to the bewildered San Franciscans who called loudly for aid.
Those who worked with and assisted the Oakland Masonic Relief Bureau, have not looked for nor did they expect that they would receive any
words of praise for their many worthy acts, but to give succor to the hungry,
to hunt out homes for the needy and to do other such deeds of valor, place
such men side by side with those who have made history through times of
war and troublous periods. The man who will aSl:!istanother man and neglect his own affairs and relatives to do so, is· a man, every inch of him. And
the world-knows it, knows that Oakland produced more real men than has
been the fortune of any other city within the confines of the Un.lied States.
For the occasion presented itself and those in charge of things, were not found
wanting.
Money was no object to those doing ~lief work. The pinched, drawn,
miserable faces and bodies of the women and children as well as men who
came here for succor and relief, were too much a lesson of self denial to allQw
any to stop to think of self gain or self sacrifice. Taken from the outset the
the affair was well and most thoroughly handled. While the members of the
Masonic Bureau were doing all in their power to relieve suffering, there were
others in Oakland doing the same. And when the needy were concentrated
in the camps on the Oakland shores of San Francisco bay, the efforts of all
were doubled.
Nightly meetings of the ·executive committee were held while the crisis
was on and they were all well attended. Questions of vital moment were
discussed and considered from every view-point and in most instances were
decided with practical unanimity. And the financing of this emergency enterprise was no small matter of itself. The money raised in Oakland was
supplemented by generous contributions from many outside points. The
difficulty and rather delicate duty of determining the demands made upon
the treasury was carefully and conscientiously perfonned and a system of
vouchers was devised that saved many dollars for the Masonic Bureau and
guaranteed the.disbursement of money without fear of favor or mistake.
The ladies who gave su~h great and willing assistance during the days
of trials and troubles following the earthquake and fire, should come in for
much deserving praise. Their knowledge of humanity and their quicR sense
of justice, worked much toward the splendid ends attained. They were here,
there and everywhere, looking out for the interests of the affiicted and had
it not been for their hearty co-operation with the male sex, who were also
hard and willing workers, it is more than probable that it would have taken
much more time to right affairs than it did.
There is one individual whose position was most trying and yet who wa~
never heard to enter a complaint and that person is Robert G. Evans, chief

322

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

of the Commissary department. Although his duties were many and varied,
he attended to them with such exa.c tness and business ability, that there was
no -confusion in obtaining and distributing food to the refugees.. At one time
shortly .after the overwhelming disaster, the banquet hall in the Masonic
Temple proved inadequate for the horde of needy who were served with meals
and a coffee and sandwich line was instituted on the street. · For a number
of days there were hundreds who satisfied their appetites in this manner ·and
the line was done away with only after affairs had become largely settled.
Mr. Evans had much assistance from the ladies in his work and felt thankful
for it.

It might be said again that it w.o uld be utterly useless to give a detailed
statement of the work done or to personally mention each and every one who ·
had a hand in the work, but they have satisfaction in the fact that t heir work
was appreciated, it having been done well-extremely well. Those who
toiled in Oakland and those who labored in San Francisco well realize that
if it had not been for united effort on the part of all concerned, no such worth)io
and commendable actions could ·have been carried out and no such self-satisfying results have been obtained. There is not a man, woman or child,
Mason, or members of other organizations who can help but admit that the
liberality of Most Worshipful Motley H. Flint was not excelled by any individual nor can they deny that Dr. R. W. Meek, Chairman of the Executive
committee and President of the Oakland Masonic Relief Association did not
do everything in his power to aid the afflicted and to give his assi~tance to
every m~"l who willingly gave time and attention to the work of relief. Neither
can it be denied that each and every member of any of the committees under
the Masonic order did all within human reason and endurance to rarry out
the work laid down for them. The sick were sen t to proper institutions or
to friends, the naked were given clothing, the hungry were liberally fed, the
strangers were given transportation to their homes and everything was done
that could be done for the welfare of the unfortunate visitors from San Francisco.
Despite the fact that t he offirers and committeemen as well as many
others did all in their power to give comfort to the needy, they would have
been powerless to act without the aid of those who contributed so liberally
to the relief fund of the Masonic Relief Bureau of Oakland. Money poured
in from every direction and was put to the best of use. Everything was
carried on along strictly business lines and the financial report shows that the
O~kland Masonic Relief Bureau ha d on hand at the meeting of September
10, 1906, the splendid sum of $1 1,046.08. As the relief work is to be continued
throughout the year, this money wili be used in the general work of relief
and that it will be iu.diciously distributed, goes without saying.

ALAMEDA RELIEF BOARD.
Alameda, Cal., Sept. 16, '06.
Motley H. Flint,
Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Los Angeles, Cal.
Dear Sir and Brother:We submit herewith statement of the relief extended by Oak Grove Lodge
No. 215, F. & A. M.
9n April 19th, 1906, a special. meeting was called for the purpose to.
provide ways and means to secure aid for .the refugees. A motion was made
and seconded that the Master be authorized to spend $500. 00 and appoint a
committee of fifteen to assist him in caring for them.
The committee was divided into squads of three who worked on all the
local trains coming into our city and turned them over to others who were
in waiting to receive them and conveyed by vehicle to our hall, where they
were fed and made as comfortable as possible.
. A quantity of bedding was bought, used for making beds for the many
-~fugees, the large hall being for families and women, the .s mall hall being
used for the men.
A number were permitted to take bedding where shelter could be provided
in different parts of our city.
The Temple was thrown open on the morning of April 20 and was kept
open for twenty-four h?urs per day till Thursday, May 3, 1906, when t he dining
room was closed.
No account was kept of the number of meals served.
No one was turned away, no questions asked as to sect or opinion, t hat a person who came up the steps was in need was sufficient.
Through the aid ol the Ladies of the Eastern Star, and others, the dining
room was handled splendidly, flowers brightened the tables and t he sympathetio
touch of these kind hands gladdened the hearts of many a sufferer.
The committee are indebted to many who gave their time and Bervice
and others who refused pay for service and supplies;Received from Grand Master, _______ __ __ _

SAN JOSE RELIEF BOARD.

With great gratitude to those jurisdictions and lodges who contributed
it, your fund has been drawn against to the amount of Seven Thousand Dollars.
Some thirty odd casei. have been attended to out of this fund, amounting in
all to the sum of $3,577 49 and leaving a balance on hand to date as noted below

To Motley H. Flint,
Grand Master F. &. A. M., of California.
M. W. Sir and Brother:
The great calamity of April last , occasioned special and immediate
acti~n in doing our part toward rendering every kind offiee that might be

required of the Masonic Fraternity in those trying days.

.

Many thoughtful and kindly acts had already been performed by member~ of the craft, both as citizens and Masons and by the Masonic Board of
Rehef ot Sa~ Jose, .when a special gathering of Masons took place on
Sunday mornmg, April 22nd at the Masonic Temple at San Jose, called by
the. Masters of the Lodges of that city at which I was L-ppointed permanent
chairman. A secretary and twQ assistants were chosen and arrangements
made · for · systematic relief work at the railroad depots and elsewhere
Inside of an hour after adjournment, a large tent had been erected at the S.· p.
Depot and headquarters established there. The trustees of the Unitarian
Church kindly tendered the fraternity the use of the church and the edifice
was immediately supplied with cots, blankets etc. for caring for the refugees
from San Francisco.

•

Books were also at once opened by the Secretaries to record the name.~
of Masons who had rooms at their homes that might be used for bretherrt in
need ~f such .and many hundreds were cared for in that manner, thereby
rendenng a kmdly office as well as spreading the cement of · brotherly love
and affection.

Receipts and Disbursements are appended;
·Funds were received from the Grand Master as follows :

May 26, - - - - -- - --- -- - -- -- -- -- --- - --- ------ -- -__ _- ----- - --- -- -- __ - -- - -- - -- --- __ __ ___ 2000 . 00
Sept. 7,

. . This class of work went on for many days, regular changes being made
m the personnel of the members stationed at the depots and el~ewhere.
The headquarters were kept open all night for over a week.
With thankfulness I note that not a death occurred among the members
of the craft in this district, as a result of the catastrophe ; though several
members were injured and a great many lost a portion or all their possessions.
The whole-heartedness with which the Masonic fraternity here and
e~ewhere entered into the work of relief occasioned not only all the commendation of members of the Craft, but received the benediction of the people
at large
·
Thanks is due to the railroad companies for carrying many members to
an? fro~ this city free of charge for transportation, some members indeed
bemg given t ransportation a great distance

One of my first actions was to enter into communication with those of
our brethern residing in San Francisco, to ascertain, as well as we might,
their condition and needs. With many of these letters we Eent receipt for
dues and assured the brethern of our desire to assist them at once. Those
residing in our own midst who could be assisted, were personally visited an<l
promptly given assistance. In some cases it was to rebuild chimneys or
repair houses ; in others to care for the injured. In two cases the lumber for
two cottages was furnished. Several professional members were enabled
to secure a new start in their professions. Other members were prov~ded
with funds to secure provisions and clothing etc. Of course this does not
include the many cases that were looked after by individual Masons.
It is pleasant to note in this connection that so far as I know, no case
went unrelieved·, nor was relief extended beyond an amount that seemed
judicious.
All bills contracted for are paid with the iixception of one which cannot
be paid until the repairs are completed.
In connection with t he relief work I wish to say that a splendid display
of self-denial was exhibited by many members of the Craft in their eagerness
to do their utmost for those less fortunate. May the blessings of Heaven
rest upon them.

SACRAMENTO RELIEF BOARD.
M. W. Motley H . Flint
Grand Master of Masons of Calif.
Dear Sir and Brother:As requested by you, I attach report showing relief given to San Francisco Fire Sufferers by Sacramento Masonic Board of Relief.
Our Board, which is composed of the Masters and Wardens of the five
Lodges here, met on the day following the catastroph~ to make arrangements
to take care of all who might come this way. At the Board's request, I made
a trip to Oakland and personally offered you our assistance. ~he Masters
reported to the Board that their Lodges stood ready to assist us financie.lly
as did the Masonie Hall Ass'n, Sacramento Chapter No. 3, R. A. M. and the
Scottish Rite Bodies and also appointed members to act in conjunction with
the Board. Committees were appointed to remain on duty at the Hall, and
arrangements were made to furnish Board and Lodgings. We did not.have as
many cases as we expected, but this was due to the fact that the majority
of those who left San Francisco continued on to Eastern points .
The report shows a balance of $278.60 and the Board thinks that if
you decide to allow us to retain this balance, it will, with the amount we have
in our General Fund, last us through the winter.
Trusting the report meets with your approval, I remain·,
Yours fraternally,
F . A. Roblin,
Secretary.

Vouchers have been retained in all cases.
I am of the opinion that this balance should shortly be turned over to
the Masonic Board of Relief of San Jose to be retained for the purpose of
caring for such cases of relief as may yet arise, and in assisting those who
may need further aid.
The thanks of those who have been assisted as well as all members of
the Craft go out to those of our brethern who so promptly and efficiently
extended their sympathy and relief.
My personal thanks are due to the Masters of the San Jose Lodges
and the members of the Board of Relief for their assistance.
While some of the Lodge rooms in this district were damaged and in
some instances totally destroyed, yet the losses to the Lodges were in all
cases, I am glad to report, trifling.
I recognize with pleasure and cordiality, M. W. Grand Master, your
promptness, solicitude and cooperation during a per:od that required strong
executive ability.
Respectfully submitted,
Delos W. Smythe,
Chairman Special Committee.

FRUITVALE RELIEF BOARD.
Fruitvale, Aut,'Ust 18, 1906.
Motley H. Flint, M. W. Grand Master of F. & A. M. of Cal.,
Dear Sir and Broth~r
Your request concerning the relief work done, at hand. At the call of
the Master of Fruitvale Lodge, a meeting of the members convened for the
express purpose of providing some ways and means to take care of refugees,
masons and others who might come from San Francisco
· The most feasible plan proposed and adopted as the best, was the establishment of Masonic Headquarters on the main thoroughfare and the appointment of a committee to act in conjunction with the officers of the lodge,
to visit San Francisco and also to wait upon the local trains which arrive
every 20 minutes in Fruitvale from San Francisco. To aid and assist refugee
Masons and other needy persons, the committee made themselves conspicuous by the Masonic badges they wore. In this way Masons were easier
identified, located and temporary . shelter provided.
At a call meeting of the Lodge on April 30, arrangements were formulated
to have a committee of brethern in the· vicinity surrounding their homes
visit their neighbors and ascertain if there were any Masons stopping with
them and whether they could provide room for any refugees. This committee which consisted of thirty-six members, made this search on the day
following and secured places of shelter for a large number of families. A
committee visited the Oakland Masonic Board of Relief and were informed
by that body that whatever provisions were needed for refugees in Fruitvale
might be obtained from them for the expressing of them to Fruitvale. The
expressing was provided for and the provisions taken to the Fruitvale headquarters and distributed to the needy, although a numberwere provided with
provisions in this manner. A great number were taken care of at the homes of
brethern who did not call on the Relief Board for assistance
One hundred and twenty-seven Masons were taken care of i.I1 this manner.
· Doctors of the Fruitvale Lodge gave their attention to the sick free of
any charge.
·
·
I only mention the above to have it clear in your mind that the brethern
of Fruitvale Lodge met their obligations without any shirking of their duty.
I will concede to your request regarding the expenses, but with the understanding that Fruitvale Lodge does not wish to be re-imbursed. The brothers
appreciating the fact that they were called upon to help in the hour of need.
·

SAN RAFAEL RELIEF BOARD.
SAN RAFAEL, CAL., Sept. 13, 1906.
MoTLEY H. FLINT, Grand Master,
DEAR BROTHER:-;Your kind letter of recent date to Marin Lodge No. 191, F. & A. M. is
at hand and was read at our stated meeting last ·night. I was directed to
answer it as follows:
"Directly after the disaster of April 18th, we met and intended to organize a Board of Relief, but soon changed our minds and concluded to work in
conjunction with the General Relief Committee in San Rafael. Our Lodge
contributed $150.00 to the Relief fund, besides assisting Brethren and the
Relief Committee in numerous ways. We held advisory meetings every
night, and kept the Lodge room open daily with some one in charge.
On April 21st we conducted the funeral of a Brother who was killed in
Santa Rose by the earthquake. The Brother belonged to Santa Cruz Lodge."
I think this covers the ground, at least in a general way, and I hope it
will answer the requirements.
Fraternally yours,
DR. G. G. v ANDERLIP,
Secretary.

ALCATRAZ RELIEF BOARD.
OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA, Sept. 16, 1906.
MuTLEY H. F·LINT, EsQ.,
Grand Master of Masons of California,
Los Angeles,
W OHSHI PFUL SIR : -

As an or.ganization Alcatraz Lodge took but little part in the relief work
incident to the disaster of April 18th.
As individuals many of our members took active parts. Matters so
shaped themselves that the lodge was not called on for any particular action
in the relief work-in fact, but one brother has asked for assistance since the
date mentioned.
When the influx of refugees from San F rancisco commenced, the Officers
of Alcatraz Lodge immediately transformed our Temple into a temporary
hotel, and invited all comers, without reference to fraternal connections, to
partake of our hospitality. We fully expected to continue this course in. definitely, and were preparaed to empty our treasury, if necessary, in the good
cause. But fortunately for us the General Relief Committee soon heard of
ur situation, and immediately offered to furnish us with all .the provisions

334

. PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIF.ORNIA.

required. Needless to say the offer was gratefully accepted, and up to the
time of the concentration of the _refugees in one general camp, we were supplied
with groceries, vegetables, etc., in the greatest profusion. Our entire outlay
as a Lodge will not exceed $125, and while we thank you most sincerely for
your offer to reimburse us for our expenditures, we most respectfully decline
as we feel we can stand this small amount without inconvenience. Neither
do we expect to call on the Grand Lodge for funds during the coming winter,
as, although it is true we have several Brothers on our rolls who will undoubtedly require assistance, we are quite confident that the funds of the Lodge
will be ample for all demands.
We desire to callyourspecial attention to the noble work performed by
the ladies of Unity Chapter, No. 65, 0. E . S. without whose assistance we could
have accomplished but little. They responded to the call for help instantly
and willingly, and for nine days worked early and late in ministering to the
wants of hundreds of refugees, as well as three companies of soldiers who
were quartered on us at different times.
· No account was kept of the number of meals served, but a conservative
estimate would place the number at four thousand.
Our main Lodge Room was used as a dormitory by the refugees, and the
large assembly hall on the first floor was placed at the disposal of the soldiers.
All who made themselves known as being in any way connected with the
Masonic Fraternity were directed to the Masonic Committee's headquarters
at 12th and Washington Sts., where special attention was accorded them.
Several of our members were active participants in the work of this Committee
whose endeavors can only be commended in the highest terms, a full account
of which will doubtless be rendered to you from other sources. .
Special mention must also be made of the other Fraternal organizations
who occupy our Lodge room, and who for over three weeks surrendered their
rights without a murmur-neither asking or expecting any rebate in their
rent, and many of the individual members offering contributions of money
supplies and services.
Thanking you most sincerely for the interest you have displayed in Alcatraz Lodge, I remain,
Fraternally Yours,
H. A. GLJNES,
Secretary.

LOS ANGELES RELIEF BOARD.
To the Most Worshipful
Motley Hewes Flint Grand Master of Masons
State of California:
()ear Sir and ·Brother:Complying with your request of August 16, 1906, concerning the action
which this Board of Relief took in the matter of the dirnster cccasioned by
Earthquake and fire which befel the Cen tral po1tion of our glorious State,
on the 18th ·day of April, 1906, will say:That immediately upon the realization•of that awful calamity, a special
meeting of t he Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles, was called on April
22nd, 1906, at which meeting I was directed to cornmunicafo with each Masonic Body of this City, and request a contribution of One Dollar ($1.CO)
i}er capita, to enable our Board ·to relieve the distress of the rr.ernbers of the
craft, and those dependent upon them who might take refuge in our City.
This request was promptly complied with, and there came into my hands,
as Secretary, from the vario.us Masonic Bodies of our city, together with
individual contributions; and also from Mount Zion lodge of Troy, N. Y.,
the sum of Three Thousand One Hundred and Seventy-Four Dollars and
Fifty Cents ($3,174 . 50 ).
Arrangements were made that the Masonic Board of Relief, should
establish Headquarters at the Masonic Temple, and notices were placed in
all the Newspapers of the City, calling attention to that fact. We secured the
use of the Banquet Room and I\itchen for the purpose of providing meals ;
also the Lodge Room recently vacated by the Scottish Rite Bodies, was filled
with cots and bedding for use of the ladies.
We secured the upper floor of the Lexington Hotel (now the Rosselyn
Hotel) for t he use of the gentlemen.
A cook was hired, and with the assistance of the Ladies of the Eastern
Star, meals were provided at the Masonic Temple; committees were appointed,
who met all trains corning from the North, and brought the members of the
fraternity to the temple, and after a bath, a good meal, and a rest, positions
were secured, as best the:i< could be, for employment.
Those of the unfortunates who were in feeble health, were sent to the
Southern California Masonic Home at t;ian Gabriel, at our expense, and when
they were recovered, they sought employment.
Quite a number of refugees being aged, and having relatives in other
cities, were furnished with transportaiton, as they desired.
It is estimated that at least One Thousand (1000 ) Meals were furnished
at our expense.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the
Grand Lodge as follows :
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master
and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I beg to submit this brief report upon the condition and needs
of the Lodges in the several Masonic Districts of this Grand Jurisdiction.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

367

In Augu?t last a circular letter was sent to each District Inspector, which was intended as a sort of guide to them, pointing to
the matters which, as Inspectors, it would be their especial duty to
investigate.
It is gratifying to be able to say that nearly all the Inspectors
have sent in their reports conc.e rning the work they have accomplished and the condition of the Lodges over which they have been
called to exercise supervision and impart the necessary instruction
in the Ritual and Work.
·
From the reports of the Inspectors, it is found that with few
exceptions the Lodges are in a prosperous condition; that the work
is in accordalice with the Ritual and fairly well done ; that the books
· of secretaries are neatly and correctly kept; that the minutes are
prop.e rly transcrib.e d by the secretaries and signed by the W.'. M.'.
as required by the Grand Lodge; that the dues, though not collected
in advance, as required by the Uniform Code of By-Laws, are generally paid at or before the annual election of officers. In this con·
nection I might say that the custom of paying dues at the end of
the Masonic year has grown almost into a law.
The Inspectors report that they have been busy in the discharge of their official duties and have visited and instructed the
Lodges of their respective districts at all times when requested
by the Lodges to do so, and more than this, have voluntarily gone
to the Lodges and proffered their assistance.
It is to be regretted, however, that some Lodges, notably those
which are in the greatest need of instruction and assistance, are
the ones that not only refrain from asking the Inspectors for help,
but also fail to get together when notified by the Inspector in
advance of his coming.
It would be of great benefit if the Grand Lodge should adopt a
regulation providing that where the Inspector is cognizant of a
Lodge in his district that from carelessness or lack of interest is
not able to confer any or all degrees in a creditable and proper
manner, the Inspector be authorized to forbid further work in the
Lodge until the fault be remedied.
I hold that the Inspect or is
now so authorized; and I know of an instance where the Inspector,
knowing a certain Lodge in his district was not able to c·o nfer the
degree as it should be done, went to the W.'. M.'. of that Lodge
on the day the degree was to be given and forbade it, until the
Lodge had been called together and practiced on the work until
the W.' . M.'. and his officers had acquired the necessary proficiency.
It was a splendid lesson, not only to the Lodge itself, but to the
other Lodges of that district. It was a glorious example of the
stam~na of that Inspector and worthy of emulation by other Inspectors.

368

369

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

It has been apparent to me for several years that it would be
of benefit to the Lodges to require Junior Wardens~elect before
being installed, to be able to confer the E. A. degree, :nd that
Senior Wardens be able to confer both E. A. & F. C.
Were this provision embodied in a Regulation, it would not
make it necessary for the Master-elect to cram into his memory in
a short time the entire work of the three degrees.
It would lessen the strain and confusion consequent upon
burdening the mind so much in so short a time, and it would lighten
the task of the Inspectors by having them examine the Masterelect only in the Ritual of the Third Degree and the law governing
Masonry in general and his duties as Master in particular. Upon
this question I have sounded the several Inspectors, and through'.
them the ·o fficers of the Lodges, and the result has shown the great
majority of all concerned very much _in favor of such a regulation,
and I therefore respectfully suggest that such a regulation be
adopted by the Grand Lodge.

I presume that the Inspectors whose reports have not reached
me have, through business pressure or forgetfulness, neglected this
duty.
I regret that it has been impossible for me to do as much work
during the year as I had hoped and planned to do.
The great cal1amity of last April so much disturbed the whole
State that for several months it seemed impossible to settle down
to the usual order of everyday business, and later the intense summer heat rendered work in the Lodge-rooms so disagreeable that
it would have been little less than torture for the brethren to assemble.
However, I have done the best that was possible under the
circumstances.

It is known to the Grand Lodge and the membership throughout the State that at all times since I have held the office of Grand
Lecturer, I have been engaged in professional work in the city of
San Francisco and could only devote such time to Masonry as
was not occupied in my profession.

reposed in me, and thanking the brethren for the many kindnesses
ancl courtesies extended me, I am,
Sincerely and fraternafiy,
WILLIAM H. EDWARDS,
Grand Lecturer.

There seems to be a sentiment among the Lodges that the
time has come when the Grand Lodge of California should have
its Grand "Lecturer devote his entire time to the business of lecturing the Lodges, not only in the Ritual and Work of the Fraternity
as used in the conferring of degrees and the proper transaction
of the business of a Lodge, but also in the principles and groundwork of this greatest of all societies.

Which report was ordered to be referred to a Special
Committee of three, and the Grand Master named the following brethren to constitute such committee-

It is well known many of our brethren know less about the
history and symbolism of Masonry than they should. They are
eager to learn more. Nothing could be. of more benefit to the
Grand Lodge than to have a Lecturer go from Lodge to Lodge,
stirring up interest, awakening enthusiasm and so bringing into
our brotherhood the good and the true of every community in our
glorious State.

The Grand Treasurer presented his Annual Report to
the Grand Lodge, as follows :-

370

I cannot close this report without saying something concerning "Anderson's Manual." When the author of thaot book had completed that most valuable volume and offered it to the Masons of
California, it was a complete compendium of the Constitution,
· Regulations, Decisions, and Forms of every kind and character,
clearly and accurately stated and in all up to date in every partic·
ular, and it was a source of genuine pleasure to know that if one
wanted any form for any Masonic purpose, he had only to look in
"Anderson's Manual," and, like a dear friend, it was there to greet
him. If one wanted to find any Masonic law or decision for California, he had only to search "Anderson's Manual" and he found it.
If one sought to establish a new Lodge, every form of procedure
was in it. If a cornerstone· was to be laid, the form was there,
and so on throughout, everything could there be found.
But one by one the forms have been dropped out, the decisions
which have been reversed do not now appear, and if we de5ire to
trace through them the rise and progress of Masonry in this State
we cannot do h.
I believt> from the comments of the brethren throu1rhout the
::itate upon the changes and omissions above named that the Grand
Lodge should refer the book to its author that it may be by him
revised, and that all that original volume contained should again
appear between its covers with whatever has since been ordained as
law or decision.
And now, thanking the Grand Lodge for the confidence it has

On Grand Lecturer's Report
Rodolph W. Meek,
Dana R. Weller,
Arthur J . Thatcher.

The Grand Secretary presented his annual report to the
Lodge, as follows:
To th<:l M. ·. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:
The undersigned submits his Sixteenth Annual Report, and notwithstanding the awful disaster of April last, he believes that all
transactions of his office for the year as should necessitate action by
the Grand Lodge will be fully presented for its consideration.
At the earliest day possible after the close of the last Annual Communication, seventeen hundred copies of the Proceedings were distributed, or reserved for future binding, in the customary manner,
viz.: one copy to each of the present Grand Officers; one copy to each
of the elective Past Grand Officers; three eopies to each of the Grand
Bodies, American and }'oreign, with which we are in correspondence;
one copy to each Inspector, and two copies to each of the Lodges of
our Jurisdiction.
New editions of the Constit;ition, Anderson's Manual, Monitor,
Example Lodge, Installation Service, Form for Record of Trial, ~ni­
form Code of By-Laws, Funeral Service and Ceremonies for Laymg
Corner·Stones, Dedicating Halls and Constituting Lodges have been
issued, all of which had been destroyed by fire.
The Proceedings of all the Grand Lodges of the United States, for
the year, have been receive<l and placed in the hands o~ the Chair~n
of the Committee on Correspondence, with the exception of Georgia,
Indian Territory New Mexico, and Tennessee, as have also those of
British Columbi:, Canada, England, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova
Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec.
The seven Lodges to which Charters were granted at the last
Annual Communication were, in due season, properly constituted; four
by deputies specially appointed for that purpose, as follows:

The work of this Board of Relief for the year 1906 has been inc11eased by the unfortunate disaster which befell the City of San
Francisco on the 18th day of April; for which reason many unfortunate
brethren, or their families, sought refuge in our own beautiful city,
and called upon us for aid. However, a word from · this Boarcl to
the several Lodges of our c~ty, brought a ready, generous response,
and thereby we were enabled to relieve the suffering with little difficulty; and we believe no worthy brother, or any member of his family,
has suffered for the necessaries of life.
To all° who contributed to this Board of Relief for the benefit of
the San ~rancisco sufferers pe extend our fraternal thanks.

MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU.
Through the efforts of Most Worshipful Grand Master Motley H.
Flint, a Masonic Employment Bureau has been established, through
which several hundred positions have been secured for needy Masons,
their widows or orphans. This we deem a most worthy charity,
enabling one to become self-supporting.

Complying with your request of August 16th, 1906, concerning the
action which this Board of Relief took in matter of the disaster occasioned by ear t hquake and fire, which befell the central por t ion of our
glorious State, on t he 18th day of April, 1906, will say:
That immediately upon the r ealization of that awful calamity,
a special meeting of the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles was
called, on April 22d, 1906, at which meeting I was directed to communicate with e.ach Masonic body of this city, and r equest a contribution of One Dollar ($1.00) per capita, to enable our Board to r elieve
the distress of th e members of t he craft and those dependent upon
them, who might take r efuge in our city. This r equest was promptly
complied with, and ther e came into my hands as Secretary, from the
various Masonic b odi es of our city, together with individual contributions; and also from Mount Zion Lodge, of Troy, N. Y., the sum
of Three Thousand One Hundred and Seventy-Four Dollars and Fifty
Cents ($3,174.50).
. Arrangements were made that th e Masonic Board of Relief should
establish headquarters at the Masonic Temple, a nd notices were placed
in all t he newspapers of th e city, calling attention to that fact.. We
secured the use of the banquet room and kitchen for the purpose oi
providing meals; also t he Lodge Room r ecently vacated by the Scot·
t l.sh Rite Bodies, was filled with cots and bedding for use of the
ladi es.
We secured the upper floor of the Lexington H otel (now the
Brooklyn Hotel) fo r the use of the gentlemen.

402

PROCEEDINGS OF 'i'HE

A cook was hired, and with the assistance of the Ladies of the
Eastern . Star, meals were provided at the Masonic T emple; committees were appointed, who met all trains coming from the North, and
brought the members of the fraternity to the Temple, and after a
bath, a good meal, and a rest, positions were secured, as best they
could be, for employment.
Those of the unfortunates who were in feeble health, were sent
to the Southern California Masonic Home at San Gabriel, at our expense, and when they were recovered, they sought employment.
Quite a number of the refugees being aged, and having r elatives
in other cities, were furnished with transportation as they desired.
It is estimated that at least One Thousand (1000) Meals w~ re furnished at our expense.

The M. :. W. :. Charles L. Patton presented the fbllowing:
To the M. w. Grand Lodge of California:
The undersigned, on behalf of the Masonic Hall Association of the
City of San Francisco, and in order that the matter of the sale of the
Temple site may be fully understood by the Grana Lodge, submits
the following for consideration:

The purchaser is now examining the title and this sale will be consummated in a very short time.
Upon receipt of this money it is the intention of the Hall Association to obtain an order of Court permitting the distribution of all the
funds on hand among the stockholders and, for the reason that there
is no power in the Hall Association to acquire a new site under its
Articles of Incorporation, the Directors propose to proceed to disin·
corporate.
The Directors have, however, been advised that nearly all the Masonic Bodies owning stock in this corporation desire to invest all 'or
nearly all the amount to be received from the sale of the Temple site
to build a new Temple on ·a new site to be selected, are about to
formulate a plan whereby a new hall association shall be incorporated
with a capital stock equal in amount to the price received from the
sale of the Temple and ·divided into twenty-five thousand shares of the
par value of thirty dollars each, so that each stockholder in the
present Hall Association may either receive the amount due him on
dissolution in. cash or may receive an equal number of shares of equal
valu·e in the new hall association in lieu of shares in the old asso·
ciatiOn.
The fact that the purchase price of the Old Temple site has not
yet been paid makes it impossible to fu:rnish the Grand Lodge at this
time with a more detailed statement of the plans for the erection of
a new Temple.
As the decision of thiji Grand 'Lodge in :reference to investing the
funtls received from the sale of the Temple site in a new and modern
'J'emple for the use of the Craft, will have great weight in accomplishing this most desirable purpose it is suggested that a committee
be appointed at this session of the Grand Lodge with power to act for
the Grand Lodge in all matters connected with the consummation of
the sale of the Temple site and with the erection of a new Temple in
San Francisco.

The M. :. W. :. George W. Hunter, from the special committee on the Grand Ma~ter's Address and Grand Secretary's· Report, presented the following reports:
To the M . W. Grand Lodge of Califomia:Your committee to whom was r ef erred the address of the M. W.
Grand Master, Motley H. Flint, beg leave to submit the following:
0

It has been the fortune of Grand Master Flint to serve t his Grand
Jurisdiction in the most eventful year of its history, and in a capacity
which, for taxing one's powers and r esources, has never before fallen

414

415

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

to the lot of any Grand Master of this or auy other Granu Jurisdiction.

Although brief, the report is complete · and bears evidence of the
accuracy of all the work of the Grand Secretary's office.

•

The awful calamity which befell the City of San Francisco in April
1ast was so sudden and appalling that thousands of ih 'inhabitants
were not only deprived of their homes, but of the actual r.ecessaries
or life. It required _a man of great executive ability to take charge
of the relief work and organize committees to perform the service
demanded, and Grand Master Flint, by reason of his business experi·
ence, was specially qualified tp grasp the situation and render the niost
efficient service.
We commend his untiring zeal and personal efforts in aiding the
needy, and heartily approve of his action in helping, not only the
members of the Masonic fraternity and their families, but all who
were in distress in those trying hours.
The generous response of other Grand Jurisdictions; in contributing
so liberally, for the· relief of San Francisco and other stricken cities
in our State, shows how universal was the sympathy' of our Masonic
brethren and how true and loyal the -fraternal spirit when a great
occasion calls it into activity. The funds donated were gratefully
r eceived, worthily bestowed and faithfully accounted for, and the
report of the Grand Master on the relief fund, and the record of relief
work as shown by his special report, is a tribute to Masonry throughout the world.
•
we note with pleasure the gain in membership during the year, and
the satisfactory condition of Masonry in general in this Jurisdiction.
We recommend that so much of the address of the Grand Master
as deals with decisions be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence;
that portion which r elates to the amendment of the constitution in
regard to granting Dispensations for the formation of new Lodges
upon the recommendation of the Grand Master where the nearest
Lodge declines to give its conse-n t, be referred to the same committee;
that portion _which relates to Masonic Temple matters in San Francisco be ref erred to a special committee for consideration and report;
that portion relating to ~ Dispensation for a n ew Lodge in · the Philippi ueR be r eferred to a special committee, and that portion relating
to printing a list of members of Lodges be submitted to the Grand
Lodge for its considera tiOn and decision.
Grand Secretary, Bro. Johnson, has been able, notwithstanding the
great loss sustained by him in the destruction . of th<i records, 0f his
office, to present to this Grand Lodge a full account of all transactions
of his office for the year requiring consideration by this Grand Body.
That portion of his r eport realting to unfinished business has
already been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

Respectfully and Fraternally submitt.ed,
EDMUND C. ATKINSON,
JAMES B. STEVENS,
GEO. W. HUNTER,

Bro. J ohn Hosmer, Chairman of the Committee on Grievances presented the following reports:
~o the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:

· Your Committee have had under consideration and have care·
fully examined the following records of trials had in subordinate
Lodges, from which no appeals have been taken, and find them all
to be in substantial compliance with our law, and the respective
judgments are sustained by evidence, to wit:
William Silver Grover, expelled by "California" Lodge, No. 1.
Harvey Irwin, an Entered Apprentice Mason, expelled by '' Aca·
cia'' Lodge, No. 92.
William Clawson, expelled by "Chico" Lodge, No. 111.
Benjamin Beatty Duncan, expelled by "Mission" Lodge, No. 169.
Alexander .Isaac Gray, expelled by ''Elk Grove'' Lodge, No. 173.
Charles W. Koerner, expelled by ''Marin'' Lodge, No. 191.
•Tohn Duncan Cummings, expelled by ''Dunsmuir'' Lodge, No. 297.
James Francis Beahan, expelled. by "Manila" Lodge, No. 342,
and Emil Julius Kanngeisser, expelled by ''Presidio'' Lodge, No. 354.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of the several Lodges upon the cases
herein particularly specified be, and the same is, hereby affirmed.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record of the
case of A. A. Manuel, sentenced to reprimand by "Monterey" Lodge,
No. 217, and from which ·judgment the accuser, George W. Mease, has
appealed, have had the same · under consideration, and report as
follows:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

417

The accused was the Treasurer of ''Monterey'' Lodge, and was
charged with the embezzlement of $176.74 of the funds of the Lodge,
set forth in six specifications. Among other matters the specifications
related offensive and defiant actions on the part of the accused when
requested to make payment of these funds, even afte'r a successor had
been appointed and de~and made.
. Upon the trial before the Commissioners, through his counsel,
the accused himself being present, he pleaded guilty to the charges,
and such was the finding of the Commission. In sentencing the
accused to reprimand the Commission evidently took into consideration a promise to repay the money in six months, or sooner if possible.
If a Brother so far forgets his Masonic duty as to appropriate
money of the Lodge, en trusted to him as an official, he should ·be
subjected to such discipline as shall, at least, convince the Lodge
that he is penitent for his act, and worthy to mingle with his 'Masonic
Brethren. While a reprimand may work reform for small offenses,
the good faith of the Brother will be better shown if he is deprived,
for a season, of Masonic rights, and displays to his Brethren a bearing that will justify them in again receiving him into full fellowship.

Your Committee is not satisfied that the sentence is sufficient
or adequate punishment for the offense of which the Brother has
acknowiedged. himself guilty. Such conduct warrants the severest
punishment known to our law, but as the trial Commissioners have
shown such great leniency, and there may be circumstances of which
we are not cognizant, which may be urged in mitigation, we are disposed to recommend a milder judgment.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of the Trial .Commissioners of "Monterey" Lodge, No. 217, sentencing A. A. Manu.~l to a reprimand, be,
and the same is, hereby reversed, and that the said A. A. Manuel be,
and he is, hereby suspended from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record in the case
of Robert Emil Goeritz, expelled by "Chico" Lodge, No. 111, have
had the same under consid.eration, and beg leave to report.
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct in four specifications, but evidence was introduced to the Commission only as to
one, which was that during the month of April or May, 1905, the said
Goeritz came to me (the accused) and said he was in trouble ancl

418

419

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

asked me as a Mason to assist him by letting him have some cattle
to tide him over his difficulties, and that in a few days he would p·a y
me for them without fail. I (the accuser) gave him the assistance
he desired, and he took niy cattle and disposed of them, and· took the
money and left the State, and I have no doubt but it was his intention at the time he secured the cattle to rob me of my property.

would not accept of it. If there was dishonesty in procuring the cattle the evidence do es not sho~ it. At most, it shows that in his busin ess he estimated beyond his ability.

At the time that charges were preferred the accused was in Butte,
Montana, and wrote to the Ma~ter, asking an extension of the time
of trial for at least sixty days, which was granted, and at the expiration of that time the trial proceeded and the accused was present.
In his statement to the Commission he said : "Everybody knows the
way I started in business, and as soon as I made a few dollars, I spent
it in improving my business with fixtures, etc., and finally I got married and my expenses were higher and business was pretty good, and
I improved my business, and in one way I made a mistake. I risked
too much, and I thought . busi11ess was getting better, and it got
worse, prices declined, competition was harder, and I could not meet
my bills; consequently, my' family expenses were awfully high, it was
impossible for me to cut them down, which I can prove by my books.
Through this came my family trouble, and I made a mistake by
starting in drinking, and for this I ask forgiveness from my brothers.
I tried to beat nobody out of a cent ; that is why I came back and
took charge of the market, where I take only my living expenses,
a~d I will pay everybody dollar for dollar.''
Upon the trial the only evidence offered was by the accuser, who
testified ''all the charges preferred by me were on the hearsay of
Brothers, except the first charge; relating to cattle.''
The accuser was apparently not even half-hearted in his prosecution, for when asked, ''Where did you get the other information
preferred in charges'" answered, from Brother J. D. March; and
when further asked, ''Why did you not get the witnesses here to
prove thatf" answered, "Because I did not care to." He also stated
that he received a ' Jetter from Brother Goeritz offering to square the
first charge, relating to the cattle, but that he wrote. him an answer
th.at he would ~ot do so, as it was too late, and he was advised by
Masonic authority that he could not do so.
The transaction disclosed by the charge gave the accused the
privilege of using the cattle, and in the absence of fraud, such use
would not subject ·him to censure. The only thing looking towards
fraud is that he went away, but before the completion of the trial
he returned and went to work, and was only taking his living expenses,
and would pay everybody dollar for dollar. According to the prosecutor he had offered to square his indebtedness, but the prosecutor

·The charge of fraud, a serious offense, especially when committed
by a Mason against a Brother, should be fully and clearly substantiated by the testimony. Anderson's Manual, Sec. 203, page 250.
'
by the testimony. Anderson's Manual, Sec. 203; page 250.
We are not satisfied that the evidence in this case is sufficient to
justify the finding of the Commissioners.
We therefore offer t he following resolution and r ecommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of "Chico" Lodge, No. 111, expelling
Emil Goeritz be, and the same is, hereby reversed and set
aside.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record of tl~e
case of Charles F. Mugridge,· expelled by ''Naval'' Lodge, No. 87,
and from which judgme:nt the accused has appealed to this Grand
Lodge, has had the same under consideration, and r eport:
The charges preferred against the accused are that on divers occasions he violated the chastity of Katherine C. Macdonald, the wife
of· Angus E . Macdonald, the accusing Brot her.
·
The appeal is upon the ground that the ·evidenc·e is insufficient
to support the finding of guilty of the charges, and that error was
committed in allowing in evidence over the objection of the accused,
of an ex ·parte affidavit of Katherine C. Macdonald.
The accused denied the charges. The evidence of the ,accuset
was wholly hearsay, aside from the affidavit of Katherine C. Macdonald, which was admitted in evidence over the objection of the accused,
that it was incompetent, irregular and not taken in accordance with
Masonic law. This document was offered as a deposition, but it is
wholly in narrative form, reciting the a cts charged in the complaint
of the accuser, but not by question and answer, nor do.es it appear that
the accused had an opportunity to appear and cross-examine the witness.. The only reference to the matter in the transcript is: "The Sec·
retary was instructed to notify the Master of 'Sacramento' Lodge, No.
40, F. & A. M., to accompany a Notary Public for the purpose of
taking the testimony of wife of Angus E. Macdonald, Katherine
C. Macdonald. Accused was also notified in person.'' But it nowhere
appears that notification of the time and place of taking the deposition was given. The only apparent whereabouts of the wife is indi-

420

421

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

cated in a letter from Macdonald to the. Master of "Naval" Lodge,
speaking of her condition, written from Broderick, Yolo County. The
alleged deposition was atteste~ by William F. Renfro, Notary Public
in and for the County of Sacramento, and the record shows it was
received from H. H. Stephenson, W.:. M.:. of "Sacramento" Lodge,
NCI'. 40. We do not think this a substantial compliance with our law,
as provided by the Constitution (Part VI, Art. IV, Sec. 5), "The
t~stimony of witnesses who are not Masons shall be taken by depositions before some officer authorized by the laws of the State wherein
he resides to administer oaths, and at such time and place and upon
such notice to the adverse party as shall be designated by the Master,
upon the application of the party desiring the testimony.''

. It is the duty of the Master, if he deem the application for a

the deposition before some officer authorized to administer oaths,
after such notice to the adverse party as may be prescribed by the

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record in the
case of Frank Ridgway Todd, expelle·d by "Hartley" Lodge, No. 199,
beg leale to report as follows:
This is the second time tliat this case has come before the Grand
Lodge. The action of ''Hartley'' Lodge was reversed by the Grand
Lodge at 'its annual session of 1904, on account of the charge being
supported by hearsay evidence.
The new trial was had under the charges preferred by the Junior
·Warden, under direction of the Master in 1904. And while it does
not appear from the transcript, it is a fact shown by the records
· of the Grand Lodge, that the officers at the trial were different persons from those who officiated in 1904.
The accused was charged with having committed embezzlement in
Santa Ana, Orange County, and having pleaded guilty to the charge,
The whereabouts of the accused was unknown, and the trial proceeded
ex parte. The charge was sustained by the evidence.

•

The Trial Commissioners were elected March 31st, 1906, and the
Master named April 5th, 1906, as the time for the first meeting of
the Commissioners, and ordered the Secretary to prepare a summons
to ace.used, w~ch summons. was served upon the accused April 1st,
1906. The accused was at the tim~ under arrest by the United States
military authorities, and General Wood refuse~l to allow him to
appear before the Commission. This fact was made known to the
Commission and on motion it adjourned until April 10th, 1906, authorizing a brother to take the deposition of the accused, and to notify
him of his right to be represented at the trial, and also to give him
sufficient time to prepare for his defense. Upon April 10th the . Com.mission again met, and the accused's deposition not being received,
another adjpurnment was had, until April 14th, 1906, at which time
no objecti~n was made to the Commissioners, and the accused filed
an answer, which was witnessed by the accuser and a Brother Lawrence S. Carson, of "Minrehohn" Lodge, No. 5, of Sioux Falls, South
Dakota, who represented the accuaed upon the trial. In the answer
the accused admitted the charge, and upon the trial there was evidence
of other witnesses, that justified the action of the Commis~ioners.
These µroceedings were not in compliance with our law, and if
the accused liad not appeared by answering and being represented,
the sentenc04of the Lodge could not stand. Our law is very plain.
(Const., Part VI, Art. IV, Sec. 3.) "If the accused be within the
jurisdiction of the Lodge, the summons ancl a copy of the charges
shall be issued at least ten days prior to t he day appointed for the
trial, and shall be served personally by the Tyler, or some other member of the Lodge, authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall

422

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

be left at his ordinary residence or place of business,'' ·and we cannot too seriously commend to our Brethren having trials, that they
closely read and pursue the practice laid out for them in· the law,
thereby avoiding the necessity of reversal.

Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record in the
case of William Dean, sentenced to reprimand by "Palo Alto"· Lodge,
No. 346, and from which an appeal has been taken to this Grand
Lodge, has had the same under consideration, and report:
The Brother was charged with unmasonic conduct in using vile,
profane and indecent language towards a Brother, and in charging
him with dishonesty and making threats of violence towards him.
The affair was evidently an outcome of business difficulties. The
accused Brother appeared, confessed the charge and expressed sorrow
for his acts, and showed a penitential disposition. The Brethren of
the Commission were, no doubt, impressed with his statement, for they
all concurred in the adoption of reprimand al\ a punishment, and
we cannot say, in view of the facts, that a more serious penalty was
nllcessary.
We therefore offer the ;ollowing resqlution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of "Palo Alto" Lodge, No. 346, sentencing William Dean to be reprimanded be, and the same is, hereby
affirmed.

Congratulations are again due this Grand Body and the subordinate Lodges on the very marked ·increase in membership. It is unnecessary to call attention to the immense handicap resultant upon the
earthquake and fires, which took the homes from many of the subordi'late Lodges, and for a period covering several months made work
extremely difficult and, in many instances, impossible.
The returns show a gain of 2,208, having increased from 31,561 in
1905, to 33,769 in 1906.
The report, therefore, is particulariy pleasing and serves to empha1Size the strong hold that Masonry has upon the minds and hearts of
. honest men.
For the information of those Brethren who take an interest in the
growth of our Fraternity your Committee submits the following, which
shows the membership of the ten largest Lodges:

We note with particular · pleasure the sentiments of the Grand
Lecturer upon the subject of devoting his entire time to the work of
thi11 office. It may not be amiss to say in this connection that other
Jurisdictions, notably New York and Missouri, require the whole time
of the Grand Lecturer and pay him a salary commensurate with such
requirements. Masonry has reached such a point in California that
such a requirement on the part of the Grand Lodge seems absolutely
essential if we are to retain our present high standard among the
jurisdictions of the United States. It is not alone instruction in the
ritualistic work which we ought to require of th.e Grand Lecturer, but
having a man capable of doing so, it would immensely add to the edu·cational value of the office, if we could receive from him lectures and
instructions upon the history, principles, ground work, symbolism anrl
the law and jurisprudence of the Order. But it is totally out of the
question to expect such services from our Grand Lecturer unless he
can devote his whole time to the office, and if we ask that of him we
must be prepared to pay him a salary in accordance with the demands which we make upon him. We are asking the entire time and
attention of an expert, and we must be prepared to pay according to
the services which we receive. So while we hesitate to r ecommend a
figure, for the purpose of bringing the matter in concrete form before
the Grand Lodge, we would r ecommend that the salary of the Grand
Lecturer be fixed for the ensuing year at Twenty-five Hundred Dollars,
with the usual allowance for traveling expenses.
In conclusion, we would again reiterate our appreciation which we
feel confident is concurred in by the Grand Lodge and Masons throughout the State, of the magnificent administration of the Grand Lecturer,
and while Brother Edwards in his usual modesty has r efrained from
touching upon a greater part of his achievements, a perusal of the
Grand Lodge report, showing the growth of this Order in this State
and our own personal contact with his delightful personality, speak
volumes for him in his work and as a man and a Mason.
Respectfully submitted,

Freemasonry as an institution and }'reemasons as individuals cannot be separated from the ordinary affairs of life. It is not a mere
toy, serving as a mental diversion at each annual Communication,
nor on idle lip service to be performed in the Lodge room. It is a
great, living moral fo·r ce which should pervade and regulate human conduct from childhood to age, at the hearthstone, on the marts of trade,
in the social and business intercourse between man and man. Its principles express and their practice should exemplify the cardinal virtues which should be part and parcel of our every-day exiStence.
Never in the history of civilization since the elimination of religion from government has there been a time when a proper application
of 1\~asonic virtue could accomplish so much for the pEirpetuity and
peace of beneficent institutions. We are taught that time, patience
and perseverance, with proper exercise of temperance, fortitude, \ervency and zeal, will accomplish all things. Let each party to existing
controversies, standing upon that common level established by our
magnificent institution, with patient zeal endeavor to bring about .an
adjustment of differences, and persevere in his efforts, let each with
temperate consideration for the judgment of his fellow, and courageou~ fortitude ·i n the hour of trial, zealously seek the right and fervently pursue it, and in God's own time honor, justice and truth will
ultimately prevail.

Past Grand Master Edmund C. Atkinson then addressed

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
As we assemble in Annual Communication to resume our accustomed duties for the benefit of the Craft, and for the exchange of fraternal court'esies, we are saddened by the. appearance of vacant places,
and vrie note with sorrow the absence of son:ie of our most faithful colaborers.

A few months ago I stood in the .gallery of that Temple where for
so many years we were wont to assemble-that dear old Temple now
laid in dust and ashes, and as I gazed upon the life-like portraits of
my departed brothers with whom I had associated in this Grand
Lodge, a feeling of sadness came over me that defied my soul's resistance, and, like the lonely cavalier in Locksley Hall, I seemed to hear
the phantom years whispering, "Never! Nevel'! "
Never to hear
their voices again! Never to stand in the living presence and receive
the hearty, fraternal greeting! ·
What a mystery is death! Philosophers tell us that God never
gives to man the key that opens the golden gate of Eternity until hi~
time shall come to enter there. The only proof they give us of
immortality is that the desire to live again is implanted in every
human breast; that the sun-browned children of the forest see God in
clouds and dream of happy hunting grounds beyond the star-gemmed
sky; that the polished and imaginative Greek in fancy walks in Heeperian gardens and roams iD; .Elysian fields. This is their conclusion:
It must be so!

Plato, thou reasonest well,
Else why this longing for immortal!ty?

But, my brethren, ou;r faith requires a firmer foundation. The
philosophy of six thousand years has failed to search the chambers of
the human soul. Reason, unless it be illumined by inspiration, leaves
us in the cold and chilling atmosphere of uncertainty and doubt.
Intellect is not our highest endowment. Imagination is not our crowning faculty. Every form of genius is inferior to conscience, to faith,
to sympathy and love. Man became a living soul when God breathed
into him the breath of life. The soul is then divine-a part of the
Infinite life, similar in essence but different in degree. If God is the
Infinite Spirit of Life back of all, from whfoh all comes, then clearly
our life, as individualized spirits, is continually coming from that
Infinite Source by divine inflow.

Our departed brother was born in Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, June
2, 1825. He came from rural parentage and of a long line of tillers of
the soil. In youth be labored on his father's farm in summer and
attended the district school in the winter months. From qoybood he
was a diligent workel', doing with all his might what his bands found
to do. So diligent was be in his studies and so rapid was his progress
that at the age of 19 years ll.e became a teacher in the public schools.
The following year he fell a victim to the "gold fever"; he joined a
large ~art~ of neighbors and friends and journeyed across the plains
t~ Cahforma, the El Dorado of the West. He crossed the snow-capped
Sierras and descending the western slope came into the Sacramento
valley; and at sight of a beautiful spot on the bank of the Sacramento
river be exclaimed, "Here I pitch my tent." His first night's rest
was b.eneath a giant oak, which in after years shaded bis beautiful
dwelling. He secured a tract of land . in accordance with bis means,
and later purchased large outlying tracts until be came into possession
of one of the largest and most fruitful farms on the Sacramento river.
He. built an elegant residence and braug'b.t around it everything that
eould conduce to the comforts and enjoyments of home. Peace and
Plenty sat smiling at his door.

It was my privilege to enjoy an intimate acquaintance with our
brother for more than thirty years. I was often a visitor at his home
and he a guest at mine. Foi; nearly twenty years we met once a week
as directors of a corporation which was the cutsodian of the poor
man's savings, the widow 's mite, and the orphan's heritage. It was
in this relati~n ~bat I learned to . admire our brother for his rigid
adherence. to Justice and right.
Brother Johnston's every act was the sequence of mature .t hought.
He made no f ailure, left nothing undone, improved every hour, and
every year's effort tended to material prosperity.
He was also a man of public spirit; he did much for the general
prosperity of the State, and served in many positions of trust. His
advice was eagerly sought in private and public enterprises. His hand
and heart were ever open to _public and private charities.
As a public speaker he aspired to no 'flights of eloquence, he used
no smooth and rounded p.erio.ds. His words were simple, plain,
straightforward, and big with meaning. He held the attention of bis
audiences and impressed his hearers with the superiority of bis judgment. Many times I listened to. his words in the balls of legislation
and observed him in the dignified position of :rresident of the State

As Grand Master of the Grand Lodge he was ever faithful in the

Grand Master's warning to gather up his working tools and prepare
to quit ea;th 's field of labor. He had suffered from a stroke of paralysis, and could with difficulty converse with the brethren. A short
time thereafter a second admonition was given and he entered into
a state of mental decline. He was often oblivious to time and place,
and a guide attended him wherever he went. At 1'ast came the third
warning. ''God's finger touched him and he slept.'' On the fourteenth ' of last November, as the shades of night were gathering round
his beautiful home on the banks of that river which for more than
fifty years had gladdened his heart with its musical cadences, our
brother bade adieu to the scenes of earth and passed into the Silent
J,and.

To the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:-

•

It is not often that we are so forcibly reminded of the uncertainty
of human life as we were when, on the 13th day of December, 1905,
our friend and Brother, the M. :. W.:. Hiram Newton Rucker, Past
Grand Master of this Jurisdiction, was, without a moment's warning,
called from a life of usefulness among us to the Grand Lodge above.
He had been in attendance upon a meeting of the' Board of Trustees
of our Masonic Home, of which he was the Superintendent, and was
returning to the Home, when the accident occurred which caused
bis death. One moment vigorous and strong, filled with enthusiasm
for the work for which he was so well fitted, looking forward to
many ;rears of usefulness and companionship with his Brethren, the
next, be had gone to join the innumerable throng in ''that undiscovered country, from whose baurne no traveler returns.''

I see many new faces before me. My brothers, you, who are here
for the first time, are not expected to enter fully into our deep sorrow,
for you did not know our departed brother. But the lessons of this
hour and the influence of this sacred observance should make deep and
lasting impressions upon your minds and heart~. You have, no doubt,
f elt the pangs of separation from friends and brothers and, even now
you may be cherishing the memory of loved ones lost. Unite then
with us in the comforting assurance that, if our Masonic faith b e not
founded upon the quicksands- if our hope be not a delusion and a
will-o '-the-wisp, the separation is not final; that when the storms of
life are past, when the mistakes and discords of time no more annoy,
when the clouds of sorrow and the mists of doubt have rolled away,
there will be an unbroken r eunion out beyond life's golden sunset
where earth 's shadows n ever fall.

B_rother Rucker lived practically his whole life in California; he
was born on September. 6th, 1844, at Arrow Rock, in ·the State of
Missouri, and came to this State with his parents at the age of six
_years, and thenceforth continually resided here. His first home here
was in our beautiful Santa Clara Valley, where he was educated in
our public schools and at the Unive~sity of the Pacific, from which
he graduated (with the first class of the medical department) in the
year 1870. · For the following eighteen years he made his home and
practiced his profession fa Merced County. He was one of the prominent citizens of the county for many years, and always took a
commendable interest in public affairs. For a. Jong time he served
his· fellow citizens in the official capacity of Coroner and Public
Administrator, and was also Chairman of the Democratic County
Central Committee. In the year· 1884 he was appointed by the
Governor o;f the State to be a Director of the State Hospital at Stockton, and in the year 1888 .he was elected to the important office
of Superintendent of that institution, which office he held for four
years. In the year 1892 he removed to Oakland, where for the
following nine years he resided and practiced his profession, and was
for a season President of the Board of Health. In the year 1901 he
returned to the scene of his early labors in Merced County, where
he continued to reside until, in 1904, he responded to the insistent
call of his Brethren to take upon himself the ·duties of Superintendent
of the Masonic Home at Decoto, which office he most acceptably'
Jilled until the time of his death.

Brother Ruck er was made, passed and raised in our ''La Grange''

that Lodge for the year 1877, and again for the year 1902. From
the year 1877 he was a faithful attendant upon the communications

of the Grand Lodge. His sterling worth was soon recognized in this
bocly, and he was made a member of the Committee on Grievances,
where he served until, on October 12th, 1883, he .was elected Junior
Grand Warden. He was re-elected to that office for a second term
on October 17th, 1884. On October 16th, 1885, he was elected Senior
Grand Warden, and on October 15th, 1886, Deputy Grand Master.
On October 14th, 1887, he was elected Grand Master of Masons of
the State of California. An examination of the record of his year's
service in that exalted position will suffice to show his high idea
of its duties arid responsibilities, and his appreciation of the honor
bestowed upon him by his Brethren. He gave practically all of his
time to the many duties of the office, and he discharged those duties
with signal ability. It was well said of him by the Special Committee
to whom was referred his annual address: "Weighed in the balance
of duty, our present Grand Master is not found wanting.'' His
interest in the Fraternity did not cease with his retirement '.from the
Grand East, but each succeeding communication of the Grand Lodge
found him present, ready and glad to serve his Brethren in any. place
where his experience and wisdom might make him useful. For many
years he was a member · of our Committee on Jurisprudence, and his
associates on that committee can testify to .the value of his services
and the beneficent effect of his presence.
We shall sorely miss Brother Rucker at our annual communica·
tions. To those who knew him an'd loved him, the r ecord he has left
behind him will, however, be a solace and an inspiration. It is a
record without a blemish. He lived the life enjoined upon him upon
his admission to our Fraternity. He was a good man, a good citizen,
a good Ma~on. He was faithful to the trust committed to his care.
Although we shall s~e him no more, the good influences of his life
will be effective among us for many years to come.
Brother Rucker was, on December 29th, 1873, united in marriage
to Emma T. Abbott, a native of Massachusetts, who, with ~>ne daugh·
t er, E. Robin Rucker, survive him. Our heartfelt sympathy is theirs
in the hour of their affiiction, deprived as they are of the loving
companionship and protection of the devoted husband and the affec·
tionate father.

The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct, consisting of,
first, that on or about the 5th day of November, 1905; he did attempt
unlawful and immoral carnal intercourse with one Dorothy Olsen, and
did persist in such attempt until frightened away by people passing
along the public street, and second, that on or about the 16th day of

had been made public through San Francisco and other newspapers,
and when he was visited at his home by a delegation of his Masonic

with . a view of re1.1dering him such fraternal aid and advice as might
be deemed proper, he did then and there absolutely and repeatedly
deny that he was the person complained of, or that he had any knowledge of the matter referred to. All of which denials were false and
calculated to deceive and mislead his brethren, who were seeking in
a fraternal way to aid him. All of which has tended to and has
brought scandal and disgrace upon himself in particular and upon the
body of Masonry in general.

the decision rendered by· him upon · questions of M;aso nic law. It is
evident that the Grand Master has given very careful consideration
to this portion of his work, and his conclusions are in the main fully
in accord with our view ·as to the, iaw obtaining in this Jurisdiction.
..1.n only one or two particulars do we deem any modification necessary.
The Grand Master was asked to ·determine the status in this Jurisdiction of a brother who was a Past Master of a Lodge in a foreign
Jurisdiction, and . had thereafter affiliated with a Lodge in California.
Is he a Past Master in California, with the rights and privileges of a
Past Master, including the right to be carried on the rolls of the California Lodge as a Past Master, and also the right of membership in
the Grand Lodge' H e was also asked to determine the same question
as to one who had acquired t he rank of Past Master by service in a
California Lodge, and who had 'dimitted therefrom and affiliated with
another California Lodge, of which he is still a member. · He answered
these questions in both cases in the affirmative. We have no doubt as
to the correctness of the decision so far as the brother who had become a Past Master .by service in a L odge in this Jurisdiction is concerned; but it appears to us to b e ·incorrect as to the brother whose
only service as Master was in a foreign jurisdictfon. The whole matter is covered by the expr ess language of our Constitution, where, in
Art. II of Part VII) under the h ead · of ''Definitions,'' we find the
following:
"Past Master,-This title applies only to one who has b een regularly elected or named in a charter a nd installed, and has served a
term as Master of a chartered Lodge within the juri.sdiction of this
Grand Lodge, and who remains a member in good standing of one of
its subordinates.''
This provision is, of course, controlling as to the meaning of the
term "Past Master" wher ever it is used in our Constitution. Only
those who come within its terms can be held to b e entitled to the
rank and privileges of a Past Master in California, and one whose
only service as Master was in a Lodge of another jurisdiction, is
plainly not within its terms.
We therefore recommend that this decision be modified to .conform
to these views.
