The Grand Mas'tElr was also asked as to the status of a Mason
under the following conditions: He is a member of one of our
Lodges, and while such member, without first withdrawing from his
Lodge, applies, under Sec .. 8, Art I, Part V, for affiliation with another
Lodge, upon a certificate of his standing in the Lodge of which he is
a member. He is elected to membership in the Lodge to which he
applies. When does he cease to be a memb.er of his old Lodgef When
does he commence to be a member of the new L odge to which he is
eiected ~ when does his liability for dues in the old Lodge end~ and
when does his liability for dues begin in the new Lodge~ The Constitution provides in t he section just cited : "If such applicant be
elected to affiliate with a J,odge, he can become a member thereof,
only by filing with the Secretary, at a stated meeting, the certificate
of his withdrawal from the Lodge of which he was last a member."

In regard to the question presented to the Grand Master as to the
right of a Lodge to pay from Lodge funds for services rendered by a
brother in assisting candidates in the work and lectures of the first
and second degrees, we are of the opinion that the Grand Master's
view that no such use can qe made of lodge funds, under our existing
law, is correct. It is the settled law of this ,Jurisdiction that t he
funds of a lodge are dedicated solely to charitable purposes, and the
ne~ssary expenses of the Lodge, the only exception being that provided by General Regulation 57, under which not to exceed five (now
tel\) per cent of the yearly revenue niay be used for purposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal int.ere>ourse. The proposed
expenditure is not, in our judgment, within any class of expendituns
now au~horized. It is, of course,. within the power of this Grand Lodge
to authorize subordinate Lodges to expend a portion of .their funds
for the purpose, just as it has authorized such an expenditure for
purposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse.
whether it would be for the best interests of Mason~y that this
should be done is a question of policy for the Grand L odge to determine; .and as to which we make no recommendation. If it be desir€d
to do this, it can be done by a regula.tion authorizing the expenditure,
and it will 11ot be necessary to create any new office in the Lodge or
to amend the by-laws.

It is clear that the mere election of the brother to membership in
the new Lodge under these circumstances in no way affects his standing as a member of the old Lodge. H e continues a member of the
old Lodge and liable for all dues that me:y accrue until such time as ·
he formally withdraws therefrom, which he may do, under section 6
of the same article, by giving notice of his intention so to do at a
stated meeting, when, he being in good standing, and his dues being
paid, he will receive a certificate of withdrawal or dimit_ F rom that
moment he is not a member of. any Lodge until he becomes a member
of another Lodge, and he can become a member 'of the new Lodge to
which he has been elected only upon filing s\lch certificate of withdrawal or dimit with the Secretary thereof at a stated meeting. His
dues in the new Lodge do not commence to accrue until such filing of
the certi1icate. During the time that may elapse before his withdrawal from· the old Lodge and the filing of his certificate of ')Yithdrawal or dimit in the new Lodge, he, not being a membel'" of any
Lodge, is not liable for dues to any Lodge. The certi1icate of standing or membership contained in the Grand Master's ·decision, and
taken 'py him from Anderson's Manual, at page 77, we find on investigation has never been adopted as a part of our Constitution or law,
and is no part thereof. As we understand the Grand Master's decision, he ruled that the brother was liable to the old Lodge for such
dues .as might accrue to the time when he formally withdrew therefrom, ·and such ruling is strictly in accord with our law, and we recommend that it be approved. We have discussed this matter at
length for the purpose of maki11g clear the status of the brother from
the time of his withdrawal to the time of filing his certificate of
withdrawal with the Se~retary of the new Lodge, a matter that does
not appear to be explicitly cove.r ed by the decision of the Grand
Master.

0

'

)

The decisi~n of the Grand Master relative to the right to use wine
at a banqul:lt held outside of the lodge-room, where such wine is paid
for othei:wise than from lodge funds, is in accord with our existing
written law on the subject. The only written prohibition now in our
law is as to the payment for spirituous,. malt or fermented liquor from
lodge funds. It has also been decided that it is contrary to Masonic
usage to serve such liquors in a Masonic hall. If· it be desired to
prohibit the use of such liquors at any Masonic banquet or gathering,
wherever held, a regulation to that effect will a ccomplish the desired
purpose.
The various other decisions rendered, including t hat in regard to
life membership, are clearly in accord with our law, and do not
require special mention. We recommend ·that they be approved.

Your Committee have had under consideration the recommendation of the Grand Master that our Constitution be amended so as to
authorize the issuance by him of a dispensation for a Iicw Lodge
without the r ecommendation of the nearest or most convenient cba;rtered Lodge, when sueh L odge, after r eqt\est, r efuses to grant such
recommendation, and the Grand Master, after investigation, considers
it proper that such dispensation should issue. The restriction upon
the power of the Grand Master to issue a dispensation for a new
Lodge without the recommendation of the nearest or most convenient
chartered Lodge, has been a part of our fundamental law for many
years, and has always beeil considered a wise and necessary provision
for the protection of existing Lodges. Doubtless, there may have .
been cases where the r ecommendation of the nearest or most convenient chartered L odge has been withheld without good r eason, b_u t we
do not think that this demands the practical abolition of what was
consideren a necessary safeguard by the framers of our Constitution,
and this would be the effect of the amendment recommended. It
often happens that a good and necessary law works injustice in a
particular instance, but this is not a good reason for the practical
repeal of the law. On the whole, doubtless the provision in question
bas wor~ed for tne general good of Masonry in this Jurisdiction. If
any ehange at all in the direction suggested is to be made to meet
exceptional cases, we are of the opinion that the change should not
authorize the issuance of a dispensation without the consent of the
nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge, except under direction
of the Grand Lodge itself, given after notice to such L odge that such
relief will be sought and an opportunity to such Lodge · to be heard
thereon.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WILLIAM S. WELLS,
JAMES B. STEVENS, ·

To the M.:. W.:. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee have hacl under consideration that portion of the
Grand Lecturer's report reeommending legislation whereby Inspeetors
may be clothed with authority to forbid and prevent further work
in a Lodge when satisfied that the Lodge from carelessness or laek
of interest is not able to confer . any or all degrees in a creditable
manner .
An Inspector has, of course, no such power under existing law.
His powers are defineu by express premises, and we find no such power
anywhere conferred.
Nor do we think it advisable that any legislation of the nature
proposed should be adopted. The 'power of suspending any funetion
of a Lodge is an extraor<linary one, to be· exercised only where the
necessities of the case elearly demand it. That, however, is now
vested exclusively in the Grand Master, and .we deem it inexpedient
that it should be exereised, in whole or in part, by any other oflieer.
If for any r eason whatever a Lodge should not be permitted to contmue to exercise any of its functions, it is clearly the duty of th.e
Inspector to immediately aequaint the Grand Master with the condi. tion. The Grand Master can at any time take such aetion in this
direc.t ion a s is for the best interests of Masonry.

.

,

480

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We therefore recommend that ~o legislation of the character
1mggested be adopted.
·
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WILLIAR S. WELLS,
JAMES B. srrEVENS,
THOMAS FLINT,
CHARLES W. NUTTING,

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:'l'hat portion of . the report of the Committee on address of Grand

That at the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge a
proposed General Regulation; to be known as ''General Regulation
No. 82,·•' was referred to them. This General Regulation is found on
page 154 of the Proceedings of 1905. Your committee at' that time
· reported that they found that the proposed regulation in no way conflicts with any constitu.tional provision and reported it back to the
Grand Lodge without any re~ommendation as to whether it be adopted
or rejected, as it involved quite a radical change in existing methods,
they recommended that the same be referred to the next Annual
Communication. This recommendation was adopted and the only
thing to be done at this .time is to determine as to whether or not they
desire to adopt such r <:'gulation, and the proper way to dispose of this
matter would be· to eithH adopt or reject the General Regulation
No. 82, as presented last year and ·found on said page 154.

Bro. Henry M. Owens, presented the following:To the M.:. W.:. Grantl Lodge of California:Your committee to whom wa~ referred that part of the Grand
Master's address which 'contained the communication from the Special Representative of "Manila" Lodge, No. 342, requesting this
Grand Lodge to define our Masonic relations towards other Masonic
powers in the Philippine Islands, to wit: The Grand Orients of Spain
and France.
From a iack of information and the limited time at the command
of this committee, it recommends that the final disposition of this
question be referred to the next Communicii.tion of this Grand Lodge,
and in the meanwhile (the regularity of the aforesaid Masonic bodies
being discussed by other Masonic powers), that no Masonic communication be held with said Masonic bodies or their subordinate bodies.

AMENDMENTS
AMENDMENT

TO

THE

CONSTITUTION.

Sec. 2, Art. ·I, Part III, adding, after the words, "the lectures
thereunto appertaining":
Provided, always, that whenever the nearest or most convenient
chartered Lodge refuses to grant its recommendation, the Grand
Master may, if after full investigation he deems it to be for the best
interests of Masonry, grant such dispensation without any such recommendation having been gi11en.
AMENDMENT TO GENERAL REGULATION No. 57.

Substitute, aft er the words, '' su_m not exceeding,'' the word ''ten''
for the word ''five.''
NEW GENERAL REGULATION.

No. 82. No Junior Warden of a Lodge shall be installed until he
shall have produced to the installing officer the certificate of the
Grand Lecturer or of the Inspector of the district in which his
Lodge is situated, certifying that he has personally examined such
Junior Warden-elect and that he is qualified to give the work and
lecture of the First Degree; and ·no Senior Warden shall be installed
until he shall have produced a like certificate of his qualification to
give the work and lectures of the First and Second Degrees. Such
eertifica tes shall be sent to the Grand Secretary and filed in his office.

To THE M. ·. · W. ·. GRAND LoooE,
F. and A. M. of CALIFORNIA:

..

The str'enuous season' through which we have passed, and from
which we have hardly yet emerged, is a good reason for the brevity
of this Report, were it not for the additional and more weighty
reason, the wish of the Grand Lodge, as expressed in it s action of
the preceding session, when it not only cut off the nub of the story
and. denied it publication; but expressed its opinion of the value
of the work by ·a n appropriation of fifty dollars for the present
Report.
But as time is money, and money is scarce, without wasting niore,
we . will take up our friend, Beauchamp of Alabama, to stand at the
head. of the line and ask hii;n to lend us his countenance in the making up of a brief R eport.
ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of Alabama held its Eighty-fifth Annual, De·
.cember 5, 1905, under the direction of the M.-. W. :. Henry H.
Matthews, Grand Master; R.·. W.:. Geo. A. Beauchamp being Grand
Secretary, and Judge Wm. I. Titcomb, Chairman of Correspondence.
Three hundred and :fifty L odges were represented. Eleven new
Lodges were ,instituted, several weak Lodges were consolidated, eight
corner-stones of public buildings were placed, and five Representat i ves
near other Grand Lodges appointed.

4

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Bro. Titcomb presents a Report of two hundred and seventy pages,
-good, square work, closing his summary with this self-evident prop·
osition, which, we venture to say, no experienced Mason will deny:
''In some quarters the unworthy use of the black ball is greatly
deplored-and justly so. But as we have taken occasfon to observe
heretofore, the improper use of the white ball is vastly more injurious.
If a good soldier and ·upright man, is shut out of the citadel, ·a serious
deprivation is the result: if, on the other hand, a traitorous miscreant
is admitted, no end of disaster may ensue. Let us guard well the outer
door.
· "It strikes us that the use of cipher or printed Ritual is an ever
present source of trouble in those Jurisdictions in which it is allowednay, in which it is fondly cherished. The good old way is the best.
Let's keep the cipher out of symbolic Maso~ry.
.
"As a last word, we crave Heaven's abundant blessings for the
Guild and the. }'raternity."
The Grand Master and Grand Secretary were re-elected.
ARIZONA.
The Grand Lodge of Arizona held its Twenty-fourth Annual in the
town of Flagstaff, November 14, 1905,-The M.'. W.:. Grand Master,
George Shand, being absent, the R.'. w ... Edwin Seymour Miller,
Deputy Grand Master, presided; the v ... W. '.. George James Roskruge
.being Grand Secretary.
Arizona has nineteen Lodges on the Roll, of which number fifteen
were represented, together with twenty-one other Grand Jurisdictions.
The M.'. W.:. George Shand, Grand Master, sent his Address by
mail and it was read by the Deputy Grand Master. He sent affection·
ate greeting to Grand Lodge, regretting his unavoidable absence,
caused by · ill-health, ·obHging him to leave the .Jurisdiction for an
indefinite period.
The Representatives of other Grand Jurisdictions were introduced
and welcomed by the Grand Master, the response thereto being made
by Past . Grand Master Morris Goldwater, for himself and his asso·
eiate Representatives, as follows:
"Most Worshipful Sir and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:-For
myself and the Grand Representatives of Sister Jurisdictions, standing
before you, I thank you for the honor of our reception. Realizing that
by this ceremony it is the intention of this Grand Lodge to honor so
far as is in its power, those Jurisdictions with which it has fraternal
relations, we make bold to say, although we ·have no written authority,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

5

that our several Grand Lodges send you their good wishes and fra·
tern.a l greetings. They trust that peace and harmony may continue
to pre;vail among the Craft you govern, and that Masonry in Arizona
may ever merit and receive the approval of the Grand Architect of
the Universe.
· ·
"Permit me, sir, a few words as Grand Representativ~ of the
Grand Lodge of California, a position I have held since 1889. At the
formation of this Grand Lodge those who were active in the work
desiring to compliment California, which was the Masonic horn~ 0 ;
many of the brethren and w:hich Grand Lodge had first introduced
Masonry into Arizona, adopted her Constitutio-n By-Laws Rules
R egu1a t'10ns and even decisions and Work as our own.
'
'
Since that
time'
whenever any doub.t or difficulty has arisen in ou~ ·minds over Masonic
matters, it has been promptly settled by asking, 'What would Cali·
fornia do in _a like case ~'
. '' Fo~lowing California's example, we exchanged Grand RepresentatIVes with, the. Grand Jurisdictions which acknowledged and accepted
us as a sovereign Grand Lodge. In 1904, at its 55th Annual Session
Grand Master Nutting delivered his Annual Address, in which not ~
word was written referring to the Representative system. His
Address was referred to the usual committee for distribution and ref·
erence. When this committee reported, at the close of the Report it
said:

" 'It will be patent to any one who will give the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges
proper consideration that this custom is_ as useless as the ''appendix
. vermiformis" in the human body. It seems to us that the custom
must have originated in a desire to decorate members with a mere
·title. The only proper way for one Grand Lodge to communicate with
another ·is through the Grand Masters. Your. committee can see no
necessity for the continuance of the custom and therefore recom·
mend that it be abolished.'
''The report of the committee was adopted.

It was afterwards

~aid that this was done without consideration, the members sup~osing

it was the usual stereoty:ped report, and paying no attention to its
contents. The Grand Secretary of California took this action, how· .
ever, as conclusive, and, I understand, notified many Grand Representatives of it, and discontinued to publish the list. I did not receive
any notice nor did I receive any copy of the Proceedings. When my
1
attention was called to the matter I wrote to Grand· Master G. W.
Hunter, and asked him if I was or was not the Grand Representative
of California. In his letter of October 2d, conveying his good wishes

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

for the ·Craft in Arizona, he told me of the action taken, and that
I was down and out. But on October 23d I received from him ·a nother
letter in which he said that the 'Resolution' had been declared void,
as being in conflict with the Constitution.,, and that I still represented
California.
·
''The action tak,en at the Grand Lodge Session of 1904 caused
considerable comment in other Jurisdictions. Louisiana, fearing for
the safety of its Grand Representative, Bro. Frank W. Pierce, withdrew his commisssion. Past Grand Master Buck of Louisiana, in an
address to the Grand Representatives, when they were received with
the Grand Honors, said:
"'The .Grand Representative is not appointed for business purposes-he merely rises, if you will, as an' evidence, a tangible symbol
expressive of the friendship and fraternal relations which exist between the Bodies-a link in the chain of unity-oneness-identity
of being and purpose of all the Masonic Bodie.a on earth.'
"I have gone into this affair at some length; as it is probably the
last time I shall answer the roll call as t _h e Representative of California. I shall not resign, I hope I shall not be called hence; but I
presume that those who began the crusade will continue their efforts
until California discontinues the system. When that time comes I
trust that the Grand Lodge of -Arizona will disregard precedent and
not follow in California's footsteps. When that day comes, and we
call the roll of Sister Jurisdictions, when California is reached . our
GraI!d Pursuivant will answer, 'Non est inventus,' and I will add,
'Farewell, farewell, the pride_, pomp and circumstance. Othello's
occupation's gcine.'
"It is hard to conceive of the reasons which induced the California
Committee to make its remarkable report. But, sir, wben you look at
the brethren before you, bedecked with the jewels whicn are indicative. of their years of service to Masonry, it will not require much
stretching of the imagination to hear the small, envious voiCe misquoting Scripture and ~aying: 'Consider the "daisies" of the Lodge,
how they grow; they toil not, nei~her do they spin, and yet I. say
unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like •
one of these.' ''

The M. ·. W. :. Edwin Seymour Miller was elected Grand Master,
and Grand Secretary Roskruge was re-elected.

ARKANSAS.
The Grand Lodge of Arkansas held its Sixty-third Annual. Communication in the City of Little Rock, November 21, 1905,-The
M.-. W. -. Styl~s T. Rowe, ?rand Master; the R.·. W.·. Fay Hempstead
being the Grand Secretary.
Arkansas has enrolled 460 live Chartered Lodges, and twenty-two
brand new ones Under Dispensation, with a tQtal of nearly 19,000
members. Four hp.ndred and· twenty-six Lodges were represented at
the present Annual, and thirty-seven other Grand Jurisdictions.
The Grand Master gives the condition of the Jurisdiction as excellent, with progress and prosperity on the right, left and front.
Two Emergent Communications were held, one for t he placing of
the .corner-stone of the St. Alban 's ·Episcopal Church, on May 2d1 at
Stuttgart, and t}le other for the same purpose at Hot Springs, August
15th.
A fine portrait of the present Grand Master, M.·. W.:. A. B. Grace,
appears on the opening• page, and a beautiful view of the home of
Albert Pike when he lived at Little Rock.
The Grand Orator, R.-. W. ·. Bro. F. G. Lindsey, delivered an excel·
lent Address, taking as his text from the Book of the Law: "In the
beginning God created the heavens and the earth.''
We note the appointment of a Committee on Correspondence, with
Bro. George H . Lyman of Fort Smith as Chairman, but fail to find
Report,
CANADA.
The Grand Lodge of Canada, in the Province of Ontario, held its
Fiftieth Annual in the City of Hamilton, July 19, 1905,-The M.-. W.·.
Benjamin Allen, Grand Master, on the Throne; the M.-. W.- . Bro.
H11gh Murray being Grand Secretary. There was a very full attendance of dfficers and members, Past Grand Officers and visitors. The ·
Grand Lodge of Canada has r egistered on its roll 386 Chart ered
Lodges, with five Under Dispen.s ation; of these, all except thirty-five
were represented, together with forty-four other Grand Jurisdictions.
· Bro. Past Grand M~ster ·J. Ross Robertson, in his intensely interesting historical Address before it at. the Fiftieth Annual, says of the
or~gin of Freemasonry in Canada:
''Canadian Masonry was founded in Nova Scotia between ·the years
1737-40. On the 13th of November, 1737, Erasmus James Phillips, an
officer of the Fortieth Regiment, who was stationed at Annapolis
Royal, visited Boston, · and was made a Mason in the first Lodge in
Boston.

8

HEPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

"Bro. Phillips was a nephew of Colonel Richard Phillips, the first
Governor of Nova Scotia, and was Secretary of the Governor's Council.
Bro. Price, as Provincial Grand Master, also appointed Bro. Phillips
as his Deputy, with power to organize Lodges in that Province.''
And with apparent satisfaction he observes, in closing:

CONNECTICUT.

''And here we are to-day, with 390 Lodges on our roll, and a
membership of 35,0001 doing a work for Masonry that has earned for
us not only the good words of the Grand Lodges of the world, but the
esteem and respect of the people at large in this happy land that is
our home.''
The Grand Lodge of Canada is advancing in progress and prosperity.
On the opening page of the present number of .t he Journal is a fine
engraved portrait of the present Grand Master, the M ... ·w... James
H. Burritt, K. C.
Three Especial Communications were held during the year for the
placing of corner-stones of St. Andrew's Presbyterian Church, at
H anover, the public school at the village at Dunnville, and the Ascension Episcopal Church, at the village of Kinlough.
The present number also presents for the consideration of the
Brethren the Revised Constitution.
COLORADO.
The Grand Lodge of Colorado held its Forty-fifth Annual in
Denver, September 19, 1905,-The M.:. W.:. Benjamin L. James, Grand
Master, presiding; the V.·. W.·. Charles H . . Jacobson being Grand
Secretary.
The Jurisdiction consists of 107 Lodges, with a membership of
11,000.
Six Called Communications were held during the year, oj' which two
were Emergent. Nearly all the Lodges were represented, together
with fifty other Grand Jurisdictions. Of the condition of the Jurisdiction, Bro. Ernest Le Neve Foster, Grand Lecturer, says in his
Report: "The Lodges are working with great uniformity and conforming to the Standard Work of the Grand L odge.''
This number of the Journal contains the portraits of Grand Master
George Keith Kimball, of 1887, and the present M. " w... Charles
Fremont Painter.
The Report on Correspondence is from the pen of the ''ready
writer," Bro. Lawrence N. Greenleaf; he reviews sixty Grand Jurisdictions in a thorough and a ble Report of two hundred pages.
Tl1e Committees on Correspondence and Necrology were continued.

9

The Grand Lodge of Connecticut held its One Hundred and Eighteenth Annual in the City of Hartford, January 17, 1905,-The M... W.:
Asa P. Fitch,. Grand Master; the Veteran Bro. John H. Barlow being
the Grand Secretary.
An Emergent Communication was held in the City of Danbury,
September 5th, for the dedication of the n ew hall of "Union" Lodge,
No. 40, a Lodge holding a Charter under the Seal of the Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts, dated March 23, 1780. There are many items of
interest in this history of this Veteran Lodge of ''ye olden tyme, ''
which would be voted decidedly out of order in many of our modern
Jurisdictions. As t he record evidences:
' " In 1785 a worthy Brother was helped to the value of five dollars.
Inste11-d, however, of giving him the money, some of t he Brethren
were empowered to spend it in buying small shoes for his children.
In 'aiding a poor woman, who does not appear to have been a relative
of a Mason, one Brother agreed to board one of her children for one
quarter of the school year and another assumed the expense of the
tuition of one of the children for the same time. It is shown from
the reC'ords that it was the custom of the Lodge to buy a cow occasionally and to pass her around from time to time to Brethren who
were in need of lacteal sustenance. Whether the benevolence of t he
Order extended so far as to appoint a Brother to milk the cow does
not appear. There are one or two instances where the Lodge voted
to buy lottery tickets. In 1801 three tickets to the Episcopalian
church lottery were purchased. But, alas! they proved to be blanks.
"In.1779 a vote appears authorizing the purchase of 'a 1¥2-gallon
or 2-gallon stone jugg for . the use of the Lodge.' One Brother was
charge'1 with the duty of filling the jug. The names of the Brethren
who assisted in emptying the jug are n ot r ecorded. Probably the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

· ·One of the Grand Stewards, Bro. W.·. M.:. Burbank, was ill.. A
Committee was appointed to wait upon him, and convey to him the
sympathy of the Grand Lodge. That Committee, in its Report, called
upon a friend and Brother of the Steward, who had accompanied
them to point the way to Brother Burbank's home, to supplement
their Report, which he did ii\ the following words; which so impress
us that we place them on record here.. The chaperon in this case,
Bro. Edward Cook, said:
"I don't know that I can add an,rthing to the very touching and
appropriate Report that has been made by the Committee.
"It is perhaps proper to give a little further information as to
the conditions in this case. .

"The Brother's office and home have long been at 3035 South
Park avenue, at the corner of Thirty-first street, where he and his
· wife grew old together, until two or three years ago, when she went
to visit a son in California, and died there, since which time this
dear Brother, who is nc,w approaching his. eighty-fifth birthday, has
lived alone. The growing years have made it impossible for him to
remain in ·the active practice of his profession as a physician. His
income has dwindled. But the officers and members of ·'Lakeside'
Lodge, No-. 730, of which he is a Past Master, and its most hon(!red
member, have been true Brethren to him. They have looked after
his wants. 'l'hey have seen to it that he· was provided for. He has'
been kept in his dear old home to which he is much attaehed. They
have engaged the services of a capable and kind woman of mature
years, who spends her time in caring for him. All this the Brethren
of 'Lakeside' Lodge, the Chapter and Commandery have provided for.
He is in comfortable circumstances so far as environment and daily
wants are concerned, and he has the attention and heartfelt love and
sympathy of .his Brethren-all of which he abundantly . appreciates.
"I feel constrained, Most Worshipful Grand Master, to say a
word further. At the solicitation of the Committee which you ap·
pointed, they not being particularly familiar with that portion of
the city and its means of transportation, I went with them on this
visit as a sort of pilot, or, as they were pleased to term me, a
chaperon, and they being rather young ( f) needed some one to guide
their footsteps, and so it fell to my good fortune to go with them,
upon a mission such as rarely falls to the lot of man.
'_'Here were three Brethren, aged respectively 71, 76 and 77 year~.
who have not been honored because of their appointment to a place
in the official roster of this Grand Lodge, but who have honored us
and our institution by accepting the position of Grand Stewards,

GRAND LODGE OF 0.ALI)!'ORNIA.

15

going to visit the fourth member of that beautiful group who stand
as th.e noblest exemplars of what is best in life and best in Masonry,
and who so well represent the four cardinal virtues, Temperance,
Fo;rtitude, Prudence and Justice.
"Brethren, the scene which presented itself when these three
Brethren gath'e red about the couch of the fourth, was s~ch as mortals
seldom witness. It was a picture of Brotherhood, sublime in its
pathos; and most beautiful in its impressiveness. Just' think of it!
H ere was this once stalwart specimen of humanity, long so strong and
vigorous, but now stricken by age infirmities, laying prostrate upon
his b.ed, p})ysically disabled, but mentally strong, and . morally pure,
waiting, with clear inward vision for the future; his· eyes were growing dim; he was evidently listening for the 'knocking at the door! '
And shall we not say, 'He is already beginning to hear· the footsteps
o{ the angels! '
''But he is approaching the end :firm in the consciousness of
having lived an upright life; of having been a just and loyal Mason;
·one of the best exemplars of thll teachings of our institution, and,
having lived thus, he can view the end calmly, and with an abiding
faith.
''His physicians tell us he may make a partial r ecovery, and be
spare·d to us for some months, but they give no ground to hope for
strength sufficient to enable him to get about.
''He appreciated your remembrance and the visit of his colleagues
beyond anything that I have words to express. He wanted you all to
know how thoroughly he felt it, how much he tha.nked you, and how
dearly he loved you.
''And as we turned away· the unbidden tears would come to the
eye. And yet with faith and confidence we could but say: 'Let my
death be like_ that of the righteous man, and may my last end be
like' his r' "

"The Grand Representative system was abolished on the recommendation of the Committee on Address, who say that it is as useless
as the appendix vermiformis in the human body, a remark whereat
we protest because the Almighty may not have yet disclosed to the
California Committee the last word concerning the appendix against
which they take up the hue and cry. To vindicate the truth of
history we are also compelled to take exception to the statement
that many of the Grand Lodges are dispensing with the system, as
only a few of them have done so. For a more w eighty reason wt'l
desire to recur to an evil which t}lis incident serves to illustrate
just as well as though something more was at stake than the unimportant question whether a Grand Lodge. should k eep up the simulacrum of a diplomatic court or not. We ref.er to reporting by the
Committee on Grand Master's Address of recommendations involving
final legislative action. This is outside the proper function of such
a Committee, whose sole duty it should b e to r eeommend the proper
reference of the vari?us topics treated in the Address, that each
subject requiring action may be presented separately and in a digested
form to the Grand Lodge. This incident illustrates the widest possible
departure from their proper sphere of action by the Committee, b e.·
cause they dealt with a subject not referred to them, the Grand Rep·
resentative system not being so much as alluded to in the Address.''

A fine portrait of the Grand Master-elect appears on the opening
page. The Committee on Ways and Means, considering the proposition to establish a ''Grand Charity Fund,'' reported as follows, and
the R eport was concurred in :
"Your Committee are, therefore, of the opinion that the true
meaning and intent of Masonic Charity can be the better ex emplified by each of the Lodges in their r espective communities than by
any Committee appointed by this Grand Lodge so widely separated
from those who may b e in need of immedia t e assistance.''
Chairman Emerson E. Ballard of Committee on N ecrology, in
closing his Report, gives expression to his meaning in these beautiful
lines :
"The services of this hour demonstrate that we have not forgott en.
our dead; that our souls are thrilled afresh by recalling the virtues
of those for whom we now mourn. It would take only a little more
effort to ext end the same r espect and charity we give the d ead to all
the living; and how the world might thus be brightened! Take then
this suggestion, that from every coffin , mingled with the perfume of
the flowers spread by loving hands to hide its horrors from view, there
should rise a sweeter incense in the form of an inspiration to all the
living to weave into their lives with fresh vigor the virtues of the
dead. This is immortality her e and now. Let us seize hold of and
possess it."
The r etiring Gra nd Master was presented. with a Past Grand Master's J ewel by the Senior Grand Deacon, on behalf of the Grand
Lodge, in ·a most eloquent and impressive Address, and several Representatives of other Grand Jurisdictions addressed the Grand Lodge.

W. ·. Calvin W. Prather, Grand Master in 1880·82, was re-elected
Grand Secretary, and M. ·. W. · . Daniel McDonald, Grand Master in
1875-76 _was continued as Chairman of· Correspondeµce. His present
Report is an elegant paper of 123 pages, in which the conditions of
the sev:eral Jurisdictions is placed before the inquirer intelligently and

Officer in some other Masonic Grand Bodies, and our experience has

one Grand Lodg.e to communicate with another is through the Grand
Masters' is amusing. The same argument .m ight dispense with Grand
Masters, as every practical Grand Lodge man knows t hat ninety per

''It may be that' the office of Grand Representative is as useless
as the vermiform appendix in the human body, but we are skeptical
· as to the wisdom of many so-called medical authorities upon this latter proposition. We are just old-fashioned enough to prefer the judgment of the C.reator, who placed that little sac in our bo\}y, and no
meilical carver gets ours without a fight.''

'' 'It will be patent "to any one who will give the matter of the
appointment of Representatives to and from other Grand Lodges
proper consideration, that this custom is as useless as the appendix
vetmiformis in the l\_uman body. It seems to us that the Cll;Stom must
have originated in a d esire to decorate members with a mere title.
The only proper way for one Grand Lodge to communicate with an~ther is through the Grand Masters.
Your Committee can see no
necessity for the continuance of the custom, and therefore r ecommend
that it be abolished. Ma ny of the Grand Lodges are dispensing therewith, and we think the Grand Lodge of California should do likewise.'
'' 'The record states that the Report was concurred in and the
recommendations accompanying were unanimously adopted.
"We do not :find any record of Report on this matter by the Com•
mittee on Jurisprudence, and our guess would be that the adopting of
the recommendations of a Special Committee of r eference would
have no legislative force, especially in view of the fact that the office
of Grand Representative and the power of the Grand Master to appoint and accredit such Grand Representatives is recognized in the
Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California.
''Our attention, however, has been called to an official communication received by our Grand Secretary from the Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge of California, in which this recommendation is quoted as
the action of the Grand Lodge, and we therefore t ake it that the
Grand Secretary at l east is t r eating the system as legislated out of
California.
"We admit that we like the Grand Representative system and
arc not in sympathy with this expression of the Special Committee
out in California. Of course, the system makes some ad.d i tional work
for a Gr an d Secretary, and, if properly conducted, it costs a Grand
Lodge something to maintain it, but we are constrained to believe that
it is worth all it costs. It is possibly true that the custom originated
in a desire to decorate some Masons with a title, but many Masons
appreciate it, and the natural effect is to create · and· foster a strong
feeling· of interest and fraternity in the accredited representative
toward the Grand Lodge he 'represents. This in itself is worth the
work and the expense. The writer has the honor to be the Recording

''The work of this office for the past year has been arduous and
exacting. I have done my best to serve you and hope my efforts have

all the Officers of the Grand Lodge and the Officers and members of

which I have been in'Vited, although I have attended not a few. In

32

- REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA.

Power Monument.
"In compliance. with the order of° the Grand Lodge and of the
Grand Chapter and Grand Commandery, I contracted with the W. G.
Sharkey Stone Company of Atlanta, Ga., to make and up set a suitable
monument to John Logan Power, where he is interred in the cemetery
at Jackson, after a design, which was kindly dra~n for me by
Worshipful Brother William A. Stanton, of Vicksburg, at a cost of
nine hundred and ninety-five dollars. It is to be in the form of a
Masonic Altar and I think is very chaste and elegant, as · well as
appropriate. I regret that owing to the disturbing conditions caused
by the prevalence of the yellow fever ip the summer and fall months,
I was unable to procure the plans until it was too late to make the
monument and have it set up in time for the dedication by the Grand
Lodge at this Annual Grand Communication, but an engraving made
from a photograph of the monument, furnished by the contractor, will
be ready for distribution and show its beautiful proportions. While if
we were to build a monument; measured by our affection for Brother
Power, it would tower higher than the Capitol at Jackson and · cost
as much, I felt that it would be more in accordance with the simplicity
of his noble character to set up a monument of mod,erate cost and
proportions, but which would be as enduring as our love for him will
be lasting.''
The Committee on Law and Jurisprudence presented a Report on
constructi)lg the law on such questions as. had been referred to it. A
most intere.sting Report.

We quote the following as one of the events of the Sixteenth
Annual of the Grand Lodge of North Dakota.
''Just as the tellers had finished counting the ballots for Bro.
Grant S. Hager, Deputy Grand Master, an awful hail storm broke
over the city, destrdying all of the windows at the Grand East, and
the wind scattered the Grand Secretary's papers and the ballots
promiscuously over th e Lodge room. The brethren rushed to the
dining room for tables and barricaded the windows of the Lodge room
with them, holding them in place through great efforts. The streets
wer e filled for the time b eing with runaway horses, it being impossible for the drivers to li~e in the fusillade of hailstones which _fell.
The Grand Secretary had fortunately made a memorandum of the
ballot which he preserved from the ravages of the storm. Some were
unkind enough to say that the storm came as a result of Brother
Hager's election, but Brother Hager declared that it was the applause
of H eaven. Whatever the cause, it was an event which the members
of the Grand Lodge will not soon forget. It is needless to say that
confusion prevailed among the Workmen, and the dignity of the
occasion was forgotten in the excitement of the moment. In due
time order was ·restored, none of the brethren were injured, and
Peace and Harmony p revailed.''

·The Grand Master appointed the Standing Committees and the
Grand Lodge closed, Peace and Harmony prevailing. '

The Grand Lodge of New York held its One Hundred and Twentyfifth Annual Communication in Masonic Hall in the city of New York,
May 1, 1906,-The M.··. W.:. Frank H. Robinson, Grand Master, pr.esiding, the M.:. W.•.. Edward M. Ehlers being Grand Secretary.

This Grand ,Jurisdiction has on its Roll 772 Lodges, .:Vith 139,203
members. The Address of the Grand Master is a lengthy paper, as it
necessarily must be for the amount of business to be considered in so
great a Jurisdiction. We quote his r efer ence to the great disaster.in
California as of interest to our readers:
"Week before last a great city was almost completely destroyed by
earthquake and fire. Thousands of our brethren, their families and
friends, were left homeless . and penni.less. No American city has
ever suffered such a shocking calamity. Starvation and death on
every hand .in the great city of San 'Francisco touched the hearts of
our people throughout the civilized world, unloosed the purse strings,

and almost an unlimited supply of food, clothing and money have

fraternal sympathy for the sufferers and invited him to draw on the

''The startling increase in numbers which is apparent in Masonry
everywhere, being no less than fifty thousand in the United States
alone, must give thoughtful Craftsmen food for serious reflection. It
shows that men are seeking Brotherhood in its unmodified characterBrotherhood ! and that alone . .And it behooves us to see that they get

Brotherhood the one thing needed in this world whereby we may
withstand the. destructive forces which instantly origi.nate to undermine every new development of human progressi Great prosperity is

societies have some divergence which makes them fail of the ideal of
Universal Brotherhood; and the danger is that we also shall fail, for
it may be that our Br·3tl;iren will not exemplify our noble principles.
Now is the time for every true Son of Light to bestir himself and be
in his . place in Lodge to show the seekers that which is being sought.
Many societies seek to cultivate the mind; it is ours to cultivate the
heart. Great is the glory of the mind; but the heart-that is the best.
The great mind may do great harm; but the great heart-it can do
naught but good.

M. ·. W. ·. Bro. Bellinger delivered an excellent Address, and the
eighteen District Deputies each made a detailed Report of the condition of the Lodges in his district. Of the general conditions Grand
Master Bellinger says:
"During an my thirty years' experience as a ·Mason, I have never
known Masonry to be in a more prosperous condition, or working upon
a higher plane. From every quarter of the State the same report
comes to me. The old Lodges are growing in membership and in
financial strength, and new ones are being formed. Better still; the
new members are composed of the finest and most intellectual members
of their several commanities-men who are honored and respected by
their fellows, and, therefore, men who must be of benefit to Masonry,
and to whom Masonry must do good. Brethren, I believe that the
hand of the Almighty is with us; that He is guiding and directing us,
and I pray that th e influence of the Holy Spirit may always abide
with us, and direct, strengthen, conti.rm and assist us in all that is
good. and noble and true. Thus influenced, Masonry will continue to
grow, and to spread its benign influences wider and wider over the

The Grand Lodge of Washington held its Forty-eighth Annual
Communication in the city of Bellingham, June 13, 1905,- M.:. W.:.
Edwin Hugh Van Patten, Grand Master, presiding. Washington has
a registry of 128 chartered Lodges, with a membership of nine thousand, and .in addition at the date of this Report nine Lodges under
Dispensation. Of these one hundred and eleven Lodges were represented, together with thirty-three other Grand Jurisdictions. The
portrait of the Grand Master Edwin Hugh Van Patten appears on the
opening page of this number of the Journal, and "In Memoriam" that
of Rev. Da,niel Bagley, Grand Master in 1861. The Grand Master appointed Horace W. Tyler Grand Secretary, in the absence of the Grand
Secretary Thomas Milburne Reed, prevented by illness from responding to the present Annual Roll Call. Thirteen Past Grand Masters
were in attendance and the Delegates from eight of the nine Lodges
under Dispensation.
The Hon. J. W. Romaine, Mayor, welcomed Grand Lodge to the
city of Bellingham and Junior Grand Warden McAlaster responded
on behalf of the Grand Lodge. The Grand Master in his Address paid
eloquent ancl affectionate tribute to the dead brethren who had
passed to rest during the recess of the Grand Lodge. 'In the Address
of the Grand Master we note the granting of a D~spensation for the
forming and opening of "Anvil'' Lodge at Nome, Alaska. We also
ncite in the Address tbe statement that the Grand Lodge of California
has abolished the system of Grand Representatives. Not so, Bro. Van
Patten; it has been attempted in a clumsy sort of a way, but has not
succeeded yet. Consequently, the M .·. W.:. William H. Upton represents the Grand Lodge of California at the Grancl Lodge at Washing-

The Grand Lodge may well appreciate our feelings upon this happy
consummation of an unpleasant incident, and the delicate compliment
paid our Worthy Grand Secretary, by the sending of such ~ communication on the anniversary of his birth.
M.·. W.-. P. G. M., Wm. H. Upton, introduced R.:. W.-. Brother
W. A. DeWolf Smith, Grand Historian and Com,iittee on Foreign Correspondence of the Grand Jurisdiction of British Columbia with a
fitting tribute to his worth and ability as a Masonic writer, to which
th<i R. ·. W. ·. Brother ably responded and. expressed his pleasure in
being present.
The Special Committee on Obituaries, Past Grand Master W. H.
White, Chairman, made a feeling and eloquent Report on the life and
character of Rev. Daniel Bagley, Past Grand Master, who passed to
rest in April, 1905.
The usual routine of business being completed, the election of
Officers was held and the H.:. W. :. Abraham Lincoln Miller was
chosen Grand Master, the M.-. W.:. Thomas Milburne Reed being reelected Grand Secretary.
On motion of Past Grand Master Upton, a Committee was appointed to visit the Grand Secretary in his illness and express to him
the love and veneration of all the members of this Grand Body for
him personally and their prayers for his future happiness.
·
The Grand Master having made his appointments, all were installed
except the Grand Secretary, the Grand Chaplain, Grand Marshal and
Grand Steward.
•
The Grand Master named the Standing Committees and Grand
Lodge closed. .

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Report on Correspondence by Past Grand Master Wm. H.
Upton is one of his very best, and we regret very much our lack of
time and space to review it as it deserves, but what does the following mean 9
Farewell.
But the hour is at hand. Brethren of the Guild, I shall be with
you no more. In spirit I pass silently around the table where you sit
and tender to each of you the warm grasp of a hand that never knowingly did any man a wrong. May the work which we 'h ave all been
doing, in diverse ways and from different points of view, redound to
the good of Masonry; may you long be spared to continue that work;
may success attend all your efforts for. good; may happiness mark your
days ~nd the lives of those dear to you; and may our Father in
Heaven have you ever in His holy keeping. So mote it be.
''Fraternally submitted,
.''WILLIAM H. UPTON,
"Walla Walla, 5905.

WEST VIRGINIA.
The Grand Lodge of West Virginia held thirteen Special Communications during the recess. Six for the placing of corner-stones
of public buildings, three for the constitution of Lodges, four for the
dedication of Masonic Halls, and an Emergent on the 25th of October,
1905, for the exercise of the miraculous power and Grand Master's
prerogative of · making a Mason at sight.
.
The Forty-first Annual was held in Masonic Temple, in the city of
Charleston, November 15, 1905,-M. ·. W. ·. Luther H. Clarke, Grand
Master, presiding.

charter ed Lodges, with a membership of 10,121, with six under Dispensation. Of these 123 were represented, with two of the Lodges
under Dispensation. }'ifteeil Past Grand Masters wer e present and the

WISCONSIN.
' The Grand Lodge of Wisconsin held its Sixty-first Annual Com- ...
municl'ltion in the Masonic Building, Milwaukee, June 13, 1905,-The
M. :. W. ·. David H. Wright, Grand Master, presiding, the R.·. W.·.
William W. Perry being Grand Secr etary.
Wisconsin has registered on its Ro1! 254 Lodges, 239 of which were
tepresented at this Annual. The Lodge membership is 21,251. Fortytwo other Grand Jurisdictions were also represented. Fourteen Past
Grand Masters were in attendance.
In his Address the Grand Master reported a prosperous year. Peace
and harmony ruled within its Lodges, with progress and prosperity
on every hand. He reported the passing to rest of two Past Grancl
Masters, M. :. w ... Bro.there Oliver Libbey, who was Grand Master in
1884-85, and E. E. Chapin in 1 880 ~81. He announced a number of appointments of Representatives near other Grand Lodges. Under
Decisions, he reported' a number of answers to questions for the construction of certain laws, but made· no important decisions. The
Grand Master closed his Address with a brief statement that might
cause him to be dubbed the veteran Grand Master. We salute you
Grand Master Wright and wish you many years of refreshment after
'so much labor. We quote:
"I have witnessed forty-eight sessions of this Grand Lodge. I
first came to Grand Lodge in 1857, as Secretary of "Madison"' Lodge,

The several Committees reported and the Grand Master, having
made the appointments, all were installed by Past Grand Master
Nathan C. Griffin, Past Grand Master Aldro Jenks acting as Master
of the Ceremonies.
The retiring Grand Master was presented with a Past Grand
Master's Jewel in a most eloquent Address by Past Junior Grand
Warden Franklin P. Ainsworth. The Grand Lodge was then closed.
Past Grand Master and Chairman of Correspondence Bro. Aldro
Jenks. Bro. Jenks' Reports are never other than intelligent and able,
the present conclusion, the subject whereof is "The Recognition of
Grand Lodges and Their Effects,'' a generally neglected subject in
Masonic jurisprudence.

The Grand Master named the Committees and proceeded to deliver
his Annual Address. He congratulated Grand Lodge that although the
year just closed had been uneventful, yet Masonry had prospered with
them as never before in the history of Wyoming. No st.artling events
had occurred. He would express the thanksgiving they were in duty
bound to express that while other Jurisdictions nad been sadly afflicted
with the loss of leaders eminent in the Fraternity, they had been
spared, and not a member of the official household had been summoned. No impor~ant decisions were reported. The year had been
prosperous, although a quiet one, the Session consequently was confined
to the transaction of the routine business of the Jurisdiction. Bro.

WYOMING.
The Grand Lodge of Wyoming held a Special Communication in
the town of Thermopolis, July 25, 1905, for the purpose of placing the
corner-stone of the Masonic Temple in course of erection for "Malta"
Lodge, No. 17, and in the town of Douglas, August 2d, in the Hall of
'' Ashler'' Lodge, No. 10, for the placing of the corner-stone of the
Converse county courthouse; and, again, in th~ town of Sheridan, assembling in the Hall of "Sheridan" Lodge, No. 6, to place the
corner-stone of the Sheridan county courthouse.
The Thirty-first Annual Communication was held in Laramie, Sep·
tember 6, 1905 1-The M. ·. W. :. Frank A. Luckfield, Grand Master,
presiding. ,
There are twenty-three Lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction, with a
membership of 1,819 Master Masons. Of these seventeen Lodges were
represented at the present Annual. Seven Past Grand Masters were in
attendance.

"In concluding this, my nineteenth Report as your Grand Secre. tary, it may not be out of place to say that in the roll of Grand
Secretaries I now rank as number twelve in length of service. My
name as Grand Secr13tary is attached to every Lodge Charter in the
State except the first· six. During my service membership has in.
creased from 493 to 1,809, and I have recei.ved in Grand Lodge funds
altogether the sum of $25,600.94, · every cent of which has been
promptly paid to Grand Treasurer, as printed Annual Proceedings
show. Of this record I am, as I believe, entitled to here say that I am
proud; and yet I am prouder still of the long-continued confidence I
have enjoyed at your hands, for which I thank you.
·'Respectfully submitted,
''W. L. KUYKENDALL,
''Grand Secretary.''

Johnston was chosen Grand Master, and the R.-. w ... Bro. William.
L. Kuyli:end~ll was re-elected Grand Secretary and Correspondent.
A photogravure of the new Grand Master appears on the opening
page of this number of the Journal: The Grand Master made his
appointments and all were installed by Past Grand Master J. M. Rumsey, Bro. Hugh Hynds acting as Master of the Ceremonies. The
Standing Committees. were appointed and after prayer by the Grand
Chaplain the Grand Lodge closed in Ample Form.
Bro. Kuykendall submits his usual review of other Grand Jurisdictions composing the Masonic World'. That the Report is an excellent review of the transactiosn in Masonry for the year 1905 goes
without saying. Masvnry is both prosperous and progressive. "So
say we all of us. ' '

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
CONCLUSION.

We submit the fore.going as our Report on Correspondence. We
had not intended to write it, but the Grand Master,. having thought
proper to name us again for the work, and in delaying the explanation
to him of our reasons for not wishing to discharge the duty until too
late to give him a fair chance to select another, we have written
the paper we submit herewith as our :final Report.
Respectfully submitted,
WM. A DAVIES,
Chairman.
